This is a digital copy of a book that was preserved for generations on library shelves before it was carefully scanned by Google as part of a project to make the world’s books discoverable online.

It has survived long enough for the copyright to expire and the book to enter the <term>public domain</term> <note>A work enters the public domain when its legal copyright term ends, meaning it is no longer owned by an individual and belongs to the community at large.</note>. Whether a book is in the public domain may vary country to country. Public domain books are our gateways to the past, representing a wealth of history, culture and knowledge that’s often difficult to discover.

Marks, notations and other <term>marginalia</term> <note>These are handwritten notes, stamps, or sketches made in the margins of the pages by previous readers or librarians.</note> present in the original volume will appear in this file—a reminder of this book’s long journey from the publisher to a library and finally to you.

## Usage guidelines

Google is proud to partner with libraries to digitize public domain materials and make them widely accessible. Public domain books belong to the public and we are merely their custodians. Nevertheless, this work is expensive, so in order to keep providing this resource, we have taken steps to prevent abuse by commercial parties, including placing technical restrictions on automated querying.

We also ask that you:

+ *Make non-commercial use of the files* We designed Google Book Search for use by individuals, and we request that you use these files for personal, non-commercial purposes.
+ *Refrain from automated querying* Do not send automated queries of any sort to Google’s system: If you are conducting research on machine translation, optical character recognition <note>Often abbreviated as OCR, this is the technology used to convert images of typed or handwritten text into machine-encoded text.</note> or other areas where access to a large amount of text is helpful, please contact us. We encourage the use of public domain materials for these purposes and may be able to help.
+ *Maintain attribution* The Google “watermark” you see on each file is essential for informing people about this project and helping them find additional materials through Google Book Search. Please do not remove it.
+ *Keep it legal* Whatever your use, remember that you are responsible for ensuring that what you are doing is legal. Do not assume that just because we believe a book is in the public domain for users in the United States, that the work is also in the public domain for users in other countries. Whether a book is still in copyright varies from country to country, and we can’t offer guidance on whether any specific use of any specific book is allowed. Please do not assume that a book’s appearance in Google Book Search means it can be used in any manner anywhere in the world. Copyright infringement liability can be quite severe.

# Preface.

If I am once again taking up the discussion on the same subject—following my last short work "In the Matter of Psychophysics" <note>original: "In Sachen der Psychophysik" (1877)</note>—and doing so in a much more thorough manner, it is for the following reason.

Almost simultaneously with the publication of that work, a very noteworthy book by G. E. Müller <note>Georg Elias Müller (1850–1934) was a prominent German experimental psychologist who became one of the leading critics—and later developers—of psychophysical methods.</note> appeared. In it, the entire field of <term>psychophysics</term> <note>the scientific study of the relation between physical stimuli and the sensations they produce</note>, as it had been presented by previous contributors, was subjected to sharp and thorough criticism. This critique was almost entirely opposed to my own formulation of the doctrine in the "Elements of Psychophysics" <note>original: "Elementen der Psychophysik," the author’s foundational work published in 1860 which established the field.</note>; furthermore, new or newly adapted objections from various other authors were raised. This has prompted me to rethink the entire doctrine according to its main points, and the result of these considerations is presented in this writing. Although it mostly builds upon Müller's critique and takes into account the objections of other authors, this work goes far beyond a mere <term>counter-critique</term> <note>original: "Antikritik"; a formal rebuttal to a published criticism.</note> in almost every respect. The psychophysical principles of measurement and methods of measurement, the formulation of psychophysical formulas, the question of the validity of <term>Weber's Law</term> <note>the rule that the change in a stimulus that will be just noticeable is a constant ratio of the original stimulus</note>, the experiments to confirm it, the controversy between the so-called "psychophysical" and "physiological" interpretations of this law—and thus between two fundamentally opposing views of psychophysics as a whole—various main subjects of <term>inner psychophysics</term> <note>the study of the relationship between sensation and the nervous system, as opposed to "outer" psychophysics which looks at external stimuli</note>, and above all, the question of the scope of psychophysics in its entirety, have

<summary>In this preface, the author explains that this new work is a comprehensive response to criticisms of psychophysics, particularly those raised by G. E. Müller, and aims to re-examine the field's fundamental laws and measurement methods.</summary>
<keywords>Psychophysics, G. E. Müller, Weber's Law, inner psychophysics, measurement methods, Elements of Psychophysics, scientific rebuttal</keywords>

In doing so, I have, of course, had to waive the registration and discussion of a larger number of new <term>specialized studies</term> <note>detailed research focused on specific, narrow aspects of a field</note> that fall within the field of <term>psychophysics</term> <note>the scientific study of the relationship between physical stimuli and the sensations they produce</note>, provided they do not challenge or even concern any main points of this doctrine and would only provide an occasion for a report rather than a discussion or revision; however, I gladly take this opportunity to express my thanks to those authors who have sent me treatises regarding their investigations in the field of psychophysics.

Since, at my age, I will no longer be able to publish a new edition of the "Elements of Psychophysics" <note>original: "Elemente der Psychophysik" (1860)</note>, which has been out of print for several years, the present work can serve as a substitute for it within certain limits, as a supplement to it in other respects, and again as preparatory work for a new treatment of the entire doctrine in still others. It can serve as a substitute to a certain extent for my presentation in the "Elements" insofar as it was necessary to return to the main points of the earlier presentation—and even to repeat some things—in order to connect them with the new considerations and proceedings; but, so as not to repeat everything, it will also frequently have to refer back to the "Elements" and the work "In the Matter" <note>original: "In Sachen der Psychophysik" (1877)</note> and present itself in this regard as a mere supplement, while from a third perspective it presents facts and controversies whose consideration can no longer be avoided in any new treatment of psychophysics.

Indeed, the time and effort I have devoted to the preparation of this writing would have been more than sufficient to produce a new edition of the "Elements," expanded compared to the previous one and corrected in individual points, if only the...

->V<-

...the investigations and proceedings undertaken here had already been available to me, so that I could refer back to them, since they could for the most part only be included in a new revision of the "Elements" itself based on their results. Moreover, it can only be beneficial if a younger force takes up the task anew from fresh perspectives.

After these preliminary remarks regarding the intent and content of this writing, I wish to state the most general result of the deliberations and discussions contained herein: I have not been led in any essential way to abandon the principles established in the "Elements" <note>Fechner refers to his 1860 book, *Elemente der Psychophysik*, which founded the field</note> or the conclusions and formulas derived from them; on the contrary, they have been confirmed. But that does not exclude the fact that I have found it necessary to yield to some counter-remarks made to me, and to correct, complete, or treat more thoroughly aspects of the earlier presentation on my own initiative. A new and far-reaching doctrine cannot, after all, be finished and perfected with the first attempt—especially one that presents difficulties making its very mission appear a risk from the start (see "Elements" vol I, p. 1). However, it is certainly a good thing that objections that could be raised have indeed been raised. A post becomes looser by being shaken; a tree, if it is not toppled by it, only takes root all the more firmly because of it. In my opinion, no one has yet performed greater service to <term>psychophysics</term> <note>the scientific study of the relationship between physical stimuli and the sensations they produce</note> in this regard than Müller <note>Georg Elias Müller (1850–1934), a younger psychologist who published a major critique of Fechner's work in 1878</note>, before whose keen insight—specifically sharpened for this purpose—hardly a possible objection could have remained hidden.

How little I underestimate the significance of this primary opponent at all, and how much merit I find not only in the suggestions originating from him but also in his positive results—so far as these have been presented by him—is proven, beyond the course of this work itself, by the [fact that] with his name particu...

->VI<-

the section titled (XXIII). However, whether I am wrong—despite this general recognition—to find all his main objections against me to be in error, and to wish that his own critique were less in need of criticism itself, the reader may judge for themselves by following the course of the following discussions with some attention.

Next to G. E. Müller, it is especially Wundt <note>Wilhelm Wundt (1832–1920), often called the "father of experimental psychology"</note> and Delboeuf <note>Joseph Delboeuf (1831–1896), a Belgian philosopher and psychologist</note> with whom I will have to contend, partly in the course of this writing and partly in special sections (XXII, XXV). The section that Ribot dedicated to my presentation of psychophysics in his work, *Contemporary German Psychology* <note>original: "La psychologie Allemande contemporaine. Paris 1879."</note> p. 155 ff., makes a seemingly great claim for consideration. However, since I find his critique to be essentially only a repetition of Delboeuf’s objections, I have no reason to address Ribot specifically.

Not to be confused with my main opponent, Prof. Dr. G. E. Müller in Göttingen—who is always intended whenever I cite the name "Müller" on its own—is Dr. F. A. Müller. In his work *The Axiom of Psychophysics* (1881), he sought to uproot my psychophysical principles from an even greater depth than the Müller from Göttingen; indeed, he sought to uproot the latter as well, insofar as the Göttingen Müller still allows for the validity of <term>psychophysics</term> <note>the scientific study of the relationship between physical stimuli and mental sensations</note> at all, whereas according to the other Müller, there is fundamentally nothing to it. Other philosophers have declared themselves partly in an equally fundamental and disparaging way against it, or have otherwise contributed "water to the sea" of objections against it. Although I believe that psychophysics can generally no more be refuted than established from a philosopher’s desk, I have nonetheless not wanted to simply ignore the attacks coming from that side. Thus, a collective article (Section XXVI) will appear under the titles of the authors to be named in this regard (Gutberlet, Koch, v. Kries,

<meta>This page continues the Preface from page VI. Fechner is moving from specific criticisms to a defense of the scientific legitimacy of psychophysics as a field, despite ongoing academic debates.</meta>

(*G. A. Müller*, *Ulrici* <note>Hermann Ulrici (1806–1884), a German philosopher who sought to bridge the gap between science and religion</note>, *Zeller* <note>Eduard Zeller (1814–1908), a prominent theologian and philosopher of the history of Greek philosophy</note>) to engage with them at least up to certain limits.

After the many disputes regarding **psychophysics**, which have been discussed in this as well as in my previous writing, the thought easily presents itself that **psychophysics** is generally only a playground for dispute, in which nothing positive or lasting can be reached. Yet that would be an error. As unfinished as **psychophysics** still is, it nonetheless possesses achievements that are no longer in question—no matter how much is still questioned regarding the 'hows' and 'whys'—in **Weber's Law** <note>original: "Weberschen Gesetz"; the principle that the smallest noticeable difference in a stimulus is proportional to the original intensity of the stimulus</note>, in the **Law of the Threshold**, in the **Parallel Law**, in the **methods of measuring sensitivity**, and I dare to add, in the **measurement principle of sensation** itself. Thus, one can argue about the limits of validity and the degree of approximation of **Weber's Law** within given boundaries, since in **external psychophysics** <term>external psychophysics</term> <note>the study of the relationship between physical stimuli and mental sensation</note> it does not appear as a strict law; but as far as it exists, it is—just like the **Law of the Threshold**—a directly decisive explanatory principle for a multitude of the most important phenomena, not only in everyday life but also in **sensory physiology**, and furthermore offers a starting point for fundamental conclusions regarding the laws of **internal psychophysics** <term>internal psychophysics</term> <note>the study of the relationship between internal physiological/neural activity and mental sensation</note>. While these laws are themselves still subject to dispute, if they are to be decided, they cannot be decided without regard for this law, whereby **philosophy** has, so to speak, only to look on <note>original: "nur das Zusehen hat"; implying philosophy must defer to the empirical findings of psychophysics</note>. The **methods of measuring sensitivity** offer cause for dispute regarding their relative importance, their most practical application, and the way they are best calculated; but these are all only secondary questions which do not at all cancel out the importance of those methods for practice and science in general. The psychical measurement, insofar as it rests upon **Weber's Law**, can be contested in its universality if **Weber's Law** itself is not universally valid, but the general **measurement principle** still remains...

<summary>Fechner defends psychophysics against claims that it is merely a field of empty dispute, listing core scientific achievements like Weber's Law and the Law of the Threshold as foundational and lasting principles. He argues that while details and limits are debated, the empirical methods and measurement principles remain vital for both sensory physiology and philosophy.</summary>

<keywords>Weber's Law, Law of the Threshold, external psychophysics, internal psychophysics, sensory physiology, scientific measurement, G. A. Müller, Ulrici, Zeller</keywords>

VIII

persist, as set forth in the *Elements of Psychophysics*, Vol. I, p. 54 ff. and Vol. II, p. 19 ff. It can be incomprehensibly misunderstood—as has occurred with *Delboeuf* <note>Joseph Delboeuf (1831–1896), a Belgian philosopher and psychologist who criticized Fechner’s logarithmic law</note> and, echoing him, *Ribot* <note>Théodule-Armand Ribot (1839–1916), a French psychologist who helped establish psychology as an independent science in France</note>—as if no psychological unity <term>psychische Einheit</term> <note>the concept that mental states form a cohesive, measurable whole</note> lay beneath it; but that is merely an incomprehensibility on the part of these authors (see p. 300 ff.). It can be defined away according to *Kantian* principles, as by *F. A. Müller* <note>Friedrich August Müller, a neo-Kantian philosopher who argued that mental states lack the spatial properties required for measurement</note>, on the grounds that there are no psychological magnitudes <note>original: "psychischen Größen"</note> and thus no measurement of them; or it can otherwise be speculated away philosophically (see Section XXVI); but its mathematical foundation on an empirical basis is not affected by this at all. In all of this, however, psychophysics possesses points with which it can meet the reproach from the side of philosophy—namely, that in a field of a task common to them both, psychophysics only shares the uncertainty of the former.

Whether, of course, psychophysics can attain an even more general and higher significance beyond these points will depend primarily on two questions: first, whether one is willing to concede and pursue the scope of psychophysics beyond the sensory into the higher spiritual realm and into the world-totality—concerning which one should compare *Elements*, Vol. I, p. 13 ff., Vol. II, p. 543 ff., and the following first section; second, whether the so-called psychophysical or physiological conception of psychophysics, as distinguished in Section XVII of this work, will gain the upper hand. According to the first, *Weber’s Law* and the **Law of the Threshold** are transferable as pure laws from the external to the internal <note>This refers to the transition from "outer psychophysics" (stimulus vs. sensation) to "inner psychophysics" (neural activity vs. sensation)</note>; according to the other, they are not. For with the loss of this transferability, the most important consequences also fall away regarding the first-mentioned relationship. History alone can decide this.

For my part, I stand decisively against the physiological view in general, based already on the reason asserted on p. 225 f., and against *Müller’s* representation of this view in particular through the explanation on p. 204 (with regard to p. 223 under point 5). But since I am a party in this matter

<summary>Fechner defends psychophysics against philosophical critics, arguing that its mathematical and empirical foundations remain valid regardless of metaphysical speculation. He highlights the central debate over whether psychophysical laws describe a fundamental relationship between soul and body or merely physiological processes.</summary>

### Finally, concerning some points regarding the external arrangement of this work.

Page references to the current work are generally denoted by **p.** <note>original: "S." for "Seite"</note>, while page references to my earlier or other writings are denoted by **p.** <note>original Latin: "p." for "pagina"</note> or simply by the page number. — Parentheses within literal quotes signify, as in the previous work, insertions made by the authors themselves; brackets signify those inserted by me.

As in the previous work, **psychophysical** is frequently abbreviated as **ps. ph.**, and **sensation** <term>Empfindung</term> as **S.** <note>original abbreviation: "E."</note>. Furthermore, in sections where the following expressions recur frequently, abbreviations are used as follows: **Difference** by **D.** <note>original: "U." for "Unterschied"</note>, **Difference-Sensitivity** by **D. S.** <note>original: "U. E."</note>, **Difference-Threshold** by **D. Th.** <note>original: "U. Schw." for "Unterschiedsschwelle"</note>, **Probability** by **Prob.** <note>original: "W." for "Wahrscheinlichkeit"</note>, **Attention** by **Att.** <note>original: "A." for "Aufmerksamkeit"</note>, and **Consciousness** by **Cons.** <note>original: "B." for "Bewußtsein"</note>. The measurement methods of difference-sensitivity—namely, those of **just noticeable differences**, **average errors**, and **right and wrong cases**—are mostly denoted respectively <note>original: "respectiv"</note> by the abbreviations Method of **J.N.D.**, **A.E.**, and **r. and w.** cases.

In the usual manner, **$\pi$** always refers to the Ludolphian number <note>The mathematical constant pi, named here after Ludolph van Ceulen</note> and **e** refers to the base of natural logarithms.

I cite my ***Elements of Psychophysics*** briefly as "Elem." I or II to distinguish between the two parts (not chapters) of the same; my work ***In the Matter of Psychophysics*** <note>original: "In Sachen der Psychophysik" (1877)</note> is cited as "**In the Matter**". Insofar as it concerns references to the writings of **G. E. Müller**, **Wundt**, **Volkmann**, or **Delboeuf**, the simple addition of a page number to **Müller’s** name, or within an account provided by him, always signifies a reference to his primary work, ***On the Foundation of Psychophysics*** <note>original: "Zur Grundlegung der Psychophysik" (1878)</note>. However, where the reference concerns his review <note>original: "Recension"</note> of my previous work in the ***Göttingen Notices*** <note>original: "Göttinger Anzeigen"</note>, or the self-announcement of his primary work in those same notices, or his treatise "**On the determination of measures—**"

<summary>Fechner defines the technical abbreviations and citation conventions used throughout the text, identifying key reference works by himself and his contemporaries like G.E. Müller.</summary>

## Part Two

Fechner, Psychophysics. 1

# First Division.

## I. On the Scope of Psychophysics.

The mind, with its content of sensations, thoughts, and feelings, can only appear to itself—or, as I will say for brevity, **internally**; the body, with its parts and movements, can only appear to a being standing opposite it—or, as I will say for brevity, **externally**. For while I can indeed see my own leg, I cannot see *by means of* the leg itself; rather, its appearance requires my own or another person's eye to be positioned opposite it. Meanwhile, my sensations and thoughts, inaccessible to any foreign being, are only partial self-appearances of my own mind. Thus, everything mental, soulful, or psychic in the broader sense is a matter of internal appearance, while everything bodily, material, or physical in the broader sense is a matter of external appearance or perception. One classifies something into one field or the other depending on which mode of appearance it belongs to. This is not the declaration of a hypothesis, but merely the identification of the characteristic by which common and scientific language alike distinguish the two main domains of existence ¹), whether clearly or unclearly. <note>Fechner is establishing that the difference between "mind" and "matter" is a matter of perspective (how we observe them) rather than necessarily being two different "substances."</note> And no differently than is done in **psychology** on the one hand, and **physics** and **physiology** on the other, these two domains are also distinguished by **psychophysics**, a point which one may adhere to hereafter regardless of the previous explanation ²).

---

1) In fact, the hypothesis only begins when one explains both factual and factually distinct areas of appearance either as **monistic** <term>Monistic: The philosophical view that variety in the world can be explained by a single substance or principle.</term> (as the concern of the same being) or as **dualistic** <term>Dualistic: The view that the universe is composed of two fundamental, distinct principles, such as mind and matter.</term> (as the concern of different beings). This, however, is no longer a matter of conceptual distinction, but of factual relationship.
2) The subtle movements in our brain, which **psychophysics** <term>Psychophysics: A term coined by Fechner for the exact science of the functional relationships between body and soul (or stimulus and sensation).</term> must also address, certainly cannot appear externally in an immediate sense, but they still fall— <note>The text cuts off here at the bottom of the page.</note>

<summary>Fechner defines the fundamental distinction between the mental (internal appearance) and the physical (external appearance), establishing that psychophysics studies the relationship between these two modes of perception.</summary>

--- Page 21 ---
<meta>This page continues the first chapter regarding the "Scope of Psychophysics." Fechner is transitioning from definitions of "internal" and "external" to the core question of whether all mental life—including higher reasoning—is governed by the same physical laws as basic sensations.</meta>

From a philosophical perspective, thinkers seek a fundamental relationship between these two domains, though they have certainly not reached an agreement on it yet. Psychophysics, however, does not involve itself in this debate at all; instead, it focuses solely on the **lawful** relationships or dependencies between both realms of appearance as facts given by experience. That such relationships exist at all is itself a fact. However, the question remains: to what degree and how far do they extend? Depending on whether one views these laws as permeating both domains entirely, or reaching only to certain limits—and thus being trackable by psychophysics only to those limits—one can speak of either an unlimited or a limited scope for psychophysics. Philosophers are generally inclined to allow only a limited scope for psychophysics; and since this question interests not only philosophy but psychophysics itself, the reflections regarding this matter already found in the "Elements of Psychophysics" <note>original: "Elem. d. Ps." (I. 13 f.); Fechner refers to his foundational 1860 work, *Elemente der Psychophysik*.</note> will be partly generalized and partly expanded upon in the following.

Against an unlimited scope of psychophysics in the aforementioned sense, one might say: certain lawful dependencies between soul and body are actually only demonstrable and proven in the sensory realm. A sensation of light is lawfully tied to certain changes in the nervous system; wherever these exist in a living creature, the sensation of light is also present, and vice versa. But for that which reaches beyond this as **higher** spiritual activity, a psychophysical representation is neither demonstrable nor even thinkable—if, for brevity's sake, we understand "psychophysical representatives" of the mental to be the physical processes upon whose existence the existence of the mental is lawfully tied, and with whose changes it changes in lawful dependency. The physical element that stands in such a relationship to the mental can then be called the "carrier" or "substrate" of the mental, without implying anything other than this lawful relationship of dependency of one upon the other.

---

...insofar as they belong to the realm of the bodily and are categorized as such by physiology, because they are inferred from the connection of external phenomena as determinations of the externally apparent brain and contribute to completing this connection; furthermore, because they are themselves conceived under the form of externally apparent processes, and would actually appear externally if the obstacles to external observation were removed and the means of external observation could be sufficiently sharpened. <note>Fechner argues that even "internal" thoughts are physical processes in the brain that we simply lack the technology to see yet.</note>

<summary>Fechner addresses whether psychophysics applies to "higher" thoughts or just basic senses, arguing that even if we cannot yet "see" the brain activity corresponding to complex thought, it still constitutes a physical process that would be visible with better instruments.</summary>

...should be. But, it is said and thought, the higher spiritual world will simply neither have nor need such a carrier; indeed, the most essential difference between the sensory and the higher spiritual realms ¹⁾ can be found in the fact that the former, but not the latter, can be represented <term>psychophysically</term> <note>Psychophysical representation refers to the idea that every mental event has a corresponding, measurable physical event in the brain or body.</note>. The fact that the spirit, even in its highest functions, still requires a brain at all to be planted into earthly existence, and makes use of certain brain apparatuses and functions for its expressions, does not yet prove that it is bound to lawfully corresponding physical ones in all its determinations and activities. From the countless experiences—such as the <term>materialist</term> <note>In this context, a philosopher who believes that only physical matter exists and that "soul" is just a byproduct of the brain.</note> tirelessly asserts—that the highest spiritual functions can be damaged by injuries, illnesses, or abnormalities of the brain, it only ever follows that the spirit may thereby experience obstacles and disturbances to its activity in this world in general. It does not follow, however, that every specific movement of its activity is accompanied by an equally specific brain activity by law, or that such accompaniment is required for those thoughts to occur. Moreover, there are even aspects of the sensory realm where the physical side cannot keep up with the psychic side; instead, the soul experiences an "addition" for which there is no physical "cooperation," a point we shall return to later (p. 11). Therefore, if the psychophysicist <term>postulates</term> <note>To assume or claim the existence of something as a basis for reasoning.</note> a lawfully corresponding change in the body for every change in the soul, wanting to find everything spiritual to be psychophysically representable and thereby claiming an unlimited scope for psychophysics, he lacks the factual and conceptual justification to do so.

To all this, it must first be replied that it is not inherent in the principle of psychophysics to assert a lawful dependence between soul and body further than can be justified through experience or inference. Thus, the requirement of a comprehensive psychophysical representation of the spiritual realm is not its core "mission." It is only that, until now, research has found no rational or empirical reason to accept boundaries in this regard from the outset. On the contrary, there are reasons to push those boundaries further than has been attempted from a philosophical side

1) Not infrequently, both areas are distinguished as **soul** and **spirit** in a narrower sense, whereas in the broader sense, which I follow here, **spirit** <note>original: "Geist"</note> encompasses both. I have discussed the terminology—which is generally very fluctuating in this regard—in more detail in the small publication "On the Soul Question" <note>original: "Über die Seelenfrage", p. 7 ff.</note>.

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s argument from page 3. ...as commonly happens; and this is what the current section will explore in more detail.

The restriction customary among philosophers, which limits <term>psychophysical</term> <note>The study of the relationship between physical stimuli and mental phenomena.</note> representability to the sensory realm, may seem tenable only as long as one remains within general ways of speaking and <term>a priori</term> <note>Knowledge that proceeds from theoretical deduction rather than from observation or experience.</note> definitions. But if one examines the actual conditions of what, according to common linguistic and conceptual usage, falls into the "lower" and "higher" realms, one easily finds that if one concedes psychophysical representability to sensory sensations, perceptions, feelings, and drives—and one does indeed do that—then one cannot deny it to the higher spiritual phenomena built upon them without abandoning a rational connection altogether. Indeed, one can assert a very general principle in this regard, which I established in the *Elements of Psychophysics* (Vol. II, p. 370) under the admittedly not very descriptive name of the **Principle of Function**. I reproduce it here because of the frequent references that will be made to it in the future. It reads:

> "To be sure, we can in no way infer from the nature of mental movements the nature of the underlying bodily movements—that is, we cannot conclude which <term>substrate</term> <note>The physical matter or substance (like neurons or brain tissue) that underlies a mental process.</note> or what form these movements take; however, we can conclude that to a mental connection there corresponds a psychophysical connection, to a mental sequence or succession there corresponds a psychophysical one, and to mental strength or weakness there corresponds a psychophysical strength or weakness, insofar as the mental has its foundation in the physical."

By <term>psychophysical</term>, we mean here, as always, the physical acting as the foundation of the mental.

It appears that, independently of me, <term>Mach</term> <note>Ernst Mach (1838–1916), a physicist and philosopher who influenced Einstein and logical positivism.</note> (in his treatise "On the Effects of Light Stimuli, etc." in the *Reports of the Meetings of the Vienna Academy*, Volume II) put forward essentially the same principle and described it as productive.

->Hiezu ein erstes Beispiel:<-
->**A first example of this:**<-

The sensations of melody and harmony are admittedly higher spiritual phenomena than the sensory sensations of tone between which they exist. Now, the sensory sensations of tone depend on vibrations that propagate from the outside world into our auditory apparatus, and from there further inward—in all probability also in the form of vibrations. In these internal vibrations, we have the psychophysical representatives of the sensations of tone, provided that the latter are lawfully linked to the former and with...

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s argument for the "Principle of Function," specifically applying it to the perception of music to illustrate how "higher" mental experiences (like harmony) correspond to "higher" physical relationships (like mathematical ratios in vibrations). ...change the former. However, the sensations of melody and harmony are linked to the same **proportions** <note>original: "Verhältnisse"; here referring to the mathematical ratios or relationships between sound waves.</note> between the internal vibrations as those which exist between the external vibrations upon which they depend. They find in these proportions their <term>psychophysical</term> <note>The study of the relationship between physical stimuli and mental phenomena.</note> representation or their carrier; again, insofar as their existence is tied to them and they change according to the changes of these proportions in a lawful manner. The sensations of individual tones, as well as their higher relationships, fall into our spirit, insofar as their psychophysical representatives fall into the more general psychophysical system that fundamentally underlies our spirit.

Here we have, in any case, a simple example showing that the elevated nature of the spiritual does not, in itself, lead beyond the possibility of psychophysical representation. One only has to think of the "higher" elements in the spiritual realm as being represented by the corresponding and existence-linked "higher" elements in the physical realm. After all, relationships in the physical realm are, in the same sense, something "higher" than the individual parts underlying them—just as sensed relationships, or "relational sensations" between individual mental processes, are in the psychic realm.

One must only be careful not to count those relationships that exist between details in the physical realm as belonging to the spiritual realm itself simply because they can only be grasped by the spirit; for by doing so, one would lose the basis for distinguishing the two realms altogether. Even the physical world, within which these relationships exist, must be grasped by our spirit in order to be present for us at all and for us to be able to speak of it. Yet, on the basis of this commonality, we distinguish that which appears externally and internally as two distinct realms. We must therefore distinguish their qualities as belonging to one or the other, and not mix or confuse them, as occasionally happens in certain philosophical circles. 

In any case, psychophysics understands it this way and thus avoids this confusion. Depending on whether something appears as a relationship, a change, a difference, simplicity, composition, and so on—generally as a determination of the physical or the psychic, abstractable from the realm of one or the other—it is categorized into its respective realm. This is done in both psychology and natural science. Thus, it is indeed possible to find the "higher" in one realm represented by the "higher" in the other realm, without identifying the two as being the same thing. Looked at more closely, it is the ratios of periodicity <note>The frequency and timing of repeating patterns in waves.</note> between vibrations which act as the psychophysical representatives of melodic and harmonic...

...sensations occur; yet the former are something very different from the latter.

The following remark is added to pull the physical relationships we are discussing here out of the realm of abstraction. Two different tones can be heard by two different people, or by the same person—one today, the other heard years ago—and no melodic or harmonic (in short, musical) relationship will be felt between them, despite the fact that the necessary **ratio of periodicity** <note>original: "Periodicitätsverhältniß"; the mathematical frequency ratio between two sound waves that creates harmony.</note> between the underlying vibrations exists for our thinking—that is, abstractly. But it is also necessary that the vibrations between which the relationship exists enter into a physical **functional relationship** <note>original: "Wirkungsbezug"; a state where physical processes actually interact or influence one another in real-time.</note> with one another. Insofar as they do so, however, it is that specific periodicity ratio upon which the sensation of the specific musical relationship depends for its existence, and by which it is, in our sense, carried.

Now one might ask: if the same external music with its given vibration ratios can only evoke those same vibration ratios internally, how can it affect different people so differently? The same music leaves one person cold while strongly exciting another, and every other person is inwardly tuned differently by that same music. Here, one might think, <term>psychophysics</term> <note>The scientific study of the quantitative relationship between physical stimuli and mental sensations.</note> fails us; here we have something that is purely a **matter of the soul**. But why should that be? In one person, the physical functional relationships that matter will be weaker than in another—they may even fall below the **threshold** <note>original: "Schwelle"; the limit below which a stimulus is too weak to be consciously perceived.</note>; and in everyone else, the music—maintaining the same ratios—interacts with a different **total psychophysical system** <note>original: "psychophysisches Totalsystem"; the complete physical and mental state of an individual, including their memories and temperament.</note>. It finds within that system other factors and connections with which it relates, stimulating and pulling them along through association.

The same applies to melodic and harmonic tone relationships as it does to the relationships that appear in the perception of spatial forms and colors—which include symmetry, color harmony, and color contrasts—without it seeming necessary to go into further detail here.

Let us imagine the brain as a harp strung with countless differently tuned strings, which hears its own playing, while we can only see the external movements of it—or rather, only the strings themselves (**brain fibers** <note>original: "Gehirnfibern"; an early term for nerve fibers or neural pathways.</note>) undergoing these movements. But why, if even with the few strings of our external harps...

...if such high and manifold harmonies and melodies are possible with strings, should they not be all the more possible with the strings of our **soul-harp**? Indeed, they should be of a completely different order, since the strings of our soul-harp do not merely ring in tones, but also in colors, scents, and so on, leaving behind "after-echoes" that interweave with one another.

Now, of course, not everything categorized as belonging to the realm of the **higher spiritual** can be traced back to relationships such as those just mentioned. Rather, memories grow out of sensory sensations and perceptions—memories which are already considered something higher than the sensory phenomena from which they grow. Not only the <term>Monadologists</term> <note>Followers of the philosopher Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, who believed the universe was made of "monads"—indivisible units of consciousness that do not physically interact but follow a pre-established harmony.</note>, but also many other philosophers, are not inclined to believe that memories are as strictly tied to material processes as the sensory sensations from which they arose. Instead, they suggest the soul should be able to reproduce previously held sensations and perceptions through a "free act," so to speak. The original sensations provide only an initial occasion, a preparation, or a precondition, whereby the capacity to produce certain memories is planted in the mind; meanwhile, the actual production of these memories is left to the mind's own inherent conditions or its own "sovereign power," without further material cooperation. This sounds quite plausible as long as one stays in the realm of the abstract; indeed, one could build an entire psychological system upon it.

In the meantime, I have shown in detail in the *Elements* <note>original: "Elem."; referring to the author’s seminal work, *Elemente der Psychophysik* (Elements of Psychophysics), specifically Volume II, Section 43.</note> that if one holds sensory phenomena themselves to be **psychophysically represented** <note>The theory that every mental experience has a corresponding, measurable physical process in the body or brain.</note>, one would have to misunderstand or tear apart the connection of facts (from a different perspective than before) to avoid holding memory-images to be similarly represented. Here, I will only return to the general viewpoints regarding this.

The material or physical processes which admittedly underlie the sensory sensations within us do not vanish without a trace when the sensation fades; after all, no physical process ceases without a continued effect. It can propagate itself or transform into other processes, but it does not vanish from the world. And so, the continued effects of the physical processes upon which sensations depend propagate from the centers of the sensory nerves in the brain further into the brain. The conducting pathways for this are even visible to the eye, thus providing the ground for the connection of corresponding mental after-effects. This causal consideration, however...

<meta>This page continues the argument from page 7, where the author began discussing whether memories require a physical basis or are purely "free acts" of the soul. — 8 —

...is supplemented by a related and consistent view based on the **Functional Principle** <note>The "Functional Principle" is the core idea of psychophysics: that mental experiences (functions) and physical processes are two sides of the same coin, always occurring together in a predictable relationship.</note>.

How do memories actually differ from the <term>sensations</term> <note>Immediate raw data from the senses, like seeing a flash of red.</note> and <term>perceptions</term> <note>The mind's interpretation of those sensations, like recognizing that the red flash is a rose.</note> they reproduce? Firstly, memories are weaker; secondly, they carry the feeling of being generated from within; and thirdly, they carry the feeling of being related to the earlier sensations and perceptions upon which they causally depend. All of this, however, is represented quite simply and naturally according to the Functional Principle. The physical processes underlying memories will simply be weaker than those underlying sensations and perceptions; they will be generated from the internal physical context just as memories are generated from the internal psychological context, and the psychological feeling of causality will be supported by physical causality. In all of this, the consistency of the Functional Principle suffers no breach.

And finally, there are transition phenomena leading from sensations and perceptions to memories. These include actual <term>afterimages</term>, so-called "memory afterimages," the phenomena of so-called "sensory memory," and hallucinations—in short, a series of phenomena through which the apparent chasm between the original sensory phenomena and the memories of them is bridged, as explained in a special section of the **"Elements"** <note>referring to Gustav Fechner’s seminal 1860 work, *Elemente der Psychophysik* (Elements of Psychophysics), specifically Volume II, pages 467 and following.</note>.

Now, of course, the philosopher—in order not to let the soul's "free act" be diminished—can imagine and thereafter assert that the propagation of physical excitation beyond the sensory centers in the brain, further into the interior of the same, no longer signifies anything psychological. Furthermore, he need not concern himself with the Functional Principle, just as he has not concerned himself with it until now; he can view those transition phenomena as mere abnormalities in which the "free act" of the soul is still mixed with a more or less material additive. But one cannot blame the **psychophysicist** if he prefers to stick to the interconnected and consistent paths of knowledge offered by experience and empirical deduction in this field of inquiry, rather than following the philosopher when he cuts them off.

Now, it may pose difficulties to represent the long-term storage of memories and their undisturbed coexistence up to certain limits, or their emergence from consciousness and sinking into the unconscious, but these...

<meta>This page continues the author's defense of the "Functional Principle"—the idea that every mental state has a physical counterpart. Difficulties are not yet impossibilities; rather, several paths open up to our imagination—even if they are currently only hypothetical—that align well with what we know about how to overcome these difficulties. I will go into this in more detail in a later section (XVIII). The simple fact is that nature itself was only able to overcome these difficulties through an extraordinarily complex brain apparatus. Why would such an expense be necessary if the soul had the power to produce memories, and everything that follows from them, purely out of itself once the initial spark was given? Simply *ascribing* this power to the soul does not mean the soul actually possesses it; and the more easily one makes it for themselves with such an "explanation"—or rather, by sparing oneself any explanation at all—the less weight that explanation carries.

Of course, one cannot say that Herbart's <term>psychological mechanics</term> <note>Johann Friedrich Herbart (1776–1841) was a philosopher who tried to describe the mind using mathematical formulas, treating ideas like physical forces that push and pull against each other.</note>, which brings the relationships of memories into its domain, has made things easy for itself. Indeed, it required a whole series of <term>premises</term> <note>Vordersätze; the foundational assumptions or logical steps at the beginning of an argument.</note> to build its system, which I, for my part, find impossible to grant (Compare my *Propaedeutics of Aesthetics*, II. 272 f. <note>original: "Vorsch. d. Aesth." refers to Fechner's 1876 work *Vorschule der Ästhetik*.</note>). But even if one were to grant the possibility of a psychological mechanics *at all*, it would by no means be granted that it could exist in the abstract without a <term>psychophysical</term> <note>The study of the relationship between physical stimuli and mental phenomena.</note> foundation. One cannot have memories and spin thoughts by means of the mind alone in an empty brain-case, or one filled with a sponge. In fact, if such a thing as psychological mechanics were to be discussed at all, it could only be established and carried out as a psychophysical one. This is because mental measurement can only be grounded psychophysically, and mental relationships of scale can only be tracked psychophysically.

But let us go even higher than memories; for it does not stop at memories as simple reproductions of earlier sensory impressions. Instead, as memories of earlier and later things, and memories from one sense meet those from another, a complex mental play arises from which new and higher results can emerge. Memories provide the material for comparisons, distinctions, concepts, and higher <term>thought operations</term> in general. The material is combined, broken down, reshaped, and brought into new forms in which higher relationships emerge. Will psychophysics be able to keep up with all of this using its "representations"? — Well, corresponding operations are not foreign to the physical world either; there are also

To do so, the elementary psychophysical relationships and laws would first have to be developed and established to the point where the rest follows partly mathematically and partly according to the functional principle. If the philosopher wishes to claim that **psychophysics** <term>Psychophysics: the branch of psychology that deals with the relationships between physical stimuli and mental phenomena.</term> will certainly get stuck here, then it must at least be admitted that it is still far from the goal in this regard.

To the higher mental phenomena considered above, **attention** is added as something that people are usually accustomed to regarding as a purely spiritual matter. That even this does not escape psychophysical representability will be taught in a later section specifically relating to it.

If, after all this, there is no decisive reason in the so-called mental "heights" to limit psychophysical representability and thus the scope of psychophysics, one might instead seek a limitation "deep below." This would involve holding the various basic qualities of sensory perceptions—such as seeing or hearing—to be **psychophysically** unrepresentable. Instead, one might see them as something that grows purely out of the soul, without the body’s own contribution or merit; and indeed, I have encountered an idea of this kind from the philosophical side. Against this, however, it cannot be denied that differently qualified sensory perceptions are awakened by different types of physical stimuli...

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s exploration of how physical processes in the body correspond to mental experiences. He is addressing a major hurdle in his theory: if everything is made of vibrations, how do we tell the difference between hearing a sound and seeing a color?</meta>

— 11 —

...be produced, which will also create diverse effects within our physical organism, and that the soul would have no basis at all to meet them with differently qualified sensations if it did not receive different occasions for them from the body, which will then form the <term>psychophysical representatives</term> <note>original: "ps.-ph. Repräsentanten"; these are the physical processes in the brain or nerves that "stand in" for a mental feeling.</note> of these different sensations. On the other hand, however, it must be admitted that a closer examination leads to a difficulty of the following kind, which, while not decisive, is nonetheless not easily dismissed.

All possible *sensations of tone* and the relationships between *sensations of tone*—such as *intensity, pitch, timbre, overtones, melody, harmony*—can be sufficiently represented in our minds by *vibrations, amplitude, period, composition,* and *ratios of vibrations*; but since these physical properties (or definitions of the physical) are, so to speak, "used up" for the representation of properties of tone sensation, they seem capable only of being used for that purpose. How is it then that *sensations of color*, which are so entirely heterogeneous to *sensations of tone*, are also supposed to be linked to *vibrations*? And what else could they be linked to? Certainly not to currents within the *nervous system* ¹). The fact that *light vibrations* are faster than *sound vibrations* certainly does not lead, according to the <term>functional principle</term> <note>The author's theory that every mental change corresponds to a specific physical change.</note>, to attributing the difference between *sensations of light* and *sensations of sound* to that fact. For when *sound vibrations* become faster, the *pitch* may change, but it remains a *sensation of tone*. Furthermore, in the progression of the *speed* of *light vibrations* through the *spectrum*, qualitative changes occur from *red* through *yellow* and *green* to *blue*, whereas the scale of *tone vibrations* shows nothing analogous. Other differences also exist between the two sensory domains (compiled in "Elements" Vol. II, p. 270 ff. <note>A reference to Fechner's own foundational work, *Elemente der Psychophysik* (1860).</note>), which call for a fundamentally different representation of *color sensation* and *light sensation* in general than for *tone sensation*—but what should we imagine? Indeed, what are we to think when *sensations of smell, taste, touch, and warmth* also demand to be represented in their distinctness?

I admit that we are by no means yet in a position to [provide] any...

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s discussion on the physical nature of sensation. Having established that light and sound both involve vibrations, he is now looking for a more sophisticated way to explain how they feel so different, moving away from his earlier theories toward a model involving particle arrangements and "chemical" senses.</meta>

— 12 —

...to provide a reasonably certain foundation for a thought we wish to grasp in this regard, and I myself no longer place any weight on the hypothesis I established in *Elements of Psychophysics*, Vol. II, p. 299 f., regarding the difference between the sensations of light and sound. However, one must speak out against the claim that nothing at all can be imagined in this respect, as long as there are perfectly conceivable possibilities. Why shouldn't the quality of sensations depend not only on the speed of vibrations but also on the number and arrangement of the particles that mutually determine each other's vibrations? Strictly speaking, all particles in the world—even the most distant—determine each other’s vibrations, but according to the <term>threshold principle</term> <note>Fechner’s foundational idea that a physical stimulus must reach a certain intensity (the "threshold") before it can be perceived by the mind.</note>, the effects of more distant particles may become imperceptible to sensation. Furthermore, the terminal apparatuses of the various sensory nerves could be organized such that the vibrations of a certain kind of combination gain dominance over all others. In the case of the so-called chemical senses—sight, smell, and taste <note>Fechner classifies sight as a chemical sense here, likely referring to the photochemical reactions in the retina.</note>—major differences in this regard could be chemically mediated, which fits well with many modern views. In general, however, a wide-ranging field of possibilities presents itself within the framework of the previous general hypothesis. We are prevented from pursuing these not so much by the road being cut off, but by the darkness that still surrounds it at this time. Consequently, until a new, luminous point of view illuminates the path, it is indeed best to concern oneself with the <term>psychophysical</term> <note>original: "ps.-ph."; the study of the precise mathematical and functional relationships between the physical world and mental experience.</note> relationships within each specific sensory domain rather than with their fundamental qualitative differences.

Finally, I want to mention **pleasure** and **displeasure** <note>original: "Lust und Unlust"; the basic spectrum of positive and negative feeling or affect.</note> as mental phenomena whose physical representability may be considered. They can possess either a sensory or a higher character, upon which sensory drives and higher motives respectively depend, eventually manifesting in active behaviors. Now, in his *Book of Comets* (1st edition, p. 325 ff.), Zöllner <note>Johann Karl Friedrich Zöllner (1834–1882), an astrophysicist interested in the physical basis of consciousness.</note>—following more general views—has already attempted a psychophysical representation of pleasure and displeasure, according to which an increase in physical <term>living force</term> <note>original: "lebendige Kraft"; a historical term for kinetic energy.</note> should be linked with pleasure, and a decrease with displeasure. However, it seems to me there are many objections to this, which I discussed in my *Introduction to Aesthetics*, Vol. II, p. 266; another hypothesis seems more promising to me, which I proposed in that same work and developed further in my book on the *Day View* <note>original: "Tagesansicht"; Fechner's philosophical worldview that the universe is conscious and full of light, as opposed to the "Night View" of cold, dead materialism.</note> (Section XIII), although I do not yet consider it mature enough to claim authoritative significance...

<meta>This page transitions from Fechner's technical discussion of sensory vibrations to a defense of his broader philosophical project. He addresses the "most general objection" to psychophysics—that it leads to materialism—by arguing for a dual-aspect theory where the material world is a representation of a universal spirit.</meta>

to be assumed for psychophysics. Nonetheless, I wish that some attention were paid to it.

After all the detailed considerations I have explored thus far, I arrive at the most general objection against the unlimited scope of psychophysics. This objection forms the true background and root of all philosophical opposition, though I cannot delve too deeply into the arguments here. A philosopher would likely have no issue with the broad reach of psychophysics in the sense described, if they did not feel that more general interests were being endangered by it. Above all, they raise the concern—or even the blunt accusation—that applying <term>psychophysical representation</term> <note>Fechner’s foundational concept that every mental event has a corresponding physical event; essentially, that the mind and body are two sides of the same coin.</note> to the entire mental realm, without exempting any "higher" faculties, leads directly to **materialism** with all its consequences. Indeed, they claim that the very essence of materialism is found within it.

And yet, only someone who focuses solely on the materialistic side—which undeniably exists in this application—could reach such a conclusion. They fail to consider the opposing side: that the entire material world is the continuous representation of a universal **spiritual being**. Psychophysics has never been conceived by me in any other relation than this, and in the ultimate generalization of its principles, it cannot be understood otherwise. If someone chooses to view it differently, that is their own affair and to their own detriment, but it is not the fault or the business of psychophysics itself. Admittedly, it is also not the primary task of psychophysics to fully develop this "other side" of its nature. To do that, the field must be supplemented by other considerations, through which it finally becomes a complete whole. One cannot say that I have been lacking in providing such considerations, even if there is still a lack of people who care to study them. <note>original: "Es ist eben noch nicht aller Tage Abend."</note> The final word has not yet been spoken.

In fact, I see the main defect of the currently prevailing worldview—in all its various branches—in the fact that people do not know how to unite these two points of view. Herein lies the reason for the conflict between **religion** and **natural science**, a conflict from which no one seems to know how to escape. For this is how things stand even today: people are just as unwilling to accept a physical equivalent for every mental process as they are to accept a mental equivalent for every physical process. They only allow for an exceptional psychophysical connection between the two within the **nervous system** of humans and animals. They see this as the only "knot" that links these two otherwise diverging realms, and

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s critique of the "Night View" of the world. He transitions from a general philosophical objection to a specific critique of the scientific assumption that consciousness is limited to nervous systems, arguing instead for a world permeated by spirit.</meta>

the abstract idea of God hovers over a world devoid of spirit. This makes the entire world—beyond humans and animals—blind and deaf; light does not shine "out there," sound does not ring "out there"; and so I have called this view the "Night View," although there are other reasons to name the prevailing worldview this way. <note>Fechner contrasts the "Night View" (the materialistic belief that the universe is dead, dark matter) with his "Day View" (the belief that the universe is conscious and filled with light and spirit).</note>

And what are the reasons for seeing the exclusive carrier of psychic phenomena in nerve vibrations? How illogical and incorrect the empirical <note>Based on observation or experience rather than theory.</note> arguments put forward for this are—and there are no *a priori* <note>original: "aprioristische"; referring to knowledge that proceeds from theoretical deduction rather than observation.</note> ones at all—I have shown too often ¹) to return to them here; I only marvel at the satisfaction generally found in these reasons, and the readiness with which people subscribe to the Night View. However, not only is there nothing *a priori* preventing us from seeing a unified <term>psychophysical</term> system in the whole world, which includes that of humans only as a part, but also arguments from analogy, causality, and teleological <note>Relating to the explanation of phenomena by the purpose they serve rather than by postulated causes.</note> conclusions—starting from the fact of our own <term>soul-life</term> <note>original: "Beseelung"; the state of being endowed with a soul or consciousness.</note>—lead to a generalization of consciousness beyond ourselves. Not without thorough care have I developed these in other writings; but I have, of course, been unable to prevent them from being dismissed as fantasies when compared to the lucubrations <note>Laborious or pedantic study; Fechner is likely being sarcastic about the "Night View" scholars.</note> of the Night View.

Aside from these conclusions, it can be asserted on the very ground of <term>psychophysics</term> <note>The scientific study of the relation between stimulus and sensation.</note> itself (*Elements*, Vol. II, Section 46), that no fundamental property of the psychophysical movements within us can be found or conceived that would establish an essential difference between them and the movements occurring outside of us. Accordingly, there is no reason why movements beyond our nervous system should not be just as psychophysical for a more general spirit as the movements in our nervous system are for our own spirit—which is thereby only planted in a special way into the general spiritual being. To this end, Zöllner and others have rightly asserted that if a "psychic carrying capacity" did not depend on the elementary aspects common to physical movement both inside and outside of us, such capacity could never arise through any complexity of movement within organisms. But none of this is of any use; for, if one cannot speculate it away, one simply speculates right over it—as has always been done—and so, in the progression through Kant, Fichte, Schelling, Hegel, Herbart, Schopenhauer—

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s argument for a scientific-philosophical worldview that bridges the gap between the material and the mental. ...hauer, <note>Likely referring to Arthur Schopenhauer (1788–1860), who emphasized the "will" as the inner essence of the world.</note> Hartmann <note>Eduard von Hartmann (1842–1906), known for his "Philosophy of the Unconscious."</note> have finally come so far as to say: should we not rather begin again with Kant.

For my part, however, I seek a true new beginning behind Kant <note>Fechner suggests looking at the foundations Kant laid rather than just his conclusions.</note> by returning to the elementary and fundamental factual and lawful relationships between bodily and spiritual things, based on observations and inferences from observations of human beings; for it cannot be done any other way. From there, one can go beyond by generalizing, expanding, and elevating these findings according to principles which—though they can never lead to a logical certainty (which is impossible in these matters)—lead to the greatest probability that can be gained in such things, and at the same time to the unified satisfaction of our religious requirements of faith. Now a principle asserts itself within us, which I have called the <term>synechological</term> <note>From the Greek *syneches*, meaning "continuous." This principle suggests that our unified mind is connected to a complex, many-parted physical system.</note> (Elem. II. 526 ff., Day View 246 ff.), according to which "the psychically unified and simple is linked to a physical manifold 1), and conversely, the physical manifold contracts psychically into the unified, simple, or at least the simpler"; and so, following an inference from ourselves to what lies beyond us, the same principle will also assert itself in the general <term>psychophysical</term> system. Thus, we do not have to demand a singular psychical phenomenon for every physical detail beyond us; rather, every physical detail, both within and beyond us, will contribute to a psychical resultant. For the distinguishability of psychical resultants, however, special <term>psychophysical</term> rules will still apply.

Meanwhile, <term>psychophysics</term> must leave the application of its general laws to the world-whole to a <term>Philosophy of Nature</term> <note>original: "Naturphilosophie"; a movement in German philosophy that sought to understand nature as a whole system of organic development rather than just mechanical parts.</note>, which presents itself as nothing other than a continuation and extension of <term>psychophysics</term> in the narrower sense (that is, the human sense). Thus, we shall not go further into considerations that lead beyond this. These previous brief remarks and references were only intended to counter the most general objection to which <term>psychophysics</term> is subject.

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s defense of psychophysical parallelism—the idea that mental and physical events are two sides of the same coin. He is addressing the objection that if the mind is tied to the physical body, human free will must be an illusion because the body follows strict laws of cause and effect.</meta>

independently of it. What becomes of human and divine freedom if all spiritual activities, even in their highest realm, are tied to material activities? For they would then also be bound to the necessary causal sequence of those material activities.

To this, one must first reply that it remains a point of contention among philosophers themselves whether an "indeterministic" freedom—that is, one that escapes the law of causal sequence—truly exists in the spiritual realm. I also believe I have shown in the 16th section of the work "On the Day View" <note>Fechner’s *Die Tagesansicht gegenüber der Nachtansicht* (1879), where he argues for a world filled with soul and life rather than dead matter.</note> that determinism can perfectly well coexist with religion and morality, provided one understands it in the sense of the "Day View," which, of course, does not happen under the prevailing "Night View" <note>Fechner calls materialism the "Night View" because it views the universe as dark and dead; his "Day View" sees it as light and conscious.</note>. But regardless, even if one does not wish to give up an indeterministic view of freedom for the spirit, nothing prevents us from imagining it represented psychophysically. We can think of the break in the law of causal sequence through freedom as belonging to both realms simultaneously. In fact, we already do this if we imagine that the otherwise lawful progression of the physical world is altered by the free interventions of the spirit—not as a secondary consequence, but as a direct, simultaneous occurrence.

In fact, if the spiritual change $\alpha$ is supported by the physical change $a$, and the spiritual change $\beta$ (which follows $\alpha$) is supported by the physical change $b$, then the lawful **causal connection** can be interrupted by freedom on both the spiritual side (between $\alpha$ and $\beta$) and the corresponding physical side (between $a$ and $b$). By this, new beginnings in the realm of events are established on both sides at once, without the psychophysical connection between $\alpha$ and $a$, or $\beta$ and $b$, suffering in the least. There is no difficulty in this at all. Causal connection and the break of that connection simply always coincide in both realms. Of course, we are very accustomed to thinking of indeterministic freedom and causal necessity as being divided between the two realms, rather than coinciding in both; but that is simply a <term>petitio principii</term> <note>Latin: "begging the question." A logical fallacy where the conclusion is assumed in the premises. Here, Fechner means people assume the physical world *must* be strictly deterministic while the mind is free, without proving they are separate.</note> based on habit—and bad habits must eventually come to an end.

Finally, if one wishes to find an *a priori* <note>Latin: "from the former." Knowledge that proceeds from theoretical deduction rather than from observation.</note> difficulty in the idea that such incomparable phenomena—for example, simple sensations and complex movements like vibrations—should belong together in a relationship of mutual dependence, then psychophysics itself does not need to concern itself with the explanation, but only...

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s discussion on the relationship between the mind and the body. He is transitioning from a defense of determinism to explaining his "Identity View"—the core philosophical foundation of his psychophysics, which suggests that the "mental" and "physical" are simply two different ways of looking at the same underlying reality.</meta>

...to keep in view and pursue that very fact, which cannot be dismissed even by the simplest logic. This fact may pose difficulties for every philosophical view regarding the connection between **body and soul**, though the least difficulty, it seems to me, for the view I placed at the head of my "Elements" <note>Fechner refers to his 1860 book, *Elements of Psychophysics* (*Elemente der Psychophysik*), which founded the field.</note>—not as a guide *through* psychophysics, but as a point of connection *to* philosophy. 

According to this view, it is the fundamental difference between the **inner** and **outer standpoint** of perceiving the same being that determines the difference between the spiritual and material world ¹). From this perspective, that which appears to itself internally as a simple unity can, through the variety of relationships it develops outwardly, appear to the external observer as something complex and composed; it is upon this that the **synechological principle** <term>synechological principle (from the Greek *syneches*, meaning "continuous"; Fechner’s idea that all things in the universe are fundamentally interconnected and continuous rather than isolated atoms)</term> depends. Furthermore, whatever contributes to a general mental phenomenon—whether in the universe as a whole or merely within an individual—may require a certain strength before it can be distinguished from the general background as a specific phenomenon; it is upon this that the **threshold principle** <term>threshold principle (the "threshold" or *Schwelle* is the point at which a physical stimulus becomes strong enough to produce a conscious sensation)</term> depends.

To say one more word on the matter, a consequence of this general fundamental view is that there can certainly be a "pure psychology" just as there is a "pure physics" or general natural science, which need not concern themselves with one another nor with psychophysics. Each of these former sciences considers the world in its context from its own specific standpoint—either the inner or the outer—and why shouldn't they be allowed to do so? Only, in the end, neither should forget that its view is merely one-sided. There is still a need for a doctrine that links these one-sided perspectives together. That doctrine is **Psychophysics**.

(A more detailed discussion on the relationship of these respective doctrines to one another can be found in "*Zendavesta*" Vol. II. 312 ff. <note>*Zend-Avesta: On the Things of Heaven and the Hereafter* (1851), a work where Fechner argued that plants and stars have souls.</note>).

# Section Two

## Psychophysical Principles and Methods of Measurement

### II. Concept and Measurement of Differential Sensitivity

A fundamentally critical view held by Müller—one which forms, so to speak, the guiding thread through his entire critique of the methods for measuring differential sensitivity (D.S.) <note>original: *Unterschiedsempfindlichkeit* (U. E.); the ability of a person to detect a change or difference between two physical stimuli, such as two weights or two lights.</note>, but which is also most disastrous for this critique—is as follows: **that only the reciprocal value of the difference threshold (D. Th.) <note>original: *Unterschiedsschwelle* (U. Schw.); the minimum difference between two stimuli that is just barely detectable.</note>, designated by him as S, may serve as the measure of D.S.; that is, the value of the difference which must first be exceeded before the difference (D.) is recognized as such.** According to Müller, any value other than S that one might wish to use for this measure, whether directly or by its reciprocal value—be it the mean error of the method of mean errors (m. E.) <note>original: *mittlere Fehler* (m. F.)</note>, be it the difference that yields a given ratio of right, wrong, and doubtful cases (r, w, d) <note>original: *richtige, falsche und zweifelhafte Fälle* (r, f, z)</note> in the method of right and wrong cases (r. and w. C.), or be it the measure of precision derived from this ratio—is only useful as a measure of D.S. insofar as its direct or inverse proportionality to the D. Th. has been proven, and then only by virtue of this proportionality or reciprocity <note>original: *Reciprocität*; the mathematical relationship where one value increases as the other decreases (1/x).</note> and only as far as that relationship extends. Müller claims this proportionality is by no means self-evident, and that not only has no theoretical or empirical proof been provided by me or anyone else, but that no investigation into the matter has even been undertaken. Consequently, everything that has hitherto been based on the assumption of such proportionality—specifically the formulation of Weber's Law <term>Weber's Law (a fundamental psychophysical principle stating that the smallest detectable change in a stimulus is a constant proportion of the original stimulus intensity)</term>, insofar as it rests upon it—would entirely lack a secure foundation.

The primary passage in which Müller expresses this view, along with the reasons upon which he bases it, is this (p. 2).

Yet, that this must be required in order to validate the general significance which Müller ascribes to the D. Th. is something Müller seems not to have considered, as nothing regarding it is found in his work. 

However, there are also differences above as well as below the threshold, and there exists a differential sensitivity regarding these differences, for which a measure can be demanded just as well as for the sensitivity regarding the threshold difference itself. ...wrong cases <note>original: *f. F.*, for *falsche Fälle*.</note> and mean errors <note>original: *m. F.*, for *mittlere Fehler*.</note> are present. Through the measurement values of D.S. <note>Differential Sensitivity; original: *U. Thus, I can find no rational motive for Müller’s demand that every value other than the D.T. must prove its proportionality (or reciprocity) with the D.T. in order to demonstrate its usefulness as a measure of D.S. One could just as well—indeed with even more right—demand the inverse: that the D.T. prove itself against the measures that extend above and below it, because it provides only one very specific measure. Suppose the required proportionality did not occur, or did not occur consistently; one would then have to reject neither one nor the other of these scales, but rather apply each only within its proper limits. One should not demand that one of these scales base its validity on the fact that it aligns with the other.

The actual reason that led Müller to restrict the measure of D.S. to the D.T. can only be found, in my view, in the way he understood and handled the "Method of Right and Wrong Cases" <note>original: *r. u. f. F.*, for *richtige und falsche Fälle*.</note> and the "Method of Mean Errors." He could not recognize the significance of the precision measure and the mean error as scales of D.S.; consequently, nothing remained for him but to reduce the measure of D.S. to the D.T. However, these methods are to be understood and handled differently than he has done, for which the later sections should be consulted where I come to the discussion of these methods.

When Müller asserts, in favor of preferring the Difference Threshold value as the measure of D.S.
