However, the point is not to determine the D.S. with respect to a single difference value. I do not see why a certain ratio of *r, f, z* <note>Referring to the categories of Right (*richtig*), False (*falsch*), and Doubtful (*zweifelhaft*) judgments in a trial.</note> in the "Method of Right and Wrong Cases," or a certain mean error in the "Method of Average Errors," should not—just as well as the D.T.—in principle [correspond to] a precisely fixable degree of noticeability, or distance from noticeability, identically reproducible by different observers...

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s rebuttal of G.E. Müller. Fechner is arguing against Müller’s narrow focus on the "Difference Threshold" as the only valid way to measure sensitivity. He suggests that Weber’s Law—a fundamental principle relating physical stimuli to mental perception—should be understood more broadly across different experimental methods, not just the one Müller prefers.</meta>

If the law’s relationship were restricted only to the **Difference Threshold** <note>original: *U. Schw.* (Unterschiedsschwelle); the minimum difference between two stimuli that a person can detect.</note>, then it would in fact have very little significance. It only gains its very general and important meaning because the concept of **Difference Sensitivity** <note>original: *U. E.* (Unterschiedsempfindlichkeit); the capacity to perceive differences between stimuli.</note> is measured in a way that allows the law's application to other types of differences to be generalized. The fact that Weber himself only proved his law using the **Method of J.N.D.** <note>Just Noticeable Differences; original: *e. m. U.* (eben merklicher Unterschied)</note>—and thus only by the **Difference Threshold**—is irrelevant to the matter at hand. Rather, it makes the question of the law's general validity all the more urgent, for which other methods must be employed.

In order not to withhold Müller’s own remarks regarding this latter question, he says during his discussion of the **Method of Mean Errors** <note>original: *m. F.* (mittlere Fehler); a statistical method where a subject tries to match a standard stimulus, and the average error is measured.</note> (p. 73 and more briefly p. 213): "One can, of course—if one finds pleasure in doing so—define **Difference Sensitivity** without further consideration however one likes, and thus in any case set it simply as the **reciprocal** <note>In mathematics, the reciprocal is 1 divided by the number. Here, it means if the error is large, sensitivity is considered low.</note> of the mean error. However, if one wishes to use the behavior of **Difference Sensitivity** defined in this way to draw conclusions about the validity or invalidity of **Weber's Law**—which, after all, primarily states that for one and the same stimulus quality, the relative size of the **Difference Threshold** value possesses a constant value—one must first and foremost know how the mean error relates to the **Difference Threshold**. As long as this is unknown, one can indeed—and this will always be instructive when using a suitable experimental procedure—conduct as many experiments using the **Method of Mean Errors** as one wishes, and set the relative **Difference Sensitivity** as the reciprocal of the relative value of the mean error; only, one must not then transfer what applies to the **Difference Sensitivity** defined in *this* way to the sensitivity that is set as the reciprocal of the relative size of the **Difference Threshold**, the constancy of which is what **Weber's Law** asserts."

But I return all of this to Müller. If Müller finds pleasure in restricting the measure of **Difference Sensitivity** and the application of **Weber's Law** to the **Difference Threshold**, no one can prevent him from doing so; however, he thereby places himself in a position where he cannot satisfy the more general conceptual and factual demands of this field.

Consequently, I for my part stand by the general meaning and definition of the measure of **Difference Sensitivity** that I provided in the *Elements* <note>Fechner is referring to his 1860 book, *Elements of Psychophysics*, the founding text of the field.</note> (I. 47), though I wish to explain it here somewhat more specifically than was done there ¹).

1) What applies here is **Difference Sensitivity** in itself, from which the *relative* **Difference Sensitivity** is derived by dividing the former by one of the two stimuli or their average.

--- Page 42 ---
<meta>This page continues Fechner’s defense of how Difference Sensitivity (U.E.) is calculated. On the previous page, Fechner argued that Weber’s Law remains valid across different experimental methods, even those Müller criticized. He is specifically addressing the relationship between physical stimulus changes and the mental perception of those changes, using the concept of the "reciprocal" to link them mathematically.</meta>

**Difference Sensitivity** <term>U.E.; original: *Unterschiedsempfindlichkeit*</term> cannot be measured in an absolute sense, but only comparatively. In general, I define it as being **reciprocal** <note>Inversely proportional; as the physical difference required to notice a change gets larger, the sensitivity is considered lower.</note> to the objective size of the **stimulus variation** or stimulus difference that produces a subjectively equal impression in the cases being compared. This means it is felt to be the same size, appears equivalent in sensation, is recognized with the same ease, or can be substituted for another without the impression of size changing; these are all merely different expressions for the same factual point.

Initially, of course, this explanation seems to apply only to **Difference Sensitivity** regarding differences *above* the **threshold** <note>The "Schwelle" is the point where a stimulus becomes just barely perceivable.</note>. However, in the **Method of Mean Errors** <term>m. F.; original: *Methode der mittleren Fehler*</term>, one observes only errors—differences *below* the threshold—since these are intentionally brought down below that limit. In these cases, errors of very different sizes produce the same sensation of a "missing difference." But this simply implies that we cannot judge **Difference Sensitivity** here based on a single difference below the threshold. Instead, we must judge it based on the sum or the average of the differences that fall below the threshold across a large number of comparable trials, setting the sensitivity as proportional to the reciprocal value of that average.

This explanation is entirely consistent with the explanation regarding cases above the threshold. In both cases (below and above the threshold), we set the **Difference Sensitivity** as the reciprocal of the differences that *appear* equal. Because there are many various differences below the threshold that all equally appear to be "missing," we use the total sum (given an equal number of trials) or the average obtained through the **Method of Mean Errors**. To do this, however, the method must be carried out differently than Müller describes—partly because he misunderstands the method and partly because he prescribes it incorrectly, a point I will return to in Section VII.

Based on this, we can add a further point to the definition: **Difference Sensitivity** is reciprocal to those differences that are recognized with equal ease—that is, with equal probability—across a majority of comparable trials. Furthermore, following the general concept of **Difference Sensitivity**, we can say it is reciprocal to those differences that are equally easily *misidentified*. These are the **estimation errors** <note>original: *Schätzungsfehler*</note> one commits when trying to judge two given magnitudes as being equal. We obtain these very errors specifically by means of the **Method of Mean Errors**.

While the measurement of **Difference Sensitivity** via the **Method of Mean Errors** regarding these errors aligns with the general principle of measurement in the manner just described, the measurement regarding

[...] of the differences above the threshold through the **Method of Right and Wrong Cases** <term>Method of r. and f. C.; original: *Methode der richtigen und falschen Fälle*</term> in the following way. If, in this procedure, two stimulus differences **D** of different magnitudes are subjected to the procedure in a comparable manner under the same external circumstances, they will yield a different ratio of **right, wrong, and doubtful cases (r, f, z)** <note>These are the three possible categories of participant responses in a discrimination task: "heavier," "lighter," or "uncertain."</note> at the same degree of **Difference Sensitivity** <term>U.E.</term>. If, however, despite their objective difference, they yield the same ratio, this can only be understood to mean that the influence which the varying magnitude of **D** would have exerted under equal sensitivity is balanced out by a difference in sensitivity. Thus, according to our principle of measurement, the sensitivity in these two different states must be set as reciprocal to the **D**s that yield the same result—that is, the same **r, f, z**.

There is nothing hypothetical in this; it is a matter of definition that the **Difference Sensitivity** is reciprocal to the differences that achieve the same for the sensitivity; it is a case of "the same by the same" <note>original: *idem per idem*; a Latin logical term for a definition that circles back on itself, here used to mean the relationship is true by definition.</note>. Now, in practice, it is admittedly not easy to adjust the variation of **D** during different levels of sensitivity to produce the exact same **r, f, z**. But if one had brought them close to it through experimentation, any interpolation formula would suffice to finalize the calculation. Naturally, however, a formula would be preferred that corresponds to the actual law of probability for the **r, f, z** in relation to the size of the errors committed. And according to the most probable hypothesis, the **Gaussian Law** <note>Also known as the Normal Distribution or Bell Curve; Fechner used this mathematical model to describe how human judgments vary around a mean.</note> presents itself as such. **Müller** <note>Georg Elias Müller (1850–1934), a prominent experimental psychologist and contemporary of Fechner who refined many of these methods.</note> also makes use of this law. By utilizing the **r, f, z** in the sense of this law—in a manner that differs from Müller’s, which I will discuss in Section IV—I obtain a **precision measure *h*** ¹), which is reciprocal to the **D** that yields the same **r, f, z**, and thus corresponds to our general concept of measurement for **Difference Sensitivity**. ¹) Namely, the **precision measure *h*** I use to measure **Difference Sensitivity** is determined such that when **D** changes in different series of trials, ***h D*** remains the same, provided the trials at the different **D** values are brought to the same **r, f, z**. If, however, ***h D*** is to remain the same when **D** changes, ***h*** must change in the inverse ratio to the **D** that yields the same **r, f, z** (and thus appears identical to the sensitivity); it therefore corresponds exactly to the concept of the measure of **Difference Sensitivity**. ### III. On the so-called accidental error processes.

In the **Methods of Right and Wrong Cases** as well as the **Method of Mean Errors**, those factors which Müller calls **accidental error processes**—often referred to by me simply as **random occurrences** <note>original: *Zufälligkeiten*</note>—have a great influence on the results. They have less influence in the **Method of Just Noticeable Differences**, although they are not entirely absent there either. What I was able to say about this in the "Elements" <note>Fechner’s foundational 1860 work, *Elemente der Psychophysik*</note> (Vol. I, p. 76 ff.) is essentially contained in the following remarks:

> "In all three methods, irregular **random occurrences**—which partly adhere to the physical manipulations and partly lie grounded in subjective conditions of how the compared magnitudes are perceived—play a major role... If the manipulation changes in any way during the experiments, a different play of random occurrences immediately sets in, and the measurements cease to be comparable; likewise, one cannot assume the same latitude for random occurrences across different individuals due to possible variations in internal conditions."

---

1) If one accepts the calculation of the experiments according to the Gaussian Law, the significance of the measure of precision I have derived for the measure of **Difference Sensitivity** <term>U.E.</term> can be explained in another way, as will be done in Section VI.

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s discussion of Georg Elias Müller’s critiques. On the previous page, Fechner defended the "measure of precision" (h) as a valid tool for calculating sensitivity. Here, he transitions into a more specific debate about the "accidental errors" or "contingencies" that occur during sensory experiments.</meta>

> “There is absolutely no way to obtain a measure free from these random contingencies; their average magnitude always enters into the measurement. This does not, however, prevent one from gaining comparable measures of sensitivity as long as this factor remains constant—that is, as long as the irregular contingencies maintain the same average size. Indeed, without these contingencies, the measurement methods of ‘right and wrong cases’ <term>a method where a subject compares two slightly different stimuli and the frequency of correct vs. incorrect judgments is recorded</term> and ‘mean errors’ would not exist at all. But attached to the previous consideration is the important caveat: to regard only those measures of sensitivity as comparable where one can assume an equal play of contingencies, which requires exact comparability of external and internal conditions.”

Now, Müller <note>Georg Elias Müller (1850–1934), a German experimental psychologist who frequently critiqued Fechner’s work</note> is right in a certain sense when he says (p. 335), while partially reproducing the previous passage, that I “unfortunately did not go into the question of what kind of accidental error processes are at play in the perception of a given sensory stimulus”; for at the very least, I did not go into it as deeply as it was possible to do, or as deeply as he himself has done. In my work *Elements* <note>Referring to Fechner's seminal 1860 book, *Elemente der Psychophysik*</note>, I simply did not know more to say about it than the generalities above, and I believed I had done enough to address the considerations necessary for the measurement methods. However, it is to Müller’s credit that he has examined the question of the nature of those processes more specifically; it would be even more so if he had also answered them convincingly, which is something I cannot concede. The matter concerns three main questions in particular: **First**, are the accidental error processes that play a role in measurement experiments primarily internal or external in the sense of the distinction to be made further on? **Second**, are the changes that the magnitude of psychophysical excitations <term>the internal neural or mental response to a physical stimulus</term> suffers through accidental error processes independent of this magnitude, or dependent on it—specifically, proportional to it? **Third**, how is Weber's Law <term>the principle that the perceived change in a stimulus is proportional to the initial intensity of the stimulus</term> to be related to the actual circumstances of the accidental error processes, and does an advantage for one or another interpretation of this law perhaps emerge from this? On none of these points, however, could I agree with Müller based on the following considerations.

As far as the first question is concerned, generally speaking, neither Müller nor I deny that the accidental error processes in the experiments can be both internal and external; but while I, for my part, in the *Elements*...

...can be attributed. Indeed, one can imagine from the outset that even with the most careful maintenance of external circumstances—which I have taken into account in my experiments—a weight might be lifted in a more slanted direction, or with a hand rotated differently, or gripping more or less firmly, or by a hand that is more or less fatigued or carrying over a lingering effect from the previous trial, compared to another time or compared to the other weight. These circumstances, which I briefly categorize as external ^1)), vary according to the laws of chance.

Now let us consider the shadow experiments using the **method of just noticeable differences** <term>Methode der eben merklichen Unterschiede: a procedure where a stimulus is adjusted until the observer can barely detect a difference between it and a reference</term> by contrast. If, in these experiments, one reduces the difference between two adjacent shadows, or between a shadow and its background, until it is imperceptible—that is, slightly below the **difference threshold** <term>Unterschiedsschwelle: the minimum amount of change in a stimulus required for a person to detect it</term>—then according to Müller, it should reappear from time to time due to internal error processes, then fade again, or perhaps seemingly flip into its opposite, just as we see the corresponding effect in the weight experiments when the difference between the two weights is small.

*But it does not.* <note>original: "Quod non."</note> One looks for the border between the two shadows or between the shadow and its surroundings in vain; one continues to look in vain, and **the difference never switches its sign in our perception** <note>meaning the observer's mind does not suddenly mistake the lighter area for the darker area</note> ^2)). Even two very similar shades of clouds, whose difference is slightly above the threshold, do not do this. 

And Müller should see for himself whether, in the practically countless experiments with shadows and rotating discs—or indeed in any experiments using the method of just noticeable differences to test **Weber’s Law** <term>the rule that the change in a stimulus that will be just noticeable is a constant ratio of the original stimulus</term>—there is any mention of such changes. These changes play a major role not only in the **method of right and wrong cases** <term>Methode der richtigen und falschen Fälle: a method where a subject compares two stimuli and says which is greater</term> but also in the **method of average error** <term>Methode der mittleren Fehler</term>. 

But where lies the essential difference between these methods? It can only be found in the fact that in the former <note>the light and shadow experiments</note>, unlike the others, there are no spatial, temporal, or movement differences inserted between the comparison of the components of the difference, which would give room for external chance occurrences.

We have compared weight experiments with light experiments here; however, even in the weight experiments themselves, the influence of external circumstances in the sense described can be shown by the following fact—

---

1) Irregular changes in fatigue and lingering effects fall into the category of external factors insofar as they depend on the influence of the external weights themselves.
2) With repeated adjustments to the "just noticeable difference" via external manipulations, one will of course be able to find a play of accidental error processes, and to that extent, the method of just noticeable differences will also be susceptible to them.

<meta>This page continues Gustav Fechner's argument against Georg Elias Müller. ...to prove, which Müller himself can verify on my weight apparatus, currently in his hands—a fact which I confess formerly puzzled me, though it is now explained quite simply by the predominantly external nature of the accidental error processes in the sense indicated.

One may set up a single-handed experimental series with two completely identical weights under the normal conditions specified in my "Elements" <note>Referring to Fechner's foundational work, *Elemente der Psychophysik* (1860)</note> (or chosen by oneself); that is, lift one weight to a given height for 1 second, set it down for 1 second, then after a 1-second interval do the same with the other adjacent weight after having let go of the handle of the first and grasped that of the other with the same hand, and so on. Repeat this double-trial after a 5-second interval, and so on. Despite maintaining these seemingly identical external experimental conditions and despite the objective equality of the weights themselves, one will obtain a very similar irregular change of cases as if one were conducting a corresponding experimental series under the very same normal conditions with two weights that differ by only a little. Now one will appear larger, now the other; now both will appear equal. I have entire large series of trials (so-called <term>Reihen ohne D: "series without D," referring to experiments where the objective difference between two weights is zero</term>) as proof of this.

But does this not speak precisely in favor of Müller? If the external circumstances and the weights remain the same, from where else should the change of cases arise but from internal changes? But patience! After this, under otherwise identical circumstances, lift only the one weight—identical to itself—with one and the same hand, at the same time intervals as before with the two, so that two lifts of the same single weight take the place of the previous lifts of two identical weights. However, do so without letting go of the weight's handle or changing the hand's position or pressure upon it for the entire duration of the trials. In comparing any two such lifts, one will obtain—not exclusively, but far more predominantly than in the previous experimental method—<term>Nullfälle: "null cases," instances where the subject perceives no difference between two stimuli</term>; that is, one will find the difference to be zero or ambiguous. Why? Because the manner of gripping and moving a single weight, held continuously with the same hand and only moved straight up and down, cannot vary in the same way as the transition from one weight to another.

Regarding the interruptions of very weak auditory sensations (such as the ticking of a watch) mentioned above, which he attributes to internal error processes <note>original: "Fehlervorgänge"; accidental internal fluctuations or "noise" within the nervous system that interfere with perception</note>, he says: "Why do these error processes not also cause complete interruptions of strong auditory sensations? If the accidental error processes were dependent on the occurring nerve excitations—specifically, if the magnitudes of $\epsilon$ were proportional to the latter—then obviously strong nerve excitations would also have to be completely extinguished by the accidental error processes from time to time. However, this is not the case at all, precisely because the magnitudes of $\epsilon$ are generally independent of the nerve excitations; they are therefore smaller in comparison to the existing intensity of excitation the larger that intensity is, and accordingly, they are only capable of completely extinguishing very weak nerve excitations."

But Müller completely neglects to consider the circumstance that weak stimuli are close to the threshold <note>the "Schwelle" or point at which a stimulus becomes strong enough to be perceived by the mind</note>, while strong stimuli are far from it; thus, the former can fall below the threshold through the same proportional change, while the latter remain elevated above it. Let us suppose, for example, two impressions, one of which is 10 times as strong as the other. If an error process reduces both proportional to their size by half, then the weak impression (set at 1) is reduced to 1/2, and the other is reduced to 5. The impression of 1/2, however, falls below the threshold—whether that threshold lies at 1, 2, 3, or 4—while the impression of 5 still remains above it. Now, to be sure, Müller, in accordance with his physiological view, does not accept an internal sensory threshold; rather, according to him, even the smallest internal psychophysical <note>ps.-ph.; the relationship between physical stimuli and mental sensations</note> excitation produces a minimal sensation. A weak internal excitation, however, can more easily fall below the mixing threshold than a strong one. Finally, it is sufficient to consider that attention is more easily maintained above the threshold by strong stimuli than by weak ones, in order to explain those facts—which Müller believes can only be explained in the sense of his own view—in a different way.

The manner in which weights are lifted has such an influence on the effect that each weight exerts in producing an internal <term>psychophysical</term> <note>original: "ps.-ph."</note> excitation, as if the weight had been objectively increased or decreased by a certain amount. We call this the "apparent change" of the weight (substantively agreeing with Müller's "random observation error"), while the weight imagined as increased or decreased in this way can itself be called the "apparent weight." Insofar as all parts of a given weight are simultaneously affected by the same influence, the apparent change of the weight can be considered proportional on the one hand to the intensity of the changing influence, and on the other hand to the magnitude of the weight itself. Or, at the very least, this can be assumed hypothetically at first, to be justified later through its consequences. [...proportional to the magnitude] of the weights; from which it follows naturally—given the previous assumption—that the random changes in the internal impressions are themselves proportional to those internal impressions ¹). However, even if we were to follow the physiological view defended by Müller—that a logarithmic relationship rather than simple proportionality exists between the "Internal" and the "External" (to put it briefly)—it would still not result in the independence of random changes from the magnitude of the internal impressions that Müller claims. Instead, rather than simple proportionality, there would merely be a different kind of dependency between them. In our current main inquiry, however, we are concerned with whether there is *any* dependency or non-dependency in this regard at all, rather than the specific mathematical nature of that dependency.

If the internal changes of the impressions were truly independent of their magnitude, then the random changes of the external weights would also have to be independent of their magnitude. One might perhaps charge my previous justification for the proportionality between the two with a lack of rigor, and in a certain sense, that might be conceded. However, if at least an approximate proportionality did not exist between them, then—according to the discussions following under the third main question—it would remain inexplicable for both the physiological and <term>psychophysical</term> <note>The study of the relationship between physical stimuli and the mental sensations they produce</note> interpretations of <term>Weber’s Law</term> <note>original: "Weberschen Gesetzes"; the principle that the perceived change in a stimulus is proportional to the initial intensity of the stimulus</note> how an approximate confirmation of this law could ever be achieved through experiments involving <term>random error processes</term> <note>original: "zufällige Fehlervorgänge"; internal or external fluctuations that create "noise" in scientific measurements</note> and by means of those very processes.

In order to now also take into account the internal random error processes—which undoubtedly are not entirely absent—it must first be noted that although these occur within our organism, they still behave "externally" in relation to the internal impressions derived from the outside world. This is because they are the product of a general organic activity that fluctuates independently of those specific impressions. Here, we shall first address Müller’s own way of representing this by assuming that these fluctuating processes join the internal impressions as modifiers, adding their random **+ e** and **– e** <note>positive and negative error values</note> to them. Everywhere else I see that when *magnitudes*, however they may have arisen—whether through external or internal causes—vary randomly, they generally vary in proportion to their (average) *magnitude*. And how could they not, since having more parts and components also offers more points of attack to both internal and external causes of change? In addition to the *magnitude* itself which varies, the *magnitude* or *range* of the changing causes will also come into consideration, as will the specific susceptibility of the *magnitude* to changes in general. Thus, given the same nature of the *magnitude*, the *magnitude* of the random variation will stand in a composite relationship to this *magnitude* and the changing influences; one must also take into account that if external changing influences do not act upon all parts of the *magnitude* in question with equal strength, only the relevant proportional part of the effect is factored in. This is not merely a matter of rational reflection, but also of such universal experience in the most diverse fields that we can see <term>induction</term> <note>The process of drawing a general conclusion from a set of specific observations.</note> rather than <term>analogy</term> <note>A comparison between two things to highlight a similarity.</note> in it. Thus the wave, although raised by the external wind, fluctuates in dependency not just on the strength of the wind, but also on its own average *magnitude*; the strength of the wind itself, the rumbling of thunder, the height of the fir tree, the *size* of the mouse and the elephant (among various individuals of the same species) all fluctuate in dependency on the one hand on their average *magnitude*, and on the other on the changing causes. Why should it be any different with the random fluctuations of internal impressions?

I do not wish to conceal an objection that might be raised against the previous observation. I can cut a piece off any object without the change it undergoes being proportional to its *size*; and if I strike a billiard ball with a given force, neither the quantity nor the <term>kinetic energy</term> <note>original: "lebendige Kraft"; literally "living force," a historical term for kinetic energy or the capacity of a system to perform work.</note> of the resulting motion will grow proportionally to the mass of the ball. Countless examples of various forms could be cited where our *law of proportionality* fails. But these are all changes in a one-sided direction, the production of which exhausts the effect of a limited force. In our case, however, we are dealing with random changes of direction caused by forces originating from the ongoing <term>kinetic energy</term> of the *whole organism*; and even if the abstract possibility exists that they nevertheless behave regarding the question of proportionality like those former examples—which I cannot *absolutely* refute—one would...

Finally, to the third main question, namely: how *Weber’s Law* is to be related to the actual conditions of random error processes, and whether an advantage for the *psychophysical* or *physiological* interpretation of the law arises from this.

In my opinion, this question is answered as follows: *Weber’s Law* can be stated in the following form: when the difference between two stimuli changes proportionally to the stimuli themselves, the sensation of the difference remains the same. According to this, for example, the difference between stimuli 1 and 2 is felt to be just as great as the difference between 2 and 4, despite the fact that the second difference is twice as large as the first. 

<note>Weber's Law is a fundamental principle in psychology stating that the minimum increase in a stimulus required to produce a noticeable change in sensation is proportional to the original intensity of the stimulus.</note>

Now, provided that the changes in the stimuli caused by random <term>error processes</term> <note>Fechner refers to 'Fehlervorgänge,' which are the unpredictable, random fluctuations in physical stimuli or internal nervous system activity.</note> are proportional to the stimuli, the change in their difference also remains proportional to the stimuli. Thus, the law—insofar as it exists without the random error processes—cannot be altered by them. Consequently, every procedure that involves random error processes can serve to confirm it; indeed, the changes caused by these processes themselves can be used for testing, provided only that the changes in stimuli through random error processes really remain proportional to the stimuli.

Now, the point of view was stated above (p. 34 f.) under which one can understand the occurrence of this proportionality; but it is also admitted that this should not be viewed as strictly certain and that something of a hypothesis still clings to it. Thus, one cannot claim <note>original: "a priori"</note> from the outset that this proportionality is strictly maintained everywhere. Well, insofar as this is not the case, the confirmability of the law through experiments will also suffer; and this may possibly contribute to the empirical deviations from the law in **external psychophysics** <note>The study of the relationship between physical stimuli and the mental sensations they trigger.</note>; conversely, the confirmability of the law within given limits also speaks for the proportionality in question within those limits; and, as already noted above, not even an approximate confirmation of the law could take place if an approximate proportionality did not occur.

This latter consideration seems to me equally valid, whether one accepts the *psychophysical* or *physiological* interpretation of the law (see XII.), and therefore no decision between the two can be found in the conditions of random error processes at all, which would only be the case...

After all this, one might ask what the random <term>error processes</term> <note>German: 'Fehlervorgänge.' They would mean nothing for the sensitivity to differences and could lead to no measurement of it, if their external occurrence were not accompanied by an internal effect, which can be larger or smaller according to the internal conditions of perception; thus, the internal factor of sensitivity to differences also comes into play. Indeed, just as an external stimulus can appear larger or smaller depending on the internal conditions of perception, so too can the changes to which the external stimulus is randomly subjected. This internal factor is always involved in the effect of random error processes. 

Suppose, for example, two individuals, *a* and *b*, whose sensitivity to differences is different due to this internal factor (greater for *a* than for *b*). Meanwhile, it does not contribute to the average error for *a*, which is therefore smaller than for *b*; this proves the greater sensitivity to differences in *a*.

## IV. The Method of Right and Wrong Cases (r. w. c.) Applied to the Measurement of Differential Sensitivity*) from a Practical Viewpoint.

Müller has so completely overturned and remodeled my treatment of the <term>method of right and wrong cases</term> <note>German: *Methode der richtigen und falschen Fälle*. Since it may not be convenient for those interested in the practical application of the method to immerse themselves in a theoretical dispute in order to extract what they need for practice, I have specially compiled the essentials of this latter relationship in this section. I have done so both in the sense of my earlier view—which I will continue to defend—and in the sense of Müller's new view. This may be welcome even to those who might prefer the latter, as Müller himself has not made it particularly easy to follow him in this regard. The next two sections will then go into the reasons that allow me to maintain the second of the above alternatives, while acknowledging the great ingenuity Müller has displayed in his contestation of my work.

The minimum physical difference between two stimuli required for a person to notice that they are different.</note> derived by him; that he rejects my equal division...

### 1) Preliminary remarks on the essentials of the method and the chosen terminology.

Let two stimuli be given, generally designated as **A, B** (in the weight experiments as **P** and **P'**). They can be equal or unequal. In the case of inequality, let **B** be the larger, and the real difference (**U.**) of both be **B — A = D**. If this same difference is observed in repeated cases—let us say **n** times—it will, by virtue of chance occurrences, so-called <term>accidental error processes</term> <note>German: *zufälligen Fehlervorgängen*. These are internal or environmental fluctuations that cause a person's perception to vary even when the physical stimulus remains the same.</note>, appear now larger, now smaller; indeed, if it is not too large, it may occasionally even appear reversed. A case where the larger stimulus **B** actually appears larger, we designate as a right or positive case with **r**; a case where **B** appears smaller than **A**, as a false or negative case with **f**; and a case where a difference (**U.**) seems to be missing or the direction of the difference becomes ambiguous, as a doubtful or null case with **z**. Simultaneously, **r, f, z** will serve to designate the respective number of these cases, so that:

**r + f + z = n** and **r/n + f/n + z/n = 1**; or, if one gives the numbers as percentages of the total number: **r + f + z = 100**.

First, he reminds us that according to **Bohn’s** photometric <note>Photometry is the science of measuring the perceived brightness of light to the human eye.</note> investigations <gloss>1)</gloss>, when comparing two light intensities, one can distinguish cases where very slightly different intensities are not distinguished at all from those where a difference is noticed, but one cannot decide which intensity is the greater. **Boas** <note>Franz Boas (1858–1942), who later became a foundational figure in anthropology, began his career studying the physics and psychology of perception.</note> claims to have made the same observation in photometric observations and corresponding ones in visual estimation experiments; in this regard he says: "When comparing two lines of very little difference in length, one judges them to be equal, or different without being able to decide with certainty on their size relationship, or considers one decidedly longer than the other," and adds: "based on these experiences, it is certainly necessary to generally distinguish two **threshold values**, by assuming that differences smaller than the smaller **threshold value** are not felt at all, while those larger than the smaller but smaller than the larger **threshold value** are felt but cannot be judged. To have a short expression for these values, I designate the smaller **threshold value** as the inner one, and the larger as the outer one, since the positive and negative values of the latter enclose the positive and negative values of the former."

For my part, in my weight-lifting experiments, I have found no occasion to make a definite distinction between equality cases (**zero cases**) and doubtful cases in the sense stated; by which I do not deny that where other observers and other experimental fields offer a reason to distinguish both types of cases, this distinction should indeed be made. That two thresholds should be assumed in that distinction instead of a single mean threshold may be theoretically possible, but practically it is likely of no advantage.

In tactile experiments relating to absolute sensitivity, the majority of experimenters distinguish **zero cases** (so-called false cases) and undecided cases in a different sense than **Boas** does here, though this will not be discussed for now.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the mathematical treatment of observations in psychophysics, specifically how "null cases" (where no difference is perceived) are reconciled with the Gaussian law of errors.</meta>

Each trial case in our method corresponds to a specific magnitude of the difference *D*, which we imagine to be altered by random chance. Similarly, the "null cases" *z* correspond to a whole series of such differences. While these differences have a certain objective magnitude as altered values of *D*, they appear subjectively as null insofar as they fall below the **difference threshold** <note>The "difference threshold" is the smallest change in a physical stimulus that a person can actually detect.</note>. Now, in calculating the values necessary for measuring **sensitivity to differences** <term>U. E.</term> <note>original: "U. E." for *Unterschiedsempfindlichkeit*</note>, both Müller <note>Georg Elias Müller (1850–1934), a pioneer in experimental psychology who refined many of Fechner’s methods.</note> and I will continue to rely on the **Gaussian principle of error probability** <note>Commonly known today as the "Normal Distribution" or "Bell Curve." This mathematical model suggests that small errors are common, while large errors are rare.</note>. However, this principle only recognizes positive and negative deviations (errors), between which lies a "null case" of infinitely small probability. At first glance, it might seem that this law is inapplicable here, since our method generally yields a large number—and in large datasets, a great many—of null cases *z*. But we must remember from the outset that in the calculations we are performing, the law is not applied to the sensations themselves, but to the underlying **apparent differences** between the stimuli that trigger the sensation. As noted, the many "null sensations" provided by our method do not correspond to zero-values of the apparent differences. Rather, according to the **law of the threshold**, small positive and negative apparent differences in the stimuli are simply lumped together as "null values" for the sensation, even though they should be thought of as distributed on either side of a single mathematical zero-point.

The entire interval of apparent differences that appear as null to our sensation is enclosed between two limit values—one positive and one negative difference. For the sake of brevity, and regardless of the mathematical sign of the differences perceived as null (i.e., according to their absolute value), this shall be called the **Total Threshold** 1) and be designated with *T*. We can then say briefly that the **Total Threshold** *T* is the interval of differences into which all *z* (the differences perceived as null) fall. This interval, however, is divided into a section of positive differences, designated with *S,*, and a section of negative differences, designated with *S'* 2), which are perceived as null; thus, it is divided into a positive and negative **Partial Threshold**—

2) I am placing the prime index at the top for the negative section and at the bottom for the positive section because, according to the "Division Principle I" for *z* (which we will consider later), the negative section turns out to be larger than the positive one.

Müller essentially sees in the *S* determined this way the same threshold of difference that one also obtains through the method of J.N.D. <note>J.N.D. stands for "just noticeable differences," or *eben merkliche Unterschiede*.</note> when the size of the difference vanishes (the so-called method of least differences), which can be explained as follows. In this method, let one of two stimuli, *A* and *B*, be fixed and the other variable. If *B* is increased from an initial state of equality with *A* until the difference just begins to become noticeable, then the distance achieved between *A* and *B* will represent the threshold of difference with a positive sign. If, on the other hand, *B* is decreased from the state of equality with *A* until the difference begins to become noticeable, one will have the threshold of difference with a negative sign. The sum of both in absolute value corresponds to our *T* <note>The total threshold.</note>, but it is not the threshold itself; for if one wanted to take the difference between *A* and *B* as equal to the entire *T*, it would far exceed noticeability, since each of the previous one-sided differences already provides the limit that cannot be exceeded without becoming noticeable.

Now, in the method of just noticeable or least differences—aside from a secondary circumstance 1) to be neglected here—there is no reason to view the positive and negative thresholds arrived at in this manner as being of different sizes; and thus Müller, in our current method, also assumes the positive and negative thresholds, into which the total threshold *T* is divided, to be equal. To be sure, it remains to be asked further on whether this reduction of threshold determination from one method to another is permissible given the different conditions of both; however, that does not concern us for the moment, as we are not yet testing the correctness of the various assumptions—

1) This secondary circumstance lies in the fact that the threshold of difference (in absolute value) grows when the stimuli between which the difference exists grow, in that it grows in proportion to the stimuli according to **Weber's Law**. <note>Weber’s Law states that the smallest change in a stimulus that can be detected is a constant proportion of the original stimulus.</note> Thus, the threshold of difference must be larger between the constant *A* and an increased *B* than between the constant *A* and a decreased *B*. However, this difference—which generally amounts to very little—only complicates the question currently occupying us, which is whether, aside from this small difference, the positive and negative thresholds of difference in our method are equal or unequal. ### 2) Purpose of the Method.

I regard the **main purpose** of the method of right and wrong cases <note>Original: *r. u. f. F.*, short for *richtige und falsche Fälle*. This is a classical psychophysical method where a subject compares two stimuli and the researcher records the frequency of "greater," "lesser," or "equal" judgments.</note> to be the determination of a <term>precision measure h or H</term> <note>In 19th-century psychophysics, *h* is a coefficient of precision derived from the Gaussian error distribution. A higher *h* indicates that the subject is more consistent and thus more sensitive to small differences.</note>, which corresponds to the concept of a measure of differential sensitivity (D.S.) <note>Original: *Unterschiedsempfindlichkeit* or *U. E.*</note> based on the viewpoints presented in Section II. I consider the **secondary purpose** to be the determination of the total threshold *T* or its half, the difference threshold *S*, and the product $h \times T$ (to be designated hereafter as *E*), which will be applied later.

For even if *S*, as the difference threshold, might in principle be just as suitable for measuring differential sensitivity as *h*, its determination is only possible with any degree of accuracy from such large series of experiments as are rarely available; it is, in all cases, less reliable than the determination of *h*. Furthermore, in the following section, an objection to the fundamental usability of *S* or *T* as the measure in question will arise.

According to [G.E.] Müller, however, the determination of the difference threshold *S*, or half of *T*, would instead constitute the main purpose of the method; meanwhile, he regards the determination of a precision measure *h*—which differs from ours—as a secondary purpose (p. 21), to which he himself attaches no significance as a measure of differential sensitivity. Müller’s *h* is actually the precision measure of what Müller designates as $\delta$, the random (apparent) changes of the smaller stimulus—that is, in weight experiments, the smaller weight *P*. Our *h* is the precision measure of what is designated as $\alpha$, the random changes of the entire difference *D*, the significance of which for the measurement of differential sensitivity follows from the discussions in both Section II and Section VI.

Henceforth, whenever I introduce the value *h*, I mean it in my sense as the precision measure of $\alpha$, unless noted otherwise. It would undoubtedly have been better if Müller—to avoid confusion and conflation between my *h* and his, the difference in meaning of which could not have escaped him—had introduced a different letter or a distinguishing index for his *h* right away. However, I find no reason to abandon the designation *h*, which I chose first, for the precision measure in my sense. To prevent confusion on my part, however, I shall explicitly refer to Müller’s *h* as "Müller's"...

### 3) Calculation of the Main and Secondary Values Relevant for the Measure of Differential Sensitivity (D.S.) According to Two Different Principles for Dividing the Undecided Cases (z).

The calculation of the main and secondary values at issue here, based on the experimental data, can be carried out according to the two different principles for dividing the undecided cases (*z*) <note>Original: *z* refers to "Zwischenfälle" or undecided/equal judgments where the subject cannot perceive a difference.</note> between the positive and negative sides. I distinguished these on page 46 and designated them as I and II respectively. The first is advocated by me, while the second is advocated by [G.E.] Müller. Although I do not see how the second principle can still be considered valid according to the reasons to be cited in the following section, I will—since some may find the entire question thorny, and because many have already deferred to Müller's authority, and because the invalidity of his principle can only be demonstrated by its consequences—present without argument or theoretical justification how the determination of the relevant values is performed according to each method of division (in my sense and Müller's, respectively). Every reader can then choose between them after weighing the reasons to be discussed in the next section.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of statistical methods in psychophysical measurement. Having previously compared Principle I and Principle II, the author now addresses how to handle "constant errors" (systematic biases) and how to manage data when the frequency of correct responses falls below the level of chance (0.5).</meta>

...mental <note>original: "mental"; likely the conclusion of the word "fundamental" from the previous page</note>, when such [influences], as is generally the case, are present; however, these first require an **elimination of constant errors** <term>constant errors; systematic biases in an experiment, such as a preference for the left side or a tendency to judge the second stimulus as heavier</term> in order to be applied, for which the rules given elsewhere apply. A brief and incidental summary of this follows here.

In order to assume the application of Principle I (with Principle II to be handled analogously), then in the determination of **h** <note>h represents the "measure of precision" in the Gaussian distribution</note>, the value $t_0$ found for the given $\frac{r'}{n}$ is not set equal to h D, but rather $= \text{h (D + c)}$ or h (D $-$ c), where $\pm$ c signifies the **constant error**, which may be positive or negative depending on the circumstances. This $\pm$ c is to be eliminated by conducting two comparable **experimental series**, where c maintains the same magnitude but receives the opposite sign (through opposing spatial or temporal positioning). By adding the values obtained therein, $t_0 = \text{h (D + c)}$ and $t_0 = \text{h (D $-$ c)}$, and dividing by 2, one returns to $t_0 = \text{h D}$ and $\text{h} = \frac{t_0}{D}$. This is the procedure of so-called **complete elimination**.

If two types of constant errors, $\pm$ c and $\pm$ c₁, were present, one would have to conduct 4 experimental series with the opposition of the constant errors, in order to obtain a $t_0$ freed from $\pm$ c and $\pm$ c₁ by summing the four resulting $t_0$ values and dividing by 4; as is detailed further in *Elements of Psychophysics*, Vol. I, page 112 ff., and to which we shall return in Section IX.

### b) Consideration of cases where r or r' is smaller than 0.5.

In the case of the absence of constant errors, with a larger number of trials, one would always find not only $\frac{r'}{n}$ but also $\frac{r}{n}$ to be greater than 0.5, because the constant influence of the positive D (the stimulus difference) across all trials causes the positive cases **r**, and even more so $r' = r + \frac{z}{2}$, to outweigh the remaining cases. <note>In these experiments, 0.5 represents the threshold of chance; a value higher than 0.5 indicates the subject is successfully perceiving the difference.</note> 

However, with a smaller **n** (number of trials) or in the presence of constant errors, the positive D can be outweighed by random error processes or constant errors in a negative direction, and $\frac{r}{n}$ or even $\frac{r'}{n}$ can turn out to be smaller than 0.5. The **Fundamental Table**, however, only contains values of $\odot$ <note>This symbol refers to the probability integral or the frequency of cases</note> that exceed 0.5. Quite generally, if one has to look up the associated **t** for a value of $\odot$ obtained through experiment or calculation that is smaller than 0.5, one should instead look for $1 - \odot$ (consequently, instead of $\frac{r}{n}$, look for $\frac{n - r}{n}$)...

### c) Concerning so-called **failures**, where *h* becomes infinite.

I briefly designate as a **failure** <term>failure; German: *Fehlschlag*. In this statistical context, it refers to a trial series where every response is correct. Because the Gaussian curve only reaches a probability of 1.0 at infinity, such results make the math "break" by producing an infinite value for precision.</term> the case where all *n* trials turn out correctly; thus *r* = *n*. In this instance, $t_o$ and $t_u$, determined in the manner above from the fundamental table, become infinite. Consequently, according to the given formulas, *h* becomes infinite, regardless of whether one applies Principle I or II. However, infinite values for *h* <note>h represents the "measure of precision." A higher h means a more sensitive or "precise" sensory judgment.</note> are not useful. Now, one must not view it as an error in the formulas, but rather in the experiments, that they lead to such failures under certain circumstances. In principle, the formulas only hold for a very large—strictly speaking, infinite—*n*. Presumably, under the conditions for the method’s applicability, one or another false case or null case would always occur if one only increased the number of trials *n* sufficiently. Therefore, generally speaking, one must assume an *n* large enough that false cases still occur; and where it is necessary to treat larger series in fractions, the *n*—which must be kept equal for all fractions—must be large enough that failures are avoided.

If such cases do occur exceptionally, it is always an inconvenience. One cannot exclude the fractions with failures when calculating the entire series without, on the one hand, disturbing the entire calculation system—which is to be built on an equal number of equivalent fractions for every condition being tested—and on the other hand, finding resulting *h*-values that are too small for the condition in which failures occur, since the failures in reality correspond to very large, though not infinite, *h*-values. But what should one substitute into the formulas instead of ∞ for $t_o$ and $t_u$ in such exceptional cases? For the time being, there remains no other choice than to combine the failing fraction with another non-failing one—conducted under as similar circumstances as possible, particularly with the same temporal and spatial positions—into a double *n*, to calculate *h* from this, and then [to use] the same *h* for...

#### a) The question of under which conditions the method is applicable.

In *Studien* <note>Referring to the journal *Philosophische Studien* (Philosophical Studies), founded by Wilhelm Wundt in 1881 as the first journal for experimental psychology.</note>, p. 12, Wundt seeks to specify the conditions under which the method of right and wrong cases <term>right and wrong cases; German: *richtige und falsche (r. u. f.) He concludes his discussions on the matter (*Studien*, p. 14) with the following explanation:

> “According to this, we can briefly summarize the condition for the applicability of the method of right and wrong cases as follows: it is permissible wherever the objective tools for measuring stimulus intensities are far superior in accuracy to our sensation, and where, therefore, the errors committed during the variation of objective stimulus intensities remain vanishingly small compared to the errors of our sensory estimation. In all other cases—and as we have seen, these concern precisely some of the more perfect sensory domains—the method is inapplicable, or, where it might nevertheless be applied, it yields in any case far less accurate results than the method of just noticeable differences.” <note>The "method of just noticeable differences" (*eben merkliche Unterschiede*) involves finding the smallest change in a stimulus that a person can detect.</note>

Meanwhile, I confess that I cannot agree with the viewpoint that is supposed to determine and limit the applicability of our method, for the double reason that I do not find it precise enough myself, and that I find it replaceable by another.

> “Indeed, in a series of important areas of investigation, the difference threshold of sensation seems to roughly coincide with the limit of physical differentiation. <meta>This page continues the transition from technical methodology to the foundational philosophy of psychophysics. Now, from a philosophical perspective, one also seeks a fundamental relationship between both domains to establish a basic distinction, though agreement on this has certainly not yet been reached. Psychophysics, however, does not involve itself in this at all; rather, it focuses merely on the *lawful* relationships or dependency ratios between the two domains of appearance as actually given facts. That such relationships exist between them at all is itself a fact. But the question is: in what way and to what extent do they exist? Depending on whether one views them as permeating both domains entirely or as reaching only to certain limits—and thus only followable by psychophysics up to those points—one can speak of either an unlimited or a limited scope of psychophysics. Philosophers are generally inclined to allow only a limited scope for psychophysics; and since this question interests not only philosophy but also psychophysics itself, the considerations regarding this already found in the **"Elem. d. Ps."** (I. 13 f.) <note>original: "Elem. d. Ps."; referring to Gustav Fechner’s 1860 work *Elemente der Psychophysik* (Elements of Psychophysics), which founded the field.</note> may be partly generalized and partly expanded upon in the following.

Against an unlimited scope of psychophysics in the aforementioned sense, it is often said: Specific lawful dependencies between the soul and body are actually only demonstrable and proven in the sensory domain. A sensation of light is lawfully linked to certain changes in the nervous system; wherever these are present in a living creature, the sensation of light is also present, and vice versa. However, for that which reaches beyond this as *higher* mental activity, a psychophysical representation is neither demonstrable nor conceivable—if, for the sake of brevity, we understand "psychophysical representatives" of the mental to be the physical elements upon whose existence the existence of the mental is lawfully tied, and with whose changes it changes in lawful dependence. The physical element that stands in such a relationship to the mental can then be called the carrier or the foundation of the mental, without designating anything other than this lawful relationship of dependency of one upon the other

insofar into the realm of the bodily and are classified as such by physiology, insofar as they are inferred as determinations of the externally apparent brain from the connection of external appearances and contribute to the completion of this connection; furthermore, as they themselves are imagined under the form of externally apparent processes and would truly appear externally if the obstacles to external observation were removed and the external means of observation could be sufficiently sharpened.

The restriction, common among philosophers, of <term>psychophysical representability<gloss>The theory that every mental state or process has a direct, specific physical counterpart in the body or brain.</gloss></term> to the sensory domain may seem sustainable as long as one moves in general phrases and <term>a priori<gloss>Knowledge that proceeds from theoretical deduction rather than from observation or experience.</gloss></term> conceptual definitions. However, if one looks into the technical details of what, according to common linguistic and conceptual usage, falls into the lower and higher domains, one easily finds that if one grants psychophysical representability to sensory sensations, perceptions, feelings, and impulses—and one does indeed do that—one cannot deny it to the higher spiritual phenomena built upon and above them without giving up a rational connection altogether. Indeed, one can assert a very general principle in this regard, which I established in the *Elements* <note>original: "Elem." refers to Fechner's 1860 work, *Elemente der Psychophysik* (Elements of Psychophysics), the founding text of the field.</note> (Vol. II, p. 370) under the admittedly not very descriptive name of the **Functional Principle**, and I reproduce it here because of the relationship that will be drawn to it several times in the future. It reads:

> "To be sure, we can in no way conclude from the nature of mental movements the nature of the underlying bodily movements—that is, conclude which substrate and which form belongs to these movements—but we certainly *can* conclude that to the mental connection there corresponds a psychophysical connection; to the mental sequence and succession, a psychophysical one; and to the mental strength and weakness, a psychophysical one, insofar as the mental has its foundation in the physical." By "psychophysical" <note>original: *Psychophysisch*</note> we mean here, as always, the physical acting as the foundation of the mental.

It seems that independently of me, **Mach** <note>Ernst Mach (1838–1916), a physicist and philosopher famous for his work on shock waves and his influence on the philosophy of science.</note> (in his treatise "On the Effect of Light Stimuli, etc." in the *Reports of the Vienna Academy*, Volume II) established essentially the same principle and described it as fruitful.

After all, ratios in the physical realm are "higher" than the individual elements underlying them in the same sense that perceived relationships or relational sensations between individual psychic processes are "higher" than the sensations themselves.

One must only be careful not to count ratios that exist between details in the physical realm as belonging to the mental realm simply because they can only be grasped by the mind; for in doing so, one would lose the ground for distinguishing between the two realms at all. Even the physical elements between which these ratios exist must be grasped by our mind to exist for us at all and for us to be able to speak of them; yet, on the basis of this commonality, we distinguish between the externally and internally apparent as two distinct realms. Thus, we must also distinguish their characteristics as belonging to one or the other, rather than mixing or confusing them, as occasionally happens in philosophical circles. In any case, <note>Fechner refers to his own field here: the scientific study of the relationship between stimulus and sensation.</note> psychophysics understands it this way and thus avoids this confusion. Depending on whether something—be it a ratio, a change, a difference, simplicity, composition, and so on—appears as a characteristic of the physical or the psychic, or can be abstracted from one realm or the other, it is assigned to that realm. This is how it is done in both psychology and natural science. Thus, it is indeed possible to find the "higher" in one realm represented by the "higher" in the other, without identifying the two as the same thing. Now, admittedly, not everything considered to belong to the realm of the higher spiritual can be traced back to relationships and connections like those mentioned. Rather, memories grow out of sensory impressions and perceptions—and these are already considered something higher than the sensory phenomena from which they grow. Not only the **Monadologists** <note>followers of Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz’s philosophy, which views the world as made of "monads," or simple, soul-like substances that do not interact physically.</note> but many other philosophers are disinclined to believe that memories are as inextricably tied to material processes as the sensory impressions from which they arose. Instead, they suggest that the soul should be able to reproduce previously held sensations and perceptions through, so to speak, its own **free action**. According to this view, the initial sensations only offer a first occasion, a preparation, or a precondition, whereby the capacity to produce certain memories is planted in the mind. However, the actual production of these memories is then left to the mind itself, according to its own inherent conditions or out of its "free plenitude of power," without further material cooperation. Again, this sounds quite plausible as long as one remains in the realm of the abstract; indeed, one could base an entire psychological system upon it.

Here, I will return only to the general viewpoints on the matter.

The material or physical processes which admittedly underlie our sensory perceptions do not vanish without a trace once the sensation fades. After all, no physical process disappears without some **after-effect** <note>original: "Fortwirkung"; the physical principle that energy or movement is transformed rather than lost.</note>; it may propagate or transform into other processes, but it does not vanish from the world. Thus, the after-effects of the physical processes on which our sensations depend propagate from the centers of the sensory nerves in the brain further into the brain itself. The pathways for this are even visible to our eyes, thereby providing the ground for the linking of corresponding mental after-effects. This causal consideration, however...

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s argument that memories, like direct sensations, are governed by physical laws. He is contrasting the "functional principle"—the idea that mental states correlate to physical brain states—with philosophical views that attribute memory solely to the "free action" of the soul.</meta>

...is supplemented by a related and consistent view according to the **functional principle** <note>The principle that every mental change corresponds to a specific physical change in the brain or nervous system.</note>.

How, then, do memories differ at all from the sensations and perceptions they reproduce? Firstly, memories are weaker; secondly, they are accompanied by the feeling of being generated from within; and thirdly, they carry a sense of being related to the earlier sensations and perceptions upon which they causally depend. All of this, however, is represented quite simply and naturally according to the functional principle. The physical processes underlying memories will likewise be weaker than those underlying direct sensations and perceptions; they will be generated from the internal physical context just as the memories arise from the internal psychological context, and the psychological feeling of causality will be supported by physical causality. In all of this, the logical consistency of the functional principle remains unbroken.

And finally, there are **transitional phenomena** between sensations and perceptions on one hand and memories on the other. These include actual **afterimages**, so-called **memory afterimages**, the phenomena of what is called **sensory memory**, and hallucinations—in short, a series of phenomena that bridge the apparent gap between the initial sensory experiences and the memories of them, as detailed in a specific section of the *Elements* <note>Fechner is referring to his own foundational work, *Elemente der Psychophysik* (Elements of Psychophysics), specifically Volume II, page 467 and following.</note>.

To be sure, a philosopher—in order to avoid diminishing the soul’s "free action"—might imagine and claim that the transmission of physical excitement beyond the sensory centers of the brain and deeper into its interior no longer signifies anything psychological. Furthermore, he need not concern himself with the functional principle, just as he has ignored it until now; he can view those transitional phenomena as mere abnormalities in which the free action of the soul is still mixed with more or less "material ingredients." But one cannot blame the **psychophysicist** <note>A researcher who studies the quantitative relationship between physical stimuli and the sensations they produce.</note> if he prefers to stick to the consistent and coherent paths of knowledge offered by experience and empirical reasoning in this field, rather than following the philosopher who cuts them off.

Now, it may pose difficulties to represent the long-term storage of memories and their undisturbed coexistence up to certain limits, or their emergence from **consciousness** and sinking into the **unconscious** <note>Fechner was one of the first to treat the "unconscious" as a threshold of mental intensity that could be studied scientifically.</note>; but these

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s argument that mental processes like memory cannot be viewed as purely "spiritual" acts of the soul, but must correspond to physical brain activity (the functional principle).</meta>

Difficulties are not yet impossibilities; rather, many paths open up to the imagination—paths that, though currently only hypothetical, harmonize well with what we know—to overcome these difficulties. I will address this in more detail in a later section (XVIII). Simple facts teach us that nature itself has only been able to overcome these difficulties through an extraordinarily complex **brain apparatus** <term>Gehirnapparat: the physical structure of the brain viewed as a biological machine for processing information</term>. Why this immense expenditure of physical effort if the **soul** <note>In Fechner's 19th-century context, "soul" (Seele) refers to the mind or the seat of consciousness, which he argues is inextricably linked to physical processes.</note> has the capacity to produce memories—and everything that follows from them—entirely from within itself once a stimulus is given? Simply ascribing this power to the soul does not mean the soul actually possesses it; the more easily one accepts such an explanation (or rather, avoids any explanation at all by simply "attributing" it), the less weight that explanation carries.

Admittedly, one cannot say that **Herbart’s** <note>Johann Friedrich Herbart (1776–1841) was a philosopher who attempted to use mathematics to describe how "ideas" (Vorstellungen) compete and interact in the mind.</note> **psychological mechanics**, which brings the relationships between memories into its domain, has taken the easy way out. Indeed, it requires a whole series of premises for its construction which I, for my part, find impossible to grant (Compare my *Propaedeutic to Aesthetics*, Vol. II, p. 272 f. <note>original: "Vorsch. d. Aesth.", referring to Fechner’s *Vorschule der Ästhetik*.</note>). But even if one were to grant the possibility of a psychological mechanics *in general*, it would by no means follow that such a system could exist abstractly without the foundation of a **psychophysical** mechanics. One cannot have memories and spin thoughts using mental mechanics alone within a skull that is empty or filled with nothing but a sponge. Indeed, if such a thing were possible at all, a psychological mechanics could only be established and executed as a psychophysical one, because psychological measurement can only be grounded psychophysically, and mental relationships of scale can only be tracked through their physical counterparts.

But let us move even higher than memories; for the mind does not stop at memories as mere reproductions of earlier sensory impressions. Instead, as memories of things earlier and later—memories from one sense meeting those from another—a complex mental play arises from which new and higher results can emerge. Memories provide the material for comparisons, distinctions, concepts, and higher thought operations in general. This material is combined, disassembled, reshaped, and brought into new forms in which higher relationships emerge. Will **psychophysics** <term>Psychophysics: the scientific study of the relationship between physical stimuli and the sensations/perceptions they produce.</term> be able to keep pace with all of this through its physical representations? Well, corresponding operations are not foreign to the physical world either; there are also

If we imagine the entire **psychophysical system** <note>original: "pf.-ph. System"</note> involved in a continuous vibratory process that carries a certain **mental state**—and it is difficult to conceive of any other representation at all—then through the reflection of the entire wave train of these oscillations, or a part of them, back into itself, the spirit of the mental state attached to the first wave train can perceive itself in **self-reflection**.

However, it must be admitted that it would be uncertain and therefore troublesome to go into detail with the pursuit and elaboration of such representations. To do so, the elementary **psychophysical relationships** and **laws** would first have to be developed and established to such an extent that the rest follows partly mathematically and partly according to the functional principle. If, therefore, the philosopher wishes to claim that **psychophysics** remains stuck here regardless, it must at least be conceded that it is still far from its goal.

To the higher spiritual phenomena considered above, **attention** is added as something that people are particularly accustomed to regarding as a purely spiritual matter. A later section, specifically relating to this, will teach that even attention does not escape **psychophysical representability**.

If, after all this, there is no decisive reason in the so-called spiritual heights to limit **psychophysical representability** and thus the scope of **psychophysics**, one might instead look for a limitation deep below. This is done by considering the different basic qualities of **sensory perceptions**, such as **seeing** and **hearing**, to be **psychophysically unrepresentable**; rather, one sees in them something that accrues to the soul purely from within, without the physical excitation contributing anything of its own merit. Indeed, I have encountered a thought of this kind from the philosophical side. Against this, however, it cannot be denied that differently qualified sensory perceptions are awakened by different types of physical stimuli...

The fact that light vibrations are faster than sound vibrations does not, according to the functional principle, lead to attributing the difference between light and sound sensations simply to that speed. For if sound vibrations become faster, the pitch certainly changes, but it remains a sensation of sound. Furthermore, in the progression of the speed of light vibrations through the **spectrum**, qualitative changes occur from red through yellow and green to blue, whereas the scale of sound vibrations shows nothing analogous, and other differences (compiled in *Elements of Psychophysics* <note>original: "Elem." referring to Fechner's *Elemente der Psychophysik*, 1860</note> Vol. II, pp. 270 ff.) occur between these two **sensory domains**, which demand a fundamentally different representation of color and light sensations than that of sound sensations. But what should we think of instead? And finally, what should we think of when sensations of smell, taste, touch, and warmth also want to be represented in their distinctness?

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s defense of the "unlimited scope" of psychophysics.
