...to be assumed for psychophysics. Still, I would wish that some attention were paid to it.

After all the specific considerations I have entered into so far, I come to the most general objection against an unlimited scope of psychophysics. This objection forms the actual background and the root of all philosophical objections, though I will certainly not be able to delve deeply into negotiations regarding it here. The philosopher would have nothing against an unlimited scope of psychophysics in the sense described, if he did not find more general interests endangered by it; and above all, the concern—or even the unhesitating accusation—arises from his side that carrying out <term>psychophysical representation: the theory that every mental process has a corresponding physical process</term> through the entire spiritual realm, without exempting any higher domain, leads to materialism with all its consequences—indeed, that one basically finds the whole cause of materialism within it.

And yet, only someone who considers the materialistic side (which undeniably exists in this implementation) without also taking into account the opposite side can reach that conclusion. That opposite side is the fact that the entire material world is the continuous representation of a universal spiritual being. Psychophysics has never been conceived by me in any other way than through this relationship, and in the final generalization of its principles, it cannot be conceived otherwise. If someone chooses to do so anyway, it is their business and their loss, but not the business or the loss of psychophysics—though, admittedly, it is also not the business of psychophysics to elaborate on this "other side" of itself. Rather, for that purpose, it must be supplemented by other considerations, through which it finally becomes a whole; and one cannot say that I have been lacking in such considerations, even if there is still a lack of those who care to examine them. It is simply not yet the end of the day <note>original: "noch nicht aller Tage Abend"—a German idiom meaning it is not yet too late for a final judgment or for things to change.</note>.

In fact, I find the main defect of the currently prevailing worldview—in all its branches—to be that people do not know how to unite both points of view. I see this as the reason for the discord between religion and natural science, a conflict from which people do not know how to escape. For this is how things stand even today: people are just as unwilling to accept a physical equivalent for everything mental as they are to accept a mental equivalent for everything physical. They only permit an exceptional psychophysical connection between the two within the nervous systems of humans and animals. They see this as the only "knot" that links two otherwise diverging realms, and

Aside from these conclusions, it can be asserted on the very ground of psychophysics itself (“Elements” Vol. II, Section 46) that no fundamental property of <term>psychophysical: relating to the relationship between physical processes and mental experiences</term> movements can be found or conceived within us that would establish an essential difference between them and the movements occurring outside of us. Accordingly, there is no reason why movements beyond our nervous system should not just as well be psychophysical for a more general Spirit, as the movements in our nervous system are for our own spirit, which is thereby merely implanted in a special way into the general spiritual Being. <meta>This page continues Fechner’s discussion on the relationship between the physical and the spiritual. He is addressing potential objections to his theory—specifically the concern that if mental states are tied to physical ones, human free will might be lost to mechanical necessity.</meta>

...this also occurs independently of that. What becomes of human and divine freedom if all spiritual activities, even in their highest realms, are bound to material activities? For they would then also be bound to the necessary causal sequence of those activities.

To this, one must first reply that philosophers themselves still argue whether an "indeterministic" freedom—that is, one that escapes the law of causal sequence—really exists in the spiritual realm. I also believe I showed in Section 16 of the work *The Day View* <note>Original: "Über die Tagesansicht." Fechner’s "Day View" is his philosophy that the entire universe is conscious and alive, as opposed to the "Night View" of a dead, mechanical world.</note> that determinism can perfectly well coexist with religion and morality, provided one understands it in the sense of the Day View, which certainly does not happen according to the prevailing Night View. One can think of the break in the law of causal sequence through freedom as belonging to both realms together. We already do this anyway if we think of the otherwise lawful course of the physical as being altered by free interventions of the spirit—not as a secondary consequence, but as something directly belonging to it.

Indeed, if the spiritual change $\alpha$ is carried by the physical change $a$, and the spiritual change $\beta$ following $\alpha$ is carried by the physical change $b$, then the lawful **causal connection** can be interrupted by freedom both on the spiritual side (between $\alpha$ and $\beta$) and on the corresponding physical side (between $a$ and $b$). Through this, new beginnings can be set in the realm of events on both sides at once, without the psychophysical connection between $\alpha$ and $a$, or $\beta$ and $b$, suffering at all. There is no difficulty in this. Causal connection and the break of causal connection always meet in both realms. To be sure, people are very accustomed to thinking of indeterministic freedom and causal necessity as being divided between the two realms, rather than coinciding in both, based on a prior reasoning <note>original: "a priori"; knowledge that proceeds from theoretical deduction rather than from observation.</note>. But that is simply a begging of the question <note>original: "petitio principii"; a logical fallacy where the conclusion is assumed in the premise.</note> based on habit; and bad habits must eventually come to an end.

Finally, if one wishes to find a theoretical <note>original: "aprioristische"</note> difficulty in the fact that such incomparable phenomena—for example, simple sensations and complex movements like vibrations—should belong together in mutual dependence, then psychophysics itself does not need to worry about the explanation for this, but rather only

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s argument that his psychophysical theory, rather than complicating philosophy, actually resolves the tension between the physical and the spiritual. Thus, that which appears simple to itself internally can appear as complex to the external observer through the multiplicity of relations it develops outwardly—upon which the <term>synechological principle: a concept based on continuity (from the Greek *syneches*), suggesting that the seemingly simple soul is connected to a complex physical system.</term> depends; and that which contributes to a general mental phenomenon within the world-whole, or even just within the individual, may first require a certain strength in order to appear as a distinct phenomenon distinguishable from the general one—upon which the <term>threshold principle: the law that a physical stimulus must reach a certain intensity, or "threshold," before it can be consciously felt.</term> depends.

One consequence of this general basic view—if I may lose one more word on it—is that there can indeed be a pure psychology just as there is a pure physics or general natural science, which concern themselves neither with each other nor with psychophysics. Each of the former considers the world in its context from its particular, respectively inner or outer standpoint; and why should they not be allowed to do so? Only, in the end, none should forget that they are but a one-sided perspective; for which reason a doctrine is still required that links these one-sidednesses. Such a doctrine is <term>psychophysics: the scientific study of the functional relationship between the physical and the mental.</term>.

<meta>This page marks a transition from Fechner’s philosophical defense of his "Identity View" to a technical discussion of experimental methods. Müller regarding how we measure a person's ability to perceive differences.</meta>

# Second Section.

## Psychophysical Principles and Methods of Measurement.

### II. Concept and Measurement of Differential Sensitivity.

A quite fundamental view held by Müller—one that forms, so to speak, the guiding thread through his entire critique of the methods of measuring <term>differential sensitivity: the ability of a person to detect the smallest possible difference between two stimuli, such as two weights or two lights (German: *Unterschiedsempfindlichkeit* or U. E.).</term>, but which is also most fateful for this critique—is this: that only the reciprocal value of the <term>differential threshold: the minimum amount of change in a stimulus required for a person to notice a difference (German: *Unterschiedsschwelle* or U. Schw.).</term>, designated by him as **S**, should count as the measure of differential sensitivity; that is, the difference which must first be exceeded so that the difference (**D.**) is recognized as such. 

Any value other than **S** that one might wish to use for this measure—whether directly or by its reciprocal value—be it the <term>average error: a statistical measure of how much individual trials deviate from the average result (German: *mittlere Fehler* or m. F.).</term> of the method of average error, or the difference that yields a given ratio of right, wrong, and doubtful cases (**r, w, d**) <note>The original uses "r, f, z" for *richtigen, falschen, und zweifelhaften Fälle*.</note> in the <term>method of right and wrong cases: an experimental setup where a subject must judge whether a second stimulus is greater, smaller, or equal to a first.</term>, or the measure of precision derived from this ratio, is only useful as a measure of differential sensitivity to the extent that its direct or inverse proportionality to the differential threshold has been proven, and then only by virtue of this proportionality or reciprocity and as far as it extends. This proportionality, however, is [according to Müller] not at all self-evident; and not only has no theoretical or empirical proof been provided by me or anyone else, but no investigation into it has even been undertaken. According to this view, everything that has hitherto been based on the assumption of such proportionality—specifically the formulation of <term>Weber’s Law: a historical psychological principle stating that the just-noticeable difference between two stimuli is proportional to the magnitude of the stimuli.</term>, insofar as it rests upon it—completely lacks a secure foundation.

The primary passage in which Müller expresses this view, along with the reasons upon which he bases it, is this (p. 2).

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s technical response to G. E. Müller. On the previous page, Fechner introduced Müller’s specific definition of differential sensitivity—that it should only be measured by the "threshold." Here, Fechner quotes Müller directly before beginning his counter-argument, arguing that sensitivity exists for all differences, not just the smallest detectable one.</meta>

> “We generally define <term>differential sensitivity (U.E.): the ability of a subject to detect a difference between two stimuli.</term> as the reciprocal of the magnitude of that stimulus difference which, under given experimental conditions, possesses a certain degree of noticeability. The only question remains as to which specific degree of noticeability of stimulus difference is most suitable to serve as the basis for the measure of differential sensitivity. . . . . Without doubt, the only difference whose noticeability is—at least in principle—an exactly fixable magnitude and exactly reproducible by different observers, must be considered that which only needs to be decreased by the smallest amount to become just unnoticeable, or which only needs the smallest increase to become noticeable. We therefore generally define the differential sensitivity as the reciprocal of the magnitude of the <term>just noticeable stimulus difference: the smallest change in a stimulus that a person can detect (German: *eben merklicher Reizunterschied*).</term>, which appears to differ from the just unnoticeable difference only by an infinitesimal amount.”

Thus, Müller himself proceeds from essentially the same general definition of the measure of differential sensitivity that I gave in the <note>original: "Elem." refers to Fechner’s 1860 foundational work, *Elemente der Psychophysik* (Elements of Psychophysics).</note> "Elements" Vol. I, p. 47, and which I will subject to an even more definite explanation below (p. 23); however, he believes that for the reasons he added, he must restrict it in the manner stated.

Against this, one can remark from the outset that since Müller wishes to use only a single magnitude out of all possible difference magnitudes—the <term>differential threshold (U. Schw.): the point at which a difference is first perceived.</term>—as the measure of differential sensitivity, it follows that this measure can fundamentally only be applied to this one single difference. In fact, it follows that if two thresholds $S, S_1$ are found for two given states of sensitivity, it does not follow <note>original: *a priori*, meaning "from the start" or "by logic alone."</note> automatically that two differences $D, D_1$ above the threshold, which relate to each other as $S$ relates to $S_1$, appear equally distinct. Müller does not seem to have considered that this requirement is necessary to justify the general significance he ascribes to the differential threshold, as nothing regarding this can be found in his work. 

Yet there are, after all, differences both above and below the threshold, and there exists a differential sensitivity regarding these differences for which a measure can be requested just as rightfully as for the sensitivity regarding the threshold difference itself. Now, we certainly have no practical means of determining the differential sensitivity regarding individual specific differences above and below the threshold in the same way we have for the threshold itself via the <term>method of just noticeable differences: an experimental procedure where the stimulus is changed until the observer first notices a difference (German: *Methode der e. m. U.*).</term>; however, we do have the means to determine it regarding the average values above and below, for which the <term>methods of right and wrong cases: an experimental setup where subjects judge whether a difference exists across many trials, used to calculate statistical probability (German: *Methoden der r. u.*).</term>

<meta>This page continues Gustav Theodor Fechner’s rebuttal to Georg Elias Müller. Fechner is defending his "Methods of Constant Stimuli" and "Average Error" against Müller’s assertion that only the "Threshold" (the smallest detectable difference) is a valid measure of sensitivity.</meta>

<note>original: "r. u. f. F. und m. F." refers to the *Methode der richtigen und falschen Fälle* (Method of Right and Wrong Cases) and the *Methode der mittleren Fehler* (Method of Mean Error).</note> Method of Right and Wrong Cases and the Method of Mean Error are present. Through the measure-values of <term>differential sensitivity (U.E.): the ability to distinguish between two slightly different stimuli</term>, which can be obtained by means of these methods—the **measure of precision** and the **mean error**—the measure-value gained via the <term>difference threshold (U. Schw.): the point at which a difference becomes just barely noticeable</term> is fundamentally completed, as these other measures extend over the remaining part of the scale of difference.

Thus, I can find no rational motive for Müller's requirement that every value other than the difference threshold must prove its proportionality (or reciprocity) with said threshold to prove its usefulness as a measure of differential sensitivity. One could just as well—indeed, perhaps with even more right—demand the opposite of the difference threshold regarding the measures that go above and below it, because the threshold provides only one very specific measurement. Even if the required proportionality did not occur, or did not occur consistently, one would not have to reject one or the other of these scales. Instead, one should simply apply each within its proper limits; one should not demand that one scale base its validity on how well it conforms to the other.

The actual reason that led Müller to restrict the measure of differential sensitivity to the difference threshold can only be found, in my view, in the way he understood and handled the Method of Right and Wrong Cases and the Method of Mean Error. He could not recognize the significance of the **measure of precision** and the **mean error** as scales for differential sensitivity. Consequently, nothing remained for him but to reduce the measure of sensitivity to the threshold. However, these methods are to be understood and handled differently than he has done, for which the later sections should be compared, where I come to the discussion of these methods.

Müller argues for the preference of the difference threshold value as a measure of sensitivity (according to its reciprocal value) by stating, "that it is the only stimulus difference whose noticeability is, at least in principle, an exactly fixable magnitude that can be exactly reproduced by different observers." This may hold true in a certain sense as **individual values**; but the point is not to determine differential sensitivity regarding a single difference value. I do not see why a certain ratio of right, wrong, and doubtful cases in the Method of Right and Wrong Cases, or a certain mean error in the Method of Mean Error, should not—in principle—be just as well-regarded as an exactly fixable degree of noticeability (or distance from noticeability) that can be identically reproduced by different observers.

If the law were restricted solely to its relationship with the <term>Difference Threshold (U. <meta>This page continues Fechner’s technical defense of his psychophysical methods against G. E. Müller. Fechner is clarifying how "Difference Sensitivity" (U. E.) is defined and calculated, specifically addressing how it applies to trials where differences are too small to be noticed (below the threshold).</meta>

The <term>Difference Sensitivity (U. E.): the capacity to perceive differences between stimuli</term> cannot be measured absolutely, but only comparatively. I generally define it as the reciprocal <note>original: "reciprok"; the mathematical inverse (1/x)</note> of the objective magnitude of the stimulus change or stimulus difference which, in the cases being compared, produces an equally noticeable, equally distinct subjective impression; one that is felt to be equally large, appears equivalent to the sensation, is recognized with equal ease, or can be substituted for another without the impression of magnitude changing. These are all merely different expressions for what is essentially the same thing.

At first glance, of course, this explanation seems to apply only to the <term>Difference Sensitivity (U. E.)</term> regarding differences *above* the <term>threshold (Schw.): the point at which a stimulus change is just barely perceptible</term>. However, in the <term>Method of Mean Errors (m. F.): an experimental procedure where a subject attempts to match a comparison stimulus to a standard, and the average inaccuracy is measured</term>, one observes only errors—differences *below* the threshold—since one intentionally brings such differences down below the threshold. In this case, errors of very different sizes produce the same impression of a "missing difference." But this simply means that one cannot judge the <term>Difference Sensitivity (U. E.)</term> here by a single difference below the threshold, but rather by the sum or the average of the differences that fall below the threshold during a large number of comparable trials, by setting the <term>Difference Sensitivity (U. E.)</term> proportional to the reciprocal value of that average. Furthermore, this explanation is entirely consistent with the explanation regarding cases above the threshold; for in cases both below and above the threshold, we set the <term>Difference Sensitivity (U. E.)</term> as the reciprocal of differences that appear equal in size. Because there are many various differences below the threshold that equally appear to be "missing," we use the total sum (given an equal number of trials) or the average of those differences which can be obtained through the <term>Method of Mean Errors (m. F.)</term>. To achieve this, the method must, of course, be carried out differently than Müller partly describes through misunderstanding and partly prescribes incorrectly—a matter to be addressed in Section VII.

Accordingly, to the explanation that <term>Difference Sensitivity (U. E.)</term> is the reciprocal of differences that are recognized with equal ease (i.e., with equal probability) across a majority of comparable trials, we can add another definition connected to the general concept: it is the reciprocal of the differences that are equally easily *misperceived*. These are the estimation errors one commits when judging magnitudes of a given kind as being equal; such errors are precisely what we obtain by means of the <term>Method of Mean Errors (m. F.)</term>.

While the measure of <term>Difference Sensitivity (U. E.)</term> via the <term>Method of Mean Errors (m. F.)</term> subordinates itself to the general principle of measurement regarding these errors in the manner just described, the measure regarding...

Thus, according to our <term>Measurement Principle (Maßprincip): the fundamental rule used to assign numerical values to sensations</term>, the sensitivity in these two different states must be set as reciprocal <note>original: "reciprok"; the mathematical inverse (1/x)</note> to the differences (D) that yield the same result—that is, the same r, f, z. ## III. On the So-Called Accidental Error Processes.

In the methods of Right and Wrong Cases as well as that of <term>Average Errors: a method where a subject adjusts a stimulus until it matches a standard, and the variation in their attempts is measured</term>, what Müller calls "accidental error processes"—often referred to by me simply as "accidental occurrences"—exert a great influence on the results; this is less the case with the Method of Just Noticeable Differences, although they are not entirely absent there either. What I was able to say about this in the "Elements" <note>original: "Elementen"; referring to Fechner’s seminal 1860 work, *Elemente der Psychophysik*</note> (Vol. I, p. 76 ff.) is essentially contained in the following remarks.

> “In all three methods, irregular accidental occurrences play a major role, which partly cling to the manipulations <note>refers to the physical handling of experimental equipment</note> and partly lie grounded in the subjective conditions of the perception of the compared magnitudes. . . . If the manipulation changes in any way during the experiments, a different interplay of accidental occurrences immediately begins, and the measurements cease to be comparable; likewise, because of possible changes in internal conditions among different individuals, one cannot assume the same latitude for these accidental occurrences.”

Now, Müller is right in a certain sense when he says (p. 335), while partially reproducing the previous passage, that I had “unfortunately not addressed” the question of “what kind of random error processes are involved in the perception of a given sensory stimulus”; at the very least, I did not go as far into it as one could have, or as far as he himself has gone. I simply did not know more than the generalities above when I wrote the <note>original: "Elementen"; referring to Fechner's 1860 *Elements of Psychophysics*, the founding text of the field</note>, and I believed at the time that I had given enough consideration to what was necessary for the measurement methods. However, it is to Müller’s credit that he examined the nature of these processes more specifically, and it would be even more so if he had also answered them convincingly; which I cannot quite concede. Specifically, there are three main questions at stake:

**First**, are the random error processes that play a role in the measurement experiments primarily internal or external, in the sense of the distinction to be made later in this regard?

**Second**, are the changes that the magnitude of <term>psycho-physical (ps.-ph.) excitations: the neural or mental activity triggered by a physical stimulus</term> undergoes due to random error processes independent of this magnitude, or dependent on it—specifically, proportional to it?

**Third**, how is <term>Weber’s Law: the principle that the smallest detectable change in a stimulus is a constant proportion of the original stimulus</term> to be related to the actual conditions of the random error processes, and does this perhaps offer an advantage for one interpretation of this law over another?

On none of these points, however, can I agree with Müller, based on the following considerations.

As far as the first point is concerned, generally speaking, neither Müller nor I deny that the random error processes in the experiments can be both internal and external; however, while I, for my part, in the “Elements”...

> "According to the above, little contradiction should be expected against the assumption that the random error processes, under whose influence our perception of given sensory stimuli falls, are processes taking place within our organism that influence the intensities of existing sensory nerve excitations—for example, random fluctuations in excitability, irregular influences of blood flow, unpredictable effects of the states of excitation present in various parts of the central organ upon one another, and the like."

Regarding the second question, according to *Müller* (p. 346): "the effect of the random error processes occurring in the nervous system is entirely independent of the intensity of the nerve excitation caused by the sensory stimulus to be perceived." *Müller's* reasons for this, along with my counterarguments, will follow further on.

Finally, thirdly, based on the previous determinations and the factual reciprocity of the <term>U. Schw. (Unterschiedsschwelle): the difference threshold, or the smallest detectable difference between two stimuli</term> with the precision measure, *Müller* finds only the physiological interpretation of <term>Weber’s Law: a historical principle stating that the change in a stimulus that will be just noticeable is a constant ratio of the original stimulus</term> to be admissible.

To address the first point of inquiry now, I oppose *Müller’s* decision—that the random error processes playing a role in the experiments are internal rather than external—with the following remarks.

Factually, it is found that the random changes in the impression of stimuli, which we attribute to random error processes, vanish to the same extent as the external causes of those processes vanish in the relevant experiments. In this respect, a comparison is particularly instructive between the weight experiments—conducted using the <term>method of r. u. f. F. (richtige und falsche Fälle): the "Method of Right and Wrong Cases," where a subject judges which of two stimuli is greater</term>—and the shadow experiments, conducted using the <term>method of e. m. U. (eben merkliche Unterschiede): the "Method of Just Noticeable Differences," where a stimulus is adjusted until a change is detected</term>. Both were performed in the well-known manner for testing *Weber's* Law. In the weight experiments, the play of random error processes asserts itself in the most striking way, as the resulting correct, incorrect, and doubtful cases alternate in such an irregular manner that <term>Gauss's Law: the "Normal Distribution" or bell curve, used here to describe the statistical distribution of human errors in judgment</term> of random deviations applies to them; however, there is no lack of external causes to which this—

If one conducts a single-handed series of trials with two identical weights under the normal conditions specified in my <note>Fechner refers here to his 1860 foundational work, *Elements of Psychophysics*.</note> "Elements" (or conditions chosen by oneself)—that is, lift one weight to a given height for 1 second, set it down for 1 second, then after a 1-second interval do the same with the other weight standing next to it, having released the handle of the first and grasped the second with the same hand in the meantime, and so on; repeating this double-trial after a 5-second interval—then, despite maintaining these apparently identical external conditions and despite the objective equality of the weights themselves, one will obtain a very similar irregular alternation of outcomes as if one were conducting a corresponding series of trials under the same normal conditions with two slightly different weights. But not so fast!

Following this, under otherwise identical circumstances, lift only *one* weight—which is identical to itself—with the same hand, at the same time intervals as before for the two weights. Thus, two lifts of the same weight take the place of the previous lifts of two identical weights, but *without* letting go of the handle or changing the hand's position or pressure upon it throughout the duration of the trials. In comparing every two such lifts, one will find—not exclusively, but far more predominantly than in the previous method—<term>null cases: results where the subject perceives no difference, or the difference is ambiguous</term>. Why? Because the manner of gripping and moving the one weight, held continuously with the same hand and moved only straight up and down, cannot change in the same way as occurs with two weights when transitioning from one to the other.

We cannot, of course, look *directly* into the brain; thus, a *direct* decision on the matter is not possible, though we must seek points of reference in experience. The only thing, however, that I find asserted by *Müller* in this regard is the following:

With reference to the previously discussed interruptions of very weak auditory sensations (when listening to the ticking of a watch) caused by what he assumes to be internal "error processes," he says:

> “Why do those error processes not also cause complete *intermissions* <note>original: *Intermissionen*; meaning temporary cessations or interruptions.</note> of strong auditory sensations? Apparently, those interruptions of very weak sensory sensations occur because the [internal] *negative excitation increment*—$\epsilon$—corresponding to the present error process is, according to its absolute value, greater than or at least equal to the *nerve excitation* caused by the sensory stimulus, and consequently extinguishes it entirely. Now, if the accidental error processes were *dependent* on the occurring nerve excitations, and specifically if the magnitudes of $\epsilon$ were *proportional* to the latter, then strong nerve excitations would clearly also have to be completely extinguishable by the accidental error processes at times. But this is by no means the case, precisely because the magnitudes of $\epsilon$ are generally *independent* of the nerve excitations, and therefore are smaller in comparison to the existing *excitation intensity* the larger it is, and accordingly are only capable of completely extinguishing very weak nerve excitations.”

But *Müller* entirely neglects to consider the circumstance that weak stimuli are near the **threshold** <term>The "Schwelle" or threshold is the minimum level of stimulus intensity required for a sensation to be consciously perceived.</term>, while strong ones are far from it; thus, the former can fall below the threshold through the same proportional change under which the latter remain elevated above it. Let us assume, for example, two impressions, one of which is 10 times stronger than the other; if both are **reduced** <note>original: *reducirt*</note> to half their size by an error process, the weak one (set at 1) falls to 1/2, while the other falls to 5. The impression of 1/2, however, falls below the *threshold*, whether that threshold lies at 1, 2, 3, or 4, while the impression of 5 still remains above it. Now, to be sure, *Müller*, in accordance with his physiological view, does not recognize an internal **sensation threshold** <term>Empfindungsschwelle: The point at which internal neural activity becomes strong enough to be felt as a sensation.</term>; rather, according to him, even the smallest internal **ps.-ph.** <term>Short for "psychophysical," referring to the relationship between physical stimuli and mental sensations.</term> excitation already produces a smallest sensation. But it is precisely the internal *sensation threshold* that is at issue regarding the internal impressions we have in mind here. <meta>This page continues Gustav Fechner’s rebuttal of G.E. Müller’s views on sensory thresholds. ...to exchange them more logically (§. XII.) <note>Fechner frequently refers to specific sections (§) of his earlier works or arguments.</note>. Taking into account the undeniable **mixture threshold** (§. XV.) accomplishes the same thing as considering the simple **sensation threshold**. As long as a person is awake, they are always occupied in some way by a play of stimuli acting from both without and within; for a stimulus to be perceived as **distinct**, it must first exceed a certain limit of strength—the **mixture threshold**—in order to stand out as discernibly special from the mixture of other stimuli. A weak internal excitation can more easily fall below the mixture threshold than a strong one. Finally, it is enough to consider that attention is maintained above the threshold more easily by strong stimuli than by weak ones, in order to explain those facts that Müller believes can only be explained through his own view.

Apart from the previous empirical reason, Müller (p. 343) generally finds it "difficult to see how the positive and negative increments of the occurring nerve excitation, which correspond to the accidental error processes, should be dependent on—and indeed proportional to—the intensity of this nerve excitation, since their cause lies not in the nerve excitation evoked from without, but in other internal conditions."

But, of course, the matter appears differently—indeed, the opposite—if the accidental error processes are external rather than internal. Let us illustrate this more closely with the weight-lifting experiments.

The way in which weights are lifted has such an influence on the effect that each weight exerts in producing an internal <term>psychophysical</term> <note>Fechner uses the abbreviation "ps.-ph." for psychophysical, referring to the relationship between physical stimuli and mental sensations.</note> excitation, as if the weight had been objectively increased or decreased by a certain amount. We call this the **apparent change** of the weight (which corresponds in substance to Müller's "accidental observation error"), while the weight that is perceived as increased or decreased can itself be called the **apparent** weight. Insofar as all parts of a given weight are simultaneously affected by the same influence, the apparent change of that weight can be considered proportional, on the one hand, to the intensity of the changing influence and, on the other hand, to the magnitude of the weight itself. At the very least, this can be assumed hypothetically at first, to be justified later by its consequences. According to this, however, it is simplest to assume—and this is done in the sense of the <term>psychophysical</term> view I represent—that the internal <term>psychophysical</term> impressions made by the weights are proportional to the weights themselves, and the accidental changes of these impressions are proportional to the accidental changes...

Fechner is arguing that random fluctuations in how we perceive weights (what he calls "accidental error processes") must be proportional to the size of the weights themselves. This proportionality is essential for Weber’s Law—the rule that we notice relative changes rather than absolute ones—to hold true in scientific experiments.</meta>

...of the weights proceed proportionally; from which, under the previous assumption, it follows naturally that the accidental changes of the internal impressions <note>original: "inneren Eindrücke," referring to the neural or mental representation of a stimulus</note> proceed proportionally to the internal impressions themselves ^1). However, even if—in the sense of the physiological view advocated by Müller—a logarithmic dependence rather than proportionality existed between the "internal" and "external" (to put it briefly), the independence of the accidental changes of internal impressions from their magnitude, as asserted by Müller, would still not occur. Instead, another kind of dependence would simply exist in place of simple proportionality. But regarding the current primary question, it is a matter of dependence or non-dependence in this respect in general, rather than a specific type of dependence.

If the internal changes of impressions were independent of their size, then the accidental changes of the external weights would also have to be independent of their size. One might certainly raise the charge of a lack of rigor against the above justification for proportionality between the two, and in a certain sense admit it; but if at least an approximate proportionality did not exist between them, then, according to the discussions following the third main question, it would remain just as inexplicable for the physiological as for the psychophysical interpretation of **Weber’s Law** <term>Weber's Law: The rule that the smallest change in a stimulus that can be detected is a constant proportion of the stimulus itself (e.g., adding 1 ounce to 10 feels like adding 1 pound to 10 pounds)</term> how an approximate confirmation of this law could even come about through experiments with accidental error processes <note>Random variations in judgment or neural firing</note> and by means of those processes themselves.

To now also take into account the internal accidental error processes, which undoubtedly are not entirely absent, it must first be noted that although they occur within our organism, they behave "externally" to the internal impressions originating from the outside world. This is because they are a matter of a general organic activity that fluctuates independently of these impressions. We shall first address Müller's own way of conceiving this by assuming that these fluctuating processes join the internal impressions as modifications, adding their accidental **+ e** and **- e** <note>These represent positive and negative "error" values—random increases or decreases in the perceived intensity</note>. Regardless, however, of whether one wishes to grasp these processes as internal or external from one point of view or another, the following general consideration seems to me applicable to them.

--- Page 109 ---
<meta>This page continues Fechner’s argument for the law of proportionality in sensory perception. On the previous page, he argued that if internal mental impressions do not scale proportionally with physical stimuli, Weber’s Law would be mathematically impossible. Here, he provides broader scientific and natural justifications for why variations in any system are typically proportional to the size of that system.</meta>

<page-num>36</page-num>

In every other instance I observe that when *magnitudes*, however they may have arisen—whether through external or internal reasons—vary randomly, they generally vary in dependence on their (average) size; specifically, they vary proportionally to it. And how could they not, provided that more parts and moments <note>original: "Momente," here referring to constituent factors or elements of a physical or mental state</note> also offer more points of attack to the internal and external causes of change. In addition to the magnitude itself which varies, the magnitude—the scope—of the changing causes will also come into consideration, as well as the specific receptivity of the magnitude for changes in general. Thus, given the same nature of the magnitude, the size of the random *variation* will stand in a composite relationship to this magnitude and the changing influences—taking into account that if external changing influences do not act with equal strength on all parts of the magnitude in question, only the relevant proportional part of the effect is considered. This is not only a matter of rational consideration, but also of such universal experience in the most diverse fields that we can see it as *induction* <note>The process of deriving a general rule from specific observations</note> rather than mere *analogy*. Thus, a *wave*, although raised by external winds, fluctuates in dependence not just on the *strength of the wind*, but also on its own average size; the strength of the wind itself, the *rumbling of thunder*, the *height of the fir tree*, the *size of the mouse* and of the *elephant* (in their various individual specimens) all fluctuate in dependence on their average size on one hand, and the changing causes on the other; why should it be any different with the random *fluctuations of internal impressions*?

I do not wish to conceal an objection that could be raised against the previous consideration. I can cut a piece off any body without the change it undergoes being proportional to its size, and if I strike a billiard ball with a given force, neither the quantity nor the living force <term>living force: (vis viva) a historical term for kinetic energy or the energy of motion within a physical system</term> of the movement resulting from it will grow proportionally to the mass of the ball; countless examples of such various forms could be cited where our *law of proportionality* fails. But these are all changes in a one-sided direction, in the production of which the effect of a limited force is exhausted; in our case, however, we are dealing with random changes of direction caused by forces that stem from the persistent living force of the *total organism*; and even if the abstract possibility exists that they nevertheless behave like those others regarding the question of proportionality—which I cannot absolutely refute, I would know...

<page-num>37</page-num>

...I find no analogous example in nature to the contrary, so that in any case, a high degree of probability remains for our consideration.

Finally, we come to the third main question: namely, how <term>Weber's Law<note>A fundamental principle in psychophysics stating that the minimum change in a stimulus that can be detected is a constant ratio of the original stimulus</note></term> is to be related to the actual conditions of random error processes, and whether an advantage for the psychophysical or physiological interpretation of the law might arise from this.

In my view, this question is answered as follows. Weber's Law can be stated in the following form: if the difference between two stimuli changes proportionally to the stimuli, the perception of that difference remains the same. According to this, for example, the difference between stimuli 1 and 2 is perceived as being just as great as the difference between 2 and 4, despite the fact that the second difference is twice as large as the first.

Now, as long as the changes in stimuli caused by random error processes are proportional to the stimuli themselves, the change in their difference also remains proportional to the stimuli. Thus, the law—insofar as it exists without the random error processes—cannot be altered by them. Consequently, any procedure that entails random error processes can serve to validate the law; indeed, the changes caused by these processes themselves can even be used for testing, provided only that the changes in stimuli through random error processes really do remain proportional to the stimuli.

The viewpoint under which one can understand the realization of this proportionality was stated above (p. 34 f.); but it is also admitted that this should not be regarded as strict and that something of a hypothesis still clings to it. Accordingly, one cannot claim <term>from the outset<note>original: "a priori"</note></term> that this proportionality is strictly maintained everywhere. Indeed, insofar as this is not the case, the confirmability of the law through experiments will also suffer; and this may possibly contribute to the empirical deviations from the law in <term>outer psychophysics<note>The study of the relationship between physical stimuli (like light or sound) and the mental sensations they produce</note></term>. Conversely, the confirmability of the law within given limits also speaks for the relevant proportionality within those limits; and, as noted above, not even an approximate validation of the law could take place if an approximate proportionality did not exist.

This last consideration seems equally valid to me, whether one accepts the psychophysical or physiological interpretation of the law (see section XII). Thus, no decision between the two can be found at all within the conditions of random error processes—which would only be the case

After all this, one may ask what the random error processes—and the errors or apparent deviations caused by them, insofar as they are external (which they are for the most part)—mean for **sensitivity to differences**, and to what extent they are considered in its measurement. They would mean nothing for **sensitivity to differences** and could lead to no measure of it if their external occurrence were not combined with an effect on the internal state. This internal effect can be larger or smaller depending on the internal conditions of perception, whereby the **internal factor of sensitivity to differences** comes into play. Indeed, just as an external stimulus can appear larger or smaller according to the internal conditions of perception, so too can the changes to which the external stimulus is randomly subject. This internal factor always plays a part in the effect of random error processes. Suppose, for example, two individuals, *a* and *b*, for whom the **sensitivity to differences** is different due to this internal factor (greater for *a* than for *b*). If they perform externally comparable experiments according to the **method of average errors**, and the **normal distance N** is the same for both, and the external random error processes are the same, a small change in **N** caused by external randomness will result. Or, what is equivalent, a small difference in the **error distance f** from the **normal distance N** is obtained under the influence of randomness. This difference, which is already noticeable for *a*, will not yet be noticeable for *b*; it will still fall below the <term>threshold<note>The 'Schwelle' or threshold refers to the minimum amount of stimulus change required for a difference to be perceived.</note></term>. Consequently, it will contribute to the magnitude of the **average error**, which depends only on the deviations between **f** and **N** that fall below the threshold. However, it does not contribute to the average error for *a*, which is therefore smaller than for *b*, thus proving the greater **sensitivity to differences of a**.

Regarding the **method of right and wrong cases**, within the limits of **Weber's Law**, the ratio *r*, *f*, *z* and therefore the value *hD* (with which this ratio is connected) remains the same if both stimuli change in the same proportion. Simultaneously, their **difference D** changes in this same proportion, which entails that *h* <note>The 'measure of precision' in Fechner’s formulas.</note> changes in inverse proportion to **D**. Even where **Weber's Law** does not strictly apply, if the stimuli change in the same proportion, *h* decreases as **D** grows, and vice versa. ## IV. The Method of Right and Wrong Cases (r. and w. c.) Applied to the Measurement of Sensitivity to Differences*) from a Practical Perspective.

<term>Müller<note>Georg Elias Müller (1850–1934), a prominent German experimental psychologist who published a rigorous critique of Fechner’s mathematical methods in 1878.</note></term> has so completely overturned and remodeled my treatment of the <term>Method of Right and Wrong Cases<note>Original: "Methode der richtigen und falschen Fälle." Since a person interested in the practical application of the method may not find it convenient to immerse themselves in a theoretical dispute just to extract what they need for practice, I have specially compiled the essentials in this section. I have done so from the perspective of both my earlier view—which I will continue to defend—and Müller's new view. This may be welcome even to those who might prefer the latter, as Müller himself has not made it particularly easy to follow his reasoning in this regard. ### 1) Preliminary remarks on the essentials of the method and the chosen designations.

Let two stimuli be given, generally designated as A and B (in weight-lifting experiments as P and P'). They can be equal or unequal. In the case of inequality, let B be the larger, and the real difference (D) between the two be B — A = D. Now, if this same difference is observed in repeated cases—let us say *n* times—it will, by virtue of chance occurrences (so-called random error processes), appear sometimes larger and sometimes smaller; indeed, if it is not too large, it can sometimes even appear to be reversed. A case where the larger stimulus B actually appears larger, we designate as **right** or **positive** with *r*; a case where B appears smaller than A, we designate as **false** or **negative** with *f*; and a case where a difference seems to be missing or the direction of the difference becomes ambiguous, we designate as **doubtful** or a **null case** with *z*. At the same time, *r*, *f*, and *z* will serve as the respective designations for the number of these cases, so that r + f + z = n and r/n + f/n + z/n = 1; or, if the numbers are given as percentages of the total number: r + f + z = 100.

F.* (richtigen und falschen Fälle). A standard psychophysical procedure where a subject compares two stimuli and reports which is greater.</note></term> not merely right, false, and doubtful or equality cases, but right, false, doubtful **a n d**

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion on how "null cases" (instances where no difference is perceived between two stimuli) are handled mathematically. It bridges the gap between raw experimental data and the Gaussian probability models used to analyze them.</meta>

Each <term>experimental trial</term> <note>original: "Versuchsfall"; a single instance or trial in a psychophysical experiment.</note> of the method corresponds to a specific magnitude of the difference *D*, which is imagined to be modified by accidental factors. Similarly, the <term>null cases</term> <note>responses where the subject perceives the stimuli as equal; denoted as *z*</note> correspond to a whole range of such differences. While these differences have a certain objective magnitude—viewed as modified values of *D*—they appear subjectively as zero insofar as they fall below the <term>difference threshold</term> <note>The "Unterschiedsschwelle" is the minimum difference between two stimuli required for a subject to detect that they are different.</note>. Now, in calculating the values necessary for measuring sensory sensitivity, Müller <note>Georg Elias Müller (1850–1934), a prominent German experimental psychologist.</note> and I will continue to base our work on the <term>Gaussian principle of error probability</term> <note>Commonly known today as the Normal Distribution or Bell Curve.</note>. However, this principle only recognizes positive and negative deviations (errors), between which lies a "null case" of infinitely small probability. Because of this, it might initially seem that this law is inapplicable, as our method generally yields a plurality—and in a large total number of cases, many—null cases *z*.

But it must be remembered from the outset that in the calculations we are to perform, the law is applied not to the sensations themselves, but to the underlying *apparent differences* between the stimuli that result in sensation. As noted, the many "zero sensations" provided by the method do not correspond to zero values of the apparent differences. Instead, according to the <term>law of the threshold</term> <note>The principle that a stimulus must reach a certain intensity to be perceived at all.</note>, small positive and negative apparent differences of the stimuli simply merge into zero values for the sensation, while the differences themselves are to be thought of as distributed on either side of a single mathematical zero value.

The entire interval of apparent differences that appear as zero to the sensation is enclosed between two limit values—one positive and one negative difference. For the sake of brevity, and regardless of the mathematical sign of the differences felt as zero (i.e., according to their absolute value), this shall be called the ***total threshold*** <margin>1) This designation is newly introduced here, but will be convenient for what follows.</margin> and designated with *T*. We can thus say briefly that the total threshold *T* is the interval of differences into which all *z* (the differences perceived as zero) fall. ->$r' + f' = n$<-

Namely, the negative threshold $S'$ is larger in absolute value than the positive threshold $S$. However, one could also conceive of a different division method where both partial thresholds $S$ and $S'$ are assumed to be equal. This approach implies that the $z$ cases are distributed *unequally* between them. This method was adopted by Müller and shall hereafter be designated as **II** $^1$).

Müller considers the *S* determined in this way to be fundamentally the same <term>difference threshold</term> <note>Original: *Unterschiedsschwelle*. The minimum detectable difference between two stimuli.</note> that one also obtains through the <term>method of J.N.D.</term> <note>Abbreviation for *eben merkliche Unterschiede*, or "just noticeable differences."</note> when the magnitude of the difference vanishes (the so-called method of smallest differences). This can be explained as follows: Suppose that in this method, of the two stimuli *A* and *B*, one is assumed to be fixed and the other variable. If *B* is increased from an initial equality with *A* until the difference (*U.*) just begins to be noticeable, then the distance reached between *A* and *B* will provide the difference threshold with a positive sign. If, on the other hand, *B* is decreased from the point of equality with *A* until the difference begins to be noticeable, then we will have the difference threshold with a negative sign. The sum of both according to their absolute value corresponds to our *T* <note>The "total threshold."</note>, but it is not the threshold itself; for if one were to take the difference between *A* and *B* as equal to the entire *T*, it would far exceed noticeability, since the difference that cannot be exceeded without becoming noticeable is already given by each of the previous one-sided differences. Now, in the method of just noticeable or smallest differences—aside from an ancillary circumstance <gloss>1)</gloss> to be neglected here—there is no reason to regard the positive and negative thresholds obtained in this way as being of different magnitudes. Thus, in our current method, Müller also assumes that the positive and negative thresholds into which the total threshold *T* is divided are equal. To be sure, it will still be a question later on whether this reduction of the threshold determination from one method to another is permissible given the different conditions of both; however, that does not concern us for the moment, as we are not yet judging the correctness of the various assumptions.

1) This <term>ancillary circumstance</term> <note>Original: *Nebenumstand*.</note> lies in the fact that the difference threshold (according to its absolute value) grows as the stimuli between which the difference exists grow, in that it increases in proportion to the stimuli according to <term>Weber’s Law</term> <note>The principle that the perceived change in a stimulus is proportional to the initial intensity of the stimulus.</note>. Therefore, the difference threshold must be larger between the constant *A* and the increased *B* than between the constant *A* and the decreased *B*. Meanwhile, this difference—which generally amounts to very little—only complicates the question currently occupying us, which is whether, setting aside this small difference, the positive and negative difference thresholds in our method are equal or unequal. Indeed, Müller also abstracts from the ancillary circumstance in question. In the transition to the logarithmic treatment of the method, which will be discussed in a later section (X), the difference in question disappears entirely.

## 2) Purpose of the Method.

I regard the primary purpose of the <term>method of right and wrong cases</term> <note>Original: *r. u. f. F.* (richtige und falsche Fälle). A foundational psychophysical technique now often called the Method of Constant Stimuli, used to determine how often a subject correctly identifies a difference between stimuli.</note> to be the determination of a **measure of precision** *h* or *H*. This measure corresponds to the concept of a **measure of differential sensitivity** <note>Original: *Unterschiedsempfindlichkeit* (U.E.). The ability to perceive small differences between two stimuli.</note> based on the perspectives provided in Section II. I consider the secondary purpose to be the determination of the **total threshold** *T* or its half, the **difference threshold** *S*, and the product *h T* (to be designated as *E* in the future), which will be applied later.

For even if *S*, as the difference threshold, might in principle be just as suitable for a measure of differential sensitivity as *h*, its determination is only possible with some degree of accuracy from such large series of experiments as are rarely available; in all cases, it is of lower reliability than the determination of *h*. Furthermore, in the following section, an objection will arise against the fundamental applicability of *S* or *T* for the measure in question.

According to Müller, however, the determination of the difference threshold *S*, or half of *T*, would constitute the primary purpose of the method; meanwhile, he considers the determination of a measure of precision *h*—distinct from ours—to be a secondary purpose (p. 21), to which he himself attaches no significance as a measure of differential sensitivity. Specifically, Müller's *h* is the measure of precision of the random (apparent) changes in the smaller stimulus—designated by Müller as δ—which, in weight experiments, refers to the smaller weight *P*. Our *h* is the measure of precision of the random changes of the entire difference *D*—designated as α—the significance of which for the measure of differential sensitivity follows from the discussions in Sections II and VI.

Henceforth, wherever I introduce the value *h*, I intend it (unless otherwise noted) in my sense as the measure of precision of α. Undoubtedly, it would have been well-advised if Müller—to avoid confusion and bewilderment between my *h* and his, the difference in meaning of which surely could not have escaped him—had immediately introduced another letter for his *h* or distinguished it with a subscript. However, I find no reason to abandon the designation *h*, which I chose first, for the measure of precision in my sense. To prevent confusion on my part, however, I shall explicitly designate the Müllerian *h* as such...

### 3) Calculation of the Primary and Secondary Values relevant for the measure of Differential Sensitivity according to two different principles of dividing the *z*.

The calculation of the primary and secondary values in question—derived from the experimental data as previously discussed—can be performed according to two different principles for dividing the *z* <note>In psychophysical experiments, 'z' refers to "doubtful" or "undecided" cases where the subject cannot determine a difference between two stimuli.</note> between the positive and negative sides. I distinguished these on page 46 and designated them as I and II respectively; the first is advocated by me, and the second by Müller. Although I do not see how the second can still be considered tenable—based on the reasons to be cited in the following section—I nonetheless intend to set forth how the determination of the relevant values is presented according to one or the other mode of division (in my sense and Müller's respectively). I do this without initial dispute or theoretical justification because the entire question can be considered thorny, and many have already deferred to Müller’s authority; furthermore, the untenability of his principle can only be demonstrated through its consequences. Anyone may then choose between them after weighing the reasons to be discussed in the following section.

In this regard, it should be noted that the following formulas for both Principle I and II are directly applicable only to the case where $\frac{r}{n} > \frac{1}{2}$ <note>Where 'r' is the number of right cases and 'n' is the total number of trials; this refers to instances where the subject is correct more than half the time.</note>; however, they can also be made applicable to the case where $\frac{r}{n} < \frac{1}{2}$ through a simple change of sign, following a rule to be given later under 4) b).

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of psychophysical calculations, specifically addressing how to handle systematic biases (constant errors) and what to do when experimental results fall below the 50% probability threshold. It refers to "Principle I" and "Principle II" established on the previous page.</meta>

...experimental, when such errors—as is generally the case—are present; they first require an elimination of the constant errors <term>Conſtante Fehler: Systematic biases or "constant errors," such as a subject’s tendency to always think the second weight is heavier, regardless of the truth.</term> in order to be applied, for which the rules given elsewhere apply. Here is a brief and incidental note on this.

To assume the application of I (with which one proceeds analogously for II), then in the determination of *h* <note>The "measure of precision," indicating how consistent or sensitive a subject's responses are.</note>, the value *t*₀ found for the given *r'*/ *n* is not equal to *h D*, but is rather to be set as *t*₀ = *h (D + c)* or *t*₀ = *h (D — c)*, where ± *c* signifies the constant error, which may be positive or negative depending on the circumstances. This ± *c* is to be eliminated by conducting two otherwise comparable series of trials, where *c* maintains the same magnitude but receives the opposite sign (through reversed spatial or temporal positioning <note>For example, if a constant error is caused by the "left-hand side," the experimenter repeats the test on the "right-hand side" to cancel it out.</note>). By adding the values obtained therein, *t*₀ = *h (D + c)* and *t*₀ = *h (D — c)*, and dividing by 2, one returns to *t*₀ = *h D* and *h* = *t*₀ / *D*. This is the procedure of so-called complete elimination. If two kinds of constant errors, ± *c* and ± *c'*, were present, one would have to conduct 4 series of trials with the opposition of the constant errors to obtain a *t*₀ freed from ± *c* and ± *c'* by summing the four *t*₀ obtained and dividing by 4; as is detailed in *Elements [of Psychophysics]* Volume I, page 112 ff., and to which we shall return in Section IX.

### b) Consideration of cases where *r* or *r'* is smaller than 0.5.

In the absence of constant errors, with a larger number of trials, one would always find not only *r'* / *n* but also *r* / *n* to be greater than 0.5, because the constant influence of the positive *D* <note>The objective difference between two stimuli.</note> in all trials causes the positive cases *r* (and even more so *r'* = *r* + *z*/2) to outweigh the remaining cases. But with a smaller *n* <note>The total number of observations.</note> or in the presence of constant errors, the positive *D* can be outweighed by random error processes or constant errors in a negative direction, and *r* / *n* or even *r'* / *n* may turn out to be smaller than 0.5. However, the fundamental table <term>Fundamentaltabelle: A standardized mathematical table (based on the normal distribution) used to convert the percentage of correct answers into a statistical value.</term> contains only values of $\Theta$, which exceed 0.5. Quite generally, if one must find the corresponding *t* for a $\Theta$ obtained through experiment or calculation that is smaller than 0.5, one should look for 1 — $\Theta$ instead (and thus (*n* — *r*) / *n* instead of *r* / *n*)...

### c) On so-called "misfires," where *h* becomes infinite.

I use the term "misfire" <term>Fehlschlag: Literally a "failure" or "miss." In statistics, this refers to an experimental run where every single answer is correct ($r = n$). While this seems like a perfect result, it causes the mathematical formula for the "measure of precision" ($h$) to break, as it results in an "infinite" value that cannot be used for further calculations.</term> to briefly describe the case where all *n* trials turn out correctly—that is, *r = n*. In such a case, the values *t₀* and *tII* (determined from the Fundamental Table as described above) become infinite. Consequently, according to the given formulas, the measure of precision *h* <note>A variable representing the subject's sensitivity or consistency.</note> becomes infinite, whether one applies Principle I or II. However, infinite values of *h* are not useful.

One should not view this as a flaw in the formulas, but rather as a limitation of the trials themselves. The formulas are theoretically valid only for a very large—strictly speaking, infinite—number of trials (*n*). It is likely that under the conditions where this method is applicable at all, one or another incorrect or "null" case would always occur if the number of trials (*n*) were sufficiently increased. Generally speaking, one must therefore assume a value for *n* large enough that incorrect cases still occur. When it is necessary to handle larger series in "fractions" <term>Fractionen: Sub-groups or batches of trials within a larger experiment.</term>, one should keep *n* large enough and consistent across all fractions to avoid these misfires.

If such misfires do occur exceptionally, it is always a nuisance. One cannot simply exclude the batches with misfires when calculating the entire series; doing so would disrupt the calculation system (which must be built on an equal number of equal-sized batches for every condition being tested). Furthermore, excluding them would lead to finding resulting *h*-values that are too small, since these misfires actually correspond to very large (just not infinite) real values of *h*. What, then, should be substituted in these exceptional cases for $\infty$ in the formulas for *t₀* and *tII*? For the time being, there may be no other choice than to combine the "failed" batch with another non-failing batch conducted under the most similar circumstances possible—specifically the same temporal and spatial positions <note>The order and physical placement of the stimuli, which can influence results through bias.</note>—to form a double-sized *n*. From this, one calculates *h*, and then applies that same *h* for...

### 5) Discussions with Wundt regarding various points concerning the application and utilization of the method.

#### a) Question regarding the conditions under which the method is usable.

In *Studies* <note>Referring to Wilhelm Wundt’s foundational journal, *Philosophische Studien* (Philosophical Studies), specifically page 12 of the cited volume.</note> Wundt attempts to specify the conditions under which the Method of Right and Wrong Cases <note>original: "Methode der r. u. f. Fälle" (richtige und falsche Fälle). A procedure where a participant compares two stimuli and the researcher records the proportion of correct versus incorrect judgments.</note> is applicable and where it is not—or at least where it cannot be used with advantage. He concludes his discussion on this (page 14) with the following declaration:

> "We can accordingly summarize the condition for the applicability of the Method of Right and Wrong Cases <term>Method of Right and Wrong Cases: Also known today as the "Method of Constant Stimuli." It is a mathematical way to determine a person's sensitivity by seeing how often they correctly identify a difference between two nearly identical objects.</term> by stating that it is permissible wherever the objective tools for measuring stimulus intensities are far superior in precision to our sensation, and where the errors made in varying the objective stimulus intensities therefore remain vanishingly small compared to the errors in our estimation of sensation. In all other cases—and as we have seen, these concern some of the more refined sensory domains—the method is inapplicable, or, where it should nonetheless be applied, it certainly yields far less accurate results than the Method of Just Noticeable Differences <term>Method of Just Noticeable Differences: A method where the researcher changes a stimulus by tiny increments until the subject says, "I feel it" or "it changed."</term>."

However, I must confess that I cannot agree with the viewpoint that is supposed to determine and limit the applicability of our method, for two reasons: I do not find the viewpoint itself precise enough, and I believe it can be replaced by another.

Regarding the former, I ask myself how the reliability or precision of subjective estimation should even be compared with the reliability or precision of objective measurement in this respect; I could only find a starting point for this in the following explanation by the author (*Studies* p. 12, 13).

> "Indeed, in a series of important areas of investigation, the difference threshold <term>Difference threshold: The minimum amount of change in a stimulus (like light or sound) required for a person to detect that a change has occurred.</term> of sensation seems to coincide approximately with the limit of physical differentiation. This is the case with the discrimination of light intensities, pitch, temperatures near the skin's own heat, and finally under certain experimental conditions..."

...conditions even in the discrimination of time intervals. For light intensities, pitch differences, and temperature sensations, until now only the method of just noticeable differences—and in some cases the so-called method of supra-threshold differences—has been applied. This has happened, I believe, at least partly for the good reason that the <note>original: "Methode d. r. u. f. F."</note> Method of Right and Wrong Cases <note>A classic psychophysical procedure where a subject compares two stimuli and the researcher records the frequency of correct versus incorrect judgments to determine sensitivity.</note> becomes generally unusable here. > "Our measure of sensation is so certain here that we can state with the greatest certainty the moment when the two shadows compared with one another become unequal; previously they appear equal to us; and therefore there is no opportunity for recording right and wrong cases."

If I am not mistaken, according to this, when comparing subjective and objective accuracy—to use these terms for the sake of brevity—it would depend on whether the smallest still physically measurable difference exceeds or fails to reach the magnitude of the <term>Difference Threshold: The minimum amount of change in a stimulus required for a person to detect that a change has occurred (original: "U. But this point of view lacks definiteness insofar as the difference threshold grows with the magnitude of the stimuli, without the smallest physically measurable difference changing its magnitude. Thus, one only needs to choose the stimuli introduced into the method as small or large enough to find either the subjective estimation or the objective measure at an advantage according to this principle of comparison. Furthermore, I would not want to admit that in the shadow experiments cited by <term>Wundt</term> <note>Wilhelm Wundt (1832–1920), often called the "father of experimental psychology."</note>, we are able to "state with the greatest certainty the moment where the two compared shadows become unequal," since the fact of the difference threshold itself consists in—and can be established in these experiments—the fact that we are *not* able to do so. Only the point where the <term>Difference Threshold</term> is crossed can be stated with relative certainty; but that is not what matters here.

Accordingly, I can only seek the reason why shadow experiments lack the opportunity for recording right and wrong cases—which is indeed the case—in a circumstance other than the one asserted by the <term>Author: Referring here to Wundt, whose work is being critiqued.</term>. Specifically, regardless of the subjective sensitivity of the estimation, I find the reason in the fact that between the components of the difference, there are no temporal, spatial, or external movement factors intervening—as there are, for example, in experiments with weights—and that therefore the accidental error processes, which could give rise to such cases that essentially belong to the method, are eliminated.

### b) On the role of the precision measure.

Regarding the remark by *Wundt* (*Studies p. 8*), that the <term>Precision Measure: A statistical value (often denoted as *h*) derived from the Method of Right and Wrong Cases that indicates the consistency or "sharpness" of a subject's sensory discrimination (original: "Präcisionsmaß")</term> to be derived from experiments according to the <term>Method of Right and Wrong Cases: A procedure where a subject compares two stimuli and the frequency of correct versus incorrect judgments is recorded to determine sensitivity (original: "Methode d. r. u. f. ### c) On the dependence of null cases on the knowing and unknowing procedure and the choice between both.

*Wundt* raises (*Studies p. 17*) an objection against the <term>Knowing Procedure: An experimental setup where the subject is aware of the nature or direction of the stimuli differences beforehand (original: "wissentliche Verfahren")</term> maintained during my weight experiments according to the Method of Right and Wrong Cases. His objection is from the perspective that the estimation of doubtful or <term>Null Cases: Instances where the subject cannot perceive a difference between two stimuli and reports "equal" or "undecided" (original: "Nullfälle")</term> might be altered by it. Specifically, if one knows that both weights—or more generally, stimuli—to which one is subjected are unequal, then because of this knowledge, one will more easily estimate them as unequal than if one did not know it. Consequently, the doubtful cases would lose their correct relationship to the other cases, which requires impartiality of observation. Now, *Vierordt* <note>Karl von Vierordt (1818–1884), a physiologist known for his work on the sense of touch and blood flow.</note> has already, in the tactile experiments conducted under his direction according to the Method of Right and Wrong Cases, where it was a matter of...

Camerer’s earlier published tactile experiments prove it. Indeed, <term>Wundt</term> <note>Wilhelm Wundt (1832–1920), often called the "father of experimental psychology."</note> is quite right in his suspicion that by including <term>catch trials</term> <note>original: "Vexirversuche"; these are "trick" trials where no difference between stimuli exists, used to see if a participant is just guessing.</note>, the ratio of **r**, **f**, and **z** <note>These represent results: **r** for right (*richtig*), **f** for false (*falsch*), and **z** for doubtful/uncertain (*zweifelhaft*).</note> must change; however, it changes for the worse. This is because it also grows due to the <term>influence of contrast</term>, much like when one performs trials with a large **D** after or between those with a smaller **D**. Since **D = 0** is the smallest possible distance, its inclusion—the catch trial—acts most strongly in this regard. In short, by inserting catch trials into the main trials, one introduces a complication for which no method of <term>elimination</term> <note>Meaning a way to mathematically cancel out the bias.</note> has yet been found. Finally, the fact that in the **knowing procedure**, one can dispense with the help of an assistant and keep the methodical arrangement of the trials entirely in one's own hands, gives this procedure a decided external advantage over the **unknowing** one. Indeed, such an arrangement is generally not easily successful except in the knowing procedure. If an assistant were to carry out the trials with such methodical variety and sequence of circumstances—as well as an equal number of trials for each specific circumstance—as is necessary for the comparability of the trial fractions and the elimination of <term>constant errors</term>, the unknowing procedure would become <gloss>pointless</gloss> because the subject of the experiment would easily guess what one intended to hide from their knowledge.

### d) Question regarding the most practical D to be applied.

When applying our method, the question arises as to what difference **D** one should use between the stimuli subjected to the experiment. For example, what **additional weight D** should be added to the **main weight P** in weight-lifting experiments to create the larger weight **P' = P + D**? Naturally, one will avoid a **D** that is too small, where both weights would be nearly identical and, regardless of constant errors, the **r** (right) cases would turn out almost equal to the **f** (false) cases. Likewise, one avoids a **D** that is too large, where all cases would turn out correctly, because both scenarios evade the principle of the method. Now, while there is a certain range within which one is not bound to a specific ratio of **D** to **P**, one may still ask whether a certain ratio deserves to be preferred in practice over others, insofar as the goals

->$\frac{r'}{n} = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}} \int_0^{t = h D} e^{-t^2} \partial t$<-
