->$\frac{\partial r'}{n} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}} e^{-t^2} \partial t,$<-

->$\frac{\partial t}{t \partial r'} = \frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{n t e^{-t^2}}$<-

### V. On the Utilization of Doubtful or Zero Cases *z* in the Method of Right and Wrong Cases.

When conducting many trials to determine a physical value, one can obtain a majority of occurring zero errors <note>original: *Nullfehler*; refers to trials where no difference is perceived or recorded</note> simply because one cannot distinguish very small differences—between the object being measured and the divisions of the scale—from zero deviations. Even though these differences actually exist, the **threshold law** <note>the *Schwellengesetz*; the principle that a stimulus must reach a certain intensity to be consciously perceived</note> applies here just as it does in psychophysical experiments. And so it would seem most natural from the outset to do the same regarding the zero cases occurring there when applying the Gaussian Law to our field of observation; that is, to divide the deviations corresponding to them equally between both sides, in the sense of the Division Principle I discussed in the previous section. And indeed, this is how I handled it in the "Elements" <note>original: "Elementen"; referring to Fechner’s seminal 1860 work, *Elemente der Psychophysik* (Elements of Psychophysics)</note>. Indeed, I confess that I had not even considered that it could be done otherwise, and even now, after reasons for doubt in this regard have arisen, I still consider this equal division to be correct based on the following considerations.

However, the transferability of what is indisputably valid for zero cases in errors of observation to the zero cases of our method is really not self-evident. Errors of observation are random deviations from a single magnitude underlying the observation (for which one takes the mean of the observed magnitudes); on the other hand, in our method, there are two magnitudes, A and B, which are subject to random deviations, and from which the random deviations of their difference, D, are only then composed, which can bring other viewpoints into play. And thus, the validity of my equal division of the *z* <note>Representing the "zero" or "doubtful" cases where a subject cannot distinguish between two stimuli</note> toward both sides has been contested by Müller <note>Georg Elias Müller (1850–1934), a contemporary psychologist who critiqued Fechner's methods</note>, who instead proceeds from the principle that the difference threshold <note>The smallest difference between two stimuli that a person can detect</note> on the positive side must be taken as equal to the difference threshold on the negative side in the <term>method of right and wrong cases</term> <note>original: "Methode der r. u. f. F." (richtige und falsche Fälle); a technique where subjects judge which of two stimuli is heavier, louder, etc.</note>, just as in the <term>method of average error</term> <note>original: "Methode der e. m. U." (eben merkliche Unterschiede/mittlere Unsicherheit); a technique where subjects adjust a stimulus until it feels equal to a standard</note>. Moreover, he felt no more need to justify his principle than I did; he includes it in his formulas as if it were self-evident. Both principles—that of the equal division of *z*, designated by me as I in the previous section, and that of the equality of the threshold on both sides, designated by me as II—are, according to a remark made earlier, incompatible with each other. It follows mathematically that with an equal division of *z* toward both sides, the total threshold divides unequally toward both sides; conversely, with an equal division of the threshold toward both sides, the equal division of *z* cannot exist.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion on how to categorize and mathematically process neutral or "zero" responses in psychophysical experiments, emphasizing that empirical sensation must guide the math, rather than forcing the data to fit a preconceived formula.</meta>

...or positive, negative, and null cases according to the testimony of sensation; we must therefore base our calculations and formulas on this testimony, rather than vice versa, to avoid committing a *logical reversal* <note>original: *Hysteron Proteron*; a logical fallacy where that which should come second is put first, effectively "putting the cart before the horse."</note>. This testimony, however, does not directly reveal magnitudes but only the numbers of positive and negative difference-sensations, between which the null-sensations are to be considered divided. This is done in accordance with the principle discussed in § 41 f., in order to be able to think of the underlying apparent differences as divided into positive and negative, as is necessary for the application of *Gauss's Law* <note>The Gaussian or "Normal" distribution, often called the "bell curve," which describes how random variables are distributed.</note>. According to the testimony of the sensation itself, there is simply no reason to regard a *null sensation* as +0 rather than -0; and if a computational need arises to consider such sensations as distributed toward both sides, the division should be carried out according to equal probability or number. The corresponding division of the apparent differences should be thought of as belonging to both sides, and only then should we ask how the magnitudes of these differences on one side and the other behave under the subordination of *Gauss's Law*.

When one speaks of positive and negative difference-sensations, this can occur in various senses. A few words should be said about this to avoid confusion between the different interpretations, as only one of them will be valid in the following. Suppose a difference of a certain magnitude exists between B and A, where B > A, or conversely A < B; the difference can be taken indifferently as B — A or A — B—that is, as either positive or negative. In the first case, one keeps in mind that B is larger than A; in the second, that A is smaller than B, and this can be transferred to the sensations of difference. However, as long as we only consider the absolute magnitude of the difference ± (B — A) as well as its sensation (for which this arbitrary distinction signifies nothing), and designate it as positive as is customary with absolute magnitudes, a negative value of the difference as well as of its sensation can only signify an *impossible value* of one or the other. It is in this sense that the negative sign appears in the <term>difference-measurement formula</term> <note>original: *Unterschiedsmaßformel*; the mathematical rule used to quantify the perceived difference between two stimuli.</note> for sensations of difference *below the threshold* <note>original: *unter der Schwelle*; referring to stimuli too weak to be consciously perceived.</note>. Finally, from a third point of view, in the case of actually existing sensations of difference, we can distinguish between their directions. A difference between A and B, in which B appears larger than A, can be transformed through real or apparent changes into one in which A now appears larger than B; as the real or apparent reversal of the actual difference occurs, the direction of the sensation of difference also reverses. In this third sense, *opposing difference-sensations* are understood here.

The following remark may also be appropriate here. A sensation of difference of zero is not to be confused with a null sensation in general, but rather as the negation of the sensation of a difference between two sensations...

...distinguished from the negation of a simple sensation. To be sure, one can say that zero, as zero, is everywhere equal to itself; yet it is not equal in all its relationships, just as, for example, "no apple" is something different from "no money."

An objection may be raised against the previous *a priori* <note>Latin: "from the former"—referring to knowledge derived from theoretical deduction rather than empirical observation.</note> consideration: that the equality of the threshold on both sides is itself *a priori* necessary, and the mode of distribution of the *z* [values] to both sides should be derived as a consequence of this, rather than being taken as an *a priori* starting point. And it must be admitted from the outset that our principle comes into apparent conflict with a way of looking at things previously established (p. 47 f.), which can indeed claim to be *a priori*. Before going into this more closely, we will return to it with a clear, visual way of imagining it that simplifies the consideration.

Let the difference *D* between two stimuli <note>original: *Reizen*; singular *Reiz*. In psychophysics, a stimulus is an external energy or physical change that triggers a sensation.</note> *A* and *B* be represented by a distance between two points. If we disregard the absolute magnitude of the stimuli—which is irrelevant to the consideration occupying us here—and consider only the change in their difference, that is, the distance *D*, then this change will be represented by a relative movement of the points toward and away from each other. In the sense of a well-known fiction, we can think of one stimulus, let us say *A*, as fixed, and only the other, *B*, as movable, by transferring any movements of *A* onto *B* in the opposite direction. The equality of both stimuli will be represented as a "vanished difference" by a coincidence of *B* with *A*; and based on this, the <term>difference threshold</term> <note>The minimum amount of change in a stimulus required for a person to detect that a change has occurred.</note> will be determined by the <term>method of just noticeable differences</term> <note>A technique where a stimulus is gradually changed until the participant can just perceive that it is different from a standard.</note> as follows:

Starting from the case of equality, where *B* coincides with *A*, if we imagine *B* moving away from *A* first in one direction and then in the opposite direction, this can occur up to a certain distance, respectively $S_1$ and $S'$, from *A*, before the deviation becomes noticeable. $S_1$ and $S'$ then represent the difference threshold toward the one and the other side respectively—let us say the positive and negative—insofar as we distinguish the direction of both movements from *A*. Apart from the incidental circumstance mentioned on p. 47, which is disregarded here, no reason can indeed be found *a priori* why $S_1$ should be different from $S'$. In the <term>method of right and wrong cases</term> <note>original: *Methode der r. u. f. F.* (*richtigen und falschen Fälle*). An experimental procedure where a subject compares two stimuli and the researcher records the frequency of correct, incorrect, and undecided judgments.</note>, the starting conditions are of course different from the outset. *B* does not coincide from the outset with...

This advantage might seem insignificant; however, when one has to combine the results from many <term>fractions</term><note>Subsets or segments of a larger data set.</note> to determine a definitive $h$—as can become necessary in large experimental series—it indeed becomes quite significant.

If one were to use $S = \frac{T}{2}$, the advantage of looking things up less frequently in the <term>fundamental table</term><note>A table of values for the normal distribution, used to convert experimental frequencies into precision measures.</note> would indeed fall to Principle II. **Secondly**, generally speaking, according to Principle I, one can divide a large series of experiments into smaller <term>fractions</term><note>Sub-groups or segments of the data set treated separately to see how results vary over time.</note> to be treated individually than is possible with Principle II. Furthermore, in Principle I, one can introduce larger differences $D$ into the experiment than in II; both of these advantages exist because Principle II leads more easily to "breakdowns" (in the sense stated on page 54) when dealing with small fractions or large values of $D$. Indeed, in series—or in specific fractions of series—where there are no "false cases" at all, and therefore $r + z = n$ <note>Meaning the "right" and "doubtful" cases equal the total number of trials.</note>, one obtains an infinite value for $t_{II}$ (which is used in the formula for $h$ under Principle II). This results in an infinite value for $h$. In contrast, $t_{II}$ is not used in the formula for Principle I; instead, only the value $t_0$ (belonging to $r + \frac{z}{2}$) is used, which is itself finite and yields a finite $h$. Thus, under Principle I, a breakdown in the determination of $h$ can only occur if both false cases ($f$) and doubtful cases ($z$) are absent—that is, when $r = n$.

Finally, I come to show that the ratios of the <term>measurement values</term> $h$ and $T$, which are what matter in measurement comparisons, really do not turn out to be different to any noteworthy degree, whether one derives the relevant measurement values according to Principle I from formulas (1) and (2) on page 50, or according to Principle II from formulas (3) and (4) on page 51 <note>Fechner is arguing that the two mathematical methods are practically interchangeable for the final results.</note>. Consequently, even if Principle II had a theoretical advantage, one would not obtain any comparison results from it that deviate significantly from those obtained via Principle I. And indisputably, **Müller** <note>Georg Elias Müller, a prominent psychophysicist who critiqued Fechner’s methods.</note> would have had reason to first undertake an investigation of this himself—for which he did not lack opportunity in several experimental series I provided to him for other purposes—before he allowed himself (as, for example, on page 267) to—

...to deny the validity of results I have derived according to Principle I on the grounds that they were drawn according to I rather than II. He would be wrong to do so, even if he were correct about his Principle II—and he would be even more mistaken, of course, if he is not. I had the opportunity to establish this for myself because for a time I believed I had to abandon my Principle I and adopt Müller’s Principle II (cf. p. 72). Consequently, I recalculated all my earlier series of experiments—which involve the most diverse conditions—only to find that the results that mattered were not changed in any essential point or degree. At first glance, this seems to contradict the fact that in certain cases, which I presented above as striking evidence for the decision between I and II, the difference in results can become quite enormous; however, experimental setups where such cases occur are generally not practically suitable for drawing results at all, and in any case, they did not occur in my many varied series of experiments conducted to investigate different circumstances.

The matter is as follows. According to Principle I, one has $h D = t_0$; according to Principle II, one has:

-> $h D = \frac{t_{I} + t_{II}}{2}$ <-

However, as one can verify through random samples from the **fundamental table** <note>A mathematical table based on the law of errors (the normal distribution) used to convert the frequency of correct answers into a measure of sensory precision.</note>, this latter value is always greater in absolute value than $t_0$. A higher $h$ means the subject is better at distinguishing small differences.</note>—generally turns out larger according to Principle II than Principle I. Setting aside certain extreme cases that almost never occur, the difference is not very significant, as the example on page 52 already showed; however, it would still be wrong to neglect it if it did not maintain the same direction for both Principle I and II when the circumstances for which one seeks to determine $h D$ (and thus $h$) are changed. This carries the implication that the *ratios* of the $h$ values, which are what truly matter, remain noticeably the same regardless of whether one uses Principle I or II. I do not say *exactly* the same; but experience shows that the deviations are so minor and fluctuate so randomly in both directions that they are truly negligible for *practical* purposes. Aside from the general result expressed above, I have confirmed this specifically in two of my largest series: the one-handed No. 1 and the two-handed No. 6 (the specific conditions of which are given in a later section). I hope that the foregoing will have sufficed to restore the contested validity of Principle I over Principle II, without failing to recognize that in fact, in the "Elements" <note>Fechner refers to his seminal 1860 work, *Elemente der Psychophysik* (Elements of Psychophysics), which founded the field of experimental psychology.</note> there was still a lack of sufficiently thorough discussions for the justification of the former, so as not to allow Principle II the possibility of opposing it; except that Müller's <note>Georg Elias Müller (1850–1934), a younger psychologist who published a rigorous critique of Fechner's methods in 1878.</note> challenge to Principle I, though more ingenious, was no more thorough than its original formulation on my part. After this, however, we still have to deal with Principles III and IV.

As far as Principle III of proportional division is concerned, one could generally argue in its favor that when in doubt as to how to divide the *z* <note>The "doubtful cases" (German: *zweifelhafte Fälle*) where a test subject cannot discern a difference between two stimuli.</note> between positive and negative values, nothing is more natural than to divide them according to the ratio presented by the already existing undoubtedly positive and negative *r* and *f* <note>The "right" (*richtige*) and "false" (*falsche*) responses recorded in a psychophysical experiment.</note> in relation to each other or to the total number. This could also be more specifically motivated as follows: if we could increase our attention to the highest degree, we would obtain no *z* cases at all, but only positive and negative cases, *r* and *f*, and the ratio of the actually recognized *r* and *f* to each other or to the total number now gives us a starting point for how we are to think of the unrecognized cases as being divided between the two sides.

But it is generally an error to want to infer the probability ratio existing between the remaining parts of a positive and negative scale of random values from the probability ratio between given parts of the same; and in fact, such an inference would fail in the case of observation errors, the law of which we are applying. Furthermore, the principle contradicts the *a priori* <note>Original: "aprioristischen." Referring to reasoning that is independent of specific experience or experimental data.</note> Principle I established above regarding the division of the *z* into equal numbers of positive and negative values. Finally, the proposition that with the greatest possible attention all cases would appear as positive or negative is not tenable, as it would presuppose that the <term>difference threshold</term> <note>original: "U. Schw." (*Unterschiedsschwelle*), the smallest detectable difference between two stimuli.</note> depended solely on a lack of attention, which is not to be conceded for other reasons; and even if this were to be conceded, we could not relate the method to the ideal case of infinitely increased attention, but only to an attention level kept as constant as possible across the various experiments.

->1) Preliminary Remarks.<-

### 2) Path of determination (a) of the measured values according to Division Principle I.

I will first proceed from the case where both stimuli, $A$ and $B$, are equal to one another, and consequently $D = 0$. <note>$D$ represents the physical difference between two stimuli.</note> Without **random fluctuations** (accidental error processes), $B$ would also appear equal to $A$, and thus the actual $D = 0$ would also yield the apparent value $D = 0$. However, random fluctuations cause $B$ to appear sometimes larger than $A$, and sometimes the reverse; thus, apparent deviations between the two, which we shall call $\Delta$, occur in one direction or the other. If we assign a positive sign to those $\Delta$'s where $B$ has an apparent superiority—which in later experiments will be taken as truly larger—and a negative sign to the opposite, designating the former as $r$ <note>Right/correct cases.</note> and the latter as $f$, <note>False/wrong cases.</note> then the **probability** (W.) of the positive and negative $\Delta$'s, and thus of $r$ and $f$, will be equal. Insofar as <term>null cases<note>original: "Nullfälle"; instances where the subject reports no perceivable difference or is undecided.</note></term> (denoted as $z$) also occur alongside $r$ and $f$ and must be divided between both sides for calculation purposes, they shall in any case be divided equally between both sides in this instance. Since everything is symmetrical from $D = 0$ toward both sides, any difference between the two modes of division—which only exists for the case where $D$ has a finite value—is irrelevant. For the assumption of $D = 0$, the

-> total number of cases is thus divided into $r + \frac{z}{2} = r'$ positive and just as many, i.e., <-
-> $f + \frac{z}{2} = f'$ negative cases. <-

Now we can properly assume—and Müller will do this as well as I—that under the stated assumption of $D = 0$, the deviation of a $\Delta$ from zero caused by random fluctuations follows a...

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s mathematical derivation of the probability of detecting a stimulus difference. ...or the other side is all the more improbable the larger it is, because the random circumstances must coincide with higher values in the same direction to produce it. Consequently, a deviation is exceeded with a lower probability <note>original: "W." (Wahrscheinlichkeit)</note> the larger it is. This fits into the **Gaussian** law of dependence of the probability of random deviations on their magnitude; thus, according to the most probable hypothesis, we arrive directly at the Δ values as random deviations from **D = 0**.

This being established, in our current case where **D = 0**, we have as the probability of the total positive as well as negative Δ values on each side:

-> $\frac{r'}{n} = \frac{f}{n} = \frac{1}{2}.$ <-

If **D = 0** is now transformed into a positive **D** through the introduction of unequal weights, the probability of the positive cases increases beyond $\frac{1}{2}$ by a certain amount, let us say **C**, and the probability of the negative cases decreases by just as much; so we now have:

-> $\frac{r'}{n} = \frac{1}{2} + C; \quad \frac{f}{n} = \frac{1}{2} - C$ <-

However, **C** will functionally depend on **D** according to the following consideration.

In any case, we can think of the deviations **Δ**, which we obtained when **D = 0**, even if we do not know them, as being measured by the same unit with which we measure **D**, and thereby keep them comparable. Insofar as **D** remains constant in all trials and exerts a correspondingly constant influence, we can view it as if its positive value were added to every positive as well as every negative **Δ** that we would have obtained without the presence of **D**. Thereby, every positive **Δ** grows by **D**, and every negative one decreases by the same amount in its absolute value <sup>1)</sup>. These modified deviations **± Δ + D** we shall call **θ**; thus:

-> $\theta = \pm \Delta + D$ <-

->$\frac{f'}{n} = 1 - \frac{r'}{n} = \frac{1}{2} - C.$<-

### 3) Method of Determination b) for the measured values, according to both principles of division I and II.

First, the following applies to both <term>principles of division</term> I and II <note>These "principles" refer to different ways of statistically accounting for "doubtful" or "equal" cases in psychophysical experiments.</note> in common.

Along with Müller <note>Likely Georg Elias Müller, a prominent experimental psychologist of the era who critiqued and refined Fechner's methods.</note>, I assume that the stimuli *A* and *B* themselves vary apparently through random <term>error processes</term>; that their apparent changes, $\delta$, $\delta'$, which are thought to be independent of each other, follow the **Gaussian Law**; and that the random changes $\alpha$ of the difference *D* between *A* and *B* are to be made dependent on the changes $\delta$, $\delta'$ of the individual stimuli. However, it seems to me that by applying known theorems, this can be done in a shorter and more easily accessible way than Müller has done, by starting from the following known principle, which has already been brought to bear earlier.

If the difference *D* between two values *A* and *B* changes because the values between which it occurs change, then the change in *D* can be mathematically represented by taking one value—let it be *A*—as fixed and regarding only the other, *B*, as variable. This is done by transferring the changes $\delta$ that *A* undergoes to *B* while reversing their sign, and combining them with the changes $\delta'$ that *B* experiences. These combined changes $\delta' - \delta$ now give the $\alpha$, which are materially equivalent—only formally different—whether viewed as random changes of *B* while *A* is fixed, or as random changes of the difference *D* between both.

It is further known that if two sources of error, which independently give errors like $\delta$, $\delta'$, meet at the same value—in our case *B*—and thus give a composite error like $\delta' - \delta = \alpha$, this composite error follows the **Gaussian Law** if its components follow it. Since we assume this for the components $\delta$, $\delta'$, it will also apply to their combination $\alpha$, and $\alpha$ will be assigned a <term>measure of precision</term> that we call *H*.

This measure of precision *H* can be represented as a composite function of the precision measures belonging to the components of the $\alpha$'s (that is, $\delta, \delta'$), which will be discussed below; however, without for our...

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of the "Method of Right and Wrong Cases," specifically addressing the mathematical derivation of precision measures (h) and how to handle experimental errors when stimuli are compared. It responds to the methodological critiques of G.E. Müller.</meta>

...purpose of the derivation of measured values is necessary to return to this composition. Müller indeed believed that the varying magnitude of the **stimuli** <note>Reize: the physical inputs, such as weights or sounds, being compared.</note> gave cause for this, insofar as the average magnitude of the deviations *d, d'* and consequently their **measures of precision** <term>Präcisionsmaße</term> <note>A statistical term (usually denoted as h) indicating how closely data clusters around the average; high precision means low variability.</note> would be influenced by it. But by transferring both deviations *d, d'* to the same stimulus in the specified sense, and allowing these to be combined into deviations or errors $\alpha$, we must also recognize the consequences of this way of thinking. A composite error $\alpha$, however, follows the **Gaussian Law** if its components follow it, and the component measures of precision of *d* and *d'* merge into a single, unified measure of precision for $\alpha$, regardless of whether the average values of *d* and *d'* are equal or unequal. And it proves neither necessary to know the components to derive this unified measure of precision, nor is its method of composition taken into account when applying it to the measure of the **sensitivity to difference** <term>Unterschiedsempfindlichkeit</term>.

Accordingly, we first conduct the observation in the sense of **Principle of Division I** <note>This principle describes how to statistically categorize "doubtful" or "equal" judgments—specifically by splitting them between "right" and "wrong" categories.</note>.

Correct or positive cases are all those where stimulus *B*, just as it is physically larger than stimulus *A*, also appears larger. If we now allow *B* to change apparently by a random amount $\alpha$ to either side with equal **probability** <note>Wahrscheinlichkeit (W.)</note>, then first of all, all cases will be correct or positive where *B* changes toward the positive side, the probability of which is $\frac{1}{2}$. Added to this, however, are all cases where *B* changes toward the negative side up to the limit where *B* has decreased to equality with *A*. Beyond that point, *B* (apparently) becomes smaller than *A*, and thus the negative or false cases begin. Since *B* deviates from *A* by the amount *D* in its unchanged state, the change of *B* toward the negative side must be equal to *D* in absolute value to reach equality with *A*. The probability of $\alpha$ from the starting point, where $\alpha = 0$, up to a value of $\pm D$, amounts—according to the **Gaussian Law**—to:

->$\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}} \int_{0}^{HD} e^{-t^2} dt,$<-

where $t$ is generally $= H\alpha$ and $H$ is the measure of precision of $\alpha$. Since we now, according to Principle I, count half of the *z* cases <note>"z" refers to "zero" or "doubtful" cases where the observer cannot perceive a difference.</note> among the positive ones, the probability of the positive $\alpha$ is equal to:

->$\frac{r}{n} + \frac{z}{2n} = \frac{r'}{n}$<-

->$W^2 = w^2 + w'^2.$<-

The probable errors, however, are—as is equally well known—inversely proportional to the measures of precision. Therefore, by replacing $W^2$ with $\frac{1}{H^2}$, $w^2$ with $\frac{1}{h^2}$, and $w'^2$ with $\frac{1}{h'^2}$, we have:

->$\frac{1}{H^2} = \frac{1}{h^2} + \frac{1}{h'^2}$<-

->$H^2 = \frac{h^2 h'^2}{h^2 + h'^2}.$<-

Following Bessel <note>Friedrich Bessel (1784–1846) was a German astronomer whose work on error laws was fundamental to the development of statistics.</note> (according to a reference in the *Göttingische Gelehrte Anzeigen*, p. 162), he essentially derives the following value for the probability—denoted as $W_0^\alpha$—of $\alpha$ falling between $\alpha = 0$ and a specific value $a$:

->$$W_0^\alpha = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}} \int_0^{\frac{hh' \alpha}{\sqrt{h^2 + h'^2}}} e^{-t^2} dt$$<-

where $h$ and $h'$ are the measures of precision <note>The "measure of precision" (Präzisionsmaß) is a statistical value indicating how concentrated data is around the mean; in modern terms, it is related to the reciprocal of the standard deviation.</note> for $d$ and $d'$ respectively, and where

->$t = \frac{hh' \alpha}{\sqrt{h^2 + h'^2}}; dt = \frac{hh'}{\sqrt{h^2 + h'^2}} \partial \alpha$<-

is true.
However, if one now sets

->$$\frac{hh'}{\sqrt{h^2 + h'^2}} = H$$<-

and consequently $t = H\alpha$ and $dt = Hd\alpha$, one finds

->$$W_0^\alpha = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}} \int_0^{H\alpha} e^{-t^2} dt$$<-

The form of this equation immediately demonstrates that $\alpha$ follows the Gaussian law <note>The Gaussian Law refers to the Normal Distribution or "Bell Curve."</note> just as well as $d$ and $d'$ do, and that $H$ is the measure of precision for $\alpha$. This brings everything back to the state previously described under section 3) b.

Meanwhile, Müller himself did not arrive at this simplification. In his work, one finds neither a proof nor even a mention that $W_0^\alpha$ follows the Gaussian law, nor that the composite expression (which I represent as $H$) is the measure of precision for $\alpha$. Furthermore, he makes no use of this concept to measure the sensitivity to differences <note>original: "U. E.", likely standing for *Unterschiedsempfindlichkeit* (difference sensitivity), a core concept in early psychophysics.</note>. Instead, he continues to operate with the complex composite expression—which, based on the above, is not necessary to revert to at all—as follows:

He notes that if the difference weight $D$ is only very small compared to $P$, one can set $h = h'$ without significant error. Instead of replacing this with our $H$, he carries this latter expression through all his subsequent developments. These calculations consequently take on a cumbersome form that obscures clarity. He thus proceeds along the same path that I previously outlined under b) according to II, essentially in Müller's own—

### 5) On Möbius's Line Scheme (Elem. I. 105).

As previously noted (p. 84), in my book *Elements of Psychophysik*, instead of the path taken in points 2 and 3 above to derive the measure of precision <term>Measure of precision (h or H): a mathematical value used to describe how consistently a person can distinguish between two stimuli; a higher "h" means greater sensitivity and less "noise" in judgment.</term> $h$ or $H$, I took a different path based on the Möbius line scheme <note>August Ferdinand Möbius (1790–1868) was a German mathematician. Fechner used Möbius’s geometric diagrams to visualize how we perceive the difference between two stimuli.</note>. According to this scheme, the $h D$ in the formulas given in Section IV would be replaced by $h D / 2$. Consequently, $h$ would have to take on double the value that our current formulas assign to it, so that the earlier $h D / 2$ would equal our current $h D$ for a given $D$ <note>$D$ represents the difference between two stimuli, such as two weights.</note>. 

While this difference is practically irrelevant—as noted before—when comparing different series of experiments using the **method of right and wrong cases** regarding the resulting **sensitivity to differences** (where only the ratios of $h$ or $h / 2$ matter), it is nonetheless significant from a theoretical standpoint. It also matters if we wish to compare the results of the **method of right and wrong cases** with the results of other methods. 

Although I now recognize the inaccuracy of using $h / 2$ instead of $h$ derived from the Möbius scheme, the error lies elsewhere than where Müller looks for it. The fault is not in the scheme itself, but in how it was applied, regarding which I offer the following remarks:

> Müller says (p. 31): "We find this line example in Fechner’s work simply assumed to be applicable, without even an attempt being made to prove its validity."

But the validity of the line example depends on the validity of the way of thinking it is intended to represent. Instead of the line example simply being assumed as valid, the entire reasoning that led to that way of thinking is incorporated within it.

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s technical rebuttal to G.E. Müller’s critique of the Möbius scheme. Fechner is addressing the specific objection that the scheme assumes one variable increases exactly as much as the other decreases—a scenario Müller claims is physically unrealistic. Fechner counters by arguing that such assumptions are useful "mathematical fictions."</meta>

...increases by just as much as the other decreases; but this is completely contrary to the actual facts of the matter.

However, as striking as this objection seems at first glance, the following rebuttal of it might be even more striking.

When it is necessary to track the changes in the difference between two magnitudes A and B without knowing the individual changes of the two magnitudes—or it being important to know or track them individually, as is the case in our experiments regarding differential sensitivity <note>U.E. stands for *Unterschiedsempfindlichkeit*, the capacity to distinguish between two stimuli.</note>—we can employ a mathematical fiction to achieve the same results we would obtain if we knew the actual changes. As previously noted and applied, we can imagine that one magnitude remains unchanged while its change is transferred to the other in the opposite sense; indeed, this fiction is used often enough without claiming that it corresponds to reality. 

But another fiction—and indeed countless other fictions—can accomplish the same thing, provided they follow a certain general rule specified below. Thus, we can imagine that when a difference between two magnitudes shifts into other differences through random changes, half of the total change always falls on one magnitude and the other half on the other; or perhaps one-quarter on one and three-quarters on the other, so long as the change of one magnitude is always given the opposite sign to the other. In none of these cases would we claim that this was the actual physical process; however, in all these cases, we will obtain the same result regarding the changes of the sensitivity in question as if we had been able to adhere to the real process. The general rule is this: if the difference between two magnitudes A and B changes by an amount *c*, one can represent this by having one change by an arbitrary fraction of *c* (let us call it *mc*) in the positive direction, while the other, as a complement, changes by (1—m)*c* in the negative direction; because:

->B + mc — [A — (1 — m) c] is = B — A + c.<-

Now, the Möbius scheme <term>Möbius scheme: A geometric visualization used by Fechner to represent the relationship between two stimuli and their midpoint, named after mathematician August Ferdinand Möbius.</term> corresponds to the general requirement where B should always increase by as much as A decreases, and vice versa, by setting m = 1/2. This quite simply justifies itself against Müller.

If one then asks why, out of the infinitely many fictions that...

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s technical rebuttal to G.E. Müller regarding the "Möbius scheme," a geometric way of representing the relationship between two stimuli. generally speaking, are possible to represent the changes of a <term>difference</term> <note>Original: *U.*, abbreviation for *Unterschied* (difference).</note>, just this specific one is chosen—namely, that one magnitude changes by as much in one direction as the other changes in the opposite direction—one can answer that it is not so much "chosen" as it naturally arises from the context of the line scheme itself. However, should it need to be chosen, one would prefer this specific version for the following reason: The line scheme is intended to represent not the result of a single change, but in principle the result of infinitely many changes. In reality, while individual magnitudes vary in infinitely different ways, *on average* they will both have moved by the same amount in one direction and by the same amount in the opposite direction; both will have moved as much away from each other as toward each other. No change in the <term>difference</term> depends on the former movements; therefore, the *average* change is represented by the latter movements and depicted by the scheme.

But while the scheme represents all of this with intuitive validity, its earlier application in the "*Elements*" <note>Referring to Fechner's 1860 foundational work, *Elemente der Psychophysik*.</note> fails at one point. According to the previous presentation, one must assume that when C has moved from its starting point (where it is a distance of D/2 from M) apparently to M—that is, by a distance of D/2—the total apparent change of the <term>difference</term> is not D/2, but double that amount. This is because, in the simple movement of C, the one value A always moves by the same amount in the opposite direction as the other value B. However, the scheme was previously used as if the apparent <term>difference</term> between A and B became zero with a change of only D/2. If one corrects this interpretation based on the previous observation, the Möbius scheme remains fully valid, and the $hD/2$ previously derived from it is naturally replaced by $hD$ <note>Here, $h$ refers to the "measure of precision" in Fechner’s statistical formulas.</note>.

Here, he begins to describe the practical application of his "Method of Average Error" in experiments involving visual estimation.</meta>

— 105 —

...at that time [I] still intended to follow this with a special treatise on measurement methods, which did not come to pass. Before I now address Müller's <note>Georg Elias Müller (1850–1934) was a prominent experimental psychologist and one of Fechner's most rigorous critics.</note> critique of the method, I want to provide the most essential details in that regard, and will first explain my manner of executing the method using experiments on visual judgment <term>visual judgment</term> <note>Original: *Augenmaßversuchen*; experiments testing the accuracy of the eye in estimating distances or sizes.</note>.

A given distance—for example, between the points of a compass or parallel threads—the so-called standard distance *N*, is to have another distance, the error distance *f* <gloss>1)</gloss>, made as equal to it as is possible by visual judgment. After I have first made a rough and, so to speak, "throwaway" adjustment of the error distance to apparent equality with the standard distance—whether starting from an error distance that is too large or too small—I then check whether it truly corresponds to equality for the sensation or not. I then shift the boundary or boundaries (indicated by the threads or compass points) of the error distance back and forth, always observing what the effect is for the sensation, until equality seems best achieved in a definitive adjustment. The difference between the error distance and the standard distance, *f — N*, at which I stop, then provides the **raw error d**, which is generally still subject to a constant error *c*. From all the error distances, let their number be *m*, I now calculate the mean $\frac{\Sigma f}{m}$, designate it as the mean error distance *F*, and obtain the differences of the individual error distances *f* from the mean error distance *F*. These are designated as $\Delta$, representing the pure variable errors freed from the constant error. Finally, by taking the mean of these pure errors regardless of their sign (the so-called absolute mean), I obtain the pure mean error $\frac{\Sigma \Delta}{m}$, to be designated as $\Delta_m$. I consider its reciprocal value to be the measure of <term>sensitivity to differences</term> <note>Original: *U. E.*, for *Unterschiedsempfindlichkeit*. This is a measure of sensory precision; the smaller the error a person makes, the higher their sensitivity value becomes.</note>.

Following this, one must show how to arrive at the pure mean error $\Delta_m$ and the constant error *c* via the most convenient calculation path possible, which can happen in two ways, depending on whether one wishes to include the determination of the mean error distance *F* and skip the raw errors, or vice versa.

**First Procedure.** After the mean error distance *F* has been determined from the individual *f* values, one obtains the $\Delta$ values as the differences *f — F* according to their absolute value, and *c = F — N*, which value can be positive or negative, depending on whether *F > N* or vice versa.

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s technical explanation of how to calculate error in psychophysical experiments. He is moving from the general concept of the "Method of Average Error" to the specific arithmetic shortcuts used to process large amounts of data without making calculation errors.</meta>

returned. Now, it would not only be very cumbersome, but also—given the quantity of individual determinations to be made—likely that calculation errors would occur if one tried to take the differences <note>Original: *f — F*; where *f* represents the observed value and *F* represents the average of all observed values.</note> individually. Therefore, one proceeds more briefly as follows: one adds all values of *f* that are greater than *F*; let their sum be *G* and their number be *g*. Then, subtract the average error distance, taken *g* times, from *G*. This gives the **positive pure error sum** <term>pure error sum</term> <note>The "pure error" refers to the variation of measurements around the subject's own average, rather than the intended standard.</note>, *G — gF*, which we shall call *P*. Similarly, one adds all values of *f* that are smaller than *F*; let their number be *k* and their sum be *K*. Then, subtract *K* from *F* taken *k* times, which yields the **negative pure error sum**, *kF — K*, which we shall call *Q*. Adding the absolute value of *Q* to *P* gives the total pure error sum ΣΔ <note>The Greek letter Sigma (Σ) denotes a sum, and Delta (Δ) represents the individual pure errors.</note>. A test of a correct calculation is that *P* and *Q* should turn out to be equal; and if it were not for this test, it would suffice to determine only *P* or *Q* and double that value to obtain ΣΔ. Since the determination of the raw errors is of no fundamental importance to the method, the previous procedure—which bypasses this determination—is recommended as the most direct way to obtain the results we need. However, under certain circumstances, one might prefer the following procedure.

**Second Procedure.** Above all, one determines the **raw errors** <term>raw error</term> <note>Original: *rohen Fehler*; the direct difference between the observed result and the actual standard (*N*), which includes the subject's systematic bias.</note> *δ* as the differences of *f* from *N*, recording the positive and negative *δ* in separate columns. To save time, this could be done during the experiments themselves, but that is simply unacceptable; splitting one’s attention between the experiment and the calculation makes it easier to commit oversights that cannot be corrected later. Rather, in the experiments themselves—under the current as well as the previous procedure—only the directly observed values of *f* should be recorded, and the raw errors should only be determined after the series of trials is completed. Once this is done, one takes the sum of the positive *f* values (let it be *P'*) and the negative values (let it be *Q'*, using absolute values); then one has the constant error <gloss>systematic bias</gloss> *c* = $\frac{P' — Q'}{m}$. To obtain ΣΔ, however, one proceeds as follows: Let those raw errors on this side be those with the same sign as *c*, and those on the other side be those with the opposite sign. If *t* is the number and *T* is the sum of the raw errors on "this side" which exceed the constant error in size (which can be called the "upper" errors), one obtains ΣΔ by subtracting the *t*-fold constant error *tc* from the sum of the upper raw errors *T* and doubling the distance; thus:

->ΣΔ = 2 (T — tc).<-

First, one obtains only the sum of the pure errors on this side <note>Original: *diesseitig*. In this context, it refers to errors falling on one side of the mean value.</note> $\frac{\Sigma \Delta}{2} = \text{T} - t_c$, but since the sum of those on the other side is in principle equal to those on this side, it is sufficient to double this sum to obtain the total sum. Of course, one lacks the verification provided by determining the sum on the other side, which can indeed be done, but according to a rather impractical and cumbersome formula; therefore, one will generally prefer to seek verification by repeating the previous determination. When raw errors = *c* occur, they can be assigned arbitrarily to either those on this side or those on the other side in the previous determination, provided that it is done for *t* and *T* simultaneously.

I omit the proof of the previous determinations, which is easy to provide, as anyone can easily convince themselves—even without trials or proof, through their own samples—that both procedures merely lead by an easier path to the same determinations obtained through the direct method based on the concepts of $\Delta$ and *c*. As a rule, the sum of raw errors <term>raw error</term> <note>The total observed deviation before accounting for the subject's constant bias.</note> decreases when converted into the pure error <term>pure error</term> <note>The deviation of a measurement from the subject's own average, rather than from the objective standard.</note>; this is a reduction that is often very significant when *c* is large. The cases where an increase occurs are relatively rare, appearing only when *c* is small, and the increase is then always relatively slight.

If the constant error *c* obtained in one of the ways described above has only a small value, it can be considered, according to the laws of probability, as merely **apparent** insofar as the average error distance *F* can deviate from the normal distance *N* purely through unbalanced random chance, even without being triggered by a constant cause (upon which a true constant error would depend); here, *c* = *F* — *N*. In any case, however, one must assume a **true** constant error if, when fractioning <term>fractioning</term> <note>The process of dividing a large series of experimental trials into smaller groups to see if a pattern remains consistent.</note> a series of observations into segments that are not too small and calculating them separately, *c* retains the same sign <note>Meaning the error is consistently positive or consistently negative.</note> throughout all or a predominant majority of the fractions. It is considered an **apparent** error if the sign of *c* changes inconsistently. If one algebraically adds the values of *c* obtained from the individual fractions with the same *m* <note>In this context, *m* likely refers to the number of trials in each fraction.</note>—that is, taking the sign into account—and takes the average by dividing by the number of fractions, one obtains the same definitive *c* for the entire series as if one had treated the series as a single connected whole.

...more often from a variability of the constant error—which, in this sense, only improperly deserves its name—due to subjective conditions that bring about a different perception of the same spatial and temporal position, than from a difference in the pure variable average error in these <term>fractions</term> <note>Fechner refers to dividing a long series of trials into smaller "fractions" or blocks to monitor changes over time.</note>, even though actual modifications of the latter can certainly be caused by the progress of practice and altered levels of attention. Even if the danger of such contamination is not entirely eliminated by this, it is nevertheless reduced to a degree that is no longer significantly disruptive. In general, fractional treatment has the advantage of assuring us of the greater or lesser constancy of the results and allowing us to notice both the modifications of the constant error as well as the modifications that the progress of practice, altered attention, or other circumstances bring into the ratios of the variable errors. It is most advisable, where special circumstances do not prevent this, to perform the observations that are to be combined into a fraction and calculated together immediately after one another, giving each such fraction the same number—for example, 10—observations, and to obtain the definitive result by merging the results of the individual fractions. The division into fractions where *m* = 10 has the particular advantage of facilitating the calculation of means, insofar as it can be done simply by moving a decimal point from the sum.

This is an influence that must also be present in un-fractioned series, insofar as they can always be viewed as fractions of an even larger series with a larger $m$. The mean error also turns out smaller the smaller the $m$ from which it is derived, without this being dependent on a greater **sensitivity to differences**.

So much for my manner of executing this method; let us now turn to the critical remarks that the method has received to date.

First, I must confess that I find it quite surprising to encounter the remark in *Wundt's* *Philosophical Studies* <note>Wilhelm Wundt (1832–1920), often called the father of experimental psychology, published the journal *Philosophische Studien*.</note> (page 9) that the <term>Method of Average Error</term> <note>Abbreviated as "m. I am only aware that *Müller* <note>Georg Elias Müller (1850–1934), a rigorous experimental psychologist who often critiqued Fechner's statistical methods.</note> indeed thinks nothing of the Method of Average Error; and if I perceived it as erroneously as he does, I would think nothing of it myself. It may well be, however, that many a judgment has been swayed by *Müller*; the following will show with how much justification. 

Furthermore, the circumstance that the experiments of *Kollert*, conducted under *Wundt's* direction, favored the <term>Method of Just Noticeable Differences</term> <note>Original: *Methode der eben merklichen Unterschiede* (e. m. However, the Method of Right and Wrong Cases also proved to be at a disadvantage compared to the Method of Just Noticeable Differences in those experiments and was therefore rejected there, without that rejection being applicable everywhere. It is simply that one method is more advantageous than another under certain circumstances, for certain purposes, or according to certain modes of execution, as *Wundt* himself rightly emphasizes. 

Based on this and my own experiences, I find no reason to sign off on *Wundt's* statement above. Rather, I consider the Method of Average Error, when applied in the right place and with the correct execution, to be among the most useful methods. Indeed, it served *Volkmann* and me excellently in establishing **Weber’s Law** within the domain of **visual estimation**; one must simply not execute it as *Chodin* did (see the later section on eye-measure experiments) or as *Müller* insists it should, at best, be executed. Regarding the theory of the method, when it is carried out in my manner, it is found directly through the theory of observation errors without arbitrary or hypothetical assumptions, provided that the pure errors $\Delta$ obtained by our method correspond in all essential respects to the observation errors obtained in the determination of physical or astronomical quantities. Indeed, the origin of observation errors, like that of the setting errors in our method, comes down to this: in the attempt to make a quantity equal to one representing our standard quantity $N$, one finally arrives at a small difference which, whether for external or internal reasons, is no longer recognized, and thus falls within the limits of the <term>difference threshold</term><note>Original: *U. Schw.*, abbreviation for *Unterschiedsschwelle*. This is the smallest change in a stimulus that a person can detect.</note> and yields the observation error; however, this is determined not with respect to the actual standard quantity, which is unknown, but with respect to the mean of the quantities observed in individual cases, which represent our $f$ <note>In Fechner's notation, $f$ usually refers to the individual faulty settings or values.</note>. It is the same with the pure $\Delta$s of the method of average errors. While one does know the standard quantity $N$ here, one determines the $\Delta$—just as with observation errors—not as deviations from $N$, but from the mean error-size representing $N$ in this respect. Thus, the $\Delta$s become entirely comparable to observation errors, and when determined this way, they not only presumably obey the <term>Gaussian law</term><note>The "normal distribution" or bell curve, which describes how random errors cluster around a central value.</note> like the former, but actually do so according to my observations. Now, in the case of observation errors, the <term>measure of precision</term> $h$ <note>Original: *Präcisionsmaß*. A mathematical value used to describe how tightly data points cluster together.</note> of the error is inversely proportional to the average error, and given this agreement of fundamental proportions between the $\Delta$s on both sides, I find not the slightest obstacle to letting $\Delta_m$ in the method of average errors play the same role for the estimation of subjective accuracy as the $\Delta_m$ of observation errors plays for the estimation of objective accuracy.

->$\frac{r'}{n} = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}} \int_0^{hD = t_0} e^{-t^2} dt$<-

the <term>mean error</term><note>The average amount by which a subject's settings deviate from the target value.</note> $\Delta_m = \frac{1}{h\sqrt{\pi}}$ for the value $D$, whereby $hD$ becomes $1/\sqrt{\pi} = 0.56420$, one finds—by looking up this value of $hD$ in the <term>fundamental table</term><note>A mathematical table for the "error function" (integral of the normal distribution), used to convert experimental results into statistical probabilities.</note>—that $r' = 0.7844²)$.

The preceding theory seems to me at once the simplest and most illuminating that can be established; insofar as it is nothing other than the reduction of the theory of our method to the recognized theory of observation errors. In this regard, one may notice that although the actual size of observation errors depends on the magnitude of the <term>difference threshold</term><note>Original: *U. Schw.* (Unterschiedsschwelle). The smallest difference between two stimuli that a person can reliably detect.</note> (because only differences below the threshold can appear as errors), the expression of the threshold size does not enter into the measure of precision $h$, and thus also does not enter into the $\Delta_m = \frac{1}{h\sqrt{\pi}}$ of the observation errors. Therefore, this cannot be expected from $\Delta_m$ as the mean error of our method either; since the procedure, here as there, is not designed to teach us this dependency, but rather to give the value $\Delta_m$ directly, regardless of how it may depend on the difference threshold.

in this regard carries no weight, for the above theory and the use of the method do not depend upon it. For the sake of simplicity, I assume from the outset the absence of <term>constant errors</term><note>Systematic biases in measurement—for example, if a subject always perceives the left object as slightly larger than the right one regardless of their actual size.</note>, to which one can always return by transitioning from "raw" errors to "pure" errors.

Naturally, in my method of execution, I will stop at very different intervals of the error distance from the normal distance during individual trials. However, the assumption may be made that—given the assumed absence of constant errors—the average deviation from the normal size that occurs, in short the <term>average error Δ<sub>m</sub></term><note>The average amount by which a subject's settings deviate from the target value across many trials.</note>, is proportional to the range of individual errors. This range is the value of the <term>Difference Threshold</term><note>Original: *U. Schw.* (*Unterschiedsschwelle*). The smallest difference between two stimuli that a person can detect.</note>, which I designate as *T* for the total range, or as *S* (following Müller's notation) when tracking the positive or negative side specifically, such that *T = 2S* when *S* is considered as an absolute value (cf. p. 45 f.). And this simple perspective would suffice to establish the relationship between Δ<sub>m</sub> and *T* or *S*, if it were not also found experimentally that the average error varies indefinitely according to the <term>Gaussian Law</term><note>The "Normal Distribution" or bell curve, which suggests that small deviations are more common than large ones in nature and measurement.</note>. But we satisfy both this condition and that assumption if we imagine the <term>Difference Threshold</term> *S* itself varying through random error processes according to the Gaussian Law, and combine the first perspective with the second. Indeed, let Δ<sub>m</sub> = *pS* according to the first perspective (where *p* is a constant), and let *S<sub>m</sub>* be the average value of the varying *S*; the definitive mean Δ<sub>m</sub> will then be obtained if we replace the individual value *S* with *S<sub>m</sub>* in the equation Δ<sub>m</sub> = *pS*, thus setting Δ<sub>m</sub> = *pS<sub>m</sub>*.

What might first seem like a point of criticism for this theory is that it does not account for the random changes that *N* <note>The standard or "Normal" stimulus being compared.</note> and *f* <note>The variable stimulus that the subject attempts to adjust to match the standard.</note> must undergo during the experiments due to random error processes, but rather shifts these random changes onto the threshold itself. In essence, we are not comparing the *actual* *f* with the *actual* *N*, but rather an *apparent* *f* with an *apparent* *N*, thereby obtaining an *apparent error* *f—N*. We might think of this error as varying according to the Gaussian Law, instead of thinking of *S* as varying accordingly. —

In fact, it can be grasped in this way, but it amounts to the same thing; for it will always be possible to hold a double interpretation: either the error randomly assumes such an apparent magnitude that it falls within a fixed threshold, or the threshold randomly assumes such an apparent magnitude that the error falls into it. In the sense of the former interpretation, however, it may be that an error found to be very large on a physical scale still falls within the narrow limits of a threshold regarded as constant, because it has been seemingly reduced to that point by random variations. This way of looking at it would even have the advantage, in formal contexts...

If, therefore, the values of the smallest noticeable differences in size are relative according to <term>Weber's Law</term><note>The principle that the smallest change in a stimulus that can be detected is a constant proportion of the original stimulus.</note>—that is, they grow along with the various dimensions—then the smallest *unnoticeable* differences must behave accordingly. And I concede to Müller that, according to the literal wording, one could hardly understand Volkmann's remarks otherwise. But I would note the following:

Based on the context in which that passage appears, Volkmann did not intend to provide an actual **description** of the procedure—which one can just as easily find lacking in his work as Müller finds it lacking in mine—but rather an **interpretation** of it. He sought to explain the procedure in the way he believed its meaning should be understood, though he may have lacked a clear memory or grasp of the specifics at the time. Otherwise, he certainly would not have only emphasized the caution of reducing a noticeable difference between the standard distance <term>N</term><note>Standard distance (Normaldistanz): The fixed reference stimulus in a psychophysical experiment.</note> and the comparison distance <term>f</term><note>Comparison distance (Fehldistanz): The variable stimulus that the subject adjusts to match the standard.</note> just until it disappears. He would also, given his usual care regarding <term>constant errors</term><note>Systematic biases that consistently skew results in one direction, such as a tendency to overestimate distances on the left side.</note>, have surely mentioned that he sought to reach the threshold limit just as often from a comparison distance that was too small as from one that was too large; and he would have distinguished between those cases as well as between **right and left** positioning. However, one finds nothing from him regarding any of this, nor even a mention of the complexity that such an impractical procedure of a two-sided determination of limits would necessarily entail. And so, I believe that the most natural and simplest procedure likely suggested itself to him just as it did to me. Furthermore, on page 97 of the *Physiological Investigations*, in a brief mention of the procedure, he says quite simply that the comparison distance is "to be regulated in such a way" "that it be made equal to the standard distance, as far as visual estimation allows."

Suppose now, however, that Volkmann really did proceed as Müller claims—and I certainly cannot **prove** the opposite, only find it predominantly **probable**—even then, Volkmann’s procedure would, in a different form, achieve the same result as mine: namely, to obtain a value in the <term>mean pure error</term><note>The average of the absolute differences between the subject's settings and the true value, used as a measure of sensitivity.</note> that is proportional to the difference threshold. ->1) f = N + (S ± $\beta$) or 2) f = N − (S ± $\beta$)<-

### VIII. Method of Just Noticeable Differences.

In the *Elements* <note>original: "Elementen". Refers to Fechner’s 1860 "Elements of Psychophysics," the founding text of the field.</note> Vol. I, p. 75, I granted the <term>method of just noticeable differences</term><note>A procedure where a stimulus is increased or decreased until the observer can just barely perceive a change.</note> the advantage over other measurement methods for <term>difference sensitivity</term><note>The ability to detect the smallest possible change between two stimuli.</note> in that it leads most quickly to a result. However, I declared it the least accurate among the various methods and more preliminary than definitive. To this, **Wundt** (Stud. p. 8) objects: "this view is, I believe, untenable for three reasons: first, because the method of just noticeable differences, when applied in an appropriate manner, is much more accurate than is commonly assumed; second, because there are areas of investigation where, due to the specific conditions of sensitivity, the other two methods are not applicable at all; and third and finally, because the interpretation of the results obtained by these other methods is by no means established in all respects, so that their reliable utilization would first have to be preceded by experimental testing." While I have found much to counter the last two reasons in earlier sections (IV, VII) insofar as they argue against the other methods, I cannot help but accept Wundt’s defense of the method of just noticeable differences in general. I hereby retract my earlier subordination of this method to others, which nevertheless remains...

...retain their validity, and for that reason alone they belong to the completion of the <term>method of just noticeable differences</term><note>German: *Methode der eben merklichen Unterschiede* (m. d. e. U.). A procedure where a stimulus is adjusted until a change is just barely perceivable.</note>, because through this method only the <term>difference threshold</term><note>The minimum difference between two stimuli required for detection.</note> is determined. Furthermore, I cannot agree with Wundt’s <note>Wilhelm Wundt (1832–1920), a foundational figure in experimental psychology.</note> remark (*Stud.* p. 8) that "the only actually permissible procedure for the method has already been designated by G. E. Müller" <note>Georg Elias Müller (1850–1934), a psychologist known for his rigorous refinement of psychophysical methods.</note>. Secondly, I cannot find the execution of Müller’s principle, as specified by Müller himself, to be any more practical than he himself ultimately found it. Indeed, it has not yet been attempted by Müller, Wundt, or anyone else. By contrast, Wundt, as will be noted later, has not only proposed but also practically and successfully attempted a significantly different way of executing Müller’s principle. But before I come to that, permit me to place my own principle and procedure—in short, my own method—in what seems to me the correct light, in the face of Müller’s attacks and Wundt’s aforementioned remark. The essential difference between the two principles at issue is this:

According to **Müller’s principle**, one either decreases a difference that is too large (i.e., exceeding the threshold) until the point where it disappears, or increases a difference that is too small (i.e., below the threshold) until the point where noticeability begins, and then takes the mean of both determinations. 

According to **my principle**, one seeks through adjustments to repeatedly recreate a small difference above the threshold that remains as consistently noticeable as possible across repeated trials ^1).

It is to be noted, however, that the point of difference is not to be sought in the fact that in the **Müllerian** procedure, one proceeds once **descending** from a value above the threshold and another time **ascending** from a value below the threshold; for this rule also applies to the execution of my principle for the prevention of a **constant error**<note>In early experimental psychology, a "constant error" refers to a systematic bias in measurement, such as a consistent tendency to overestimate a weight because of the order in which it is lifted.</note>, and I myself (in "In Matters,"<note>Fechner is referring to his 1877 book, *In Sachen der Psychophysik* (In Matters of Psychophysics), where he defended his theories against critics.</note> p. 53) considered the neglect of this rule as a possible source of error. Rather, the **essential** difference lies here: since a difference that has just disappeared necessarily leads below the true threshold, and one that has just become noticeable already leads beyond the true threshold, according to **Müller’s** principle, the **mean** is drawn from a threshold that is somewhat too large and one that is somewhat too small. In contrast, according to my principle, the **mean** is drawn entirely from threshold values that are somewhat too large. The disadvantage of this compared to **Müller’s** principle is admittedly obvious; however, it is not equally obvious that this disadvantage is merely an illusion.

The **Müllerian** principle is what he and **Wundt** call the **principle of smallest or minimal differences**; mine is the **principle of just noticeable differences** in the narrower sense, though in a broader sense the former is also included under this designation.

In the following, I will now attempt to show that my principle—and the procedure adopted according to it—reaches the same goals that one seeks to achieve with **greater complexity** according to the **Müllerian** principle, but does so by a simpler path, without my being able to recognize any conditions of **greater certainty** in his method.

Previously, an objection was raised against the method of <term>j. n. d.</term><note>original: "e. m. U." (eben merkliche Unterschiede). The "just noticeable difference" is the smallest change in a stimulus that a person can detect.</note> in general: that sensations of difference that are "just noticeable"—meaning they exceed the sensation of zero by only a very small amount—can still have very different **size ratios** to one another. One might be double, triple, or ten times the size of another, and thus they could not be used at all to determine the <term>diff. thresh.</term><note>original: "U. Schw." (Unterschiedsschwelle). The minimum difference between two stimuli required for detection.</note>. But this **objection** was already refuted in "In Matters," p. 44. To be sure, the term **"just noticeable"** inherently includes a certain indeterminacy. One can, for example, regard a sensation of difference = 0.1, but also one = 0.01 (viewed in relation to a moderately distinct one), as being "just noticeable," where the first is ten times as large as the second. But far from the <term>diff. thresh.</term> derived therefrom—which concerns not the **sensation of difference**, but the **stimulus difference**—being...

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s technical defense of his "Method of Just Noticeable Differences." He is responding to criticisms from G.E. Müller, arguing that while his method might slightly overestimate the absolute value of a sensory threshold, it remains superior due to its simplicity and its ability to accurately measure the ratios between thresholds, which is the primary goal of psychophysics.</meta>

...attain, against which, however, the simplicity of our own seems to me to be very advantageous, a point to which I will return below.

Aside from this, we achieve the following advantages with our method. First, we do not fall into the method of <term>r. u. f. F.</term><note>Abbreviation for *richtige und falsche Fälle* (Right and Wrong Cases): an experimental method where a subject compares two stimuli and the researcher records the frequency of correct and incorrect judgments.</note> (and thus, according to Müller's critique, not into the formulas used for it), a method which requires its own specific way of calculation and a very large number of trials; in short, we retain the advantage of a method that leads relatively quickly to the desired goal. Secondly, while we admittedly will always obtain a value slightly too large for the <term>U. Schw.</term><note>Abbreviation for *Unterschiedsschwelle* (difference threshold): the minimum physical difference required for a person to notice that two stimuli are different.</note> through our method, it can be shown that, according to <term>Weber’s Law</term><note>A fundamental principle in psychophysics stating that the change in a stimulus that will be just noticeable is a constant ratio of the original stimulus, rather than a fixed amount.</note>, the thresholds <note>Fechner uses "S" to represent *Schwelle* (threshold).</note> exceeded by our procedure maintain the same ratio as the correct ones. Psychophysical investigations are generally only concerned with determining the correct ratios of the threshold, whereas knowing the absolute value of the difference threshold in every individual case is of no interest, since its value is exceptionally variable in any case, meaning that fixed, permanent determinations regarding it cannot be obtained at all.

In fact, let $S_1, S_2$ be two threshold values belonging to different sensitivities that are to be compared with one another; differences equal to $S_1, S_2$ will then stand at the limit of noticeability. Both, however, will become equally noticeable according to Weber’s Law if we increase them by values $x_1, x_2$ that have the same ratio to the respective threshold ($S$). Thus, if we explicitly set up the experiment to make the differences $S_1 + x_1, S_2 + x_2$ appear equally noticeable—by altering the settings until this seems to be the case—we will also be able to set $S_1 + x_1, S_2 + x_2$ proportional to $S_1, S_2$, and apply the ratios between the former instead of the ratios between the latter.

It is true, of course, that Weber’s Law holds only approximately in external psychophysics; however, if (as is the case) the threshold is always only relatively slightly exceeded during the experiments, so that the values of $x$ remain small compared to $S$, then any possible error depending on the inaccuracy of the law in determining the correct $x$ can only carry with it errors of such a small order in determining the correct ratios of $S$ (which is what matters). Such small errors are also to be expected according to the other principle, since it is, after all, not possible to measure the threshold determination on both sides so precisely that the average does not still leave a remaining error.

Suppose, moreover, where Müller's principle and procedure at least

If one were to consider such small details at all, firstly, one would commit a fundamental error if—following Müller—one took the arithmetic mean of both determinations as the true threshold. Secondly, a correction of this error could, again, only be found within <term>Weber’s Law</term><note>A principle stating that the smallest noticeable difference between two stimuli is proportional to the intensity of the stimuli themselves.</note>, however inaccurate or accurate it may be. Since the threshold decreases as the stimuli decrease, a deviation downward from the true threshold is not equivalent to a deviation of the same amount upward. Thus, according to Weber’s Law, one should instead determine the true threshold as a <term>ratio threshold</term><note>Fechner argues that because perception is proportional, the "middle" between two measurements should be calculated geometrically (using ratios) rather than arithmetically (using simple averages).</note> by taking a geometric rather than an arithmetic mean of the oversized and undersized thresholds.

Now, I am far from wanting to actually assert these theoretical <term>minutiae</term><note>original: "Quisquilien"; Latin for trifles or waste, used here to describe insignificant academic nitpicking.</note> against Müller’s principle in a practical sense. The uncertainty of psychophysical measurements is, unfortunately, far too great for other reasons for such things to be taken into consideration; however, I hope that such things are not used against my own method either. Moreover, I believe that Müller, in his striving to analyze methods to the finest detail, would have had cause to discuss these aforementioned relationships himself, yet nothing of the sort is found in his writing.

However, our method appears to be of particular advantage for testing Weber’s Law itself, especially when it is carried out by weakening or strengthening the components of a very small stimulus difference in the same proportion. (In experiments on light, this can be done through dark glasses or by changing the external lighting.) One then observes whether the difference remains equally noticeable. Neither Müller’s nor <term>Wundt’s</term><note>Wilhelm Wundt (1832–1920), a contemporary of Fechner and a pioneer of experimental psychology.</note> procedures achieve the same result so simply.

Finally, I can point out that the method specified here, including the latter modification, has actually proven itself in practice. Indeed, I have been able to track the progression of <term>warmth-sensation differences</term> in relation to temperature differences (Elements I, page 201 ff.), and I have found the relevant modification very useful for testing Weber's Law in the field of the sense of light (Elements I, page 140). Similarly, <term>Volkmann’s</term><note>Alfred Wilhelm Volkmann (1801–1877), a physiologist and frequent collaborator of Fechner.</note> sound experiments have been successfully conducted in this regard (Elements I, page 118).

Müller finds it striking that I have categorized Volkmann’s sound experiments under the concept of the <term>method of right and wrong cases</term><note>An experimental design where subjects are asked to judge which of two stimuli is greater; the results are then analyzed statistically.</note> because they do not correspond to his definition of this method; however, they do fall entirely under the concept of the aforementioned modification of my own method.
