Now, I am not claiming that all observers have proceeded exactly as I have; for the most part, specific details on this are lacking. As a rule, if one has not followed my method, one will likely have proceeded by varying the setup of the experiment between <term>supraliminal</term><note>Noticeable; above the threshold of perception.</note> and <term>subliminal</term><note>Unnoticeable; below the threshold of perception.</note> until reaching a very small interval between them, finally stopping within that interval at a seemingly just-vanished difference. Of this point, one admittedly only knows that it falls below the true threshold by a very small, presumably negligible, amount, since the true threshold simply cannot be hit exactly. And indisputably, one can also arrive at practically useful—that is, sufficiently authoritative for the given task—ratio determinations of the threshold using this procedure (which is probably the one usually followed), provided that one keeps the final shifts of the setting between supraliminal and subliminal, within which one stops, as small as possible everywhere. I even admit that one cannot assert <term>a priori</term><note>original: "a priori"; Latin for "from the beginning" or based on theory rather than experience.</note> and without experiments specifically directed toward it, that the admitted uncertainty in the reproduction of the same small supraliminal sensation of difference in my method—which cannot be entirely eliminated even in the average of many trials—is smaller than the uncertainty of the <term>trial and error</term><note>original: "Tatonnement"; a French term for a process of "groping" or tentative experimentation.</note> between a very small supraliminal and subliminal sensation that finally leads below the difference threshold.

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s rebuttal of G. E. Müller’s criticisms. ...Müller infers from these formulas against my execution of the method in fact never occurs, nor can it occur; how then can he reproach the method with it? Indeed, in practice, I set up every individual trial so that the <term>difference</term><note>Represented by "U" for *Unterschied*.</note>, which is just then vanishing for perception, is exceeded by only a small amount, rather than by a large or even an infinite amount; and naturally, I recognize the difference in all these cases as actually present, because I am specifically adjusting the trial to that point. This is the logic of facts as opposed to the logic of Müller’s formulas and his way of utilizing those formulas.

Now, one might ask what gives me the right to claim only a slight exceeding of the true <term>threshold</term><note>Represented by "S" for *Schwellenwert*.</note> through my adjustment to a "just noticeable difference," since I do not yet know the true value of $S$ during the trials, but rather intend to deduce it from them. To this, I say the following:

Since adjusting the trial to the exact $S$ has only an infinitely small probability, I can only hit values either below $S$ or above $S$. All cases where the difference still appears as zero will be cases of the first kind; all where it is noticeable will be cases of the second kind. If I now arrange the trial in every case so that I only need to ascend a very small amount from a value below $S$ (where I still perceive no difference) to reach a value above $S$ (where I do perceive one), I will naturally exceed not only the starting point taken below $S$, but also $S$ itself by a very small amount. Correspondingly, the same applies if I need to reduce a noticeable difference by a very small amount to arrive at an unnoticeable difference. This is exactly what happens in my procedure.

Following this, we come to Müller’s own method, which he calls the **Method of Smallest Differences**, which he describes as follows (p. 63):
> "One allows an existing, clearly <term>supraliminal</term><note>Noticeable; above the threshold of perception.</note> increment to the stimulus intensity—which is to be investigated regarding its corresponding sensitivity to difference—to be decreased quite gradually at as uniform a speed as possible, while attentively comparing the two components of the difference and, as soon as the difference between the two is no longer..."

...appears noticeable, one immediately puts a stop to the reduction of the same and allows its size to be determined with the greatest possible accuracy. <meta>This page continues Fechner’s evaluation of psychophysical methods. Having previously critiqued G. E. Müller’s "Method of Just Noticeable Differences," Fechner now transitions to a method used by Julius Kollert in his study of the sense of time. Fechner aims to clarify Kollert's somewhat obscure methodology and adapt its variables to his own system of measurement.</meta>

...neither more nor less [subject to] a certain uncertainty in determining the threshold than any other method, but it allows this uncertainty to be kept within small, measured limits—free from the suspicion of constant manual errors—and accordingly to be reduced through the repetition of trials.

Unfortunately, it must be said that the procedure does not emerge with simple clarity from **Kollert's** statements about it (**Studies** p. 80 and 86) ¹); however, I hope that with the following, expressed in slightly modified phrasing, I have correctly captured the essential sense of the procedure. It should be noted beforehand that the letters T, t, ϑ, and D have a completely different meaning here than in the sections IV, V, and VI relating to the method of right and wrong cases.

The <term>difference threshold</term><note>original: "Unterschiedsschwelle"; the minimum change in a stimulus required for a person to detect a difference.</note> in the field of the <term>sense of time</term><note>original: "Zeitsinnes"; the psychological perception of durations and intervals.</note>, to which Kollert’s investigation relates, is to be regarded as the value by which a given time interval t—or the so-called <term>mean estimation value</term><note>original: "mittlere Schätzungswerth"; the average duration perceived by the subject across multiple trials</note> T, which is estimated as equal to it on average in the experiments—can be increased or decreased without the increase or decrease becoming noticeable ²). Now, let a certain time interval t be given as the <term>normal value</term><note>original: "Normalwerth"; the standard or reference stimulus.</note>, and let another interval ϑ be compared with it as a comparison value. First, let ϑ be taken as equal to t; thus, ϑ will generally appear equal to t from the outset. After this, let ϑ be decreased step-by-step in very small intervals until the difference from t becomes noticeable and, as the reduction progresses, becomes all the more decidedly noticeable. Following this, however, let ϑ be increased again in no less small, measured intervals until apparent equality with the constantly maintained normal value t occurs again. The value of ϑ where this is first the case shall be designated as t₀, and the immediately preceding value of ϑ, where ϑ still appears smaller than t, as t₁. Then the threshold limit obviously lies between t₀ and t₁, most likely—though with a certain uncertainty—at <note>Mathematical fraction: (t₀ + t₁) / 2</note> $\frac{t_0 + t_1}{2}$, which

2) The mean estimation value T, determined as specified above, can differ from t itself due to <term>constant errors</term><note>original: "constanter Fehler"; systematic biases in judgment that consistently skew results in one direction.</note>; and according to this, the difference threshold, tracked separately toward the positive and negative sides, can also take on different values depending on whether it is determined starting from t or T; but the mean of both determinations is independent of the starting value, as follows from the above representation.

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s technical breakdown of Julius Kollert's experimental method for measuring the "sense of time." uncertainty decreases in proportion as the interval between t₁ and t₀ is kept smaller. Let the value (t₀ + t₁)/2 be called ϑ₁. Now, let us proceed in reverse: starting from ϑ = t, the interval ϑ is increased until the difference from t is decidedly noticeable; then, it is decreased again in small, step-like increments until an apparent equality with t occurs once more. Let t⁰ be the value of ϑ at which this first happens, and t¹ be the immediately preceding value where ϑ still appears larger than t. The <term>threshold limit</term><note>original: "Schwellengrenze"; the specific point where a stimulus transition from being unnoticeable to noticeable.</note> between t⁰ and t¹ will now most likely—though with a certain degree of uncertainty—be found at (t⁰ + t¹)/2, which we will briefly call ϑ¹ (or ϑ₂ according to Kollert). This can also be equivalently expressed as (d₁ + d¹)/2, if one sets d₁ = ϑ₁ - t and d¹ = ϑ¹ + t, following Kollert’s notation. The absolute distance of the first threshold limit from T is T - ϑ₁ (provided ϑ₁ < T), and the distance of the second is ϑ¹ - T (provided ϑ¹ > T). Consequently, the average distance of both threshold limits from T—that is, the mean threshold itself—is [(T - ϑ₁) + (ϑ¹ - T)]/2 = (ϑ¹ - ϑ₁)/2 = (d₂ - d₁)/2, for which **Kollert** uses the designation D. Instead of using T as the reference, one could just as easily take the distance of the threshold boundaries relative to t, and would obtain the same value for D, since t (just like T) disappears from the mean value of the threshold.

Now, while **Kollert** did not explicitly state that the D found in the previous manner represents the <term>difference threshold</term><note>original: "Unterschiedsschwelle"; the minimum change in a stimulus required for a person to detect a difference.</note>, one can easily see from the preceding description that this is indeed the case. In fact, according to this, Eₘ <note>Eₘ stands for *Empfindlichkeitsmaß*, or measure of sensitivity.</note> is nothing other than the reciprocal value of the relative difference value, which, as long as <term>Weber's Law</term><note>The principle that the just-noticeable difference between two stimuli is proportional to the magnitude of the stimuli.</note> holds true, must remain constant when the magnitude of *t* is changed; thus, it can serve for the investigation of said law. To be sure, to my knowledge, this has not yet happened; and there is all the less reason to already recommend it as a universally valid model.

## IX. On the Elimination of Constant Errors in Experiments on Differential Sensitivity.

Constant errors play a major role in psychophysical measurement experiments and must be eliminated in different ways and determined according to their magnitude, depending on the diversity of methods and circumstances; I do not wish to go into generalities about this here. How this is to be done with the <term>Method of Average Error</term><note>A procedure where a subject adjusts a stimulus until it matches a standard to find the average deviation.</note> was discussed in Section VII; here, we shall concern ourselves only with the elimination of constant errors in the <term>Method of Right and Wrong Cases</term><note>original: "Methode der r. u. f. Fälle" (richtige und falsche Fälle); an experimental design where subjects judge whether a comparison stimulus is greater, smaller, or equal to a standard.</note>, whereby I proceed from a recapitulation of the presentation of the procedure regarding weight-lifting experiments given in the "Elements of Psychophysics" <note>original: "Elem." referring to Fechner's 1860 work, *Elemente der Psychophysik*.</note> Vol. I, pp. 113 ff. Let *P'* be understood, as usual, as the larger weight, *P* as the smaller weight, and *D* as the difference between them, *P' - P*.

Using the Method of Right and Wrong Cases, in the manner specified in Section IV, one obtains a value *t₀* from the "correct cases" (supplemented by half of the "doubtful cases"), i.e., from *r'/n*, by means of the <term>Fundamental Table</term><note>A table derived from the Gaussian error curve used by Fechner to convert the frequency of correct responses into a measure of sensory precision.</note>. If no constant errors are present, this *t₀* is simply set equal to *hD*. By dividing this by *D*, one obtains the measure of differential sensitivity *h*, the acquisition of which is the primary objective of this method.

Now, however, it is found that *t₀* changes depending on whether *P'* or *P* is lifted first, or whether *P'* is positioned to the right or left of *P* (which entails a different way of handling the weights or encounters a different sensitivity in the hands)—in short, according to the different temporal and spatial arrangement of the weights relative to one another—and

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of psychophysical measurement, transitioning from specific experimental data to the general theory of "constant errors"—systematic biases like the order in which a person perceives two stimuli—and how to mathematically cancel them out.</meta>

One can now imagine that $D$ <note>The stimulus difference between two objects being compared.</note>, depending on the *opposition* of the position, is *seemingly* increased or decreased by a *constant error* (in the sense used earlier on page 40). Let this error be called $p$ with respect to the *time position* and $q$ with respect to the *spatial position*. Should a series of trials be conducted in only one of these positions—for example, where $D$ appears enlarged in both *time and space*, such that $t_0 = h(D + p + q)$—one could no longer obtain $h$ <note>The precision measure, representing the subject's sensitivity.</note> by simply dividing $t_0$ by $D$, but only by dividing it by $D + p + q$. However, since we only know the direction of the constant errors and not their magnitude, this is not feasible. Yet, we can achieve our goal by another route—namely, through the *elimination* of $p$ and $q$. This is done by conducting trials in both *opposing time and space positions*, assuming that the constant errors occurring therein have opposite signs, and taking the average of the $t_0$ values obtained. This average leads back to $hD$, provided that $p$ cancels out with $-p$ and $q$ with $-q$ in this average; whereby one can obtain $h$ by dividing this average by $D$ just as if no constant errors were present at all.

In the event that either only *time errors* or only *space errors* are present, the average of two $t_0$ values obtained in opposing time or space positions is sufficient. However, in the more general case—which certainly occurs in weight-lifting experiments—where both *time errors* and *space errors* are present, there are 4 *combinations* of positions. Trials must be conducted for these, leading to 4 $t_0$ values from which the average is taken: 1) where the time error $p$ and the space error $q$ both work to increase $D$; 2) where $p$ is negative (working to decrease $D$) and $q$ is positive (working to increase $D$); 3) where $p$ is positive (working to increase $D$) and $q$ is negative (working to decrease $D$); 4) where both $p$ and $q$ are negative (working to decrease $D$). By designating the $t_0$ values obtained in these 4 combinations as $t_1, t_2, t_3, t_4$ respectively, we have

Since there is no reason to assume that these two different combination methods would deviate from the "true" value in the same direction, one can expect an even closer approximation to the truth by taking both together. This is something that must be done anyway, because with smaller trial numbers, $t_1 + t_4$ often deviates quite considerably from $t_2 + t_3$, without there being any specific reason so far to prefer one combination over the other.

Consequently, I believe that discussions which call into question the adequacy of the procedure, without being able to present a more adequate one, lack practical interest. They would only possess theoretical interest if we had sufficient knowledge of the nature and efficacy of the causes of constant errors to provide a secure foundation for the investigation.

## X. Logarithmic Treatment of the Methods of Measurement.

In all methods of measuring the sensitivity to differences <term>Unterschiedsempfindlichkeit: The capacity to perceive the difference between two stimuli, such as weights or light intensity.</term>, one deals with two stimuli, A and B, which differ in magnitude. Now, while these have a **difference (D) = B — A**, they simultaneously have a ratio **B / A**, which we shall call **P**. According to a simple rule within the limits of the validity of Weber's Law <note>The principle that the smallest perceptible change in a stimulus is a constant ratio of the original stimulus.</note>—beyond which no simple rule exists at all—sensations of difference depend rather on the logarithms of the stimulus ratios than on the stimulus differences. That is, they are not generally equal when the differences of the stimuli are **D**, but rather when the stimulus ratios are **P**, and consequently their logarithms...

...are equal, and change proportionally to the logarithms of the **stimulus ratios**. Therefore, it is inherently more accurate to consider the **sensations of difference** <term>Unterschiedsempfindungen: the internal psychological perception that two stimuli, like two weights, are not the same</term>, which we deal with in our measurement methods, in relation to the logarithms of the real and apparent stimulus ratios—that is, to the ratios $\mathfrak{P}$—rather than to the stimulus differences $D$. However, since it is a known property of logarithms that in cases where a stimulus ratio $\frac{B}{A} = \frac{A + D}{A} = 1 + \frac{D}{A}$ deviates only slightly from unity—meaning $D$ is a small ratio compared to its starting value $A$—the difference is nearly proportional to the logarithm of the ratio. In such cases, one can substitute the difference $D$ for the logarithm of the ratio ($\log \mathfrak{P}$), which offers the advantage of greater simplicity in deriving measurement values, albeit at the expense of total mathematical rigor.

Insofar as we now substitute the logarithms of the stimulus ratios for the arithmetic differences of the stimuli according to this strict interpretation, I distinguish these two ways of handling the methods as **arithmetic** and **logarithmic**. I should first note in general that regarding the experimental procedure, the transition from the former to the latter treatment brings about no changes at all; they affect only the calculation process and its results. In this regard, the following should be noted:

As far as the **method of right and wrong cases** <term>r. u. f. F.: Abbreviation for "richtige und falsche Fälle," a classic experimental design where a subject compares two stimuli and the researcher records the frequency of correct versus incorrect detections of difference</term> is concerned, I can as before find a value $t_0$ from the **fundamental table** <note>This refers to a table of the probability integral (Gaussian distribution) used to convert the percentage of correct answers into a measure of sensory precision.</note>, only now it is not set equal to $hD$, but to $h \log \mathfrak{P} = h \log \frac{B}{A}$. By dividing this value by the given $\log \mathfrak{P}$, I obtain $h$ (the measure of precision) just as simply as by the arithmetic route, i.e.

-> $h = \frac{t_0}{\log \mathfrak{P}}.$ <-

As for the **threshold** $T$ <term>Schwelle: the point at which a stimulus or a difference between stimuli becomes just barely perceptible</term>, according to the logarithmic treatment, this will translate into the logarithm of the ratio which must be exceeded in order to make the **sensation of a difference** <note>original: "E. eines U." (Empfindung eines Unterschiedes)</note> noticeable. In this sense, one has:

-> $T = \frac{t_{II} - t_I}{t_0} \log \mathfrak{P},$ <-

from which the relevant ratio itself can be found.

If, given a starting stimulus $A$, one continuously increases the value $D$ and consequently $B = A + D$, then according to the arithmetic treatment of the...

While, according to the above, the method of right and wrong cases does not change so much in the execution of the calculation as in the interpretation of the final results when transitioning from arithmetic to logarithmic treatment, this transition leads to a very laborious calculation in the **method of average error** <term>m. F.: "mittleren Fehler," where a subject attempts to adjust a variable stimulus to match a standard stimulus</term>. In this case, it is necessary to translate the obtained error magnitudes $f$ individually into logarithms. The method of right and wrong cases offers no reason for this, since it provides only counts <note>the frequency of right versus wrong answers</note> rather than the actual size of the errors; Section IV should be consulted for more on this.

In the method of just noticeable differences <term>e. m. U.: "eben merklichen Unterschiede," the smallest difference between two stimuli that a person can detect</term>, it is sufficient when transitioning from arithmetic to logarithmic treatment to replace every found "just noticeable" difference $D$ between $A$ and $B$ with $\log \frac{B}{A}$.

While the arithmetic treatment of the methods of average error and just noticeable differences requires the positive difference threshold <term>U. Schw.: "Unterschiedsschwelle," the point at which a difference is perceived</term> to be considered somewhat different from the negative one, the ratio-threshold obtained through logarithmic treatment is to be assumed equal both upward and downward (See p. 47, Note).

One may observe that as the **Gaussian law of probability** <note>Also known as the Normal Distribution or "bell curve," which describes how data points cluster around an average</note> transfers from the external differences $D$ to the logarithms of the stimulus ratios—following the logarithmic treatment of the methods of right/wrong cases and average error—it consequently transfers to the sensations of difference measured by them, which are proportional to those logarithms. There is no mathematical obstacle to applying the Gaussian law to the logarithms of ratios, provided these logarithms behave like arithmetic differences that extend in opposite directions from a zero point (occurring where $\frac{A}{B} = 1$). Furthermore, in my investigations into the measurements of **collective objects** <term>Collectivgegenstände: Fechner’s term for groups of data or populations that are subject to statistical laws</term>, I have become convinced that their deviations from the most probable (so-called **most dense**) value <term>dichtesten Werthe: In modern terms, the "mode," or the most frequent value in a distribution</term> are treated more soundly—that is, more consistent with experience—according to a logarithmic rather than an arithmetic principle, in cases which generally—

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s technical discussion on why logarithmic calculations are superior to arithmetic ones when measuring sensory perception. He is specifically addressing how to cancel out "constant errors"—biases caused by the order or position in which a subject experiences stimuli—by treating them as ratios rather than simple additions or subtractions.</meta>

...are suitable for leading to a decision, though I cannot go into more detail here.

As already noted in the previous section, the elimination of constant errors in the **method of right and wrong cases** <term>r. u. f. F.: Abbreviation for "richtigen und falschen Fälle," a foundational psychophysical test where a person judges which of two stimuli is greater</term> will, strictly speaking, also be traced back to the principle of logarithmic treatment. This means that the compensation required for elimination—occurring in opposing temporal and spatial positions—can only take place if $\mathfrak{P}$ <note>the ratio between two stimuli being compared</note> is increased by a ratio $p$ in one temporal position and decreased by that same ratio in the other. One must therefore consider $p$ not as arithmetic additions $\pm p$ to $D$ <note>the physical difference between stimuli</note>, but as proportional changes $p$ and $\frac{1}{p}$ regarding $\mathfrak{P}$. In this way, through one temporal position $\mathfrak{P}$ becomes $p \mathfrak{P}$, and through the opposite position it becomes $\frac{\mathfrak{P}}{p}$. Consequently, $\log p \mathfrak{P} = \log \mathfrak{P} + \log p$ compensates with $\log \frac{\mathfrak{P}}{p} = \log \mathfrak{P} - \log p$ when combined and averaged to reach $\log \mathfrak{P}$. The same applies to the spatial error $q$.

Accordingly, due to the combination of temporal and spatial errors across the four opposing positions as $pq$, $\frac{q}{p}$, $\frac{p}{q}$, and $\frac{1}{pq}$, the elimination equations for the case of truly complete compensation are as follows:

->t~1~ = h (log $\mathfrak{P}$ + log p + log q)<-
->t~2~ = h (log $\mathfrak{P}$ — log p + log q)<-
->t~3~ = h (log $\mathfrak{P}$ + log p — log q)<-
->t~4~ = h (log $\mathfrak{P}$ — log p — log q)<-

By adding the four $t$ values and taking the mean, we arrive at a complete elimination just as we do with arithmetic treatment. However, as is fundamentally more correct, we obtain $h \log \mathfrak{P}$ as the mean $t_0$ instead of $h D$.

In my "Elements" <note>referring to Fechner's 1860 book, *Elemente der Psychophysik* (Elements of Psychophysics)</note>, the logarithmic treatment of measurement methods is not yet found, because I had not yet arrived at it then. On the whole, it is of more theoretical than practical interest.

## XI. On the Question of the Reciprocal Proportionality of the Measure of Precision and the Difference Threshold.

It is to be regarded as a merit of Müller’s <note>Georg Elias Müller (1850–1934), a prominent experimental psychologist who refined many of Fechner’s theories</note> that he not only raised the above question but also, as far as data were available to him, successfully investigated it himself (p. 96 ff., 197 ff.), specifically using two of my larger weight-experiment series according to the **method of right and wrong cases** <term>r. u. f. F.: Abbreviation for "richtigen und falschen Fälle," a foundational test where a subject judges which of two stimuli is heavier</term>—one two-handed (No. 6) and one one-handed (No. 1)—which I placed at his disposal at his request. In both, the weights *P* vary from 300 to 3000 grams, with associated *D*’s <note>the physical difference between the standard and comparison weights</note> = 0.04 and 0.08 *P*. If one now understands the measure of precision *h* and the difference threshold *S* as they were conceived and calculated by him (for which Section IV should be compared), then the inverse proportionality between *h* and *S*—or, what amounts to the same thing, the constancy of *hS*—was found to be very well confirmed when progressing through the six *P*’s in the two-handed series. Meanwhile, in the one-handed series, a somewhat different relationship between *h* and *S* emerged for the experiment with the right hand (R) than with the left (L); thus, *hS* also took on a slightly different value for R than for L. Apart from this, however, he also found (p. 335) "certain results that have emerged in the investigations of Delboeuf <note>Joseph Delboeuf, known for experiments on light and weight perception</note>, the visual measurement experiments of Volkmann, and the electric light experiments of Masson, pointing toward an inversely proportional or at least analogous relationship between those two quantities," according to which he acknowledges a very far-reaching, though not unconditional, validity of the same.

Now, it is true that Müller’s measure of precision *h*, as it refers merely to the accidental apparent changes of the smaller weight, is not to be confused in itself with our measure of precision *h*, which is to be referred to the apparent changes in the difference between both weights; and likewise, Müller’s difference threshold *S* is not identical to my difference threshold *S = T/2* <note>In Fechner's notation, $S$ represents the threshold where a difference is just barely perceptible; $T$ often refers to the 'total' interval of uncertainty</note>. Yet, Müller’s *h* and my *h*, and Müller’s *S* and my *S* run parallel to one another in this regard, and I have convinced myself through my own calculations—not only in those two experimental series—that the same result Müller found regarding his *h* and *S* is recovered regarding my *h* and *S*. Furthermore, prompted by Müller's investigation, I have since examined my other weight-experiment series regarding the question of to what extent *h* and *S*...

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s analysis of the relationship between the measure of precision (h) and the perception threshold (T). He is specifically testing whether their product (hT) remains constant across various experimental conditions, a key tenet of his psychophysical laws.</meta>

...or whether instead $h$ and $T$, calculated according to my method, follow a reciprocal path when various circumstances are altered—meaning whether $hT$ (which I abbreviate as $E$) remains constant or not. I have found the following results:

Let $P$ represent, as always, the smaller or main weight <note>The "standard" weight used for comparison</note>, $P' = P + D$ the larger weight, and $D$ the difference between the two. Provided that all experimental circumstances and the methods themselves are kept identical (aside from the specific differences to be noted between the compared series of trials), then—setting aside random variations that remain uncompensated due to the finite number of observations—the value $hT = t_{II} - t_{I} = E$ remains constant:

1) When the difference $D$ changes while $P'$ remains constant.
2) When $P$ and $D$ change in a proportional relationship to one another.
3) When the time-space positions—and thus the **constant errors** <term>constant errors: systematic biases in judgment caused by the order in which stimuli are presented or their physical position relative to the subject</term>—change.
4) When the state of fatigue of the hand changes.
5) When the duration of lifting, or the interval between the two components of each double-lifting, changes within certain limits; however, it remains questionable whether this holds outside of these limits.

In contrast, generally speaking, $E$ changes depending on whether the lifting is performed with the left or right hand in a one-handed procedure. It also changes—indeed, often to a much greater degree—if one conducts experiments with the same hand or hands at such different times that one can no longer be certain of the same state of the sensing organ. In these cases, the sensing organ (which is inherently different in different hands) becomes, so to speak, a "different" organ. 

Remarkably, however, as noted under point 4, the state of fatigue of the hand leaves the value $E$ unchanged<sup>1)</sup>. This is attributable to the fact that, according to the **parallel law** <term>Parallelgesetz: Fechner’s principle stating that changes in internal sensitivity (like fatigue) affect the perception of the stimulus in a way that is mathematically equivalent to changing the intensity of the physical stimulus itself</term>, the internal fatigue of the organ caused by a stimulus is equivalent in its effect to a reduction of the external stimulus; and as shown in the combination of points 1 and 2, the value of $E$ does not depend on the magnitude of that stimulus.

To share the specific evidence for the preceding statements would lead too far here; I must reserve this for a future, more specialized publication of my weight experiments, should that still be possible to achieve.

1) This is confirmed by conducting the same experiments for comparison immediately before and after the intermediate lifting of very heavy, and thus highly fatiguing, weights; or by periodically alternating between light and heavy weights during the experiments themselves and comparing the resulting values of $E$.

The number of trials ($n$) was 346 for both No. 1 and No. 2, and the results obtained were:

| | r/n | f/n | z/n | E |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| **No. 1** | 0.564 | 0.112 | 0.324 | 0.7459 |
| **No. 2** | 0.410 | 0.205 | 0.385 | 0.7436 |

Whether one calculates according to Division Principle I or II <note>Fechner used different statistical methods (Principles) to handle "doubtful" judgments where the subject could not perceive a difference</note>, this yields the notably similar values for $E$ shown above for No. 1 and No. 2. Meanwhile, the measure of precision $h$ is found to be 0.4248 for No. 1 and 0.1837 for No. 2 (according to Division Principle I).

To Müller <note>Likely Georg Elias Müller, a pioneer in experimental psychology who often critiqued or refined Fechner's work</note>, the inverse proportionality of $h$ with $S$ <note>Original: "proportionalität des h mit S". $S$ likely refers to the sensitivity or threshold value in this context</note> was initially striking and unexpected, based on his own way of calculating these values and the extent to which he admitted them from his own investigations. However, he subsequently tried (p. 334 ff.) to relate this to his assumptions about the nature and conditions of random error processes and the physiological view of Weber’s Law <term>Weber's Law: the principle that the just-noticeable difference between two stimuli is proportional to the magnitude of the stimuli</term>. I find it unnecessary to go into this, as those very assumptions have proven untenable—for which Section III should be consulted.

For my part, I have the following to say regarding the subject at hand.

Let $\alpha$ be the apparent deviations from the difference $D$ given in the experiment, caused by random chance. Thus $T$ <note>the threshold of perception</note> is a difference $\alpha' - \alpha$ between two values $\alpha'$ and $\alpha$, which contains the $\frac{z}{n}$ <note>the frequency of doubtful cases</note>, and, insofar as $h = \frac{1}{a_n \sqrt{\pi}}$, then

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s mathematical derivation of the constant $E$ (the product of precision $h$ and the threshold $T$). -> E = h T = $\frac{\alpha' - \alpha,}{\alpha_n \sqrt{\pi}}$ <-

If $h$ <note>$h$ represents the "measure of precision" in the Gaussian distribution; a higher $h$ means measurements are more tightly clustered around the truth</note> now changes in a certain proportion, then $\alpha_n$ <note>$\alpha_n$ is a value related to the average error or spread of observations</note> changes in the inverse proportion; and, as long as the Gaussian Law <term>Gaussian Law: the law of normal distribution, often called the "bell curve," which describes how data points naturally cluster around an average</term> holds, every value of $\alpha$ that has a specific probability changes in a corresponding proportion to $\alpha_n$.

Thus, $hT$ may very well remain constant, provided that $\alpha'$ and $\alpha$ <note>$\alpha'$ and $\alpha$ represent the upper and lower limits of the "threshold of difference"—the points where a subject can just barely tell two stimuli apart</note> change in the same proportion as $\alpha_n$, and it even seems self-evident at first that this would generally be the case. Yet it is not necessary, for it could be that the $\alpha'$ and $\alpha$ which changed in the same proportion as $\alpha_n$ no longer contain the same ratio of "doubtful" cases ($z/n$) between them, and thus can no longer be considered threshold limits. The reported experiences teach us that this is indeed not the case when the subjective conditions of the psychophysical system change in a certain respect, whereas changes in objective, external conditions—as well as internal changes in fatigue and attention—do not affect it.

The value $E$ is therefore of importance insofar as, when derived from a sufficient number of observations, its constancy or variation between two series of trials tells us whether the internal state of the psychophysical system <term>psychophysical system: the complex relationship between physical stimuli and the resulting mental sensations</term> has remained comparable or not. However, it is still unknown which specific changes in the psychophysical system cause the changes in $E$.

It should be noted well that the variability of $E$ according to internal circumstances has no influence on the validity of Weber’s Law <term>Weber’s Law: the principle that the smallest change in a stimulus that can be detected is a constant proportion of the original stimulus</term>, whether it is applied to the threshold or to the deviations $\alpha$, provided that the validation occurs while the state of $E$ remains constant.

# Third Section.

## Psychophysical Laws.

### XII. On the Question of the Validity of Weber’s Law.

The expression of **Weber's Law** <term>Weber’s Law: the principle that the smallest detectable change in a stimulus is a constant proportion of the original stimulus, rather than a constant absolute amount</term> is briefly stated as follows: the sensation of difference between two stimuli does not change if the stimuli maintain the same ratio to each other when their absolute magnitude changes—consequently, if their relative difference remains the same. Depending on the so-called **psychophysical** or **physiological** view, this law can be interpreted in different ways regarding the question of whether it can be transferred from the "outer" to the "inner"—that is, from the physical stimulus to the internal psychophysical activity. This, however, will not be addressed here, but only in Section XV. For now, I wish to focus anew on the question of its empirical validity in **outer psychophysics** <term>Outer Psychophysics: the study of the relationship between the external physical stimulus and the resulting mental sensation</term>, as the discussion led by **Müller** <note>Georg Elias Müller (1850–1934), a prominent experimental psychologist who frequently critiqued Fechner's work</note> on this matter seems to make this investigation far from redundant.

The experiments testing Weber’s Law, as far as they were available to me during the writing of my *Elements* <note>Original: *Elemente der Psychophysik* (1860), Fechner's foundational text on the subject</note>, are cited there in Volume I, page 134 ff. (1860). In my later work *In Matter* <note>Original: *In Sachen der Psychophysik* (In the Matter of Psychophysics), published in 1877</note> on pages 148 ff., they were partly summarized and partly supplemented by findings that became known to me after that first writing. Müller, in his own publication (1878) from page 102 onwards, also provided a compilation and critique of the relevant experiments independently of me. This compilation overlaps with mine regarding the facts but also supplements them, though we often diverge significantly in our interpretations and critiques.

Regarding how we supplement each other, I must acknowledge that Müller (pages 114, 164, 173, 188, 208, 215) has considered many empirical investigations that I overlooked; meanwhile, only a few investigations I considered (*In Matter*, pages 160 and 200) were overlooked by Müller.

Müller (page 813) criticizes me for involving the **sense of time** <note>Original: *Zeitsinn*; our mental capacity to perceive the passage of time and the duration of events</note> in the question of the validity of Weber's Law, arguing that in this sense it is “not in the least a matter of comparing differ-

...intensities of sensation." To which I ask: what can prevent generalizing the question of the validity of the law in question beyond the comparison of different intensities of sensation? The more various the fields in which its validity is proven—or at least an approximation of it is shown—the more, by inductive reasoning, the probability of its fundamental validity in general increases. That differences in time are something else than differences in intensity, I believe I know as well as anyone, just as I know that differences in pitch <term>Pitch: the perceived highness or lowness of a tone, which Fechner distinguishes from the "intensity" or loudness of the sound</term> are not the same as differences in the strength of tones; yet, for the reason stated above, I consider the question important whether Weber's Law does not extend just as well to the former as to the latter. 

To reproach me, Müller <note>Georg Elias Müller</note> would first have had to show that I really transfer the law from one field to another based on mere analogy; on the contrary, I have demanded specific experiments for each individual field. Now, while I find that the invalidity of the law in the field of pitch—which has been fairly well demonstrated by Preyer <note>William Thierry Preyer (1841–1897), an English-German physiologist known for his work in developmental psychology and sensory perception</note>—proves nothing against its validity for differences in brightness and sound intensity, I am nevertheless sorry to see a support for the general validity of the law as a whole lost by it. On the other hand, I continue to see a not insignificant support for it in its validity for the relationships of **"physical and moral fortune"** <note>original: *“fortune physique et morale”*; a concept from Daniel Bernoulli and Pierre-Simon Laplace suggesting that the subjective value of money (moral fortune) increases logarithmically relative to the actual amount of money (physical fortune)</note> (*"Elements"* I. 236 ff.). 

Also, without placing too much weight on it, one may consider a very peculiar application which, following the conclusion of this section, can be made from Weber's Law to the circumstance that time seems to run faster for us the older we get <note>Fechner is suggesting that our perception of a year's duration is relative to the total number of years we have already lived; to a five-year-old, a year is 20% of their life, but to a fifty-year-old, it is only 2%</note>. But let us first turn to the main question which must occupy us, which certainly has to refer to the validity of the law in the field of stimulus intensities <term>Stimulus Intensity: the physical energy of a stimulus, such as the brightness of a light or the pressure of a weight</term>, only to return at the very end to the question concerning other fields.

### 1) The Question in the Field of Stimulus Intensities.

The relationship between Müller's and my way of considering the experiments related to this is generally this:

Both of us must acknowledge that the law in outer psychophysics—that is, according to experiments with external stimuli—shows itself to be of only limited validity, yet in a majority of cases it holds very approximately; according to which the question arises whether more weight is to be placed on the deviations or on the success, so far as it takes place...

is. The former occurs on **Müller’s** part, the latter on **mine**. While I myself regard it as a fundamental law of great generality, which is only more or less disturbed by side conditions <note>The "side conditions" Fechner refers to are external or internal variables—like fatigue or lighting inconsistencies—that interfere with pure experimental results.</note> that one cannot avoid during experiments, **Müller** is inclined to turn the deviations produced by these conditions against the fundamental significance of the law itself. He does this by either not accepting the reasons I have asserted for these deviations, or by not considering them sufficient; indeed, he even counts the deviations from the law as part of the law itself, and accordingly wishes to see no actual deviations in it at all (p. 225).

Now I certainly believe that, however far one may push a <term>Specialdiscussion: a detailed, specialized analysis of specific data points or experimental conditions</term> of the relevant experiments, an absolutely *certain* experimental decision between these two views will not be gained in this way. Instead, everyone will still have the *possibility* of siding with one or the other based on their general views, where in particular the difference between the *physiological* and *psychophysical* view of the relationship between physical and psychic changes comes into consideration. But certainly, the *specialized discussion* can contribute significantly to making one view of the law more or less plausible: either as a fundamental law frequently disturbed only by secondary causes, or as a law inseparable from its deviations, which I have supposedly inflated without merit in its validity, importance, and significance. The following observations will focus on this.

In this regard, there exists from the outset a certain contrast between *light experiments* and *sound experiments*. Generally speaking, light experiments present sources of error that are difficult to eliminate and difficult to estimate. Even if they nevertheless allow the law to be recognized everywhere within certain limits and with a certain approximation, those limits and approximations vary greatly depending on the method and the observer. By contrast, sound experiments are inherently freer from demonstrable or suspected sources of error. Using two very different methods, carried out by two different independent observers (**Volkmann** <note>Alfred Wilhelm Volkmann (1801–1877), a German physiologist and close collaborator of Fechner</note> and **Nörr**), these experiments have led to a similarly far-reaching confirmation of *Weber’s Law*. One can therefore find it *probable* that, if light experiments were conducted under similarly favorable circumstances as the sound experiments, the law would also be confirmed more generally and across wider limits than has already been shown. ...hidden enough, and yet it emerges with the most desirable approximation in the light experiments of Delboeuf (*In the Matter of Psychophysics* <note>original: "In Sachen"</note> p. 178 ff.), Dobrowolsky (*In the Matter of Psychophysics* p. 159), my own experiments (*Elements of Psychophysics* <note>original: "Elem."</note> I. 140 ff.), and in the estimations of stellar magnitudes <note>This refers to the ancient system of ranking stars by brightness, which was later found to be a logarithmic scale, perfectly illustrating Weber's Law before the law was even formally defined.</note>; and even in Aubert's and Helmholtz's experiments, which people are most inclined to assert against the law, a strong approximation of it is not missing within the limits of ordinary vision, and is acknowledged by Helmholtz himself. Now, the experimental methods of those observers are different from these; and if the former have generally given a more favorable result than the latter, then according to the principle that a law can be more easily disturbed and hidden by sources of error of any kind than it can gain an apparent confirmation through them, one can suspect from the start that sources of error have gained less influence in those methods of observation than in these. To be sure, regarding Delboeuf's and my light experiments, one must not merely stick to Müller’s report on them, but also take into account what I will have to say against this report.

Now consider the beautiful confirmation that Weber's Law has received through Volkmann's and my **visual measurement** <note>German: *Augenmaß*. This refers to the ability to judge distances or sizes by eye.</note> experiments, which can be included here because they undoubtedly relate much more to intensive **muscular sensations** <note>Fechner argues that judging distance is not just a visual act but involves the physical sensation of the muscles controlling the eye's focus and position.</note> than to actual extensive sensations. Even Chodin's visual measurement experiments, despite their impractical method of setup, allow the law on the whole to prevail over the deviations; and to this, Wundt's experiments on changes in the convergence of the ocular axes also support the law. To be sure, regarding Volkmann's experiments, one must again not rely on Müller's report alone. (Compare the later section on the visual measurement experiments).

Furthermore, with the well-motivated addition of a constant, Weber’s Law is confirmed in the best possible way by my as well as Hering's **weight** experiments, and the most self-consistent experiments by Keppler on the sense of **taste** agree best with Weber's Law (*In the Matter of Psychophysics* p. 161 ff.).

And what has Müller to set against this overview? With his usual sharp-wittedness, he nitpicks as much as possible at every individual investigation, yet he still cannot break the weight of the evidence for the law as a whole.

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s systematic defense of Weber’s Law. On the previous page, he discussed how different experimental methods (such as those by Delboeuf or Helmholtz) can lead to different results, suggesting that apparent deviations are often the result of experimental "noise" or errors rather than a flaw in the law itself.</meta>

However many empirical deviations from the law exist for immediate observation, these cannot be considered true deviations—those that would challenge the law’s fundamental significance—when the incidental circumstances they depend on are demonstrable or can be assumed with great probability, or when they reveal themselves through the calculation itself as merely complicating factors. Indeed, how many deviations remain that do not fall under these categories? Even where this is not definitely the case or does not suffice, the possibility of unrecognized incidental circumstances still remains, given the nature of the situation.

Constant errors are to be named as the most general cause of deviations in the aforementioned context. In some cases, these can be eliminated by reversing the experimental conditions—such as the positioning in time and space—as is done in weight experiments <note>Fechner refers to the practice of switching the order or hand in which weights are lifted to cancel out biases like "time errors" (the tendency to judge the second stimulus differently just because it came second).</note>. Insofar as this is possible, no one would consider a deviation from Weber's Law to be established by results that, without such elimination, would occur to a high degree for each time and space position individually. But in other cases, they cannot be eliminated in this way because no reversal of experimental conditions is possible regarding them. However, elimination can still occur if the measurement values obtained through the experiments can be mathematically decomposed into a constant part and a part that obeys Weber's Law; where this is the case, a true deviation from Weber's Law cannot be assumed. This applies to the <term>lower deviation</term> <note>This refers to discrepancies observed at very low levels of stimulus intensity, near the threshold of perception, where the law often seems to lose precision.</note> in weight experiments, as well as the small lower deviations noticeable only in micrometric experiments during visual measurement trials. In the former experiments, the constant cause—which cannot be "reversed" or set against itself—can be found, at least in part, in the <term>arm weight</term> <note>German: *Armgewicht*. Fechner argues that the physical weight of the participant's own arm acts as a constant "internal" stimulus that adds to the "external" weights being lifted, thereby skewing the results if not accounted for.</note>, which adds itself to all lifted weights. In visual measurement experiments, its nature is problematic; however, this does not prevent the resulting deviation from being seen merely as a complication of Weber’s Law, provided that the law reveals itself clearly through the calculation once the complication is accounted for. Now, however, there is no lack of experiments—particularly in the field of light sensation—which have not even avoided the avoidable causes of constant errors and are nevertheless asserted against Weber’s Law.

To the previous reasons for empirical deviations from Weber's Law, two more are added, which were already discussed in *In the Matter of Psychophysics* <note>original: "*In Sachen*" (referring to his 1877 book, *In Sachen der Psychophysik*)</note> p. 51,

Now, if Müller (p. 229) <note>Referring to Georg Elias Müller (1850–1934), a younger psychologist who critically revised Fechner’s work.</note> takes all possible deviations from Weber's Law—regardless of what they depend on—wholesale into his so-called corrected measurement formulas (to be discussed later in Section XV), by giving them a corresponding indeterminacy without considering the incidental character of these deviations, and with the claim of having established in those formulas the truly fundamental ones to which one must return in the theoretical treatment of psychophysics, then I must confess—apart from everything that could be objected to these formulas in detail—that I do not understand what is supposed to be gained for a real insight into the psychophysical fundamental relationships or for a rational treatment of psychophysics in general.

There is, so to speak, a great deal of external rubble clinging to the law, from which the law must be purified; however, Müller's corrected formulas incorporate this rubble into the law itself, and with this and from this, one is expected to build. But if even outer psychophysics <term>Outer Psychophysics: The study of the relationship between an external physical stimulus and the resulting sensation</term> gains no fruit from this, how is an inner psychophysics <term>Inner Psychophysics: The study of the relationship between internal physiological/neural activity and sensation</term> supposed to base itself upon the outer psychophysics, a point which Müller does not even reach?

The preceding was only a general overview. In detail, I do not wish to return to everything that has already been said in the *Elements*, Part I, Section IX, and further in *In the Matter of Psychophysics* (Sections V, VI, VII, XVI, XVII, XVIII) regarding the question of validity and the corroborative experiments of the law. ### a) Light.

Above all, I must return here to the question—previously treated but not yet settled—of what role natural light or the so-called brightness of the <term>eye-black</term> <note>Fechner uses the term "Augenschwarz" (eye-black) to describe the "gray" sensation one perceives in total darkness, caused by the internal activity of the visual system.</note> plays in the occurrence of the lower deviation from Weber's Law in the field of light sensation. That such a deviation occurs here is certain and was first explicitly noted by myself. However, if one cannot help but acknowledge $^1$ that the sensation of a pure black in the closed eye—like the black we perceive upon objective observation of a black velvet or soot surface—is only the lowest level of brightness sensation accessible to us according to the structure of our visual organ, and which is clearly distinguishable from the "not-seeing" of the ear or finger, and which can increase through transitions to the highest brightness, then it is also certain that the existence of this subjective brightness is at least a contributing factor, if not the sole or main reason, for the lower deviation; and the only question can be whether it also suffices to explain the lower deviation. I absolutely admit that this cannot be asserted with certainty based on the investigations available so far, but I claim that the opposite can just as little be asserted, as is done by Aubert, Müller, and others; and after recapitulating what is necessary to place the question in context, I will go into it more closely in the following.

If we briefly denote with **c** the weak <term>psychophysical</term> <note>Abbreviated as "ps.-ph." in the original text.</note> excitation of the visual organ, upon which the subjective brightness of the eye-black depends without any external light stimulus, then we can think of this **c** as equivalent to a value of external light stimulus that would be capable of producing an equal brightness by evoking an equal <term>psychophysical</term> excitation. Let the intensity of the external light generally be called **i**, and at different strengths respectively **i'** and **i,,**; then every **i** that falls on a spot on the retina is to be viewed as increased by **c**, and for the validity of Weber’s Law in its thorough formulation, one must not demand that the perceived difference of two external brightnesses remains the same when their absolute strength changes if their ratio $\frac{i'}{i_{\prime}}$ remains the same, but rather the entire ratio

Now, Müller attributes the error to Volkmann’s earlier experiments and attempts (p. 117) to characterize the apparent confirmation of <term>Weber’s Law</term> <note>Weber's Law states that the smallest change in a stimulus that can be detected is a constant proportion of the original stimulus.</note> in those studies as a mere illusion by asserting a specific circumstance that supposedly did not affect the later experiments. > "We have already emphasized that in Volkmann’s earlier experiments, due to the sometimes very small distance of the two lights from the white board, the shadow of the rod probably had noticeably diffuse boundaries. Müller enters into further detail on this point.

However, it is highly unlikely from the outset that, while conducting a series of experiments across very different light distances from the board, the conditions of the penumbra should have always led precisely to the apparent confirmation of Weber’s Law; and we have nothing to support this but Müller’s vague suspicion, without any direct experiments on the effect of the penumbra in this regard. But even if the contradiction between Volkmann’s later and earlier experiments could be resolved in this way, it still, as noted, does not resolve the conflict with the experiments of other observers using different methods, where there is no question of a penumbra.

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s discussion regarding potential errors in previous psychophysical experiments. He specifically addresses how the physical size of a stimulus (like a shadow) affects whether Weber's Law appears to hold true, citing work by Förster, Aubert, and Volkmann.</meta>

...no information can be found in the earlier experiments ("Elem." <note>Likely referring to Fechner’s 1860 foundational work, *Elemente der Psychophysik* (Elements of Psychophysics), Volume I, page 149.</note>). However, it is already known from other contexts that the size of the light or dark field—the difference of which from a surrounding background is being observed—has an influence on the outcome of experiments concerning <term>just noticeable differences</term> <note>The "just noticeable difference" (JND) is the smallest detectable change in a stimulus. Fechner argues here that if the area being looked at is too small, it becomes harder to see these changes.</note>, an influence that has not yet been sufficiently explained. As the size of the field in question decreases, its distinguishability from the background also decreases. Observations on this matter are available from **Förster** ("On Night Blindness" <note>Original: *Über Hemeralopie*, Breslau 1857. Richard Förster was an ophthalmologist who studied how we perceive light.</note>), from **Aubert** (*Physiology of the Retina* <note>Original: *Physiologie der Netzhaut*, p. 83.</note>), and from **Volkmann** (*Physiological Investigations* <note>Original: *Physiologische Untersuchungen*, Vol I, p. 57 ff.</note>). This might lead one to assume that the ease of differentiation grows with the number of points to be distinguished by their brightness—a concept that is not improbable in itself, but which can remain an open question here.

At the same time, however, **Volkmann’s** experiments (p. 61 of his treatise) teach us that this influence of size decreases rapidly as the field grows larger; thus, beyond a certain limit, it should no longer be noticeable. And so the suspicion arises that, just as the smallness of a shadow influences the magnitude of the just noticeable difference, it simultaneously influences the validity of <term>Weber’s Law</term> <note>The principle that the change in a stimulus that will be just noticeable is a constant ratio of the original stimulus.</note>. It seems the shadow must first exceed a certain size if this validation is to succeed at all, because below a certain size, disruptive influences become noticeable, which then disappear once that size is surpassed.

This is also the case with the laws of <term>irradiation</term> <note>A visual effect where a bright area appears to "bleed" into a dark area, making the bright object look larger than it actually is.</note>. It is even questionable—though not yet to be asserted as certain—whether one disruption of lawfulness is somehow connected to the other, since irradiation occurs at the boundary of the light intensities being distinguished. Indeed, the law stating that when white and black are adjacent, the white "encroaches" upon the black through irradiation (thereby increasing the extent of the white and decreasing the black), no longer holds true when the black appears in a very small area against the neighboring white. For just as a white point or a white line on a black background irradiates into the black and thus appears enlarged or widened, so conversely does a black point or a black line on a white background—except that the first type of irradiation is stronger than the second. The intensity of illumination also has an influence on these irradiation ratios ¹).

To the previous point, one might object that in <term>star magnitude estimations</term> <note>The method by which astronomers categorize the brightness of stars. Fechner argued this followed a logarithmic scale, supporting his law.</note>, both components are even imperceptibly small compared to the background, and yet a beautiful confirmation of <term>Weber's Law</term> <note>A psychological principle stating that the smallest detectable change in a stimulus is proportional to the original intensity of the stimulus.</note> has been achieved there. However, the estimation here does not happen through a comparison of the star’s brightness with the brightness of the background—as is the case in the shadow experiments—but rather through a comparison of the star brightnesses with each other upon a shared background. Here, therefore, the two components are not unequal at all; additionally, there is the favorable and likely essential condition that they are distant enough from one another so as not to overlap through *irradiation*. If, indeed, anything is to be attributed to *irradiation* in this matter, then the advantage of the field's size in an extensive background can very well be interpreted as follows: the irradiated edge of the field surrounded by the background is only narrow everywhere, but it occupies relatively more of a small field than of a large one, and thus interferes relatively more. Conversely, when the field is enlarged beyond a certain limit, it no longer counts noticeably in proportion to its entire area, since we do not compare the brightness of the two components merely by a glance at their shared border, but by a glance at them as a whole. Yet, I admit the hypothetical nature of this view.

Under the same point of view as the *irradiation* borders in the respect just considered, one can also grasp the <term>penumbras</term> <note>The partially shaded outer region of a shadow where the light source is only partially obscured.</note> at the boundary of the field and background in the shadow experiments. Likewise, in these as in the rotating disc experiments, one could grasp the often very conspicuous border-glows—dependent on *contrast*—which were discussed in *“In Matter”* <note>Original: *In Sachen der Psychophysik* (In the Matter of Psychophysics, 1877), page 108. This was Fechner’s later defense of his theories.</note> p. 108, provided that the latter should not change proportionally to the external brightnesses. According to **Mach's** formulas (*“In Matter”* p. 108 f.), this remains the case as long as the brightness of the <term>retinal black</term> <note>Original: *Augenschwarz*. Also known as "intrinsic light," this is the gray sensation one sees in total darkness caused by neural noise in the visual system.</note> can be neglected.

**Volkmann** (p. 63) also mentions disc experiments, according to which a white *sector* on a black rotating disc is much more easily distinguished than a black *sector* of the same angular width on a white rotating disc; however, these experiments seem to me to prove nothing other than a well-known consequence of Weber's Law: that the same absolute difference in light is harder to recognize at a higher absolute brightness. A white rotating disc with a black *sector* gives, in fact, a greater absolute brightness for the entire experiment than a black rotating disc with a white *sector*.

As for the star magnitude estimations in themselves, I have considered them in *“Elem.”* I. 158 ff. and *“Elem.”* II. 107 ff. <note>Refers to Fechner's *Elemente der Psychophysik* (Elements of Psychophysics), Volumes I and II.</note> with the inclusion...

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s technical defense against G. E. Müller. While the previous page touched on astronomical observations, Fechner here focuses on the experimental data of Joseph Delboeuf, specifically the role of the constant "c" which represents the eye’s internal light or "noise." Fechner argues that Müller’s critique of Delboeuf’s data is unfair because Delboeuf himself admitted the experiments were preliminary.</meta>

the equality of differences for the eye should be preserved (which is indeed a consequence of the existence of the *c* <note>In psychophysical formulas, *c* represents the "intrinsic light" of the eye—the constant internal stimulation that exists even in darkness.</note> in our sense), without these experiments being able to serve in any way for a comparative determination of the magnitude of *c* under different illumination—as Müller attempts to do—nor were they used by Delboeuf himself for that purpose. Delboeuf himself calls these experiments *"grossières"* <note>original: "grossières"; French for "crude" or "rough."</note> and says explicitly regarding the numbers obtained in these trials:

> "I would by no means claim that these numbers are exact, since we did not observe the precaution of determining the numbers first with the reduction, and then with the enlargement of the bright zone,"

that is, because no precautions were taken against <term>constant errors</term> <note>Systematic biases in measurement, such as a tendency to over-estimate a value when starting from a higher point versus a lower one.</note>. However, that the neglect of this precaution must have introduced significant constant errors is evident from Delboeuf's experimental tables in *Étud.* <note>Delboeuf's "Étude psychophysique" (1873).</note> p. 73 and 88, which I mentioned in *„In Sachen“* <note>Fechner’s "In Sachen der Psychophysik" (1877), a polemic defending his theories.</note> p. 153, note. Finally, Delboeuf explains in a footnote (p. 71) regarding those very experiments to which Müller refers, that he had intended to conduct more precise experiments on the dependence of *c* on the intensity of illumination, but had not yet gotten around to it. Nevertheless, and without regard for everything noted here, Müller (p. 185) calculates from those crude experiments that with a 256-fold illumination of Delboeuf’s apparatus, *c* emerges with a value more than three times larger than with a single illumination; he finds in this sufficient reason to dismiss the consideration that Delboeuf himself gives to this value in the experiments, formulas, and tables he regarded as authoritative.

Regarding the evaluation of the role of *c* in Delboeuf’s tables, one may further note the following. To begin with, *c* is not an absolute constant; and if, according to more reliable experiments, the value of *c* really only rose threefold while the illumination increased 256-fold, the dependence of *c* on the intensity of illumination could still only be considered relatively weak. In any case, *c* remains everywhere a small magnitude, noticeably vanishing compared to stronger external illumination. It must surely be conceded that the smaller a magnitude is in relation to the other factors contributing to the result, the more precise and free from constant errors the observations must be from which one wishes to calculate that magnitude. On the other hand, a small value can vary in a much larger proportion without changing the results much, as long as its absolute value remains small compared to the contributing magnitudes. And so, in the face of stronger external <term>light stimuli</term> introduced in the experiment, *c* can not only be neglected but cannot even be determined; meanwhile, one can adhere to the average of the values emerging from experiments at weaker intensities and use this even at stronger intensities, even should it not strictly retain the same value. This is the sense in which Delboeuf introduced *c* as a constant in his main tables, without thereby asserting that it is truly entirely constant across different illuminations. I have shown in *„In Sachen“* p. 183 (bottom) that the value *c* = 0.50, which Delboeuf used for the calculation of the values in his main tables, can be seen as having arisen in such a manner. His original tables, moreover, contain a calculation for *c* = 0.12, though considering the smallness of this value, it changes little in the results that matter. Müller’s objection would, according to the data provided by Delboeuf, have to be grounded quite differently if it were to signify anything at all.

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s technical defense against G. E. Müller regarding the mathematical foundations of psychophysics. Fechner is specifically addressing the "lower deviation"—the point where Weber's Law seems to fail at very low stimulus intensities—and how the constant "c" (intrinsic light) might account for this discrepancy.</meta>

If, by the way, Müller (p. 185) notes that Delboeuf himself later somewhat changed his views regarding the significance of *c* <note>In Fechner's formulas, *c* represents the "intrinsic light" of the eye—the constant internal stimulation that exists even in total darkness.</note>, that is quite correct (cf. *„In Sachen“* p. 34), but it only concerns his theoretical view; nothing changes in his experiments and the factual conclusions flowing from them, and nothing is retracted by Delboeuf himself.

If I correctly understand a remark by Müller (p. 185), he finds the justification for considering the natural internal stimulation of the eye in experiments to test Weber's Law itself to be "extremely doubtful." However, I find no grounds for this doubt put forward; and when Müller (p. 185) calls Delboeuf's attempt to eliminate the lower deviation by considering *c* "hardly successful," I find Müller's attempt to refute him even less successful.

That some imperfections still cling to Delboeuf's procedure, making a repetition of his experiments desirable, is admitted in *„In Sachen“* <note>Fechner’s "In Sachen der Psychophysik" (1877), a text written to defend his theories against critics.</note> p. 179; and even without a specific suspicion that this only created the false appearance of a confirmation of Weber's Law, it nonetheless represents a reduction in the weight these experiments would otherwise have. In any case, they offer a sufficient counterweight to Aubert's experiments, since, as noted above, at least as many objections can be raised against those.

Now Müller mentions (p. 164) Breton's experiments, which were not conducted according to Delboeuf's method, but according to the same principle of comparing <term>supraliminal differences</term> <note>Differences between stimuli that are clearly perceptible, rather than "just noticeable" differences (JNDs).</note>, as proving a lower deviation from Weber's law. And why not? It simply seems to me superfluous to confirm through new experiments the quite undeniable fact of such a deviation—a fact I already demonstrated in the *„Elementen“* <note>Fechner’s seminal work, "Elemente der Psychophysik" (1860).</note> and which has been confirmed by Delboeuf and everyone after me. What matters would be to test the result of Delboeuf's experiments through new, ideally irreproachable trials. According to Delboeuf, this deviation is covered by a small value *c* that disturbs the law, and is thus eliminated from the law itself. In doing so, however, the sole or even the primary weight should not be placed on the question of whether and to what extent it is the <term>intrinsic light of the eye</term> <note>Also called "Eigenlicht"; the visual noise or faint light sensation generated by the retina and brain in the absence of external light.</note> on which this *c* depends; it is only most natural to accept it in this regard, since it presents itself so readily. If *c* were the unknown cause of a disturbance that could be eliminated in the stated sense, Weber's Law would retain the same advantage, and only our insight into the nature of the disturbance would suffer.

<meta>This page continues Gustav Fechner's defense of his psychophysical methods against the criticisms of G. E. Müller. Fechner is specifically addressing his experiments using darkening glasses to test Weber's Law (the idea that the ratio of a stimulus increment to the background remains constant for perception).</meta>

Following this, a few more words regarding my experiments with darkening glasses on cloud nuances and faint ink-wash shadings (*Elements*, Volume I, pages 140, 144). The procedure with darkening glasses is not only free from many complexities, but also from many sources of constant error that can play a role in other experimental methods. Its only disadvantage is that one cannot use it to measure the just noticeable difference <note>original: "e. m. U." (eben merklicher Unterschied), the smallest change in a stimulus that can be detected.</note> precisely. However, this does not prevent one from confirming—using a shading that differs only very slightly from its background in daylight (within the limits of the so-called "just noticeable")—that its distinctness remains noticeably the same as one employs more and more darkening glasses. This holds until one reaches such levels of darkness where the brightness of the eye's own "internal black" <note>original: "Augenschwarz." This refers to the "intrinsic light" of the retina, or the faint gray sensation one perceives even in total darkness.</note> can no longer be ignored. I have not been able to observe a "lower deviation" <note>The point where Weber's Law fails because the stimulus is too weak to be distinguished from the eye's internal noise.</note> that could not be explained by this factor, at least according to the admittedly subjective judgment available here. Meanwhile, under bright sky illumination, the experiment on cloud nuances can reveal a slight "upper deviation," in that the difference appears even slightly clearer when using dark glasses.

While the lack of precise measurements for the just noticeable difference remains an admitted flaw of this procedure, it does not undermine the principle of validating the law. Regarding the objections Müller (p. 102 ff.) finds against it, I cannot concede that any of them are well-founded, as per my remarks in the following insertion.

According to Müller, "very little weight" is to be given to the results of these experiments. And what are the reasons for this judgment? 1) My experimental method does not stand up to his critique of the method of just noticeable differences in general, and specifically does not agree with his "method of smallest differences." To this, I can only reply that I, for my part, find his critique and his method to be the ones that do not hold up under scrutiny; for more on this, Section VIII should be consulted. — 2) In my experiments with colored darkening glasses, it did not emerge that the relative sensitivity to brightness differences varies with different colors. — But this is quite natural, because they were not conducted to compare different colors, but only to examine different brightness levels within each specific color. — 3) According to page 105, I am said to have overlooked "that the magnitude of the just noticeable difference is significantly influenced by random error processes—which constantly change in intensity and direction—and is therefore necessarily a constantly fluctuating value itself." However, instead of overlooking anything, I simply did not see what Müller believes I should have seen according to his view of the nature of random error processes—and which others in their experiments with just noticeable differences see just as little (Cf. p. 28). —

### b) Weights.

Regarding my weight experiments conducted in relation to Weber's Law, I reported on them in *Elem.* <note>Abbreviation for Fechner's 1860 foundational work, *Elemente der Psychophysik* (Elements of Psychophysics).</note> Vol. I, page 182 ff. and *In Sachen* page 197 ff.; I also reported on Hering’s experiments (by which I mean here, for brevity, those organized by Ewald Hering) in the latter publication on page 186. I asserted those experiments, as well as these, in favor of the law and continue to do so no less now, though in doing so I must take into account some of Müller's counter-remarks, and I will precede this with a few preliminary observations.

Insofar as pressure is involved in the lifting of weights during the experiments, the confirmation of Weber's Law—to the extent it was achievable through my and Hering's lifting experiments—will relate collectively to the sense of pressure and the <term>force or muscular sense</term> <note>The "muscular sense" (kinesthesia) refers to the perception of movement and resistance in the muscles, distinct from the tactile feeling of weight on the skin.</note>, without it being necessary for the role of both senses to be the same regarding the <term>lower deviation</term> <note>The phenomenon where Weber's Law becomes less accurate at very low levels of physical stimulus.</note> that occurs in these experiments. What is certain is that, apart from an anomaly in the smallest weight I used, one can satisfy Weber's Law according to my and Hering's experiments by mathematically including a constant value, and that to this extent these experiments belong among the welcome confirmations of Weber's Law.
