## 2) The Question regarding Differences other than Intensity.
### a) *Pitch*.

In my work *In Sachen* <note>Referring to his 1877 book *In Sachen der Psychophysik* (On the Matter of Psychophysics).</note> (p. 168), I myself considered Preyer’s <note>William Thierry Preyer (1841–1897), a physiologist famous for studying child development and acoustics.</note> experiments to argue against the validity of **Weber's Law** for pitch. On the other hand, Müller (p. 290 ff.), without necessarily regarding the law as proven in this field, challenged the evidentiary force of Preyer’s experiments against it from various perspectives. However, I cannot help but allow Preyer’s appeal to the decisive points of his investigation <gloss>1)</gloss> to stand, so long as they are not refuted more effectively than they were by Müller; for the time being, I must stick with that—to me, personally—unwelcome admission. I would only like to return once more to the observation already made in *In Sachen* (p. 169 f.): that while the confirmations of Weber's Law for the dependence of light and sound sensation on the <term>vibration amplitude (a)<gloss>The maximum extent of a vibration, which determines the volume of a sound or the brightness of a light.</gloss></term> are generally only found when the <term>vibration frequency (n)<gloss>The number of vibrations per second, which determines the pitch of a sound or the color of light.</gloss></term> remains constant, it is quite conceivable that the confirmation of the law for the dependence of pitch and color sensation on the **frequency** would, conversely, only be found with a corresponding constancy of the **amplitude** *a*. The experiments asserted by Preyer offer no guarantee for such constancy. For although I added in *In Sachen* that "hardly any weight should be placed on this suspicion, because the relative strength with which we strike tones seems to have no clear influence on the sensation of their difference in pitch," upon closer consideration, I can no longer place weight on that remark. Namely, that Weber's Law seems to be confirmed for the **musical ear** <note>The ability to perceive relationships between musical notes.</note> can—according to the remark made in *In Sachen* (p. 168)—be attributed to the fact that the **musical ear** judges pitch intervals more by the ratios of the recurrence or non-recurrence of **overtones** <note>Higher-frequency tones that sound along with the main note, giving it its specific quality or "timbre."</note> (which are not entirely absent subjectively even in objectively simple tones) than by the rising and falling of the vibration frequency; however, according to this, the circumstance that the pitch intervals for the—

## XIII. The Law or the Fact of the Threshold.

So much has already been said about this, partly in the "Elements" <note>original: "Elementen," referring to Fechner’s 1860 foundational work *Elemente der Psychophysik*.</note> and partly in "In the Matter" <note>original: "In Sachen," referring to his 1877 book *In Sachen der Psychophysik* (In the Matter of Psychophysics).</note>, that in the following I will content myself with reviewing the various modifications under which the law appears, along with some additional remarks on earlier considerations.

The essence of the law, as far as it is claimed for <term>outer psychophysics<gloss>The study of the relationship between physical stimuli (like light or sound) and the resulting mental sensations.</gloss></term>, consists generally in the fact that a stimulus or a difference in stimulus—in general, a physical value to which a sensation value is attached—must first reach a certain strength or magnitude before the sensation becomes noticeable. As long as this magnitude is not reached, the sensation remains, as we express it, unconscious.

This law stands in a certain connection with **Weber’s Law**, and just as with the latter, the question arises whether it can be transferred from outer psychophysics to <term>inner psychophysics<gloss>The study of the relationship between internal physiological activities (like nerve signals) and mental sensations.</gloss></term>; that is, from the external stimulus (or difference in stimulus) capable of awakening a simple sensation (or difference in sensation), to the psychophysical excitation (or difference in excitations) that underlies these psychic phenomena. However, since this question, like the previous one, only gains interest during the dispute between the so-called psychophysical and physiological interpretations of psychophysics as a whole—and Weber’s Law in particular—we shall reserve the consideration of this aspect for the section on that dispute (Section XVII).

In more detail, we can distinguish between the **simple stimulus threshold**, the **difference threshold**, the **ratio threshold**, and the **mixture threshold**.

The **simple stimulus threshold** concerns the magnitude of the stimulus that must be exceeded for the existence of the stimulus to be recognized through a perceptible sensation. The **difference threshold** concerns the magnitude of the difference between stimuli required for the difference to be recognized as present. Since every difference between two stimuli naturally also presupposes a ratio between two stimuli, the difference threshold can always be translated into a **ratio threshold**; that is, that ratio of stimuli which must be exceeded for the difference in stimulus to be recognized as such.

The law of the **mixture threshold** consists in the fact that when

<summary>Fechner defines the "threshold" as the point where physical stimuli become strong enough to enter conscious awareness and classifies the different types of thresholds (stimulus, difference, ratio, and mixture).</summary>

a mixture of various stimuli acts on us, the existence of this or that individual one among them can only be recognized if it exceeds a certain ratio of strength compared to the others.

Various authors cited by Müller (p. 238), such as Aubert, Delboeuf, and Preyer, declare themselves against the existence of the **simple stimulus threshold**; and Müller himself, without deciding definitively, calls "the question of a stimulus threshold a tricky one." One cannot argue against the fact of the **difference threshold**; but one can attempt to eliminate the stimulus threshold by reducing it to the difference threshold. In the meantime, the experiences cited in favor of this are entirely inconclusive. In the visual organ, certainly, the proof of a simple stimulus threshold cannot be made at all, because it is always exceeded by the subjective excitation upon which the sensation of the <term>eye-black<gloss>Also known as "eigengrau" or intrinsic light; the gray background seen by the eye in total darkness due to spontaneous neural activity.</gloss></term> depends. Now, the other senses are supposedly analogous to the sense of light in this respect; but how so? Rather, if not all, then certainly most behave differently in this regard. Aubert says, of course (p. 42): "we always breathe audibly, the heart beats audibly, clothes make noise, etc." But if I breathe softly or hold my breath, I hear nothing; of my own heartbeat, I hear nothing at all; of another's heartbeat, only when placing the ear against their chest; clothes rustle only when moving, etc. Now, it may be that a weak physical noise emanates from all of this, but the fact that it is heard only at a certain strength speaks for, rather than against, the existence of an external **stimulus threshold**. I have the sensation of the eye-black as soon as I direct my attention to it; on the other hand, there is a silence where I am conscious of no auditory sensation at all, despite focusing my attention on hearing something, and despite the fact that a general noise in the air is never lacking; in this general noise, weak specific auditory stimuli can indeed disappear according to the principle of the <term>mixture threshold<gloss>The point at which a specific stimulus can no longer be distinguished from a background of other combined stimuli.</gloss></term>; but even the general noise itself disappears for the sensation if it is too weak. Now, one can speak of an unconscious sensation of stimuli. But I do that myself by saying that a sensation remains unconscious as long as its <term>psychophysical carrier<gloss>The physical or physiological process (like nerve vibrations) that underlies a mental sensation.</gloss></term> does not exceed a certain strength.

In all of this, I admit a possibility never before considered, which is suggested by newer experiments by Vierordt made known to me privately: namely, that very weak sounds in

But I ask again, why so? They are not developed enough to create mental representations upon which a higher intellectual life can be based, as is the case with the senses of sight and hearing, but they are perfectly competent to decide on simple questions of sensation; or rather, I do not see why they would not be. Now, no one will persuade me that I cannot have the feeling that the air is entirely free of smell, despite the fact that traces of odorous substances are never entirely absent. Whether one ever has a completely taste-free mouth may be debated; I believe that it is the case, even though saliva contains some salt, which one simply does not taste because there is too little of it; but no one will dispute that one does not taste quinine if it is too diluted. When **Müller** repeatedly returns to the idea (including in his *Review*, p. 825) that "the existence of the outer stimulus threshold cannot even be certainly established," he has at least done nothing to diminish the evidentiary weight of the previous facts in its favor.

A specific **mixture threshold** was not yet established in the "**Elements**" <note>original: "Elementen," referring to Fechner’s 1860 book *Elemente der Psychophysik*.</note> and was first introduced in "**In the Matter**" <note>original: "In Sachen," referring to Fechner’s 1877 book *In Sachen der Psychophysik*, written as a rebuttal to his critics.</note> on page 105 and following, from which I first recall the following illustrative example.

In a loud noise, such as that produced by an agitated crowd, the sound of a violin may be completely lost and inaudible as such, even though it contributes to the overall audibility of the noise. However, if it is to be specifically recognized according to its quality and quantity, then either the accompanying noise must cease, or the violin must rise above the accompanying noise by a certain degree of strength—that is, the **mixture threshold**. The same applies to stimuli of taste and smell.

Now, let a, b, c, d . . . be **psychophysical** conditions in general,

The higher $a, b, d \dots$ rise, the higher the mixture threshold of $c$ rises, and the harder it becomes to distinguish $\gamma$ specifically; conversely, the higher $c$ rises, the higher $a, b, d \dots$ must rise to still produce a resultant phenomenon that is particularly distinguishable from $\gamma$.

## XIV. The Parallel Law.

The so-called Parallel Law, as I named it, is discussed in more detail in "Elem." <note>original: "Elem." refers to Fechner's seminal 1860 work, *Elemente der Psychophysik* (*Elements of Psychophysics*).</note> I. 300 ff., and I will again limit myself here to adding a few things to the earlier remarks about its factual nature, though it will have to be returned to once more in Section XVII.

The main fact to which the Parallel Law relates is this: If two stimuli of different intensities act upon a sensing organ for a certain amount of time, the absolute sensations produced by the stimuli weaken through fatigue—which is understood as a matter of diminished **excitability** <term>excitability<gloss>In 19th-century physiology, 'Reizbarkeit' (irritability or excitability) refers to the capacity of a nerve or organ to respond to a stimulus.</gloss></term>—but the perceived difference between the stimuli remains just as unchanged as if the objective stimuli had been changed in the same proportion.

The Parallel Law is demonstrated very simply in the domain of the **sense of light** <note>The sense of sight or visual perception.</note> through a combination of the following two experiments. 1) One gazes at a white or generally bright field on a black or generally dark ground with one eye open, while the other...

<summary>Fechner explains the "mixture threshold," where a specific sensation must reach a certain intensity relative to others to be noticed, and introduces the "Parallel Law," which states that while fatigue reduces our sensitivity to stimuli, it does not change our ability to perceive the relative difference between them.</summary>
<keywords>mixture threshold, Parallel Law, psychic phenomena, excitability, sense of light, fatigue, psychophysics, elements of psychophysics</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s discussion on the "Parallel Law" of psychophysics. The text begins mid-sentence, concluding a description of an experiment regarding how sensory fatigue affects our perception of brightness.</meta>

...kept closed. The first eye becomes fatigued through the stimulus of the bright spot at the location of its effect, while the other eye rests across its entire surface; and that this fatigue, even if continued for only 1 minute, has a very noticeable effect in reducing the sensation of brightness, is proven by the fact that when one now opens the other rested eye and immediately creates a double image of the spot through a free adjustment of the axes of the eyes or lateral pressure on one eye, the image in the fatigued eye appears considerably darker than in the other, rested eye; a result that is very striking. 2) If one observes a bright and dark field side by side with both eyes open at the same time, the difference in brightness does not seem to change, because the fatigue caused by both spots occurs in such a proportion that the perceived difference remains the same.

Very numerous and decisive experiments for the confirmation of the **Parallel Law** <note>The "Parallel Law" suggests that if the intensity of two stimuli is changed by the same ratio (for example, through fatigue), the perceived relationship or difference between them remains constant.</note> in an entirely different field can also be found among my weight-lifting experiments (*Elements* I. p. 305 ff.); and if Müller (p. 267) dismisses the results of these experiments outright as "completely useless" because I "treated the numbers of correct, incorrect, and doubtful cases in an incorrect manner," I can bypass this judgment just as briefly with a reference to Section IV.

Incidentally, I do not claim the validity of the Parallel Law any further than the validity of **Weber's Law** <note>Weber's Law states that the smallest change in a stimulus that can be perceived is a constant proportion of the original stimulus.</note> extends, and I have already pointed out the probable connection between the two in *Elements* I. 304, 325. That it can no longer hold true in the field of the sense of light when one reaches brightness intensities—either those one starts from or those one drops to through fatigue—that approach the **intrinsic light of the eye** <term>Fechner uses the term "eye-black" (Augenschwarz) to describe the "intrinsic light" or the faint grey light we see even in total darkness, caused by internal neural activity.</term>, lies in the principle of the law itself, insofar as this brightness, although not absolutely constant, cannot fall below a certain degree due to organic structures; and the deviations from the Parallel Law that Aubert observed at low brightness levels therefore do not run counter to its principle. Also, the results of the experiments by W. Schöne (*Archives for Ophthalmology* XX. 2. p. 273 ff.) and E. F. Müller (*Experiments on the Course of Retinal Fatigue*, Inaugural Dissertation, Zurich 1866), which Müller (p. 275) briefly mentions, seem to refer to deviations from the Parallel Law in the area of lower deviations from Weber's Law, without my being able to decide upon them with certainty, as I have not had these experiments before me.

# Fourth Section.

## XV. Basic Psychophysical Formulas.

First of all, a few preliminary remarks concerning the notation to be used in the following sections.

Müller <note>Georg Elias Müller (1850–1934), a prominent German psychologist who critically examined Fechner's work.</note> has generally designated the values occurring in the following formulas differently than I have done in my works *Elements* and *In the Matter*. <note>Fechner is referring to his books *Elemente der Psychophysik* (1860) and *In Sachen der Psychophysik* (1877).</note> Since it will now be necessary to discuss these formulas with him, I will adopt his notation to avoid the need for translating the meaning of letters from one formula to another that is substantially equivalent. I am all the more willing to swap my previous designations for Müller's, as his are in any case more practical regarding sensation and stimulus, insofar as their initial letters serve as immediate reminders of what they signify. For sensation (<term>Sensation</term> <note>original: "Sensation"</note>), I used *γ* [gamma], for stimulus (<term>Reiz</term> <note>original: "Reiz"</note>) *β* [beta], and for the threshold value of the stimulus *b*; Müller uses *s*, *r*, and *ρ* [rho] respectively, which I will also use in the future. For the constants *K* and *k*, which I distinguished only insignificantly based on their relation to natural or common logarithms, I will follow Müller in using *κ* [kappa]. I also accept Müller's designation *E* for psychophysical excitation (<term>Erregung</term>), which I had not previously given a specific name; this should not be confused with the *E* I used earlier (p. 48) with a different meaning. For the ratio of two different stimuli, I used the designation *φ* [phi]; however, since Müller uses *φ* primarily as a function sign, I will replace my *φ* with *F*. The sensation of difference, for which Müller lacks a specific designation, will be denoted by me as *u*.

I will first provide, under point 1), a summary of my system of basic psychophysical formulas as set forth in *Elements* Vol. II, p. 9 ff. and *In the Matter* p. 7 ff., in order to proceed from there to Müller's critical remarks in point 2) and to the so-called "corrected" formulas he established himself in point 3).

# 1) Summary of the system of basic psychophysical formulas established by me.

The entire system of the following formulas is built upon Weber's Law <note>Weber's Law states that the change in a stimulus that will be just noticeable is a constant ratio of the original stimulus.</note> and the Threshold Law <note>The Threshold Law refers to the point (threshold) at which a stimulus is strong enough to produce a conscious sensation.</note> and is directly related to the magnitude dependence of sensation on the **stimulus**. It is thus established for outer psychophysics <note>Outer psychophysics studies the relationship between the physical stimulus and the resulting sensation.</note> within the limits of the validity of Weber's Law; however, it is also transferable to the magnitude dependence of **sensation** [E.] on **psychophysical excitation** [ps.-ph. Erregung]. It is therefore transferable into inner psychophysics <note>Inner psychophysics studies the relationship between the physiological excitation (nerves/brain) and the resulting sensation.</note> under the assumption that those laws can be transferred from the external to the internal. It will likely play an even more general role in inner psychophysics than in the field of sensation, although this will not be discussed in further detail here. Moreover, it refers not merely to simple sensations but also, in connection with them, to differences and sums of sensations.

Regarding differences, it is important to clearly distinguish between **differences in sensation** and **sensations of difference**. A **difference in sensation** [Empfindungsunterschied] or a **difference between sensations** can exist between sensations in different people, as well as between a present and a forgotten **sensation** [E.] in the same person; it is sufficient that the sensations are different in themselves. Conversely, a **sensation of difference** [Unterschiedsempfindung] or a **perceived difference** requires that the difference between the sensations is also perceived as a difference. However, no matter how great a difference between two sensations is, it will not be perceived as a difference if the psychophysical excitations underlying the sensations lack sufficient functional relationships; in this regard, the situation is the same as with the melodic and harmonic relational sensations mentioned on page 6.

Insofar as Weber's Law underlies all the following formulas, it must not be overlooked that the law cannot be proven directly through **differences in sensation**, but only through **perceived differences** or **sensations of difference**; however, from the proof of the latter, the validity of the former can be inferred, as will be shown in more detail under section 2) on page 198 ff. For now, this may be taken as a preliminary result.

I now consider the following to be the basic formulas or main formulas of psychic measurement, using the names employed for them in *Elements* and *In the Matter*. <note>Refers to Fechner’s books *Elemente der Psychophysik* (1860) and *In Sachen der Psychophysik* (1877).</note>

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s mathematical exposition of psychophysical laws. The previous page established the "cardinal value" of a stimulus and the basic measurement formula (s = log r), explaining how the threshold value (rho) influences the calculation of sensation magnitude.</meta>

...appears with a negative sign whenever the stimulus <term>r</term> <note>original: "r"; the physical intensity of the stimulus.</note> or the stimulus ratio <term>r'/r</term> falls below their threshold values. According to the meaning that mathematics assigns to the negative sign when applied to absolute magnitudes, this can signify nothing other than that the mental values in question become impossible—or "unreal"—for values of the stimulus below the threshold, which corresponds exactly to the nature of the matter. Negative absolute magnitudes are simply impossible ones. 

Some have attempted to deny the validity of our formulas by questioning the justification of these negative mental values—claiming they have no meaning at all. I shall return to this point explicitly in the following section. For now, one must not confuse (as has happened several times) a negative sensation <note>original: "E."; an abbreviation for Empfindung (sensation).</note>—such as that produced by my measurement formula for a stimulus below the threshold—with a *special kind* of sensation that exists or is supposed to exist according to my theory. Rather, it signifies a sensation that *does not exist* because the necessary conditions for it are lacking.

The more these conditions are lacking, the greater the distance of the sensation from the point where it becomes real. This is represented by the fact that the sensation assumes larger negative values the further the stimulus remains below the threshold. If the stimulus has dropped from its threshold value down to zero, it can drop no further; thus, according to its logarithmic dependence on the stimulus, the sensation reaches its greatest negative value at the zero value of the stimulus, below which it cannot sink further—that is, an infinitely negative value. This is indeed what the measurement formula for the sensation <term>s</term> gives when <term>r</term> becomes zero, and thus the condition for the sensation becoming real absolutely vanishes. If, of course, the sensation <term>s</term> were proportional to the stimulus <term>r</term>, the measurement formula would have to give the value of $s = 0$ at $r = 0$. However, such a formula cannot be established at all based on experience, as will be shown later.

It is of significant interest to find how the "difference measurement formula" <note>A formula used to calculate the perceived difference between two stimuli.</note> expresses the opposition of directions (which a sensation of difference can take) in a consistent connection with the opposition between reality and the distance from reality. While in the basic measurement formula, the opposition of signs (positive or negative) can only mean the latter—representing whether a sensation is real or below the threshold—in the difference formula, the sign represents the direction of the difference.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of mathematical formulas in psychophysics. ...formula for this relationship; only the mode of mediation between r <note>the external stimulus</note> and s <note>the sensation</note> through the insertion of E <note>internal psychophysical excitation</note> changes its position and role according to the specific viewpoint.

According to the <term>psychophysical</term> <note>original abbreviation: "ps.-ph."</note> view, the previous formulas for the relationship between stimulus and sensation—which have only limited validity for **external psychophysics** <note>The study of the relationship between physical stimuli and mental sensations.</note> due to deviations from **Weber’s Law**—can be translated into strictly valid formulas for **internal psychophysics** <note>The study of the relationship between internal nervous activity (excitation) and mental sensations.</note>. This is done by replacing the stimulus r with the psychophysical excitation E. In this view, the deviations from the law that appear in experiments with external stimuli (due to secondary circumstances) are seen as disappearing when considering the immediate relationship between sensation and psychophysical excitation in the inner self. According to the **physiological view**, at least as represented by Müller <note>Likely Johannes Müller (1801–1858), a foundational figure in modern physiology.</note>, Weber’s Law is so fundamentally tied to these deviations that one cannot speak of a pure transfer of the law to either s or E.

Whether the value κ <note>kappa; a constant in the formula representing sensitivity</note>, which must be assumed as constant for sensations of the same quality, also remains constant for sensations of different qualities is not yet decided. As for the threshold ρ <note>rho; the point at which a stimulus is first perceived</note>, when related to the external stimulus, it can change even for the same quality of sensation and within the same individual depending on sensitivity, as the conditions of transmission to the interior vary. In contrast, when related to internal psychophysical excitation, it might possibly change according to the quality of the sensation, but for **internal psychophysics**, it is to be regarded as constant for the same type of sensation.

In the preceding formulas, only the facts of the <term>stimulus threshold</term> <note>The minimum intensity required for a stimulus to be felt.</note> and <term>difference threshold</term> <note>The minimum change in a stimulus required to notice a difference.</note> (or the <term>ratio threshold</term> <note>original: "Verhältnißschwelle"; the minimum proportional change needed for a difference to be noticed.</note> naturally given with them) have been taken into account, but not the <term>mixture threshold</term> <note>original: "Mischungsschwelle"; the threshold for a new stimulus to be noticed when added to an existing "mixture" of background activity.</note> (p. 179 f.). Since every new stimulus encountered while awake finds the person already occupied by a play of various external and internal stimulations—or, to put it briefly, is added to an already existing mixture of excitation—strictly speaking, the difference threshold and its associated ratio threshold translate into a corresponding mixture threshold. There is no reason to consider the formulas changed by this, as we simply have to substitute one threshold for the other. ### 2) Müller’s Critical Remarks.

To connect to Müller’s remarks, I must return for a few words to the specific way the **measurement formula** <note>original: "Maßformel"; the mathematical equation Fechner used to quantify the relationship between physical stimulus and mental sensation.</note> (2) is justified.
As noted above, this formula can be derived from Weber’s Law in two ways, both of which initially lead to the formula:
->s = $\varkappa$ log r + Const. . . . (2.a)<-

To determine the constant, I have used the convergence of an empirical and a mathematical perspective. Regarding the former, the fact of the **stimulus threshold** <note>original: "Reizschwelle"; the minimum level of intensity a stimulus must reach to be consciously perceived.</note> proves that sensation, in order to drop to zero, does not wait until the stimulus has dropped to zero; rather, it vanishes at a finite level of the stimulus, the so-called stimulus threshold. That the objections raised against the fact of the stimulus threshold are generally not valid was shown on page 178 f.; but even if it remained doubtful from an empirical standpoint—and certainly one cannot say more than that—I showed secondly in the *Elements* <note>Fechner’s *Elemente der Psychophysik* (1860), the foundational text for this field.</note> (Vol. II, p. 17) that only by including this threshold can one arrive at a usable formula from Weber’s Law at all. In fact, if we wanted to set s = 0 when r = 0—that is, if we did not accept the fact of the stimulus threshold, according to which s instead becomes zero at a finite value of r—we would have the following to determine the constant:
->0 = $\varkappa$ log 0 + Const.<-
Since log 0 = $-\infty$, the Constant would be found to be $\varkappa \infty$, and thus:
->s = $\varkappa$ log r + $\infty$<-
That is, we would obtain an infinite value for the sensation (s) for any finite value of the stimulus (r). If, on the other hand, we assume that s becomes zero at the finite value $\rho$ <note>The Greek letter rho, used here to represent the specific value of the stimulus at the threshold of perception.</note> of the stimulus r, we obtain—

Furthermore, the previous formula—which essentially agrees with the *difference formula*—only provides the value of the *difference* between two stimuli *s* and *s₀*; however, two sensations cannot be distinguished in terms of measurement if a *determination of measurement* does not also exist for the sensations themselves. Now, one might say, in the sense of the so-called *difference view* (see "In the Matter of Psychophysics," p. 113 ff.), that simple sensations do not exist for themselves at all, but only insofar as they are distinguished from others—that is, as components of *sensations of difference*. But aside from what can be said against this generally, the *difference formula*—which, as noted, the previous formula materially matches—does not relate to *sensations of difference* at all. Rather, it relates to the *differences between sensations*, which exist regardless of whether one is actually sensing that *difference*. Thus, we must return to the fact that *differences* cannot be measured without the *measurability* of the things between which the differences exist.

Therefore, even if the *determination of the constant* in the previous formula (2.a) can be achieved by relating it to a value above the threshold to establish the *difference formula*, it still does not spare us the need for a *determination of the constant* by relating it to the **threshold**. This is necessary to establish a *measurement formula*, from which the difference formula can then be derived even without regard for the first determination. Conversely, the *measurement formula* cannot be derived from the difference formula without taking the **threshold** into account.

In the meantime, considerations of the previous kind were likely clear enough to Müller himself, and so I believe that the actual reason why Müller avoided the *determination of the constant* in formula (2.a) is instead this: Naturally, it could no more escape Müller than it did me that the determination of the constant in this formula cannot be done by setting *s* = 0 when *r* = 0. To obtain any finite values for sensation (*s*) at finite values of the stimulus (*r*), one must set *s* = 0 at a finite value of *r*—that is, one must admit a **threshold value** for *r*. But it is a necessary consequence of this that *s* assumes negative values when the values of *r* are below the **threshold value**. Since Müller considers **negative sensation values** to be **absurd** (p. 373), this method of determining the constant must naturally also appear **absurd** to him. The task of every good series of experiments in this field is to keep these secondary conditions, which could influence the modification of the perceived difference, as constant as possible throughout the entire series, or to eliminate their influence. ### 3) Müller’s so-called corrected formulas.

Although Müller not only concedes but even reproduces the derivability of the formula
-> $s = x \log \frac{r'}{r} + \text{Constant} \dots (2. a)$ <-
from Weber's Law, he does not, as noted above, assign any fundamental significance to the formula. This is because he attaches no such significance to the law itself from which it flows. Considering the deviations from it that occur so frequently in **external psychophysics** <term>External Psychophysics: The study of the relationship between physical stimuli (like light or weight) and the mental sensations they produce.</term>, he considers the law to be entirely precarious. He believes it has no decisive significance for **internal psychophysics** <term>Internal Psychophysics: The study of the relationship between the soul or mind and the underlying physiological/neural activities.</term> and, based on the available facts, should be replaced in external psychophysics by the following (p. 225):

> "With gradually increasing stimulus intensity, the relative differential sensitivity in various sensory areas—for example, also in the area of the sense of pressure—first increases, reaches a maximum at a certain stimulus intensity, and then, after having reached this maximum, gradually decreases again as the absolute stimulus intensity continues to increase."

-> $0 = - \infty$ <-

## XVI. Regarding the negative sensation values entering into the psychophysical formulas.

### 1) The negative sensation values as imaginary.

According to the measurement formula <term>Measurement formula (Maßformel): Fechner’s logarithmic equation, $S = k \log(R/b)$, which quantifies the relationship between physical stimulus and mental sensation.</term> based on Weber's Law, the sensation of a stimulus—and according to the related difference measurement formula, the sensation of the difference between two stimuli—assumes negative values when the stimulus or the difference between two stimuli sinks below a certain finite value, the threshold <term>Threshold (Schwelle): The minimum level of stimulus intensity required to trigger a conscious sensation.</term>. The meaning of these negative sensation values was discussed by me in *Elements* <note>Fechner is referring to his 1860 foundational work, *Elemente der Psychophysik*.</note> Vol. II, p. 39 ff., and I returned to it in *In Matter* <note>Referring to his 1877 book *In Sachen der Psychophysik*, written to defend his theories against critics.</note> p. 88 ff., taking into account the objections raised against it. My conception of these values was also recalled above on p. 190. But the persistence

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s defense of his mathematical interpretation of sensation. He is responding to G. E. Müller’s criticisms regarding "negative sensation values"—the mathematical results that occur when a stimulus is too weak to be consciously perceived.</meta>

The opponent's challenge to this view, and his inexhaustible variations of old objections—which, while not essentially new, offer new turns of phrase against it—prompt me to address the question once more.

I will begin with a somewhat more general observation.

There are magnitude values that can only occur or be thought of as absolute or positive; for example, the square of a number in a mathematical sense, or kinetic energy <note>original: "lebendige Kraft," a historical term for *vis viva* or kinetic energy</note> in a physical sense. If one is nevertheless led to negative values for such a magnitude in any context, one can logically only see them as impossible or imaginary values <term>Imaginary values: In mathematics, these are values that do not exist on the standard number line; Fechner uses this to describe sensations that exist below the "threshold" of consciousness.</term>; for it is already presupposed that the magnitude in question can only occur or be thought of as absolute or positive. Cases where one is actually led to such negative magnitudes occur frequently enough in mathematics, and so mathematics treats them as impossible or imaginary. Consequently, it is surprising from the outset that what is universally admitted in mathematics is not permitted in the applications of mathematics. There is nothing inherently contradictory in the idea that one magnitude stands in such a dependency to another as to retain *real* values only within certain limits, and to become impossible beyond them. This general remark addresses all objections against the imaginary meaning that I attribute to negative sensation values.

To illustrate the previous principle, I have already, in "Elements" II, page 40, and "In the Matter of" page 92, recalled the imaginary value that the *radius vectors* <note>original: "Radii vectores"</note> or guide rays take on with a negative sign in the system of *polar coordinates* <term>Polar coordinates: A coordinate system where a point is identified by its distance from a center (the radius vector) and an angle, rather than by horizontal and vertical distances.</term>, provided that in this system one considers the length of the *radius vector* only according to its absolute value, and not, as in the system of rectangular *coordinates*, with regard to the sign or direction. I believe this will remain correct despite Müller and Nitzsche, who would like to do away with this inconvenient example through counter-remarks (discussed below). However, the *radius vector* is by no means a peculiar or curious example in this regard; we can find corresponding examples everywhere in the application of rectangular *coordinates* where the condition applies that the negative sign affects a value which, according to its mathematical concept, can only be positive. Let us take, for example, the simplest equation of the parabola...

Now, one might perhaps object: what does one do with such an abstract mathematical principle if it suffers no application to reality? Sensation **s** cannot, by its nature, become negative; and insofar as my measurement formula, like Müller’s <note>G. E. Müller (1850–1934), a psychologist who criticized Fechner's interpretation of negative values.</note>, leads to negative sensation values, the character of the **imaginary** must also be assigned to them. All arguments to the contrary—claiming that this does not agree with the definition of the opposition of + and –, or with anything else—are entirely in vain if one is unable to refute the logic of the previous observations and the examples related to them. One proves only that one has either not grasped the opposition of signs generally enough, or has grasped it falsely or skewed in one's own definitions.

To the extent that the stimulus, or rather the psycho-physical excitation, sinks further below the threshold, there is, on the one hand, an increasing lack of the conditions necessary for a positive sensation <note>original: "E." is an abbreviation for "Empfindung" (sensation).</note> to occur; and, on the other hand, the sensation itself—as a function of the stimulus—falls further short of reaching a positive value. Thus, we can say briefly to describe this: larger and smaller values of negative sensation measure the degree to which the sensation falls short of a positive value, just as positive values measure the degree to which it exceeds the starting point of one. Or: the former provide a psychical measure for what is still missing for a sensation to occur, just as the latter provide a measure for the sensation that has actually occurred.

In this, I take great care not to conflate or confuse that which is lacking on the **psychical** side (according to a mathematical measure of the mind) for a real sensation to occur—or the amount by which the sensation psychically falls short of becoming positive—with that which is lacking in the **physical** conditions for the sensation to occur. I have found that this has occasionally been done by others or wrongly attributed to me. That which is missing for a sensation to occur is by no means proportional to what is missing in the physical conditions; rather, it stands in the same logarithmic dependence to it as the sensation above the threshold stands to the stimulus above the threshold.

In general, one must never forget that in psychophysics we must understand sensation not merely by its psychological value, but simultaneously by its physical conditioning. According to this view, an "impossible" value of sensation <note>Meaning a value that exists mathematically but cannot be felt consciously.</note> must be distinguished from a mere zero value. This is precisely what is achieved through the distinction between minus (—) and 0. This distinction is completely lost in the view of my opponents, who thereby conflate the tasks of psychology and psychophysics.

One can represent negative *s* <note>The variable *s* stands for "sensation."</note> according to its negative value graphically by a line drawn downwards below a zero point, just as positive *s* can be represented by its positive value through a line drawn upwards above it. This does not contradict the fact that paths or movements in **reality**, which one tracks upwards or downwards in opposite directions from the same point, can be represented in a corresponding way; the dual usage allowed by the opposition of signs (+/-) in this regard is simply transferred to its graphical representability.

It has been argued that if an opposition of signs <note>Referring to positive (+) and negative (-) signs in equations.</note> is applicable to sensations at all, it could only denote an opposition of character or quality—such as the sensations of heat and cold, or of pleasure and displeasure. But even assuming this opposition could really be designated in such a way, this does not at all exclude the possibility that the opposition between reality and non-reality—in our sense—can be designated in the same way, since the opposition of signs is, after all, useful for designating various types of contrasts. Ambiguity cannot arise from this, provided that the context in which the usage occurs automatically carries its own understanding. And so too, the derivation of the measurement formula <term>Maßformel: The mathematical formula Fechner developed to describe the relationship between physical stimulus and mental sensation</term> from experiences with sensations of light and sound does not allow the opposition of signs in this formula to be understood in any way other than how I have understood it.

Moreover, regarding the sensations of cold and heat, I still consider it very questionable whether the qualitative opposition of these sensations can really be expressed by an opposition of signs, as I also consider it questionable whether this opposition is not more apparent than real. Both sensations, cold as well as heat, are sensations <term>sui generis: Of their own kind; unique</term> <note>original: "sui generis"</note>; a sensation of cold can be just as "strong" as a sensation of heat and, depending on the presence or absence of the necessary conditions, can be real or imaginary. It will therefore—just like the other aforementioned sensations and like the sensation of heat itself—require its own measurement formula, in which it appears with a positive sign as real and with a negative sign as unreal. And indeed, I have shown in *Elements* <note>Referring to Fechner's seminal work, "Elemente der Psychophysik" (Elements of Psychophysics), published in 1860.</note> Vol. II, p. 42 ff., that since the temperatures upon which the sensations of heat and cold depend are represented respectively as positive and negative differences from a certain mean temperature, it is possible to establish connected formulas for both sensations. In these formulas, the sensations appear as functions of these opposing differences while maintaining that specific meaning of the signs <note>i.e., that a negative result always means the sensation is below the threshold of being felt</note>. On the other hand, it does not seem clear to me from the outset what might lie within the sensations of heat and cold themselves that would demand opposing signs for them;

...the character of an opposition <note>Referring to the mathematical opposition of positive (+) and negative (-) signs.</note> is merely involuntarily associated with them because they depend on opposing conditions; to the extent that these conditions transition into one another—indeed, transition within themselves—they produce no less opposing consequences.

Insofar as higher phenomena of consciousness exist beyond sensory sensations, and these can be seen as psychophysically representable (according to Section I), the concept of the <term>threshold: the point at which a physical stimulus becomes strong enough to be consciously perceived</term> and, with it, negative psychic values below the threshold will also be transferable to them. However, pursuing this further is not the task at hand.

It often seems to me that the resistance against my negative <term>sensation values: the numerical representation of how intense a sensation feels</term> lies merely in a resistance against the expression itself, which appears to contain a contradiction. How can one speak of "sensations" at all when there is nothing less than sensation present? Well, if that causes difficulty, then one should translate the expression into the factual meaning to which I have returned in repeated explanations, and not cling to the wording. In any case, one should guard against confusing the **mathematical existence** I attribute to negative sensation values with a **real existence**. I attribute the former to them insofar as they serve as a mathematical designation for the *impossibility* of sensations of a given kind under insufficient conditions; however, real existence is not granted to them by this, but is expressly denied. Yet, this particular confusion is common—even traditional, so to speak.

Only by way of such a confusion could one find my negative sensation values "absurd," which they truly would be if they were interpreted as real. At the end of a long-winded passage indulging in this confusion (p. 55), Delboeuf <note>Joseph Delboeuf (1831–1896), a Belgian philosopher and psychologist who criticized Fechner's logarithmic law.</note> asks: "What is it, then, that I feel in absolute silence?" and I simply reply: **Nothing**; rather, in *absolute* silence, I am infinitely far from feeling anything of a sound.

I should think that with the preceding explanations and clarifications, all fundamental objections against the mathematical existence of my negative sensation values in the aforementioned sense—and I have never claimed any other—would be settled. But let us nevertheless hear the newly formulated objections of the opponents themselves, to see how far they run counter to the previous considerations and what power they might have against them; in the main, they are, of course, merely conceptual...

Müller, without having noticed that his own measurement formula escapes negative sensation values just as little as mine does, counters them (p. 369) with the following explanation from Gauss <note>Carl Friedrich Gauss (1777–1855), the renowned German mathematician.</note>:

> "Thus," — says Müller — "we designate the debts someone has as negative wealth, because a positive wealth of equal size, when thought of as combined with it, results in the zero state."

Quite right; and in the same way, I designate as a negative sensation <note>original abbreviation: "E." for *Empfindung*</note> that which must be thought of as combined with a positive sensation to reduce it to zero. This is exactly what is still lacking in the occurrence of a sensation (in the sense described above) according to the mathematical context. Mathematically speaking, I superimpose the negative sensation belonging to a <term>stimulus: a physical energy, like light or sound, that triggers a sensory response</term> that falls below the threshold in a given ratio, over the positive sensation belonging to a stimulus that exceeds the threshold in a corresponding ratio, and thus arrive at zero. Of course, the mathematical definition only requires that I accomplish this conceptually; however, should one find a difficulty in the fact that I cannot do it in reality, one would find the same difficulty in combining the imaginary values of negative signs—recognized by Gauss himself—with values thought of as positively real to reach zero.

To be sure, one might want to say: If 1 is the <term>threshold value: the minimum intensity at which a stimulus is consciously perceived</term> of the stimulus, then for me a stimulus equal to ½ must yield just as large a negative sensation as a stimulus of 2 yields a positive one. This is because, in the first case, the threshold is fallen below in the same ratio as it is exceeded in the second case. Following this logic, if both stimulus magnitudes were combined—yielding 2½—one should obtain a sensation of zero through the <term>superposition: the mathematical adding together of two values or states</term> of the sensations that each yields individually; from which the absurdity of my way of thinking would be self-evident. 

But with a stimulus of 2½, one does not superimpose the sensations belonging to the stimuli ½ and 2 individually; rather, one obtains the sensation belonging to the sum of the stimuli 2½ as a single unit. This line of reasoning falls victim to the same error I previously criticized (in *In Sachen der Psychophysik*, p. 37) regarding a perspective held by Langer <note>Benedikt Langer, an early critic of Fechner's law.</note>.

### 2) Negative sensation values as unconscious.

In all the preceding, it is important that a psychophysical excitation below the threshold—without being able to let its adequate sensation emerge noticeably—can nevertheless contribute as an addition to other excitations according to the principle of the **mixture threshold** <term>mixture threshold: the concept that several stimuli, each too weak to be felt alone, can combine to cross the threshold of awareness</term>.    Generally, I also call these negative sensation values *unconscious*, because according to my conception of them, the so-called unconscious mental life <note>original: "Seelenleben," a term encompassing both the soul and the psychological mind</note> essentially rests upon them (see *In the Matter of Psychophysics* <note>original: "In Sachen [der Psychophysik]," Fechner's 1877 book defending his theories</note> p. 91 f.).    By this explanation, any conceptual dispute with me regarding "conscious" and "unconscious" should actually be cut short; I have stated what I objectively understand by them, and by remaining faithful to the use of these same designations, no objective error can arise unless I have erred from the very beginning in the matter itself. With it, he can only express the very same facts in a way that is unintelligible to everyone, whereas I express them intelligibly with my own usage.

Generally speaking, nothing could be said against this, as both common and scientific linguistic usage understand consciousness sometimes in a narrower, higher sense, and sometimes in a broader sense. In the latter sense, a person who is completely absorbed in a sensory sensation without any reflection is called no less conscious than one who reflects upon his sensations. <meta>This page continues Fechner’s rebuttal of Constantin Gutberlet’s theories regarding unconscious sensation. On the preceding page, Fechner argued that a sensation like a toothache is either felt (conscious) or not felt (below the threshold), rejecting Gutberlet's idea that a "real pain" can exist without the mind being aware of it.</meta>

Gutberlet was certainly free to follow his scientific requirements by sticking to a narrow rather than a broad usage of terms, but this does not prove or refute any objective facts. Ultimately, however, in my opinion, it is inconsistent with any standard usage of language or concepts to use **reality** and **consciousness** in such a relationship to one another that one could speak of a pain that is foreign to consciousness as a real pain, or to be able to say of a real pain that consciousness knows nothing of it—as is the case with Gutberlet’s pain that is simultaneously real and unconscious below the threshold.

Should Gutberlet find such a use of language and concepts necessary for the factual representation of his view on the relationship between body and soul, then things would look poor for this view from the very outset.

As for the second point—that we perform spontaneous movements in the unconscious (that is, when attention is withdrawn) in order to alleviate a pain, and therefore the pain must be present—the author forgets that a person paralyzed in the spinal cord can withdraw a tickled or pricked leg purely by reflex without feeling anything of the tickle or pain. The machine <note>Fechner often uses "machine" or "mechanism" to describe the purely physical, reflexive functions of the body that operate without conscious intent.</note> is simply designed for it. Thus, it also proves nothing when the author further asserts "that spontaneous movements show themselves particularly conspicuously in sleep, such as when a sleeper is tickled under the nose." Either he truly does not feel the tickle—namely, if the <term>psychophysical: the study of the relationship between physical stimuli and mental sensations</term> <gloss>psychophysical</gloss> excitation aroused thereby remains below the threshold—but still reacts reflexively against it; or the tickle is strong enough to drive that excitation far enough above the threshold that he has a dream-sensation of it, from which he does not yet need to wake; or he drives it even higher until he awakens.

"That waking is a purely psychological process" follows, according to the author (p. 169), from facts among others that he takes from my "Elements" <note>Fechner refers here to his foundational work, *Elemente der Psychophysik* (Elements of Psychophysics), published in 1860.</note> II, p. 446, such as "that even the cessation of a stimulus can wake someone, as when the miller no longer hears the turning of the mill," etc. Undeniably, these facts prove what he wants them to prove within the context of his assumptions. However, the fact that they can be explained very simply in a psychophysical rather than a purely psychological way in the context of my own assumptions is proven by the explanation itself that I provided in the cited passage. The author ignores this explanation, as it certainly has as little significance for his system as his proof has for mine; I only do not see how his system's conclusions would cause any harm to my own.

<summary>Fechner argues that "unconscious pain" is a contradiction in terms and explains that reflexive movements during sleep or paralysis are mechanical responses rather than evidence of hidden consciousness. He defends his psychophysical "threshold" model against Gutberlet’s purely psychological interpretations of waking and stimuli.</summary>

## Section Five.

---

### XVII. Dispute Between the Psychophysical and Physiological Basic Views.

This is the dispute over the central question of all psychophysics, and it therefore deserves more than just superficial attention.

As is well known, the relationship between sensation and stimulus—or more generally between psychic and physical excitation—can be understood in two very different ways. For these, [Georg Elias] Müller <note>Georg Elias Müller (1850–1934) was a key figure in experimental psychology who rigorously tested and often critiqued Fechner’s work.</note> (p. 232) introduced the convenient terms **psychophysical** and **physiological** views. For my part, I shall use these terms in the following discussion, as I have done previously.

What I have said from the beginning in my *Elements* <note>Fechner’s 1860 foundational work, *Elemente der Psychophysik*.</note> and later in my rebuttal to the objections of Hering, Delboeuf, Langer, and others in *In Matters of Psychophysics* <note>original: "In Sachen"; Fechner’s 1877 book *In Sachen der Psychophysik*, written to defend his theories against contemporary critics like Ewald Hering and Joseph Delboeuf.</note> regarding the defense of the psychophysical view, can be found in Sections XVIII, XXXVIII, and XXXIX of the *Elements*, Volume II, from pages 39, 428, and 437 onwards, and in *In Matters* specifically in Sections VIII, IX, and X. In the meantime, the psychophysical view has been attacked anew by Müller—who is also the main opponent in this dispute—and earlier attacks by others have been taken up again. However, I have found no reason in these to convert to the opposite view; on the contrary, the new considerations provoked by these attacks have only further strengthened my adherence to the psychophysical view.

Before the discussion begins, a few words should be said to characterize the two views in contrast to one another. Their main points of view have already been discussed or at least touched upon in the two previous sections, but one might appreciate finding them summarized here so as to have them at hand for the following arguments.

Insofar as it is necessary to return to the formulas of Section XV, the variable *x* will generally denote a value determined by the magnitude

1) That within the limits of validity of Weber’s Law, a logarithmic dependency of the sensation *s* on the external stimulus *r* exists is recognized by both views as a mathematical consequence of this law, but is interpreted differently. According to the **psychophysical** view, within the limits of the law, the external stimulus produces a proportional excitation *E* in the nerves and the central organ; however, the sensation generally and fundamentally depends logarithmically on the internal psychophysical excitation. According to the **physiological** view, on the other hand, within the limits of Weber's Law, the psychophysical excitation depends logarithmically on the stimulus, while the sensation generally and fundamentally depends on the psychophysical excitation according to simple proportion.

**physiologically**

-> E = x log r, s = x E. <-

2) Under the assumption that the interrelated, mutually dependent changes of *r*, *E*, and *s* are only small, then according to the **psychophysical** view within the limits of Weber's Law, the change of the psychophysical excitation *E* is proportional to the absolute change of the stimulus *r*, whereas the change of sensation *s* is generally proportional to the relative change of the psychophysical excitation, and one thus has:

-> ∂E = x dr, ∂s = x $\frac{∂E}{E}$ <-

On the other hand, according to the **physiological** view within the limits of Weber's Law, the change of the psychophysical excitation is proportional to the relative change of the stimulus, the change of the sensation is generally proportional to the absolute change of the psychophysical excitation, and one thus has:

-> ∂E = x $\frac{dr}{r}$, ∂s = x ∂E. <-

These formulas are simple consequences of the formulas under 1).

3) It follows no less directly from 1) that a <term>sensation difference</term><note>The perceived degree of change between two distinct sensations.</note> of any magnitude is, according to the *psychophysical view*, generally proportional to the difference of the logarithms of the <term>psychophysical excitations</term><note>The physical neural activity that corresponds to a mental sensation.</note>—and thus to the logarithm of their ratio—whereas according to the *physiological view*, it is generally proportional to the difference of the psychophysical excitations themselves. The former does not contradict the fact that, according to 2), a small change in a sensation (equivalent to a small difference between two sensations) is proportional to the relative difference of the psychophysical excitations. This is because the logarithm of the ratio between two magnitudes and the relative difference between those magnitudes remain proportional to each other as long as the difference remains relatively small compared to the magnitudes themselves, or, relatedly, as long as the ratio of both magnitudes approaches unity.

4) According to the *psychophysical view*, there exists an *inner sensation threshold* corresponding to the external <term>stimulus threshold</term><note>The point at which a physical stimulus becomes strong enough to be detected.</note>, which we may also call the *psychophysical threshold* in relation to psychophysical excitations. This means that not only must the external stimulus exceed a certain magnitude to awaken a noticeable sensation, but the psychophysical excitation itself—whether awakened by an external stimulus or arising internally on its own—must also exceed a certain magnitude for a sensation to become noticeable. According to the *physiological view*, however, given the proportionality between sensation and psychophysical excitation, even the smallest psychophysical excitation must awaken a correspondingly tiny sensation; thus, an inner sensation threshold is absent. In this view, the fact of an external stimulus threshold, if it is to be recognized at all, allows for no conclusion regarding an inner sensation threshold, as it is assumed that the external stimulus must first exceed a certain strength simply to extend its effect into the interior as far as the sensory organ <note>original: "Sensorium"; the hypothesized part of the brain that receives and interprets sensory stimuli.</note>.

5) According to the *psychophysical view*, for psychophysical excitations that do not reach the *sensation threshold*, as well as for differences in psychophysical excitations that do not reach the *difference threshold*, one obtains mathematical expressions for the corresponding simple sensations and sensation differences with a negative sign. These signs represent the distance from the actual occurrence of a sensation or sensation difference, just as a positive sign represents the existence of an actually occurring simple or differential sensation. According to the *physiological view*, on the other hand, there is no such contrast of signs for psychic values in this sense; there is only the contrast between sensations of heat and cold, pleasure and displeasure, thus—

Indeed, from the physiological perspective, not only the real but also the mathematical existence or meaning of negative <term>sensation values</term><note>Mathematically calculated values that fall below the threshold of conscious perception.</note> (according to the distinction made on page 212) disappears. One can certainly speak of imaginary values in dependence on real values in the sense previously stated; on the other hand, it would make no sense to attempt to establish imaginary values as a function of imaginary values. This would be the case if one tried to make negative sensations (which cannot be real) dependent on negative psychophysical excitations below zero (which likewise cannot be real).

6) According to the psychophysical view, **Weber’s Law** is a fundamental law, transferable from external to internal <term>psychophysics</term><note>The study of the relationship between physical stimuli and mental phenomena.</note> with only one difference: in internal psychophysics, it applies purely and without restriction, whereas in external psychophysics, it always applies only approximately and within certain limits. Therefore, while according to Weber’s Law—so far as it holds true in external psychophysics—the sensation of a difference between two <term>stimuli</term><note>External physical energies, like light or sound, that trigger a response.</note> remains constant if the ratio of both stimuli remains constant, and the increase in sensation for a stimulus is proportional to the relative increase of that stimulus, the same applies generally in internal psychophysics if one replaces "stimulus" with "psychophysical excitation." However, the deviations from Weber’s Law that occur in external psychophysics are, according to the psychophysical view, based on secondary conditions. By contrast, according to the physiological view, Weber’s Law possesses no pure validity for internal psychophysics at all; and insofar as it exists, it does not exist between sensation and psychophysical excitation, but rather between psychophysical excitation and the stimulus—without, however, existing generally between them, as shown by the deviations from the law in external psychophysics.

All these points are so interconnected in a consistent analysis that they stand or fall together; one can therefore approach the question of which view is preferable from any of these points. ## A) A Priori Perspectives.

One cannot attribute logical self-evidence to either of the two views, nor can one find a conceptual contradiction in the assertion of one or the other. But one can ask whether contradictions might be found in one or the other with psychological or physical principles considered beyond doubt—contradictions which are not found in the other. This allows the preference to be decided from the outset, based on what can be considered, at least relatively, as <term>a priori</term>.

To me, the following point appears quite decisive against the physiological view in this regard.

The stimulus *r* <note>original: "r" for "Reiz" (stimulus).</note> is, generally speaking, a physical process—in the case of light and sound, a vibration process; the **psychophysical excitation** *E* <note>The physical activity in the nervous system that corresponds to a mental state.</note>, which stands in a dependent relationship to it, is also a physical process, likely—though that can remain undecided here—also a vibration process. According to what physical principle should the change of a physical process *E* decrease and approach disappearance simply because the causal process *r*, on which *E* depends, increases? And yet, this is the case according to the physiological view, based on the second point of difference (p. 222); for according to the physiological view, one has as a consequence of **Weber’s Law**:

->*dE = x dr / r*<-
<note>In this formula, *dE* is the change in internal brain excitation, *dr* is the change in external stimulus, and *r* is the total stimulus level. Fechner is highlighting a paradox: as the background stimulus *r* gets larger, the resulting brain reaction *dE* to a new change *dr* becomes smaller.</note>

Thus, the larger the *r* that changes by a given *dr*, the smaller is the dependent *dE*; indeed, as *r* grows, *dE* approaches disappearance more and more.

However, even in the physical realm itself, as far as I can see, states or changes that stand in a simultaneous dependence on one another only exhibit proportionality [in magnitude] in the single case that they are of a **similar nature** 1), consequently, it is not to be expected at all that physical and psychic states, which are so different in kind, should be simply proportional to one another in their simultaneous dependence.

Regarding the examples of the simultaneous relationship in the physical realm cited in *In Sachen*, it must be noted as a correction that although the distance of a planet from the sun and its velocity in its orbit stand in simultaneous dependence on one another—no less so than the space traversed and the time elapsed—they do not, as might appear from the insufficiently distinguished way of citing them in *In Sachen*, also relate both of the first states to both of the latter. For in fact, velocity and distance at a given moment cannot be considered simultaneous with the space previously traversed or the time previously elapsed. For the same reason, one should not rightly include the example of the illumination of a surface by a light at a certain distance here, and should rather strike it; because

The correlation between pendulum length and oscillation period, for example, is first conditioned and mediated by the existence of **gravity** <note>original: "Schwerkraft"</note> and various other circumstances; therefore, if these conditions are not all fulfilled, a pendulum length can exist without there being any oscillation or oscillation period of the pendulum at all." 

Now, however, the "processes" of which Müller speaks insert themselves between pendulum length and oscillation period, or velocity and distance of a planet, etc., just as little as they do between simultaneously conditioned physical and psychic determinations. Ultimately, pendulum length and oscillation period, and so on, are connected just as immediately through basic physical laws (into which force-relationships can be translated) as body and soul are through **psychophysical** ones. And as for the remark that a pendulum length can exist without an oscillation or period being present: naturally, one can only speak of a relationship between the two insofar as both are present at the same time. Similarly, one can only speak of a relationship between sensation and psychophysical excitation insofar as both are present at the same time; resting matter would produce as little sensation as a resting pendulum length would produce an oscillation.

In any case, Müller overlooks that the similarity and dissimilarity of the relatively changing processes find their expression in the schema through the different forms of the curves representing them; the schema is designed for this, so there is no need to draw a conclusion that if the curves are similar, the processes must also be similar.

### B) Empirical Points of View.

Under this heading, I will investigate several questions which, while perhaps already partially answered and settled by conclusions from the *a priori* principle <term>a priori principle: a principle established through reasoning rather than observation</term> asserted under section A, should nevertheless be revisited directly for the revision of many previous debates conducted on the subject.

### a) The Question of Interpreting the Logarithmic Dependence Between Stimulus and Sensation.

The logarithmic dependence between stimulus and sensation established by **Weber's Law** <note>original: "Webersche Gesetz"; the principle that the perceived change in a stimulus is proportional to the initial intensity of that stimulus.</note> allows, as noted (p. 222), for two initial possibilities: either to assume that the **psychophysical excitation E** <term>psychophysical excitation: the internal physiological activity (likely in the brain) that directly produces a sensation</term> is **proportional** to the stimulus *r*, while the sensation *s* is in **logarithmic dependence** on the psychophysical excitation *E*; or conversely, to think of the **psychophysical excitation as logarithmically dependent on the stimulus *r***, and the sensation *s* as **proportional** to the psychophysical excitation *E*. The former reflects the **psychophysical view**, while the latter reflects the **physiological view**.

Now, in *Elements* <note>original: "Elem."; referring to Fechner’s founding work, *Elemente der Psychophysik* (1860).</note> Vol. II, p. 429, I had stated as a general point of view to

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s rebuttal of Georg Elias Müller’s critique of the "physiological view" versus the "psychophysical view." Fechner is discussing whether the logarithmic relationship described in Weber's Law happens between the physical stimulus and the body's internal nerve activity (the physiological view) or between that internal activity and the conscious mind (the psychophysical view).</meta>

...argued in favor of the **psychophysical view** <note>original: "ps.-ph. Ansicht"</note> that "given the essential difference between the physical and psychic domains, a logarithmic dependence between physical and psychic activity—in the sense of the **fundamental formula** and **measurement formula** <term>measurement formula: the mathematical equation Fechner developed to relate the intensity of a physical stimulus to the strength of a perceived sensation</term>—is very much conceivable. By contrast, such a dependence between two physical activities—represented on one hand by the stimulus effect and on the other by the psychophysical activity [and established by the physiological view within the limits of **Weber's Law** <term>Weber's Law: the principle that the perceived change in a stimulus is proportional to the initial intensity of the stimulus</term>]—is not conceivable."

**Müller** has declared himself against this statement (p. 234), and even before that, I myself withdrew it (in ***In the Matter of Psychophysics*** <note>original: "In Sachen," referring to Fechner's 1877 book "In Sachen der Psychophysik"</note>, p. 72), because it truly could not be established as logically self-evident, and even a factual exceptional case seemed to speak against it. In the meantime, whether one thinks of inertia, impact, mass attraction, or repulsion as causes of effects in the physical domain, the immediate effect is everywhere simply proportional to the cause. It is only that the effects of one cause come into conflict with those of another, and in the course of these effects through time and space, resistances can assert themselves. These resistances, as consequences of causes acting from elsewhere, can always be traced back to complications. And according to this, generally speaking, the possibility is indeed conceivable that a causal impulse or movement process acting as a stimulus might have a nerve process as its following process in logarithmic dependence upon it. However, it is not enough to simply appeal to this general "conceivability"; rather, it must also be shown: 1) theoretically, if and under what conditions this conceivability is realizable, and to what extent such conditions exist in our case; or 2) one must be able to refer to actual **examples** of such dependence in the physical domain, from which an **application** can be made to our case. So far, there has been no mention of the physiological view fulfilling the first requirement; even in **Müller's** work, there is no hint of it. But suppose one appealed to the difficulty of theoretical (i.e., mathematical) investigation in general—which seems to me simply enough overcome by the considerations under section A—it would then be all the more necessary to seek a foothold in **examples** of the actual occurrence of such dependence. **Müller** has not done this either, whereas the discussion in ***In the Matter of Psychophysics*** (p. 73 ff.) was already directed toward this, and the following discussion will address it more thoroughly.

...the difference in altitude from the ratio of the associated barometric readings and from Bouguer’s Law—which also leads to a logarithmic dependence—namely, “that the quantity of light penetrating through a transparent body decreases in a geometric series if the thickness of the body increases in an arithmetic progression.” However, he himself later realizes that this is not a logarithmic dependence between physical processes, which is precisely what we are discussing, and he does not consider it necessary to look for other actual examples of such things. Indeed, after I myself did so and believed I had found an example that seemed to belong here—which, upon closer inspection, does not actually belong here—he does not even allow my appeal to it to stand; and what, then, does he have on his part to rely upon?

It had occurred to me that regarding the dependence of the magnitude of a muscle twitch on the magnitude of the (tetanizing) <note>tetanizing: a stimulus that causes a sustained, continuous muscle contraction</note> stimulus applied to it, one can not only very well imagine a logarithmic dependence between them, but that such a dependence even found an experimental representative, Preyer <note>William Thierry Preyer (1841–1897), a physiologist known for his work on child development and muscle response</note>, who established exactly the same measurement formula for the dependence of the magnitude of the twitch on the stimulus as I did for the dependence of sensation <note>original: "E.", abbreviation for "Empfindung" (sensation)</note> on the stimulus. Now, I myself pointed out in ***In the Matter of Psychophysics*** <note>original: "In Sachen," referring to Fechner's 1877 book "In Sachen der Psychophysik"</note> that this formula cannot have unlimited validity; and Müller (Review, p. 820) finds the appeal to it not at all fortunate, “because physiological criticism has judged Preyer’s myophysical <term>myophysical: relating to the physical properties and laws of muscle action</term> investigations with remarkable agreement in the negative”; yet the formula represents both the circumstance that the contraction only begins at a finite degree of stimulus—thus having a threshold value <term>threshold value: the minimum level of intensity a stimulus must reach to trigger a reaction</term>—and that the growth of the contraction remains far behind the proportionality with the growth of the stimulus. To that extent, it does actually hold with a certain **approximation**; and so, from the physiological point of view, one could certainly expect the objection: since we have a factual example of an (approximate) logarithmic dependence between muscle twitch and stimulus (electrical activity) as a relationship between two physical processes, there is no reason to consider such a relationship between psychophysical activity and stimulus any less possible. Insofar as the sensation is proportional to the psychophysical activity <note>psychophysical activity: the internal neural energy or "nerve-process" that Fechner believed mediated between the external stimulus and the conscious mind</note>, the logarithmic dependence between sensation and stimulus—to the extent that it exists according to Weber’s Law—is also the result.
