<meta>This page continues Fechner’s rebuttal of Georg Elias Müller’s critique regarding the nature of Weber's Law. Fechner is arguing against the "physiological view"—the idea that the logarithmic relationship between stimulus and sensation happens entirely within the physical nervous system. On the previous page, he mentioned muscle twitches as a potential physical example of this law but began to doubt its validity.</meta>

But two things must be said against the applicability of this to our case. *First*, when a physical stimulus <term>Reiz: any external physical energy, like light or touch, that triggers a biological response</term> acts on a muscle, whether through the mediation of a nerve or directly, the magnitude of the contraction cannot grow proportionally to the magnitude of the stimulus. This is because an increasing resistance develops as the contraction increases. In this case, one can certainly imagine an approximately logarithmic relationship <term>logarithmic relationship: a mathematical ratio where the stimulus must multiply to produce a simple addition in response (e.g., doubling the light to feel one step brighter)</term> between the magnitude of the stimulus and the magnitude of the contraction—that is, between two physical processes. One might even find such a relationship with a very rough approximation. But can corresponding reasons be found for a logarithmic dependence between stimulus and nerve excitation, as is demanded by the physiological view within the limits of Weber’s Law <note>Weber's Law: the observation that the "just noticeable difference" between two stimuli is proportional to the magnitude of the stimuli</note>? Does the content of the nerve perhaps contract with increasing resistance, similar to how a muscle does, under the influence of a stimulus? Of course, that would not have to be the case; some other physical means of mediating the logarithmic dependence could take its place. However, not even a hint of such a mechanism is found in the work of Müller <note>Georg Elias Müller (1850–1934), a prominent experimental psychologist and contemporary of Fechner</note> or anywhere else; there is only the vague possibility that such a thing *might* exist. As long as no complication or resistance can be pointed out with any certainty—something that would transform the fundamental proportionality between cause and effect into a logarithmic dependence—the appeal to simple proportionality remains the stronger argument.

But now, *secondly*, upon closer and sharper inspection—which should have occurred to me sooner—the dependence of the height of a muscle twitch on the nerve stimulus (that is, on the exciting electrical process) is not the dependence of a *movement process* upon it, but rather the *final result* of such a process. Therefore, it basically provides no example at all of the logarithmic dependence of one physical movement process on another movement process, which is what we are dealing with in the case of light and sound stimuli. Thus, until now, there has been a complete lack of any such *example*, either inside or outside the organism, that the physiological view could rely upon. If, however, neither theory nor empirical observation provides any indication that examples of this kind exist at all—let alone any that could be applied to our case—then the disadvantage of the physiological view compared to the psychophysical <note>psychophysical view: Fechner's own theory that the logarithmic change occurs at the transition from the physical (body) to the psychical (mind)</note> view seems evident to me; for the latter not only...

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s technical defense of his psychophysical theory against G.E. Müller. ...a general principle of the proportionality of physical consequences to physical causes; moreover, especially when taking into account demonstrable interfering secondary conditions, it is not difficult to find actual examples of this. In particular, it is worth considering that the excitation of oscillatory processes <term>oscillatory processes: rhythmic vibrations, like those of a swinging pendulum or a sound wave</term> by other oscillatory processes already provides such examples in the external world. The internal nerve processes stimulated by external light and sound vibrations, upon which light and sound **sensations** depend, can hardly be imagined as anything other than vibrations as well (see *“Elements of Psychophysics,” Vol. II, p. 282*, and *“In the Matter of Psychophysics,” p. 117*). The fact that these vibrations propagate incomparably slower through the nerve mass than light and sound do through the ether and air does not in the least prevent them from remaining proportional in strength—that is, in *amplitude* <term>amplitude: the maximum extent of a vibration or oscillation, measured from the position of equilibrium</term>—to the stimulating vibrations in comparable experiments. Now, it is true that the transition from external vibrations to internal molecular nerve vibrations does not happen directly, but through intermediate media; at least in the senses of sight, taste, and smell, this likely occurs through the intervention of chemical processes. But even in the external world, the insertion of any media between the initial and resulting vibrations does not diminish the proportionality as long as the intermediate medium remains constant. As for the insertion of a chemical process, there is certainly not the slightest theoretical or empirical evidence that a logarithmic dependence <note>logarithmic dependence: a relationship where the input must increase exponentially to produce a linear increase in output</note> between the stimulating vibrations and those propagated through the nerves could be mediated this way. Conversely, the former could indisputably not continue into the latter as vibrations through the mediation of a chemical process unless the chemical process itself included vibrations (see *“In the Matter of Psychophysics,” p. 118*), the strength of which would then, as everywhere else, be proportional to the strength of the stimulating vibrations. More on this below.

The preceding can serve as a general reply to Müller's remark (*Review, p. 823*) that the proportionality I have established between stimulus and <term>psychophysical</term> excitation within the limits of Weber’s Law only "contains a possibility just as unfounded" as the charge I level against the logarithmic dependence of <term>psychophysical</term> excitation on the stimulus—the view held by the physiological school—within the limits of the law in question. In fact, according to the previous discussions, the matter stands as anything but equal on both sides. The <term>psychophysical</term> view can argue for proportionality within those limits...

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s argument that physical stimulus and internal nerve activity relate through simple proportionality rather than a logarithmic scale. He is addressing counter-arguments that suggest small physical triggers can have large effects, potentially mimicking the complexity of his psychophysical law.</meta>

...of the law, as well as for the deviations from it, one can assert known and recognized physical principles and facts; the physiological view, however, offers no such principles for a logarithmic dependency <term>logarithmic dependency: a relationship where equal percentage changes in a stimulus result in equal additive changes in sensation, creating a curve rather than a straight line</term>.

Perhaps one could raise the following objection against the former point. In fact, there are cases where a very small physical movement can trigger an enormously large one, whereby the proportionality between cause and consequence seems to fail entirely. For instance, when a large mass rests in balance on a sharp edge, a small sideways nudge can cause it to fall, and thereby release a powerful kinetic force. Similarly, a small spark can cause a huge mass of gunpowder to explode. The prerequisite for such a release of effects that are completely out of proportion to the cause is a labile equilibrium <term>labile equilibrium: a state of unstable balance where the slightest disturbance causes a system to move toward a more stable state, releasing stored energy</term>. Even in these cases, however, the direct or immediate effect is undeniably proportional to the cause. In the first example, if the nudge to the mass is too small, it is not sufficient to cause the fall, but only to shift the center of gravity on the edge—which must necessarily have some width—and it sets the particles of the mass into motion against those of the edge in proportion to its own speed. In this case, either the nudge is insufficient to push the particles of the mass beyond the closest ones of the edge—that is, to overcome the resistance offered by elasticity, which increases as they approach—or it is sufficient. Regarding the second example: if the heat acting upon the powder from a single point is not great enough, the powder does not explode, because it is not sufficient to drive even the constituents of the nearest particles far enough apart to cause decomposition; nevertheless, it will cause an approach toward that point, while the decomposition, once started, then propagates from particle to particle.

Now, one might think that the influence of the stimulus on the nerve is also such a triggering mechanism.

But in all known cases of such physical triggering, we see that the effect is **not** in a logarithmic dependency on the cause, but rather has no specific quantitative dependency on it at all—unlike the specific relationship that exists between stimulus and nerve excitation. Therefore, no application can be made of this to justify a logarithmic dependency of psychophysical excitation on the stimulus, and indeed, it cannot be applied to our question at all.

Naturally, all previous considerations arguing against a logarithmic dependency between stimulus and psychophysical nerve excitation would be in vain if such a thing could be proven **directly**. And this seemed to have been achieved through the experiments by Dewar and McKendrick mentioned in *In Matters of Psychophysics*, p. 75 ff. <note>original: "In Sachen" refers to Fechner's 1877 book *In Sachen der Psychophysik*, a defense of his theories</note> <note>James Dewar and John McKendrick were scientists who measured the electrical response of the eye to light in the 1870s</note>. Meanwhile, I have already pointed out there that the logarithmic dependency asserted by these observers does not exist between the nerve process itself (upon which the sensation of light depends) and the stimulus,

### b) Question regarding the existence of an internal threshold.

An **external stimulus threshold** exists insofar as the external stimulus must first reach a certain magnitude before the sensation becomes noticeable. We speak of an **internal** or **psychophysical sensation threshold** in the sense already indicated: that the psychophysical activity <note>the internal physical process, like neural firing, that directly triggers a mental sensation</note> must first reach a certain magnitude before the sensation begins to become noticeable.

The assumption of an internal threshold in this sense is solid—

---

1) That I (*In Sachen* p. 81) viewed the results of Baxt’s experiments as essentially agreeing with Exner’s was indeed a mistake, correctly noted by Müller. Similarly, the derivation of the formula cited in *In Sachen* p. 80: $\gamma = k \log \beta$ from Exner’s experiments was based on the error of taking the product $t \log \beta$ as a constant instead of the sum $t + \log \beta$. However, the formula substituted by Müller for the one above, $\gamma = k \log \beta + t$, also requires a supplement. According to his version, the just-noticeable sensation $\gamma$ would still have a finite value $= k \log \beta$ if $t = 0$, whereas in reality, the sensation only begins to become noticeable at a finite value of $t$. If, on the other hand, one sets the stimulus strength $\beta = A$ at $t = 0$, one obtains the correctly supplemented formula:

->$\gamma = k \log \frac{\beta}{A} + t.$<-

The same result would be achieved without introducing $A$ by the—admittedly not self-evident—stipulation that the value of $\beta$ occurring at $t = 0$ is to be taken as the unit of $\beta$.

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s investigation into the "internal threshold" by distinguishing it from the "external threshold." He is responding to the physiological argument that sensations fail to reach consciousness not because of a mental limit, but because the physical signal simply dissipates in the nerves before reaching the brain.</meta>

...[empirically] with the transferability of **Weber's Law** <term>Weber's Law: the principle that the perceived change in a stimulus is proportional to the initial intensity of that stimulus</term> from the stimulus to the psychophysical excitation and the resulting **logarithmic dependency** of sensation on this activity. Therefore, the primary reason for assuming an **internal threshold** <note>internal threshold: the point at which activity within the brain or nervous system becomes strong enough to trigger conscious awareness</note> is intertwined with the previously discussed reasons for this dependency. More direct proof of this is provided by the conditions of attention to be discussed under section d) (which, admittedly, are to be interpreted differently than Müller <note>G.E. Müller (1850–1934), a contemporary psychologist and rigorous critic of Fechner's methods</note> does). Thus, the assumption of an internal threshold does not rest solely on the discussions we are about to undertake, which will explore whether reasons for the existence of an internal threshold can already be found in the existence of the **external threshold**. I must admit at the outset that from this point of view, it is impossible to decide for or against it with certainty; nevertheless, it will be useful to consider the circumstances in this regard more closely.

From the start, one could certainly imagine that a weak external stimulus becomes ineffective for sensation only because, on its path of propagation to the sensory organ (the *sensorium* <term>sensorium: the parts of the brain considered to be the seat of sensation</term>), it is subject to such weakening—through resistance, absorption, scattering, or conversion into another form—that nothing of it remains in the sensory organ itself. If this were the case, it would be superfluous to assume an internal threshold. Our first task, therefore, is to see what can be argued in this regard.

Generally, the **ganglion cells** <term>ganglion cells: in 19th-century physiology, this referred broadly to the nerve cell bodies in the gray matter of the brain</term> of the gray matter of the brain are regarded as the sensory organ. Although I personally believe that the entire system of our psychophysical excitations above the threshold—insofar as it is interconnected—is the carrier of our **consciousness**, one must still assign some preferred or central significance to the ganglion cells within this system. Since that assumption is currently the dominant one, we may stick to it for the following considerations to fix our ideas. However, it changes nothing if the concept of the *sensorium* is expanded in the sense I propose.

For the sake of brevity, we shall call it an **exhaustion of the stimulus** when the excitation awakened by the stimulus weakens until it completely disappears on its path of propagation to the sensory organ. Now, Müller (p. 241) explains: if the excitation of the peripheral nerve ending by the stimulus—and thus the stimulus itself—does not exceed a certain value, to be regarded as the **external threshold value**, and "the intensity of the excitation of the sensory nerve decreases as it spreads through the same," then an exhaustion [occurs]...

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s rebuttal of G.E. Müller’s physiological arguments. Fechner is addressing the idea that a stimulus might fail to trigger a sensation simply because the signal dies out (attenuates) as it travels along the nerves toward the brain.</meta>

...must necessarily dissipate the excitation before reaching the sensorium <term>sensorium: the parts of the brain considered to be the seat of sensation</term>. But nothing is more groundless than the premise established by Müller <note>G.E. Müller (1850–1934), a major rival to Fechner’s psychophysical theories</note>. Rather, if the excitation decreases at every moment of propagation or at every point along the path by a part proportional to its current magnitude—or, what amounts to the same thing, if it weakens according to the ratio of its existing magnitude, which I will call **proportional attenuation** for short—then the excitation, no matter how small it may be initially and regardless of how long the path it travels, can never completely expire. By contrast, a complete extinction would indeed occur over a sufficient length of the conduction path if, in every new moment, an amount equal to or greater than that of the previous moment were withdrawn from the excitation **regardless** of its current magnitude; this I will call **absolute attenuation** for short. It is difficult to explain how Müller could have overlooked this distinction, which is **fundamental** for the current investigation. Or was absolute attenuation for the propagation of excitation through the nervous system perhaps to be regarded as so self-evident, or so notorious based on obvious facts, that there was no need to consider the possibility of proportional attenuation at all? On the contrary, Bernstein <note>Julius Bernstein (1839–1917), a pioneer in neurophysiology who developed the "membrane theory" of nerve impulses</note> has instead taken proportional attenuation into account as if it were self-evident when constructing his measurement formula (cf. *In Sachen* <note>original: "In Sachen [der Psychophysik]", Fechner's 1877 book</note> p. 20, 138 ff.) for the progress of excitation through the ganglion cells <term>ganglion cells: nerve cells that process and transmit signals in the brain and nervous system</term> of the brain. If he nonetheless allows the excitation to propagate only up to certain limits, he merely contradicts his own premise without discarding it. This is precisely a primary error of his theory, regarding which one may compare *In Sachen* p. 144.

Furthermore, we know that the attenuation of light and sound through reflection and dispersion occurs according to the principle of proportional attenuation; thus, the possibility of the same occurring could not be neglected from the outset in the question currently occupying us. Indeed, according to Bernstein's direct experiments (*Untersuchungen* p. 151 ff.), not only does no absolute attenuation occur along the course of the nerve, but no noticeable attenuation of the propagated excitation occurs at all. Müller himself does not fail to mention this result by Bernstein, though he admittedly mentions at the same time (p. 241) that there are also investigations with contradictory results by Pflüger, Rosenthal, Pleischl, and others <note>Eduard Pflüger, Isidor Rosenthal, and others were prominent 19th-century physiologists researching muscle and nerve stimulation</note> regarding the intensity ratios of the...

<summary>Fechner distinguishes between "proportional" and "absolute" attenuation of nerve signals, arguing that under a proportional model, a signal never truly disappears. He critiques Müller for overlooking this distinction and cites Bernstein’s research to suggest that nerve signals may not weaken significantly at all during transit.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s rebuttal of G.E. Müller’s arguments regarding the "threshold" of sensation. Fechner is now examining whether the loss of a signal could happen within the eye's fluids or the sensory receptors themselves, rather than just along the nerve fiber.</meta>

...excitation during its passage through the nerves; however, I have been informed by the most expert source (Prof. Ludwig <note>Carl Ludwig (1816–1895), a preeminent German physiologist who pioneered the study of blood pressure and kidney function</note>) that the greatest confidence is placed in Bernstein’s results.

Now, of course, it does not depend solely on the propagation of the excitation through the nerve. For example, before light can reach the optic nerve, it must first pass through the ocular humors <term>ocular humors: the clear fluids (aqueous and vitreous) that fill the eyeball</term>; could a light that is too weak not be extinguished by absorption before it even gets there? But that contradicts **Bouguer’s Law** <note>original: "Bouguerschen Satze"; this law describes how light intensity decreases as it passes through a medium. Fechner notes that the law implies light is never "totally" extinguished unless the medium is infinitely thick</note>, which Müller himself has asserted elsewhere. According to this law, the light stimulus could only be absolutely exhausted if the absorbing medium were of infinite thickness.

Following this, one might claim that the changes the stimulus undergoes in the **terminal apparatus** <term>terminal apparatus: the sensory receptor cells, such as the rods and cones in the retina, where a physical stimulus is converted into a nerve impulse</term> of the sensory nerves, before it travels through the nerve, satisfy the requirements of the physiological view. It must be admitted that, since we know almost nothing about the modifications the stimulus undergoes therein, an indefinite possibility exists to find here what the physiological view requires ¹). Müller also makes full use of this indefinite possibility (p. 239 f.), notably by pointing out that the effect of light rays on the retina is indisputably a **photochemical** one, but that a certain intensity of the acting light is required to trigger a chemical action in the terminal apparatus. From this, the <term>threshold</term> <note>the minimum level of stimulus required to produce a sensation</note> could depend, which would then be physiological instead of psychophysical: at least, that is how I believe I understand Müller. On what facts he relies for this, I do not know. It is, of course, natural—but also understandable as a result of the **psychophysical threshold**—that the effect of light on a photochemical preparation must first reach a certain degree before it becomes perceptible to the eye; yet, according to the psychophysical view, the effect can already be present before that point. Furthermore, it is certain that heat, as an agent through which chemical compounds are formed or dissolved, must reach a certain degree before this result occurs. But it cannot be the final result of a completed connection or separation that produces a lasting sensation—

---

1) What one can, in my opinion, consider probable is that the particles in the terminal apparatus of the various sense organs have such a different arrangement that a different form and composition of the vibrations, excited therein by the stimulus and propagated from there, results; however, nothing depends here on holding fast to or elaborating upon this hypothesis.

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s critique of Georg Elias Müller’s physiological explanations for the sensory threshold. On the previous page, Fechner discussed whether light is extinguished by the physical structures of the eye. He now turns to the "chemical" theories of nerve excitation and Wilhelm Wundt’s theories on the resistance of nerve cells.</meta>

...sensation <note>original: "dung", likely completing "Empfindung" from the previous page</note> depends upon the constant application of a stimulus, but rather only a constant process. How Müller <note>Georg Elias Müller (1850–1934), an experimental psychologist who often critiqued Fechner’s psychophysical methods</note> conceives of this in terms of **chemism** <term>chemism: the theory that nerve impulses are essentially chemical reactions rather than purely electrical or mechanical vibrations</term> is unclear to me—and generally unclear how it is to be thought of as anything other than a form of transmissible vibrations, if one wishes to think anything at all, which one admittedly likes to avoid by using the name "chemical process."

Moreover, even if the chemical hypothesis were applicable to the eye, and the objection could find some support there, the question remains: to what extent does it apply to the other sense organs? For these, experience provides no definite support, but only an indefinite possibility. In this regard, Wundt <note>Wilhelm Wundt (1832–1920), widely regarded as the father of experimental psychology</note> explicitly contrasts the sense of hearing with the sense of sight. I admit that a more general significance of chemism in all sensory processes might find a ground of probability in the fact that the nervous system, in order to function psychically, everywhere requires a supply of oxygenated blood. However, the same considerations that apply to the eye would then have to apply everywhere else as well.

There remains, then, the view championed especially by Wundt: that weak stimuli can be exhausted by a peculiar resistance they encounter during their passage through the **ganglion cells** <term>ganglion cells: nerve cells that act as relay points or processing centers for neural signals</term>. Yet this would be of no avail, insofar as the excitation—once it had entered the ganglion cell—would have to carry with it a sensation <note>original: "E.", abbreviation for "Empfindung"</note> dependent on its remaining strength during the passage itself, until it was exhausted therein. Furthermore, I cannot find Wundt’s view sufficiently grounded by the facts he cites (Phy.-Ps. I. 340) <note>Refers to Wundt’s "Grundzüge der physiologischen Psychologie" (Principles of Physiological Psychology), Volume 1, page 340</note>.

To be sure, a very weak stimulus applied to a muscle nerve, which is still sufficient to cause the muscle to twitch if the stimulus encounters no ganglion cell on its path, is no longer able to do so if it has to pass through such a cell. Instead, an intensification of the stimulus is required; thus, it does indeed seem to be exhausted in the cell. Furthermore: if the stimulus is sufficiently intensified to trigger the twitch after passing through the ganglion cell, the twitch occurs later and is, in exchange, more sustained than when the intervention of the ganglion cell is absent. — But these same facts can be represented by the idea that the stimulus, when passing through the ganglion cell, follows the principle of **proportional weakening**,

...which does not lead to total annihilation, but only decreases so much that it no longer reaches the threshold of muscle twitching, which was discussed above (p. 231). Since the existence of this threshold is proven, there is no need for the hypothesis of a complete extinction of the stimulus along the conduction path through the cell. Furthermore, the fact that a twitch occurring later when a ganglion cell is inserted is more sustained than without such insertion does not argue at all that the **living force** <term>living force: known in the original German as *lebendige Kraft* (and in Latin as *vis viva*), this 19th-century term refers to what we now call kinetic energy or the intensity of a physical process</term> of the excitation lost anything while passing through the ganglion cell; rather, it suggests only that it has distributed itself over a longer period in its subsequent effect on the muscle. In such cases, it can indeed happen that it distributes itself so far that at no single moment does a living force sufficient to exceed the muscle's twitch-threshold come into effect.

Although I find all previous considerations—by which one believes they can justify or make probable an exhaustion of the external stimulus before reaching the **sensory center** <term>sensorium: the parts of the brain where sensations are processed and perceived</term>—to be insufficient, recent investigations by Vierordt <note>Karl von Vierordt (1818–1884), a German physiologist who studied the conduction of sound and blood</note> have swayed me. These studies show that an absolute weakening of sound occurs when transmitted through any physical body, and this is particularly significant in organic bodies. Thus, I consider it possible that the propagation of vibrational movement through living nerves is also subject to such weakening. This naturally suggests the idea of explaining the fact of the external threshold entirely without the aid of an internal one, by arguing that the stimulus is not felt because it does not reach the sensory center at all. However, as long as the other reasons for an internal threshold remain unrefuted, one must say: a weak stimulus can be lost to sensation, firstly, because it never reaches the sensory nerves due to exhaustion through external media; secondly, because it does not reach the sensory center due to exhaustion within the nerve itself; and thirdly, finally, because even after reaching the sensory center, it remains below the **inner psychophysical threshold** <term>ps.-ph. threshold: the threshold of intensity required for a physical process in the brain to trigger a conscious mental sensation</term>.

...between the physiological and the **psycho-physical** <note>original: "ps.-ph."</note> view. Let us first recall the main fact that underlies the **parallel law** <term>parallel law: the principle that the relationship between stimuli remains constant in perception even when the absolute sensitivity of the organ changes</term> (p. 180 ff.). When two stimuli of different strengths act on a sensing organ for a certain period, the absolute sensations—and therefore the excitations produced by the stimuli—weaken due to fatigue; however, the perceived difference remains just as unchanged as is the case under **Weber’s Law** <note>Weber’s Law states that the "just noticeable difference" between two stimuli is proportional to the magnitude of the stimuli</note> when the objective stimuli are changed in the same proportion.

This fact can certainly be explained quite simply and directly according to the psycho-physical view: the psycho-physical excitations caused by the stimuli are weakened by fatigue in the same proportion, which has the same effect as a corresponding weakening of the external stimuli. However, it cannot initially be denied that the physiological view could also explain this. According to that view, the **sensation of difference** <term>sensation of difference: the mental perception of the gap between two distinct stimuli</term> remains the same not when the *ratio* of excitations is constant, but when the <term>difference: abbreviated in the original as "U." for *Unterschied*</term> of the psycho-physical excitations remains the same. One would merely need to assume that through fatigue, the excitations in question decrease by the same absolute amount regardless of their strength, rather than in proportion to it; the fact of the parallel law would be represented no less by this assumption. So far, I know of no fact that directly decides in favor of one assumption or the other. To be sure, one might recall that various experiments have already been conducted on the influence of muscle fatigue on the twitching patterns of muscles; yet I know of no unambiguous clue therein for judging the psycho-physical fatigue conditions of sensory nerves.

Accordingly, it would seem that no decision between the psycho-physical and physiological views can be found from this point either. However, insofar as the parallel law consists in the fact that the weakening of psycho-physical excitations through fatigue has the same result as the weakening of stimuli in the same proportion—namely, leaving the sensation of difference unchanged—then according to the physiological view, the constant differ—

#### d) Question regarding the interpretation of the conditions of attention, sleep, and waking.

Against my interpretation of the above conditions in the sense of the **psycho-physical** view, Müller <note>Georg Elias Müller (1850–1934), a younger contemporary of Fechner and a pioneer in experimental psychology who often critiqued Fechner's work.</note> naturally finds much to object to.     Before entering into the main points of the proceedings, a few remarks to correct their foundations.
    Müller (p. 353 ff.) rightly declares it to be a view—not only unproven by me but generally untenable—that during sleep consciousness is entirely absent everywhere, and consequently that dreams also fall below the **threshold of consciousness** <term>threshold of consciousness: the limit below which a stimulus is no longer perceived</term> (*Elements of Psychophysics* <note>original: "Elem."</note> II. 461 f.); however, I had already expressly retracted this insufficiently considered conception of dreams in my work *In Sachen* <note>original: "In Sachen" refers to Fechner's 1877 book "In Sachen der Psychophysik" (In the Matter of Psychophysics).</note> page 218, even before Müller’s counter-declaration.

Müller’s remark is correct—though not new to me—that a sleep from which we cannot remember a dream may nevertheless have carried one along with it, since the memory of it could simply have been lost. Yet I consider it probable that there is also sleep without dreams; since with the approach of sleep we can sometimes become very well aware of the approach to complete unconsciousness itself, and since the psycho-physical view that I represent makes the occurrence of dreamless sleep easily explainable.
    From another side, I must protect myself against the substitution of a view by Müller (p. 350, 365 and referring to it in his review p. 166), of which I actually hold the opposite.
    According to him, I am supposed to hold the view that "every excitation arising in any nervous organ as a psycho-physical activity, if its intensity exceeds the excitation threshold value, necessarily calls forth a conscious excitation in us"; thus, for example, in an **intestinal ganglion** <note>A cluster of nerve cells in the gut.</note>...

Against this, my view is that while the brain is certainly to be regarded as the **narrower seat of the soul** (the **sensorium** <note>original Latin: *sensorium*, referring to the seat of sensation in the brain</note> according to Müller) in the sense just stated, a **psycho-physical** <note>original: "ps.-ph."</note> change excited in the nervous system outside the brain—even if it exceeds the threshold—only becomes conscious to the possessor of the brain if both excitations above the threshold are not interrupted by an intermediate excitation below the threshold, or by a missing psycho-physical excitation in between. By saying this, I do not mean that it remains unconscious altogether; on the contrary, since I assume a **universal consciousness** <note>original: "Allgemeinbewußtsein"; Fechner’s philosophical view that a broader consciousness exists beyond individual humans and animals</note> beyond the human and animal ones—which depends on more general conditions than the special conditions for us—I believe that the excitation of the ganglion above the threshold, which is so to speak cut off from our consciousness, still falls into this universal consciousness. This can be found explained through a schematic representation in Section XLV of the *Elements*. But here, we are only dealing with human consciousness.

The intensity of consciousness with which a sensation is grasped depends on the cooperation of both; thus, a strong sensory excitation can become unconscious by withdrawing attention from it, or become strongly conscious by directing attention toward it. To this belongs, among others, the example mentioned in *Elements* II. 432, according to which intense **afterimages** of objects that fell upon the eye while attention was diverted can remain completely unnoticed until the attention turns to the visual field, where they suddenly enter perception.

### e) Interpretation of the results of Lamansky and Dobrowolsky regarding sensitivity to relative differences in the intensity of colors.

Starting from p. 246, Müller raises extensive objections against the **ps.-ph.** <term>ps.-ph. (psychophysical): Fechner’s abbreviation for the study of mind-body measurements</term> view, from the perspective that it is unable to adequately represent two facts resulting from the experiments of Lamansky and Dobrowolsky, which were mentioned in *In Sachen* <note>original: "In Sachen" refers to Fechner's 1877 book, *In Sachen der Psychophysik* (In the Matter of Psychophysics)</note> p. 157. To clarify the facts of the matter, some preliminary discussion will be required.

If one determines, for one and the same given color, the difference between two intensities of brightness that is "just barely recognizable" or on the verge of disappearing (in short, the **difference threshold**), and divides it by the absolute intensity to which the difference is nearest, one obtains the **relative just noticeable difference** <term>just noticeable difference (JND): the smallest change in a physical stimulus that a person can detect</term>. This shall be designated in the following (as well as in *In Sachen*) with **ε** <note>the Greek letter epsilon</note> (according to Müller, with **ω** <note>the Greek letter omega</note>), under the assumption that it is obtained at the maximum of relative difference sensitivity—that is, at the specific absolute intensity where the difference is smaller than at any other intensity. Due to deviations from **Weber’s Law** <term>Weber’s Law: a psychological principle stating that the change in a stimulus that will be just noticeable is a constant ratio of the original stimulus</term> at very low and very high levels, there is indeed such a minimum value of the relative **j.n.d.** at a certain intensity, below and above which the relative **j.n.d.** increases. However, **ε** refers to the smallest possible value that can be obtained. The intensity for which **ε** holds is also the intensity around which the approximation of Weber's Law is greatest.

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s technical defense of psychophysical laws. He is addressing the criticism that individual differences—like color blindness—disprove the idea of a universal law. He argues that while the mind follows a consistent law, the physical organs that receive stimuli can vary between people.</meta>

...individuals with unequal ease, and specifically the phenomena of so-called color blindness offer the most striking evidence for this. If a psychophysical <note>original: "ps.-ph.", an abbreviation for psychophysisch</note> law is to be established at all, this variance cannot stem from the fact that the same internal psychophysical color excitation produces a different mental effect in different individuals. Instead, it must be that, depending on the internal state of the perceiving organ, the same external color stimulus calls forth a different psychophysical excitation in different individuals, according to which the external stimulus threshold <term>stimulus threshold: the minimum intensity of a stimulus required to produce any sensation at all</term> is different. 

What is true for the external stimulus threshold is also well known to apply to the external difference threshold <term>difference threshold: also known as the "just noticeable difference," the smallest change in a stimulus that a person can detect</term>, insofar as the same external difference is not recognized with equal ease by different observers. In this regard, a point already made in the *Elements of Psychophysics* <note>original: "Elem."</note>, Volume II, page 104—but which Müller completely ignored in his remarks on page 258—is important: the value of the difference threshold (or, if one refers to the ratio instead of the difference of the stimuli, the value of the ratio threshold <term>ratio threshold: the constant ratio between two stimuli that allows them to be perceived as different, a core concept of Weber’s Law</term>) depends essentially on the external and internal conditions under which the components of the difference or ratio meet. It depends on what is inserted, lying around, or accompanying them externally and internally, temporally, spatially, and organically (compare page 187). However, these internal conditions can be very different for different observers even under the exact same external measures. The resulting effects for different colors do not need to run parallel for two different observers, since, according to the facts of color blindness, this does not even hold true for the perception of simple colors.

Now, $\epsilon$ <note>epsilon</note> is nothing other than the external difference threshold of a color stimulus divided by the strength of the external stimulus. If we now compare the $\epsilon$ of the same color across different individuals, the strength of the external stimulus will be independent of internal states, but the external difference threshold will depend on those internal states. Consequently, $\epsilon$ can turn out differently for different individuals without this in any way falling outside the principles of the psychophysical view.

This conception also connects quite consistently with our established difference measurement formula (*Elements of Psychophysics*, Volume II, page 96 ff. and *In the Matter of Psychophysics* <note>original: "In Sachen"</note>, page 11). This formula has the same significance for the perception of sensation differences <note>original: "E. Unterschieden"; E. is an abbreviation for "Empfindung" (sensation)</note> in the sense of the psychophysical view as the simple measurement formula has for the perception of simple sensations.

### C) Mathematical Perspectives.

Naturally, a view regarding real circumstances can neither be founded nor refuted by purely abstract mathematical means; however, it can be investigated whether the fundamental facts can be represented mathematically in a simpler, more unified, and more consistent manner depending on whether one adopts one view or the other. I contend that this is the case when assuming the psychophysical view. Based on this assumption, the entire consistent system of formulas in Section XV has developed, through which the most fundamental relationships between psychic <note>mental or psychological</note> and physical magnitudes are expressed. The physiological perspective has nothing equivalent to offer; instead, it merely seeks to break that connection from a negating standpoint and raises disputes over details, while its own insoluble difficulties come to light. — To begin the discussion on this, let us first recall those basic features of the physiological perspective that will primarily be at issue.

Insofar as the physiological perspective holds that sensations are proportional to psychophysical excitations, they must become zero at the same time as those excitations. Consequently, an internal sensation threshold <term>internal sensation threshold: a level of internal physical activity that must be reached before any mental sensation is felt</term> cannot exist—according to which the zero point of sensation would instead occur at a degree of psychophysical excitation above zero—and thus, according to this view, negative sensations cannot exist below that point; for indeed, negative values of sensation are inextricably linked to an internal sensation threshold. It is therefore a vital question for the physiological perspective whether an internal sensation threshold exists, and so it defends itself against it as best it can. Now, I for my part have had to admit that from an external stimulus threshold <term>external stimulus threshold: the minimum physical energy (like light or sound) needed from the outside world to trigger a sensation</term>, no certain direct conclusion can yet be drawn regarding an internal...

### D) General Viewpoints.

Undoubtedly, every philosopher who takes notice of the psychophysical system advocated here will judge it based on how far it agrees with their own general view regarding the relationship between **body and soul** or, more generally, between the **material and spiritual principle**; accordingly, they will be inclined to accept or reject it. Now, it can naturally not be my intention to negotiate with the various philosophical systems in this regard, and I would even leave the question of how far my psychophysics agrees with my own general—one might say philosophical—views on the relationship in question unexamined here (it being enough that I encounter no contradictions between them on my own paths) had not my opponents stirred up the question. Thus, I shall allow myself a few remarks on the matter in the following. What I have to say in reply to the many conceptual objections made from a philosophical perspective against the **measurement principle** <term>measurement principle: the rule used to quantify the intensity of a mental sensation based on physical stimuli</term> I have established can be found in the specific rebuttals against individual opponents in Section XXVI.

 I developed my general fundamental view most thoroughly in **"Zendavesta"** <note>original: *Zendavesta*, specifically referring to Fechner’s 1851 work *Zend-Avesta: Or on the things of heaven and the hereafter*, where he argues that all nature is ensouled.</note> Vol. II, p. 312 ff., and reproduced the main features of it in the introduction to the **"Elements"** <note>original: *Elemente*, referring to his 1860 foundational work, *Elements of Psychophysics*.</note>. Expressed briefly and, as it seems to me, clearly and sufficiently for popular understanding and practical application, it amounts to this: that body and soul are only two different ways of appearing of the same being or substrate for two different stand-

For me, this is explained within the context of my general fundamental view and in agreement with explanations given earlier, as follows:

Suppose I look into the brain of another; it is I who stands at an external viewpoint relative to the brain in question, and the other person's brain occupies the internal viewpoint toward itself. Is this really as incomprehensible as Müller finds it? In reality, of course, I cannot look into the living brain of another, but I assume that—based on the conclusions available to me from experience from an external viewpoint—it is possible to determine how the brain would look, according to the relationships under consideration, if I could look inside using the finest means of observation by removing external obstacles, and otherwise obtain external perceptions of it that could be tracked even further into detail through physical analysis. There I would perceive material brain processes which, tracked to the last detail, might be reduced to oscillatory processes <term>oscillatory processes (Schwingungsvorgänge): vibrations or repetitive movements, which Fechner believed were the physical basis of neural activity</term>; instead of these, the subject facing me perceives only mental processes <note>literally "soul-processes" (Seelenvorgänge)</note>, despite the fact that it is ultimately the same substrate that we both perceive. However, because the perceivers as well as the viewpoint from which the perception occurs are different, the appearance is different; for me, it is the appearance of material brain processes; for the other, it is the appearance of the associated mental phenomena. I show in the *Elements* <note>original: "Elem." refers to Fechner's seminal work, *Elemente der Psychophysik* (1860)</note> Vol. I, p. 4 ff., how the most general **f a c t u a l** <note>In the original German, the letters are spaced out (Sperrdruck) for emphasis, which is rendered here in bold.</note> relationships of the connection between body and soul align with this.

This represents the case in psychophysics where the psychic phenomenon belonging to that process is below the threshold. Initially, one might think that if the inner process does not appear to the brain standing at an internal viewpoint toward itself, it could appear even less as a physical process to the outside. ...beyond man, but including man, is a <term>psychophysical (ps.-ph.)<note>original: "ps.-ph." abbreviation for "psychophysisch"</note></term> system that supports a consciousness more general than the human one, while also including the human one. This human consciousness is subordinated and integrated into it as a specific detail, just as the human body is related to the general system of physical things on the material side, and as individual thoughts in our own minds relate to our entire spirit on the mental side. — *Secondly*, that the emergence of human consciousness from the General Consciousness <note>Fechner refers to a universal or divine consciousness (Allgemeinbewußtsein)</note> as a distinct particularity depends just as much on the underlying psychophysical process rising sufficiently above the general process, as the distinct emergence of a specific thought in our own consciousness depends on a corresponding condition according to the principle of the mixture threshold <term>mixture threshold (Mischungsschwelle): the point at which multiple stimuli, which are individually too weak to be felt, combine to become perceptible</term>.

According to this, in a human being, as long as they are awake, every specific process that is not yet above the threshold on its own still contributes to keeping the person’s consciousness awake and above the threshold. Thus, it is not lost to the *inner appearance* <note>subjective experience or "the way things look to the soul"</note>, except that the specific sensation matching that specific process does not appear as a distinct, individual experience. But when, in dreamless sleep, the *entire psychophysical activity of the human falls below its threshold*, the entire consciousness of the human will indeed vanish; however, the psychophysical activity below his threshold will still contribute to the general psychophysical process as an increment, helping it rise above the threshold and thereby contributing to the General Consciousness's inner appearance.

In short, all psychophysical processes that appear as physical to an external observer—or are inferred to be such from the context of external appearances—do not lack a directly corresponding inner appearance. Rather, they possess one either as a distinct individual experience or as a contribution to a more general inner appearance in which they are absorbed.

Along with the Principle of the Threshold, the <term>synechological principle<note>From "synechology," the study of continuity. Fechner uses this to argue that there are no absolute gaps in nature or consciousness.</note></term> (see "Elements" II. 526 and briefly above on page 15) must be applied in a general way. The entire physical process of the world is subject to periodicity, from the orbits of celestial bodies down to the vibrations of light and sound revealed by finer physical analysis. It is no wonder, then, if psychophysical processes also present themselves as <term>oscillatory processes (Schwingungsvorgänge)</term>. These can be broken down into various "moments" of motion or imagined as being composed of them, without these being internally distinguished...

## XVIII. Wundt’s psychological interpretation of Weber’s Law and the play of attention therein.

In discussing Wundt’s <note>Wilhelm Wundt (1832–1920): Often called the "father of experimental psychology," he founded the first formal psychological laboratory.</note> view, I believe I must essentially stick to the presentation of it in his “Principles of Physiological Psychology,” 2nd ed. 1880; not only because it is more recent, but also because it is relatively more oriented toward psychophysics <note>Psychophysik: the scientific study of the relationship between physical stimuli and mental sensations.</note> than an earlier presentation in his “Lectures on Human and Animal Souls” (1863. I. 118 ff.), which is primarily written only with psychological interest.

Wundt himself (Vol. I, p. 351) contrasts his interpretation of Weber's Law <note>Weber's Law: The principle that the minimum increase in a stimulus required to produce a noticeable difference is proportional to the original intensity of the stimulus.</note> as a *psychological* one, in a certain sense, with both the *psychophysical* and *physiological* views. He is of the opinion that this law certainly has a more general significance than just for psychophysics, extending instead into the psychological realm; and that, given its deficient grounding through experiments of external psychophysics, it could only truly find its justification starting from psychology. In short, he calls his view *psychological* according to his own explanation, insofar as Weber's Law “is to be derived from the psychological processes [especially the processes of apperception <note>apperception: Wundt’s term for the process by which mental content is brought into the "focus" of consciousness, involving active attention and willpower.</note>] which become effective during the measuring comparison of sensations,” and insofar as the law—regardless of accompanying physiological processes in the sphere of consciousness—“specifically in the qualitative comparison of sensations as well as in the relationship of feelings to ideas, extends far beyond the realm of sensa-

<meta>This page continues the technical breakdown of Wilhelm Wundt’s physiological model of "apperception." It moves from the general philosophical discussion on the previous page to a specific mechanical description of how nerve signals travel between sensory centers and the higher brain, ultimately attempting to derive Weber’s Law from these physical interactions.</meta>

...but if attention is not directed toward it, the stimulus is merely **perceived**; however, one toward which attention is directed is **apperceived**. <note>Wundt distinguishes between "perception"—the simple entry of a sensation into the consciousness—and "apperception," which is the active focusing of the mind's "inner eye" on that sensation to make it clear.</note>

A sensory stimulus is first transmitted through the sensory nerves to a center—**sensory center a**—in the brain, through which perception is mediated. It is assumed (an idea that aligns with the <term>psychophysical interpretation</term> <note>Psychophysical interpretation: The study of how physical stimuli (like light or sound) relate to the mental sensations they produce.</note> of **Weber’s Law**) that within the limits of Weber’s Law, the intensity of the excitation in this center is proportional to the strength of the stimulus.

However, this sensory center is connected by nerve fibers to a **center C** for the <term>processes of apperception</term> located in the gray matter of the forebrain. According to the diagram in Volume I, page 219, and the discussions on page 354, the comparison of two sensations regarding their strength is only possible because <term>centrifugal excitations</term> <note>Centrifugal excitation: In this context, a nerve signal traveling "outward" from the higher processing center of the brain back down to the sensory entry point.</note> travel from center C (the seat of apperceptive activity in the gray brain matter) to sensory center *a*, where the sensory excitations first arrive. This represents the influence of **attention**, which—according to Volume I, page 219 and Volume II, page 210—can amplify the intensity of sensory sensations.

This centrifugal excitation of attention (or the underlying physiological activity) is itself triggered by a <term>centripetal excitation</term> <note>Centripetal excitation: A nerve signal traveling "inward" from the senses toward the higher processing centers of the brain.</note>. In cases where attention is directly stimulated by the sensation itself, this signal travels centripetally from *a* to *C* (p. 354, note), meeting the centrifugal signal coming from *C* to *a*. Conversely, if the direction of attention toward *a* is determined by something other than the immediate stimulus—such as by so-called "**signal stimuli**" related to the sensory excitation at *a*—the signal is "conveyed to center C via centripetal pathways." It is also assumed that this centripetal excitation is proportional to the stimulus strength within the limits of Weber's Law.

From this, a first assumption is made: that the centripetal excitation reaching *C* must first reach a certain intensity to trigger the centrifugal response toward *a*. This is the basis for the **threshold**, which in this model is understood in purely physiological terms. Secondly, it is assumed that "while the triggered centrifugal excitation grows proportionally to the strength of the triggering stimulus, it is simultaneously **inversely proportional** to the magnitude of the excitation already existing in the organ of apperception."

Following this (p. 353): "If we now designate the latter quantity as *R*, and the increase caused by the signal stimulus as $\Delta R$, then the increase $\Delta E$ in centrifugal excitation produced by the latter will be proportional to $\frac{\Delta R}{R}$." This is, however, a relationship which—

<meta>This page continues a critical evaluation of Wilhelm Wundt’s physiological theories, specifically his model of how the brain processes attention and sensory perception. ...can be regarded as the mathematical expression of **Weber’s Law**. <note>**Weber’s Law** states that the smallest noticeable difference in a stimulus is proportional to the original intensity of that stimulus. For example, it is easier to notice one candle added to a dark room than one candle added to a brightly lit hall.</note>

For my part, the following points seem to be objections against this way of looking at things:

1) It is very complex and laden with hypotheses, and I believe one would only have to take refuge in it if no simpler way to represent the facts could be established. In this respect, however, I still prefer my own approach, which sets aside the "play" of brain processes—of which we have no detailed knowledge—and only focuses on the points that those brain processes, whatever they may be like, must necessarily satisfy if the psychological connection of the facts is to be matched by a physical one.

2) According to the author <note>Referring to Wilhelm Wundt, whose work *Principles of Physiological Psychology* is being critiqued here.</note>, even sensory impressions from which attention is withdrawn (and thus directed elsewhere) are said to be conscious (“in consciousness”) once they have reached the seat of perception. He gives the example of a word heard while one is distracted. Indeed, this is rooted in the explanation of perception given above; on page 222 of Volume I, the author also explicitly identifies **perception** with “obscure perception” <note>original: "undeutlicher Wahrnehmung"</note>—treating it as a form of perception after all—and declares that perception occurs even when an impression is not passed further along from the sensory center. For my part, I would argue against this: as long as a word is "overheard" due to distraction, it is rather something else that occupies the consciousness, and the word is displaced from consciousness by that other thing. However, one may well regard this as a dispute over the specific use of the words “conscious” and “unconscious.” (See page 217 ff.)

3) According to Wundt, increased attention should be able to strengthen the intensity of a sensory sensation or its reproduction in memory. However—and I never tire of opposing this view, which is common among others as well—a piece of grey paper, if seen at all, does not appear lighter simply through increased attention; nor does a faint sound, if heard at all, appear louder through increased attention to it. I find an explanatory perspective on this lacking in Wundt's view. Appealing to Meyer’s experiments (Vol. II, page 210, note) is of no use here, because the apparent contradiction between the previously mentioned facts and these experiments themselves first needs to be explained.

4) Wundt seeks the <term>inner threshold</term> <note>Inner threshold: In psychophysics, the point at which a physical stimulus in the brain becomes strong enough to be felt as a conscious sensation.</note>—which I have assumed in the sense of the <term>psychophysical view</term>—not only in the above formulation...

> "*Psychologically*, **Weber's Law** can evidently be traced back to the more general experience that we possess in our consciousness no *absolute*, but only a *relative measure* for the *intensity* of the *states* present within it; that we therefore always measure one state against another with which we are prompted to compare it. In this way, we can conceive of **Weber's Law** as a *special case* of a more general *law* of *relation* or of the *relativity* of our inner *states*."

But taken directly, without generalization and interpretation, **Weber's Law** says only that equal sensations of difference depend on equal stimulus ratios; thus, only an *estimation of equality* in the psychic realm by itself, as well as an *estimation of equality* in the physical realm by itself (not a mutual one), come into consideration in their *simultaneous dependence* on one another. Consequently, I am unable to put the author’s above generalization and interpretation into any clear relationship, even taking into account the explanations he has attached to it; and in any case, I find lacking a specific illustrative example of how that relationship between two simultaneous cases of equality in two different realms—so characteristic of **Weber's Law**—is to be found again in something corresponding on the purely psychic side, for which the general appeal to the *relativity* of our internal states is unquestionably not yet sufficient. In any case, a significant role is played in the establishment of Wundt's view by the following sentence put forward by him elsewhere (I. 322): Strictly speaking, “it is not the relationship between <term>stimulus<note>German: *Reiz*. The physical energy, such as light or weight, that triggers a sensory response.</note></term> and <term>sensation<note>German: *Empfindung*. The immediate mental experience resulting from a stimulus.</note></term>, but only the relationship between stimulus and **estimation of sensation** that is accessible to our measurement, while the question of how sensations might behave independently of the processes of **perception** and **comparison** involved in their estimation cannot be answered by direct investigation at all.”

I would only like to concede the second part of this, not the first. Through direct investigation, one can find a measurable relationship neither between stimulus and sensation, nor between stimulus and the **estimation of sensation**, whether one understands the estimation of sensation as a reflection on a present sensation or on one reproduced in memory. However, in my opinion, the methods of measurement must aim to combine the facts—which can be observed everywhere when stimuli act upon the sensory organ—through experiment and calculation in such a way that the influence of the processes of <term>perception<note>German: *Auffassung*. In Wundt's psychology, this often refers to 'Apperception,' the process by which the mind focuses on and organizes sensory data.</note></term> and **comparison** is eliminated, insofar as it is not a matter of the magnitude of the stimuli and the sensations dependent upon them. Thus, we may proceed from the direct observation of the equality of sensed differences (given the equality of stimulus ratios), which is still influenced by the mode of observation, to regularities regarding the equality of sensory differences, and from there arrive at measurable relationships. (Compare p. 198 ff.).

# Sixth Section.

## On Certain Subjects of Internal Psychophysics.

### XIX. Relationships of Attention.

The treatment of the relationships of attention by Gutberlet, Müller, and Wundt has already been discussed on pages 218 ff., 244 f., and 264 ff. respectively. I will not return to those points here, but will instead develop my own views on the matter somewhat more thoroughly than was done previously on pages 243 ff.

In their main points, the following considerations agree with those presented in Section XLII of the *Elements* <note>Fechner is referring to his own book, *Elemente der Psychophysik*.</note>; only in the details will they occasionally deviate through a clearer or more valid formulation. Furthermore, in the following pages, I prefer to represent these relationships directly using mathematical symbols rather than the schematic representation previously employed (the so-called <term>wave schema<note>German: *Wellenschema*. A conceptual model used by Fechner to visualize fluctuations in mental energy, where the "threshold" of consciousness is imagined like the surface of the sea, and mental activities are waves rising above or falling below it.</note></term>). I have chosen this because some have been unwilling to engage with the schema, or have even mistaken it for a mere analogy, which completely contradicts its intended meaning. Finally, Müller—as a representative of the physiological view—found it simplest to dismiss this view (which is based on the psychophysical perspective and is quite incompatible with the physiological one) using harsh language (p. 359), without having even considered its central premise.

In general, the following considerations are based on the principle expressed in *Elements* II. 454:

> "It is essentially the same principle: that the <term>psychophysical activity<note>German: *psychophysische Thätigkeit*. The physical processes (likely in the brain) that Fechner believed were the direct counterpart to mental experiences.</note></term> of a human being as a whole must exceed a certain intensity for consciousness—the waking state—to occur at all; and that during the waking state, every specific determination of this activity, whether caused by a stimulus or arising spontaneously, which is capable of producing a specific determination of consciousness..."

<summary>Fechner defends his theoretical model of attention against critics, transitioning from his earlier "wave schema" visual metaphor to a more precise mathematical description of how mental activity reaches the threshold of consciousness.</summary>

--- Page 343 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of internal psychophysics, moving from a critique of other scholars to Fechner’s specific definitions of attention and mental phenomena. He transitions from a conceptual "wave schema" mentioned on the previous page to a more formal, symbolic representation.</meta>

...to provide, it must exceed a certain strength to truly become conscious." In short, insofar as we must distinguish specific manifestations of consciousness, we must also distinguish <term>thresholds<note>German: *Schwellen*. A fundamental concept in Fechner's psychophysics, referring to the point at which a physical stimulus is strong enough to be perceived by the mind.</note></term> for them—even without knowing the specific underlying psychophysical conditions.

Attention is a mental phenomenon that, according to the evidence of inner experience, is distinct from the mental phenomena to which it refers (or which are grasped through it). When I look at a more or less bright surface, or listen to a more or less loud sound, I can very well distinguish the attention with which the perception occurs from the brightness or the volume of the sound that I feel during the process. Furthermore, the strength of attention can decrease while the intensity of the phenomenon it refers to—such as the sensation of brightness or sound—increases, and vice versa. All of this was already mentioned previously (p. 244). Consequently, I cannot share the view of those who define the intensification of attention directed at a phenomenon as an intensification of the phenomenon itself, or who unclearly conflate the two; this, indeed, seems to me to be the general case. This is not to say, however, that the two are entirely independent of one another.

For the sake of brevity, I shall henceforth refer to the phenomena distinct from attention (those to which attention is directed) simply as psychic phenomena, or even more briefly as phenomena—without forgetting in a more general context that attention is itself just a psychic phenomenon of a different kind. Nor is there anything to prevent us from referring to attention, in contrast to the psychic phenomena it focuses on, primarily as a psychic "**activity**" <note>German: *Thätigkeit*. Fechner distinguishes between the "activity" of the mind (attention) and the "phenomena" (sensations) it observes.</note>. Of course, in a broader view, the psychic phenomena to which it refers could also be considered the result of psychic activity. It would, in any case, be idle to argue over word usage in this regard. What is certain is that attention is accompanied by a feeling of self-activity <note>German: *Selbstthätigkeit*.</note> that is not present in the phenomena themselves; rather, through those phenomena, we find ourselves "receptively" determined. Indeed, this is perhaps the most characteristic difference between the two.

Finally, for the shortest designation, attention may be represented by **A**, the psychic phenomenon to which it refers by **P**, and the both—

...the underlying <term>psychophysical<note>Original German abbreviation: *ps.-ph.* refers to *psychophysisch*. This relates to the intersection of physical stimuli and mental sensation.</note></term> activities, however, are designated respectively by **A** and **P**.

The **P**, to which the **A** refers, can be sensory **P** or their reproductions in memories, or mental representations in which thinking takes place—in short, psychic **P** of any kind. With all these **P**, the feeling of the **A** directed toward them remains the same in character and can only change in strength or intensity; meanwhile, in the **P** to which it refers, both the character (quality) and the strength (intensity) can vary. Thus, insofar as we can consider **A** itself as a psychic phenomenon in a more general view, we must regard it as a *general* psychic **P** in contrast to the psychic **P** to which it refers, which are *special* phenomena.

When perceiving a **P** with a given degree of **A**, the state of consciousness—briefly **C**<note>Original German uses **B** for *Bewusstsein* (Consciousness). Translated here as **C** for readability.</note>, for which **β** may serve as the psychophysical basis—is determined in its character, on the one hand, by the general character of **A** (which it retains regarding all phenomena) and, on the other hand, by the specific character of **P**. Its strength, however, is determined by the strength or intensity of both. In this sense, we can speak of a **total consciousness** regarding a given **P**, of which **A** and **P** are the components, as well as a **total strength** or **overall intensity** of **C** regarding a given **P**, of which the strengths of **A** and **P** are the components; and what applies in this regard to the **C** of individual phenomena also carries over to the **C** of entire series of them.

Just as **A** can be directed toward a **P**, it can also be withdrawn or turned away from it by focusing on other **P**. Then the phenomenon in question disappears from consciousness. However, in the case where **A** is directed toward a **P**, the following applies:

We can perceive a weak **P** with strong **A** without the **P** itself appearing strengthened as a result; only the total strength of the **C** directed toward it appears increased. For example, gray paper does not appear brighter, nor the ticking of a clock louder, no matter how much we intensify the **A** directed toward it. No one can make gray paper appear white through attention, and no one can bring the soft ticking of a clock to the strength of a powerful hammer blow; however, we do feel the intensification of **A** as an intensification of our conscious activity directed toward the **P**. And the same applies to internally generated psychic **P** as it does to sensory **P**. A gray paper

...appears also in the memory as gray, that is, faint in light; a faint chirping appears also in the memory as a faint chirping, no matter how much we may perceive the memory image of it with an increased **A** <note>Attention</note>; it remains so, even though we feel an intensification of our activity of consciousness in the increased **A**. Admittedly, we cannot consider the strength of **P** <note>The Phenomenon or mental image</note> to be *entirely* independent of the strength of **A**. As is well known, Meyer <note>Likely referring to Georg Hermann von Meyer and his work "Elements of Physiology" (Elemente der Physiologie).</note> (“Elem.” II. 484) succeeded through “repeated practice” in actually strengthening memory or fantasy images of sensory phenomena until they were equal to sensory **P** themselves, through a strong willful intention directed toward strengthening them. Now, one could indeed say: it is one thing to perceive a **P** as it is with increased **A**, and another to produce a **P** with an increased *willful* intention to strengthen it; but undeniably, every increased **A** directed at a phenomenon is naturally accompanied by such an intention. From another perspective, the very fact that Meyer’s experience is, so to speak, a unique case <note>original: "Unicum"</note>, and that Meyer himself only succeeded in producing that result “after repeated practice,” proves that it is not a matter of the state in which we find ourselves—let us say briefly—“under ordinary circumstances.” After all, many types of movements can be produced with ease “after repeated practice” which seemingly cannot be produced at all under ordinary circumstances, although they must be producible in tiny starts even without practice through an intention directed toward them; otherwise, practice could lead no further. Thus, it might be most probable that, through increased **A**, the <term>psychophysical activity<note>The underlying physical or neural process that corresponds to a mental sensation.</note></term> of a **P** above the threshold is indeed somewhat increased even under ordinary circumstances; however, once it is above the threshold, it is increased so little that a further increase is not noticed, because it does not go as far as crossing the <term>difference threshold<note>Original: *Unterschiedsschwelle*. The minimum amount by which a stimulus must change in order for the difference to be detectable by the observer.</note></term>.

Under ordinary circumstances, according to this, we can—not merely for the sake of simpler consideration, but also to satisfy the facts of observation itself—initially abstract away from an intensification of **p** <note>The underlying psychophysical activity</note> and therefore **P** through an intensification of **A**, without thereby absolutely denying an intensification of the underlying <term>psychophysical activity<note>Abbreviated as "ps.-ph. Thätigkeit" in the original.</note></term> **P** that is simply not perceptible according to the <term>threshold principle<note>The rule governing the point at which a stimulus or a change in stimulus becomes strong enough to be consciously felt.</note></term>; it could even be relatively stronger below the threshold than above it.

From the other side, it is unquestionable that, conversely, the conditions of the <term>P <gloss>Phenomenon</gloss></term> are not without influence on the strength of the <term>A <gloss>Attention</gloss></term> relating to it, and thus of the underlying <term>A <gloss>the psychophysical activity of attention</gloss></term>; rather, the Attention is involuntarily co-determined by conditions of the Phenomenon, even if not determined by it alone, since attention can also be willfully withdrawn even from phenomena that act upon it with a strong attraction.

With the established fact that under ordinary circumstances, the Attention directed toward a Phenomenon that is already above the <term>threshold <gloss>the point where a stimulus becomes perceptible</gloss></term> can be **considerably** strengthened without the strength of the Phenomenon itself noticeably increasing, there appears at first to be a contradiction: that it nevertheless requires a certain direction of Attention just to allow a Phenomenon to be noticed at all. When I am studying, I hear nothing of the ticking of the clock in the room; the sound hits my ear, but the sensation of it escapes my consciousness because my Attention is withdrawn from the field of hearing. As soon as I direct my focus there, I hear the ticking with a certain strength; if I then intensify my Attention further, the ticking still does not seem any louder to me. A word overlooked in a moment of distraction can still come to consciousness by subsequently directing Attention toward it, without a strengthened Attention making the word seem louder in the memory. But if a relationship of Attention to the auditory sensation is necessary at all to make it perceptible, how can the strengthening of Attention contribute nothing noticeable to the strengthening of the sensation? Yet, such is the factual state of affairs.

This appears indeed to be a paradox, which the competing views in psychophysics may attempt to represent psychophysically. The purely physiological view has not even dared such an attempt; for the psychophysical view, the solution lies entirely within the following more general theory.
