From the outset, one might ask why **B** is not set as equal to **A** multiplied by **P** (**AP**), and consequently, instead of the formula $x \log \frac{A P}{a p}$, why we do not use $x^2 \log \frac{A}{a} \cdot \log \frac{P}{p}$. Well, one could certainly attempt this; but I myself would not know how to represent the relationships that must be represented using that method. Indeed, it simply does not work because, according to that logic, **B** would result in a positive value just as well if **A** and **P** were both simultaneously below the <term>threshold <gloss>the point at which a stimulus becomes strong enough to be consciously perceived</gloss></term> as it would if they were both above it. <note>Fechner is noting a mathematical problem: in multiplication, two negative numbers (values below the threshold) would produce a positive result, which would incorrectly suggest that two "unconscious" processes could combine to create a "conscious" one.</note> One might further ask whether the constant $x$ should take a different value for **A** and **B**; to which I can only reply that, for now, no reason has been found to do so. As long as that remains the case, one naturally attempts to get by with the simplest assumptions.

Just as formula (4) provides the general expression for the <term>decomposability</term> of the psychological **B** into the psychological components **A** and **P**, so formula (5) gives the expression for the decomposability of **B** according to its functional logarithmic relationship to **A** and **P**.

Finally, formulas (6) and (7) show how the expression of **B** can be reduced to the simple and unified form of the <term>measurement formula</term> by condensing $\log \frac{A}{a} + \log \frac{P}{p}$ into $\log \frac{A P}{a p}$, and further condensing **AP** into **B** and **ap** into **b**. This is of importance in cases where we are only concerned with the total strength—the existence of consciousness or unconsciousness of a phenomenon in general—rather than how much is contributed specifically by the individual components.

Meanwhile, the interest here lies more in tracking how the two components of consciousness, **A** and **P**, work together to produce the result **B** according to their functional dependence on the underlying psychophysical values **A** and **P**. This will be examined more closely after the following points have been clarified.

Insofar as in formula (4) **B** is summed from **A** and **P**, and one must be subtracted from the other if they have opposite signs, the question arises as to how these two entirely heterogeneous psychological values can be brought to a comparable scale at all—which is necessary in order to...

The answer is that **A** <gloss>Attention</gloss> and **P** <gloss>the Phenomenon</gloss> can no more be compared through measurement on a purely **mental** path than can different intensities of **A** among themselves or different intensities of **P** among themselves; however, they can be compared **psychophysically**. According to this, both numerical values can then be compared with one another. Naturally, the unit for both mental values must be linked to the logarithm of the same ratio of $\frac{A}{a}$ and $\frac{P}{p}$.

The threshold *p* of **P** is to be regarded as independent of the strength of the **A** related to it, just as the threshold *a* of **A** is independent of the strength of the **P** to which **A** refers—as can be established at least approximately. Indeed, the former can be inferred from the fact that, according to experience, the intensity of **P**, which depends on a constant stimulus, remains noticeably unchanged when the intensity of the **A** directed toward it changes; the threshold value *p*, however, belongs to the special case where **P** = zero. Nor is it contradictory that, according to <note>original: "Meyers Versuchen" — likely referring to the experiments of Georg Hermann von Meyer (1815–1892), who studied how attention affects sensory thresholds.</note> Meyer’s experiments, a **P** can be raised above the threshold by an intensified **A**, which would have remained below it with a weak **A**; in this case, one should not view the value of *p* as being lowered by the influence of **A**, but rather the value of **P** as being increased by it.

The independence of the threshold *a* of **A** from the strength of the **P** to which it refers can likewise generally be inferred from the fact that we can perceive a strong and a weak **P** with the feeling of equal **A**; however, the threshold value *a* belongs to that specific level of intensity of **A** which stands between directed and diverted attention. But if strongly contrasting **P** values preferentially attract and occupy the **A**, this is again not to be regarded as an influence on the *a* but rather on the **A**.

A **practical determination** of the constants *a* and *p* in objective measures is, of course, just as unfeasible as that of the variables **A** and **P** above and below these thresholds, since we do not possess the means to track the <term>psychophysical activities <gloss>the physiological processes in the brain or nervous system that correlate with mental states</gloss></term>, which are signified by these letters, into the interior with our measurements; but this does not hinder the usefulness of formulas in which these values appear, regarding...

As for the fourth case, a <term>Phenomenon <gloss>P, the mental representation of a stimulus</gloss></term> can, by its own strength, enter into consciousness even when <term>Attention <gloss>A</gloss></term> is turned away from it; for example, a loud bang occurring while one is deep in study. Meanwhile, one can also imagine states where phenomena occur in consciousness with a dominant **P** while attention remains continuously negative—let us say, sleeping; this is what I consider to be the state of dreams, though this will be discussed in more detail only in the following section.

Regarding the four cases of a negative **P**, they demonstrate—corresponding to the positive cases—that the values of the components of the phenomenon can play different roles in its disappearance from consciousness. The final two cases, in particular, teach us that the elevation of one of the two components above the threshold is not yet sufficient to make it conscious if its positive value is overcompensated by a negative value of the other component. The positive value is then absorbed and lost within the negative total result of consciousness. This explains the seemingly paradoxical case we mentioned above: a loud sound, which in itself far exceeds its threshold and is therefore perceived as loud when attention is not below the threshold, is nevertheless not heard if attention is sufficiently withdrawn from it. If attention is then turned toward it enough that it is heard, it enters consciousness with a strength corresponding to its **P**, which it then noticeably retains even with a further increase in attention; in that case, we certainly feel the increase in attention, but without the strength of the phenomenon increasing noticeably along with it. Similarly, for someone immersed in a concert, the extinguishing of all lamps would have the same effect as a flash of lightning: it would divert **A** from the realm of hearing to the realm of sight. Clearly, contrast—the difference between various phenomena—provides the primary determining ground for awakening involuntary **A**. As for which of the contrasting phenomena it primarily focuses on: in the case of <term>successive contrast <gloss>when one event follows another in time</gloss></term>, it naturally depends on which occurs later, as the contrast cannot assert itself during the first event. In the case of <term>simultaneous contrast <gloss>when things appear at once</gloss></term>, such as the white or black spot on an opposing background, the **P** of smaller area takes priority. This is perhaps only because the <term>activity <gloss>the physical process</gloss></term> underlying the **A** is more spread out over a larger surface and thus reaches a lower intensity; undoubtedly, the more or less central position of the spot also exerts an influence.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of attention (A). On the previous page, the author discussed how attention is influenced by external stimuli—such as rhythmic strikes or visual contrasts—and how it tends toward inertia or change. Now, the author moves toward a unified theory of attention as a fundamental "self-activity" that links mental focus, the human will, and the states of waking and sleep.</meta>

Insofar as **A** <note>original: "A" for Aufmerksamkeit (Attention)</note> retains the same character everywhere in relation to the most diverse phenomena to which it refers—permeating, so to speak, our whole being with something identical—and since the feeling of self-activity attaches itself to it preferentially over the **P** <note>original: "P" for Phänomene (Phenomena)</note>, it in any case has a more fundamental significance for our spiritual being than the changing phenomena to which it relates. But it also indisputably has a more general meaning beyond the limited reference to representations suggested by its name. Indeed, I am of the opinion that it is essentially the same activity—both psychically and psychophysically—which allows us to pursue representations and raise them into consciousness with the feeling of self-activity <term>self-activity <gloss>Selbstthätigkeit; the internal power of the mind to act upon its own initiative rather than merely reacting to external stimuli</gloss></term>, and which is active in the Will to determine our actions; that it is the same which mediates the effective relationship through which differences in sensation become sensations of difference; and that the essential difference between waking and sleep depends on the crossing or falling below the threshold <term>threshold <gloss>Schwelle; the point at which a stimulus or mental activity becomes strong enough to be consciously perceived</gloss></term>, not of total consciousness (against which dreams testify), but of this particular component of it.

Following this, it would certainly be desirable if, for scientific purposes, we had a term of more general scope to designate the broader meaning of this activity instead of the name "Attention," which points only to a specific sphere of it. However, insofar as no such term exists, it must be left to the context and the factual interpretation to allow the word to be understood in its more general meaning wherever such a meaning asserts itself.

I maintain that in dreamless sleep, if such a thing exists, the entire psychophysical activity of the human being sinks below the threshold, whereas during waking, its threshold is always crossed somewhere and somehow—that during waking, the shifting of attention between different areas of psychophysical activity can be considered a local alternation of waking and sleep in those areas—

Undeniably, according to a more general definition of consciousness, dreams do reach our awareness, otherwise we would know nothing of them; they cannot, therefore, be thought of as falling below the threshold <note>the boundary between the unconscious and the conscious mind</note> of consciousness. Even when **A** is sleeping—that is, sunk below its threshold—the underlying psycho-physical activity is not entirely absent; it is simply below the threshold. Conversely, a dream can reproduce processes of waking life whose after-effects during waking have extended into **Tr**. Conversely, during waking, abnormally strong excitations of the **stage** **Tr** may spill over into **Wch**, which may be the cause of **hallucinations**. Generally, however, the normal proportional relationships between both stages can be disturbed in various senses, and this deserves attention particularly in cases of **mental illness**.

At first glance, it merely seems to contradict the idea that the stage of dream life is supposed to be turned even further away from the external world, and lie further from its influences, than the stage of waking life. However, this only applies to the means of communication with the external world through the external senses and organs of movement. On the other hand, the seat of dream life, through its connection with the rest of the body, remains no less in connection with the whole rest of the world than the seat of waking life. It could well be that influences from afar—the nature and scope of which we admittedly do not know—would be felt all the more easily within us the less they were outweighed by the influences of the sensory world and the phenomena left behind by them, as is the case in the **Waking-stage** (**Wch**) during waking hours.

Appropriately applied pressure to the brain, according to experiments on both animals and humans who have undergone <term>trepanation</term> <note>A surgical intervention in which a hole is drilled or scraped into the human skull.</note>, reliably induces sleep. Pulse and breathing slow down during sleep, and the body temperature is lowered; these conditions, which affect the entire body during sleep, must also extend to the brain, and will in all probability involve the physical-psychical processes as well. This, however, aligns quite well with the assumption of psychophysical activity sinking below the **threshold** <note>The "threshold" (Schwelle) is a central concept for Fechner, representing the limit below which a stimulus is no longer consciously perceived.</note> during sleep.

## **XXI. Some Thoughts on the Psychophysical Representation of Memories.**

The sensory sensations and perceptions <note>original: "Anschauungen", referring here to the mind's ability to form direct mental images or intuitions of objects.</note> depend on processes mediated by sensory stimuli in our nerves, which come to consciousness by entering the general system of psychophysical processes that carries our entire consciousness. Memories, however, are linked to after-effects which these processes leave behind in the brain. In accordance with the configuration of our current anatomical knowledge, I now assume that every fiber which carries a sensory excitation into the brain branches out in different directions from a central point in the brain, marked by a ganglion cell <note>In 19th-century anatomy, a "ganglion cell" generally referred to what we now call a neuron cell body; it was seen as a hub for nervous energy.</note>. Through its branches and sub-branches, it meets with those of other sensory nerves in a network-like tissue, into which the ganglion cells are inserted as nodal points. Within this tissue, which permeates and largely constitutes the gray matter of the brain, I imagine the formation of memories to be localized. Indeed, these ideas should, in a very general way, satisfy on the one hand the current state of our knowledge regarding the structure and functions of the brain, and on the other hand the need to make mental processes—in which memories meet to produce new and higher mental products—accessible to a <term>psychophysical</term> <note>original: "ps.-ph."</note> representability.

To avoid resting on a mere analogy, however, one might look for proof that such a principle—whereby a physical system becomes better at reproducing vibrations—exists in the material world. Consider how the soundboards <term>Soundboards: The wooden part of a musical instrument, like a piano or violin, that vibrates to amplify sound.</term> of musical instruments become increasingly better at reproducing tones the more they are played. We must simply assume that this principle is infinitely more developed in the highly adaptable psychophysical system than it is in rigid wooden soundboards.

In general, we should think of the various modes of vibration, to which different sensations and their memories are tied, as being inextricably linked with different arrangements of the particles or their centers of vibration (see below, p. 298 f.). Now, if a sensory stimulus is removed and the memory fades because its psychophysical process sinks below the threshold <note>threshold: The "Schwelle," a central concept in Fechner's work, refers to the limit at which a physical process becomes strong enough to be perceived by the mind.</note>, a more or less lasting arrangement of the particles—created by that process and perfectly suited to it—nevertheless remains behind. 

This arrangement facilitates the return of a sensation or memory of the same kind. At the same time, it makes it harder for a different kind of sensation to arise in those same fiber tracts, because any new excitation finds the particles already configured for a specific type of thought or memory. For sensations mediated by specific sensory nerves, this simply means that through practice, the nerve becomes better at performing its specific function. However, for the widely branching fiber tracts that serve our memories, the result is this: even if all fibers were initially equal and capable of receiving any kind of vibration, those that are more frequently prompted to vibrate in a certain way will increasingly adapt their physical particles to suit that specific type of vibration.

With the gradual development of increasingly stable arrangements and "arrangement-complexes," a gradual differentiation <note>original: Sonderung; the process of separating and categorizing different types of information</note> of these for different memories and memory-complexes must also go hand in hand. For it is indisputable that the same fiber tracts—so long as their arrangement has not become completely fixed (and it will never become completely fixed during life)—must continue to accommodate changes in the positioning of particles and the associated modes of vibration. However, to the degree that an arrangement has already been fixed in certain memory fibers and their complexes, vibrations of a different kind will find it easier to propagate through other fiber branches and, in turn, arrange these for themselves. Through this spatial expansion of the arrangements, along with their differentiation for various kinds of memories and memory complexes, not only is the creation and repetition of memories of different kinds made easier, but also their freedom from mutual interference; and herein I seek a primary viewpoint of the <term>psychophysical</term> <note>psychophysical: relating to the relationship between physical stimuli and mental phenomena</note> memory mechanism.

Indeed, the significance that the size of the brain, and especially its gray matter, has for mental development can be understood from this. It is indisputable that within already existing arrangements of the <term>psychophysical</term> system, the same fibers and cells can serve different memory complexes up to certain limits—provided that these memories share common elements to some extent. Furthermore, even the different sequence and direction in which the memory fibers are excited can determine a difference in memories, even if their physical arrangement remains unchanged; finally, a certain reconfiguration of the arrangements of these same fibers always remains possible. But all of this only goes so far, and

For a richly developed memory system, there must also be a corresponding wealth of resources within a variety of co-existing structures. Accordingly, man—who can indisputably retain more memories than any animal—also possesses a larger mass of gray brain matter; for it is only in this gray matter that the complex web of memory <note>original: "Erinnerungsgewebe"; Fechner uses this term to suggest an intricate, interwoven physical structure for mental storage</note> is to be sought.

To be sure, within certain limits, there are very clever animals that have a very small brain, such as ants. But they will certainly have extraordinarily few memories, and these only in relation to a very specific area of life. Meanwhile, they may be so constituted from the start that, even without memory, they can react appropriately to external stimuli—both psychically and physically—within their usual sphere of life. Animals generally differ from humans in that structures for limited purposes are already provided for them <note>The author is referring to innate instincts versus learned behaviors</note>, whereas humans must first acquire them. However, this also gives humans the capacity to adapt themselves to a wider variety of purposes than animals.

Where saving space in written communication is important—as in letters with expensive postage—one might write lengthwise and crosswise, or even diagonally across each other, and the letter remains legible as long as one follows the lines in different directions. I believe that this same principle of brain-writing <note>original: "Gehirnschrift"; the idea that thoughts leave physical tracks or inscriptions on the brain, similar to ink on a page</note> may be developed to a much higher degree, where attention takes the place of the reader. Yet, even in letters, this principle of spatial economy does not reach beyond certain limits; and so, when there is much to be written, one starts a new sheet of paper. The same likely applies to the writing in the brain.

# Seventh Section.

## Discussions with Various Authors.

### XXII. Prof. Dr. J. Delboeuf.

**Delboeuf** <note>Joseph Delboeuf (1831–1896) was a Belgian philosopher and mathematician who was both a supporter and a sharp critic of Fechner's methods.</note> published a critique of my work "In Matters" <note>Referring to Fechner's 1877 book *In Sachen der Psychophysik* (In Matters of Psychophysics)</note> in the *Philosophical Review edited by Ribot* <note>original: *Revue philosophique par Ribot*</note>, Jan. and Feb. 1878. In it, he partly revived and sought to intensify previous attacks against me, and partly sought to maintain his own psycho-physical <note>original: "ps.-ph."</note> fundamental view against the objections I raised; however, I was unable to yield to his considerations in either respect.

It is mainly from mathematical viewpoints that he attacks my establishment of psychophysics. But instead of following the mathematical path by which I ascend from **Weber’s** law <term>Weber's Law: the rule that the smallest change in a stimulus that can be noticed is a constant proportion of the original stimulus</term> and the fact of the threshold <term>Schwelle: the point at which a stimulus is just strong enough to be perceived by the mind</term> to the fundamental formula, measurement formula, and difference measurement formula with their consequences, he confronts me with general discussions about the way measurements are to be understood, how units of measurement are determined, and how measurements are made functionally dependent on one another—principles which I am alleged to have violated. These discussions culminate in a primary accusation, which I will examine below under point 1; he also adds various other objections, which the following numbered sections address.

Against this, I for my part make the primary counter-accusation against **Delboeuf** that he writes against me without having looked more closely at what I myself have written; for had he done so, he could not have arrived at his main accusation at all. Given the great respect I hold for **Delboeuf** as an exact researcher, I am indeed sorry that my book did not benefit from a bit more of this quality on his part.

1) On page 60, **Delboeuf** insists, and quite rightly, that a measurement of sensation must also be based on a unit of sensation; but, he says, “in **Fechner’s** work, sensation is [measured] by the...

Indeed, Delboeuf must not have looked at my most fundamental observations at all. In "Elements" <note>Referring to Fechner's seminal 1860 work, *Elemente der Psychophysik* (Elements of Psychophysics).</note> Vol. II, p. 18, I say literally: "In the measurement formula and its derivations, both the magnitude of the stimulus and that of the sensation must each be related to a unit of its own kind. For since stimulus and sensation are of entirely heterogeneous natures, they can only be measured separately by units of their own kind; a common unit cannot be applied to both. In fact, in our measurement of sensation [E.], we do not define it as a multiple of the stimulus, but as a multiple of a sensory magnitude of the same kind used as a unit, and only the relationship of the sensation to its unit is determined by the relationship of the stimulus to its unit, as both relationships are functions of one another, such that if one relationship is given, the other can be inferred from it."

Now, the unit of measurement itself is arbitrary; however, I show in the following which unit of sensation [E.] is most appropriately adopted to represent the measurement formula as simply as possible. If one now demands a demonstration of this unit of sensation—just as one can demonstrate a physical unit of measurement, such as a pound or a line <note>original: *Linie* — a historical unit of length, roughly 1/12th of an inch or 2.25mm.</note>—this demonstration is achieved by referring to the sensation belonging to a demonstrable stimulus that exceeds the demonstrable threshold value <term>Schwellenwerth: the point at which a physical stimulus becomes strong enough to be consciously perceived</term> of the stimulus in a given ratio.

And what is this passage in which, contrary to everything stated above, I am supposed to have expressed myself "very clearly," according to Delboeuf, that I intended to measure sensation by the stimulus? According to Delboeuf, it reads literally (with quotation marks) as follows: "If it is—he says—impossible to obtain the measure of sensation by the internal superposition of sensations, in the same way that one externally measures a piece of cloth using a meter, nevertheless one can base it on the relationship of dependence that exists between the force of the excitation and that of the sensation provoked" <note>original French: "s’il est, — dit il — impossible d’obtenir la mesure de la sensation par la superposition intérieure de sensations, de la même manière qu’on mesure extérieurement un morceau d’étoffe au moyen du mètre, cependant on peut la faire reposer sur le rapport de dépendance qui existe entre la force de l’excitation et celle de la sensation provoquée"</note>

6) On page 151, Delboeuf declares himself against the view established by me—and mostly accepted among us—that the sensation of black is still to be regarded as a positive sensation of light. He believes he can find a very simple experimental refutation of this view in the fact that <term>Weber's Law: The principle that the minimum change in a stimulus required for a person to notice a difference is a constant ratio of the original stimulus.</term> can be confirmed using his method of white sectors rotating in front of a black background, but not if the experiment is reversed by rotating black sectors of a corresponding angular width in front of a white background. But that is quite natural; the brightness of white sectors is weakened by the rotation as it is, to put it briefly, distributed over the entire circumference; the brightness of black sectors cannot be weakened in this way because the black background of the eye remains behind them during the entire rotation. If a white eye-background remained behind the white sectors during rotation, Weber's Law would likewise not be confirmed by it. According to Delboeuf's own experiments with the rotation of white sectors against a black background, the law is only confirmed insofar as one takes into account the small value *c*, which can be interpreted as the brightness of the <term>Augenschwarz: Literally "eye-black"; the internal sensation of gray or "light dust" perceived by the eye even in total darkness.</term>, even if Delboeuf himself does not interpret it that way (Compare p. 152 ff.).

7) Delboeuf’s objections against my negative sensation values <note>Fechner used negative numbers to mathematically represent "subliminal" sensations—those that exist below the threshold of conscious perception.</note> have already been illuminated on pages 212 and 215. Concerning his treatment of a peculiar time phenomenon, compare page 175.

So much for the opposition recently exercised against me by Delboeuf. On the other hand, as far as the objections are concerned which I raised in *In Matters* <note>Referring to Fechner's 1877 book *In Sachen der Psychophysik* (In Matters of Psychophysics).</note> on page 27 ff. and 113 ff. against Delboeuf’s own **psychophysical theory**, I can by no means find them invalidated by his reply (p. 150 ff.).

Regarding one main objection (*In Matters*, p. 32), he says:
> "Fechner objects to me: Gray is a positive and unchangeable sensation, whether one has first observed white or black. That is purely a matter of words."

...misunderstood my objection. But on the contrary, I expressly accepted this definition of **contrast sensation** <note>German: *Contrastempfindung*</note> in the aforementioned place; I only asserted at the same time that, besides the **difference** between the contrasting sensations, the **absolute value** of each sensation is also at stake. *Delboeuf* indeed “does not deny” this here, yet his theoretical observations and formulas lack an expression for it; for these formulas provide a value for gray that is sometimes positive and sometimes negative depending on a prior viewing of black or white. However, there is no place in his work for an expression of the **absolute brightness value**, which can only ever be understood as positive, and which belongs to gray both within and outside of a contrast. And indeed, since according to *Delboeuf* **sensations** only owe their origin to contrast, his version of the matter is consistent with his logic; but the more natural view will always remain that the **diversity of the absolute values of sensations** (or rather, the <term>psychophysical activities underlying them</term>) causes the contrast, rather than contrast being necessary to call forth the **absolute values of the sensations** themselves.

The deficiency of *Delboeuf’s formulas* in this regard, compared to my own formulas, should be all the more easily illuminated when I point out that among mine, the **difference formula** <note>Fechner’s mathematical way to calculate the perceived difference between two stimuli.</note> provides the expression for **contrast** (which can be understood as both positive and negative), while the **measurement formula** <note>German: *Maßformel*. This is the famous Fechner's Law (S = k log R), used to measure the intensity of a sensation.</note> provides the positive expression for the **absolute value** of a simple, real **sensation**. It provides a negative value only to designate cases where **sensations** become impossible; insofar as **negative values of absolute magnitudes** are impossible in themselves, as discussed sufficiently on page 207 and following.

Regarding the objection I raised in "In the Matter" <note>Referring to Fechner's 1877 book *In Sachen der Psychophysik* (*In the Matter of Psychophysics*).</note> on page 33 concerning the **sensation** of **black**, *Delboeuf* believes on page 151 that he can dismiss it—partly like the previous one, and partly by not recognizing at all that "**black is something**." He thus denies a positive value for its **sensation** by seeing in it only "the result of the contrast between the **dark and the less dark**," referring to another treatise ("On the Formation of the Idea of Space"). Against this, I do not wish to repeat everything I said in "Elements" Volume I, page 165 and following <note>Referring to Fechner's foundational 1860 work, *Elemente der Psychophysik*.</note> to establish that **black** is still to be regarded as a real **visual sensation**, and of which I find nothing refuted by *Delboeuf*; an unfortunate attempt at such a refutation by him was already discussed above on page 304 and following.

## XXV. Prof. Dr. Wilhelm Wundt.

Insofar as psychophysics <term>Psychophysics: The scientific study of the relationship between physical stimuli and the mental sensations they produce.</term> must deal with the lawful dependency-relationships between physical and mental states and changes, it naturally requires an acquaintance with both sides of the relationship: anatomical-physiological knowledge on one hand, and psychological knowledge on the other. In my "Elements" <note>Referring to Fechner's own foundational 1860 work, *Elemente der Psychophysik*.</note>, well-known facts in this regard were presupposed as such, and less familiar matters were drawn from available sources and discussed only as far as seemed immediately necessary for the foundation. Given the still very limited scope of psychophysical research at that time, and the resulting limited application of our specialized knowledge in both fields, this did not extend very far.

In contrast, in the "Principles of Physiological Psychology" by Wundt <note>Wilhelm Wundt (1832–1920) is widely regarded as the founder of modern experimental psychology; he established the first psychological laboratory in Leipzig in 1879.</note> (published in a first edition in 1874 and a second, substantially revised edition in 1880), the fields to be related to one another are treated with much more independence, within broader limits, and in greater depth than by myself, without losing sight of the goal of establishing their psychophysical relationship, however distant that may yet be. This was not merely borrowed from known sources, but was done essentially on the basis of his own theoretical and experimental research. Accordingly, Wundt’s work offers—beyond the immediate and subjective needs I followed when writing my own work—more general, far-reaching, and deeper foundations for psychophysical investigation, along with such investigation itself. Faced with these commendable advantages of Wundt’s work, which I gladly acknowledge, I can only claim as an advantage of my own much more limited treatment of our shared territory that the psychophysical perspectives and facts under consideration—given the current state of our knowledge—could be more concentrated on one hand, and examined in more specific detail on the other, than was possible under Wundt’s more general plan.

Insofar as we encounter one another in the same field of investigation, we meet partly in agreement and partly in conflict; however, a detailed comparative analysis of a work that is already universally known and esteemed in this regard cannot

For my part, however, I could not attach the same significance to Wundt’s **upper stimulus limit** <term>Reizhöhe: The maximum intensity of a stimulus beyond which an increase in the physical stimulus no longer produces a change in the perceived sensation.</term> as he does, for the following reasons.

First and foremost, I find a lack of specific facts that would speak as much for the existence of an upper stimulus limit as for a **stimulus threshold** <term>Reizschwelle: The minimum intensity a stimulus must reach to be perceived at all.</term>. To be sure, regarding sensitivity to light—for I know of nothing similar regarding other stimuli—it is certain that when light intensities, between which a difference is to be observed, rise ever higher while the ratio and thus the relative difference between the two remains the same, the **sensitivity** to the difference decreases from a certain point onward, instead of remaining constant, due to the upper deviation from **Weber’s Law**. Thus, one could, if one wished, speak of a height of relative difference-sensitivity regarding light stimuli—indeed, such a thing is not to be doubted; but what follows from this for the existence of an "upper stimulus limit" in Wundt’s sense? In fact, sensation could grow **asymptotically** <note>Asymptotic growth refers to a curve that approaches a limit indefinitely but never quite reaches it.</note> or in some unknown ratio to the stimulus, and even any fatigue, should one wish to include it in the consideration, could be overcome by a new increase in the stimulus, until the sensory organ is altered or destroyed by it; however, Wundt’s upper stimulus limit does not refer to that.

In any case, in my opinion, the stimulus threshold and the upper stimulus limit cannot be brought under the same simple lawfulness as corresponding boundary cases or cardinal points. This is because the stimulus threshold, according to the discussions in Section XV (p. 174, 194), can be regarded as a consequence of Weber’s Law, whereas an upper stimulus limit in Wundt’s sense could only mean an upper deviation from it; for according to the conclusions of the pure Weber’s Law, sensation rises continuously with the stimulus, albeit in a slower proportion than the stimulus itself.

This much being granted, however, it still seems most probable to me, following the discussions in *In Matters of Psychophysics* <note>original: "In Sachen" [der Psychophysik]; Fechner’s 1877 book defending his theories against critics.</note> p. 117 ff., that the chemical process essentially carries vibrations with it (in a certain sense it certainly does). Their form, speed, and composition vary with the constitution or composition of the substances entering the chemical process and the nature of the chemical process itself. These vibrations propagate through the sensory nerves to the central organ as the carriers of correspondingly different sensations. I find a lack of consideration for this possibility, which, for my part, is the only way I could gain a certain clarity regarding the role of the chemical process in stimulation and the propagation of that stimulation.

### XXVI. Some Philosophical Opponents: Gutberlet, Koch, v. Kries, F. A. Müller, Ulrici, Zeller.

I do not doubt that, in addition to the philosophical opponents mentioned above, there are others to be counted, though I have received no knowledge of their attacks. This is because—not without benefit to my philosophical peace in old age—I no longer follow philosophical literature in general; indeed, I have never followed it as a professional specialist. I was made aware of **Gutberlet’s** <note>Constantin Gutberlet (1837–1928), a Catholic philosopher who criticized Fechner's perceived materialism.</note> treatise through a mention in the "Literary Centralblatt," and of **Zeller’s** <note>Eduard Zeller (1814–1908), a prominent historian of Greek philosophy.</note> by Prof. Wundt. The treatises of the other four authors were sent to me by the authors themselves, for which I can only feel indebted to them and feel obligated to take them into consideration—an evaluation which they themselves will surely wish to be an open one.

Following this, one might ask why I do not also include **Delboeuf**, **Müller of Göttingen**, and **Wundt** among these philosophical opponents, as they are no less professional philosophers than those named above. The reason is this: As expressly stated (in the "Elements," Vol. I, Preface), I sought from the very beginning to ground **psychophysics** <term>Psychophysics: the scientific study of the relation between physical stimuli and the sensations they produce.</term> as free as possible from philosophical interference, based only on facts, methods of inference, and the mathematical linking of facts. Therefore, in the introduction to the "Elements," I briefly indicated how I integrate psychophysics into my general views on **body and soul** <term>Leib und Seele: Fechner’s "Identity Hypothesis" which suggests that the physical and the mental are two sides of the same reality, like a circle viewed from the inside or outside.</term>, but without bringing these views further into discussion or asserting them in the actual execution of psychophysics. Those three researchers [Delboeuf, Müller, and Wundt] have engaged with this conception and intention. The other opponents named above, however, have not engaged with this conception and intention; instead, they contest me based on their own definitions, their fundamental views on the relationship between body and soul, and their philosophical postulates. They offer an arrangement and interpretation of the facts in the sense of these definitions, views, and postulates, though factual objections may occasionally be mixed in. I cannot prevent this, and I myself believe that psychophysics does not lie so far afield from philosophy as to not also draw the interest of its representatives; but it nevertheless allows me to make an essential distinction between the one group of opponents and the other, as well as their objections. To allow myself a humorous comparison: it seems to me as if some, with pistol in hand, demand the purse from psychophysics, while others, without a pistol, demand its life—or if they do have a pistol in mind, it is at least not

And so, based on a functional dependence of the psychic on the physical, a psychic yardstick can be made dependent on a physical one without being found directly within it. Before one has looked closer to see whether and how this can be done, one must not claim that it is impossible simply because one finds that it cannot, in fact, be done purely out of one's own head.

### 3) Prof. Dr. J. v. Kries¹⁾ (Freiburg in Breisgau).

*“On the Measurement of Intensive Magnitudes and the So-Called Psychophysical Law”* in *Quarterly Journal for Scientific Philosophy VI. 3.*

The author introduces his treatise with explanations that go into great detail regarding the measurability of physical magnitudes. The summarized result, as it pertains to the application intended here, seems to me to be this: for magnitudes to be measurable at all, there must be a **determination of equality** between similar elements—such as those provided in the physical realm by space, time, and mass—whereby a measurement can be obtained as a numerical expression of a multiple of the **same unit**. The measures of all physical magnitudes are traceable to these. However, according to the author, **psychic values** do not satisfy this condition. The passage in which he speaks most decisively in this regard, and which in my opinion contains the **core of his objections**, is this (p. 273):

> “To simplify our expression for what follows, let us first make the (factually neutral) assumption that the entire sensory apparatus is unchangeable—that is, that a (physically) specific stimulus always corresponds to the same lasting sensation. Let S₁, S₂, S₃ ... be the sensations <note>original: "E₁, E₂, E₃ ..." representing *Empfindungen*</note> that correspond to the stimuli R₁, R₂, R₃ ... <note>original: "R₁, R₂, R₃ ..." representing *Reize*</note> and let the series R₁, R₂, ... be a series of increasing intensities. Before any attempt at determining magnitude, the question must first be asked whether it makes any sense, and if so what kind, to say that the change in sensation from S₁ to S₂ is equal to, for example, the change from S₃ to S₄; or, what amounts to the same thing, that sensation Sₘ is so-and-so many times as large as sensation Sₙ. In my opinion, unbiased reflection inevitably shows that **no sense at all** can be attached to these statements. The **homogeneity of elements**, which distinguishes our conceptions of space and time, is precisely what is missing in the series of intensive sensations. <meta>This page continues the critique by Johannes von Kries regarding the measurability of the mind. On the previous page, von Kries began an argument claiming that we cannot mathematically compare two different changes in sensation. He uses the example of "pressure sensations" to argue that an increase in intensity at a low level cannot be logically called "equal" to an increase at a high level.</meta>

> “...then the latter two pressure sensations <note>Kries is referring to a hypothetical experiment comparing two sets of stimuli</note> lie at a completely different point in the total range of sensation than the first two. Therefore, one increase is something entirely different from the other, and at first glance, they allow for no comparison. The claim that they are equal makes no sense at all. In fact, it is nothing other than the claim of equality between, for example, a movement of sound and a movement of light. Here, as there, the claim only gains meaning when it is arbitrarily established what is to be regarded as equal, or what should be understood by 'equal.' It is perhaps regrettable, but lies in the nature of the matter, that what I am asserting here cannot actually be proven. I can only deny that the meaning of the relevant judgments of equality is immediately obvious; one can argue about such an ultimate element of our judging intellect just as little as one can describe simple elements of our sensation (such as *Red* or *Sweet*). Even if someone made an effort to determine what length of distance would be equal to a second of time, we could only tell them that equating a spatial magnitude and a temporal magnitude has no meaning for us. To the confident assertion that the task is difficult but fundamentally solvable, we would be able to oppose nothing more than the appeal to the immediate result of internal experience, which teaches us the reverse. Exactly the same applies to the equating of two different increments in sensation.”

But it is nevertheless strange that this estimation of equality between differences at various heights of the <term>stimulus scale</term> <note>the range of physical energy, such as light or weight, being measured</note>—which, according to the author, has no meaning—has been carried out by everyone who has hitherto been occupied with the experimental testing of <term>Weber’s Law</term> <note>the rule that the "just noticeable difference" between two stimuli is proportional to the magnitude of the stimuli</note>. This has been done partly directly and partly through calculation, without any hesitation, and without anyone becoming aware that they were performing "nonsense." Prof. Ulrici has published a treatise in the 72nd volume of the *Journal for Philosophy and Philosophical Criticism* <note>original: "Zeitschr. f. Philosophie und philos. <meta>This page continues Gustav Theodor Fechner’s rebuttal of Professor Hermann Ulrici. Now, however, the starlight in the daytime sky—and the same applies to all analogous examples—is by no means unnoticeable; instead, every star even increases the very noticeable brightness of the daytime sky where it is located, and thus naturally also participates in the noticeability of the brightness that is increased by it. How, then, can the noticeability of a sensation <note>original: *Empfindung*</note> depend on its discrimination from another? In my opinion, the author <note>Professor Hermann Ulrici</note> confuses the noticeability of a sensation with the noticeability of the *difference* between two sensations. For indeed, one cannot distinguish the sensation of brightness of the sky (increased by the addition of the star) from the sensation of brightness of the sky in the star's surroundings if the physical difference in brightness does not exceed a certain limit, the <term>difference threshold</term><note>The *Unterschiedsschwelle* is the smallest change in a physical stimulus that a person can detect.</note>, or if the ratio of the physical brightnesses does not exceed the <term>ratio threshold</term>. However, the fact that the same star contributes less to increasing the perceptible brightness of the sky the greater that brightness already is, and that the difference threshold for distinguishing the star grows with the brightness of the sky—while the ratio threshold, according to <term>Weber's Law</term><note>A fundamental principle in psychophysics stating that the change in a stimulus that will be just noticeable is a constant ratio of the original stimulus.</note>, does not grow with it—these are fundamental facts of <term>psychophysics</term> which must be clearly grasped, formulated, and utilized in its conclusions; and I do not understand how the author's distinction between a sensation <note>abbreviated as "E." for *Empfindung* in the original text</note> as such and a *noticeable* sensation, and the role he assigns to the activity of discrimination, is supposed to find support in these facts, or what it could contribute to their proper utilization.

Regarding this, I ask the following question: the physical difference between the star and the surrounding daytime sky exists, and the mental activity of discrimination is also present—so why is the difference still not noticed? Does one wish to say that it is not noticed because the activity of discrimination finds no sufficient cause to take effect in such a small difference? But surely this activity hovers immaterially above both physical and psychophysical differences; it can, after all, be increased at will. But let the author increase it as much as he likes; he will not be able to distinguish any star in the sky during the day—not even <term>Sirius</term><note>The brightest star in the night sky.</note>, which, with its massive physical difference in brightness from the surrounding daylight (upon which it is, so to speak, superimposed), would most helpfully accommodate any increase in the activity of discrimination.

But how do I interpret the difference of the second case from the first? In the second case, psychophysical mediations and functional relationships take place between the <term>psychophysical</term> excitations, which are absent or not strong enough in the first case. can be perceived. Between these two extremes, however, there is a certain breadth within which contrast can increase the <term>psychophysical</term><note>Fechner uses this term to describe the physical brain processes that directly correspond to a mental experience.</note> representation of the **sensation of redness** on a carmine solution—which would be below the **threshold** without contrast—until it rises above that threshold. The same applies to other examples of a similar character.

In general, because of the organic connection in which our psychophysical activities stand, their intensity changes not only according to the intensity of the stimuli, but also according to the spatial distribution of those stimuli. Ernst Mach has established general formulas for this, which are not only mentioned in Section XI of my work *In the Matter of Psychophysics*, but are also applied there to the phenomena of contrast. It is even easier to conceive of this in terms of temporal distribution: a given stimulus in a rested organ will, under otherwise identical circumstances, call forth a stronger psychophysical activity than in an organ fatigued by a continuous stimulus. This explains a whole range of contrast phenomena without one being in any way compelled to seek help from the author's <note>Referring to Hermann Ulrici's theory</note> "difference view."

Ultimately, there is no difficulty at all in imagining the psychophysical foundation of sensation and mental activity to be just as variable as the activity itself, and that the former follows the latter everywhere (though not in simple proportion), even where direct experimentation cannot follow. For my part, I pursue this possibility along the thread of my system, as I have laid out in the first section of this work; however, if this thread breaks off somewhere in the author's system, then the possibility of continuing our discussion on a common foundation regarding the questions at hand also breaks off, and I thus waive further discussion here as well.

...should be, since the difficulties he raises partly do not affect my method of substantiation at all, and partly have been considered in their proper place. That **psychical measurement** is not as simple a matter as **physical measurement** is granted by me, but the interest of psychical measurement does not lie at all in its practical feasibility.

The author <note>Referring to the philosopher Hermann Ulrici, who criticized Fechner's scientific approach to psychology.</note> misses in particular "a fixed standard that we would need to possess in order to be able to determine the absolute magnitude of the intensity of a psychical activity," i.e., he misses a psychical magnitude useful as a **unit of measurement** <note>original: "Maßeinheit"</note> that can be rediscovered everywhere, and to which other similar psychical magnitudes can be related. And indeed, such a thing cannot be found in a "just noticeable sensation"—and nothing further seems to occur to him. However, according to the principles I have established and developed, any arbitrary psychical magnitude can serve as an ever-recoverable unit of measurement for psychical magnitudes of the same kind, which belongs to a stimulus that exceeds its **threshold value** in a given ratio; and insofar as the threshold value itself is a value that can be established for every individual and every state thereof, so too is the psychical unit, which belongs not to the threshold value itself, but to its exceedance in a given ratio. Just as one can take any arbitrary spatial magnitude as a unit of spatial measurement, provided it is held fast everywhere in consistent application, so can any psychical magnitude be used as a unit of psychical measurement that belongs to an exceedance of the threshold in an arbitrarily assumed ratio.

It is well to note that this measurement by no means fundamentally or essentially presupposes the validity of <term>Weber's Law</term><note>A principle stating that the perceived change in a stimulus is proportional to the initial intensity of the stimulus.</note>, but only presents itself in its simplest form under the assumption of this validity; and the explanation of the measurement based on it in my *Elements* <note>Fechner refers to his seminal 1860 work, *Elemente der Psychophysik* (Elements of Psychophysics).</note> also has a fundamental interest because of the law's at least approximate validity in <term>outer psychophysics</term><note>The study of the relationship between physical stimuli and mental sensation.</note> and its likely unlimited validity in <term>inner psychophysics</term><note>The study of the relationship between internal physiological/brain processes and mental sensation.</note>; deviations from the law, however, once they are determined empirically, can also be included in the functional expression of the measurement, as is discussed in more detail in *Elem.* II. 191 ff. Fundamentally, the obtaining of the measurement rests upon "constating the equality of small changes—increments of sensation—for corresponding stimulus increments in different parts of the stimulus scale," for which the measurement methods of **difference sensitivity** <note>original: "Unterschiedsempfindlichkeit"</note> serve; and from this, the relationship of dependence between the sensation, grown from increments starting from zero, and the...

Let the sum of errors for a given distance D generally be called S (not to be confused with the usual meaning for the <term>difference threshold<gloss>The minimum amount by which a stimulus must change in order for the difference to be noticeable.</gloss></term>).

The confirmation of <term>Weber’s Law<gloss>A principle stating that the perception of a change in a stimulus is proportional to the original magnitude of the stimulus.</gloss></term> here depends on the error sums S being proportional to the distances D; therefore, S/D should be found to be nearly constant across the different distances, such that any deviations can be attributed to unresolved random chance. <meta>This page continues the critique of experimental data regarding Weber's Law. ...case with the experiments of Chodin. He conducted 3 series of experiments, each with 7 distances ranging from 2.5 to 160 millimeters; two of these utilized horizontal distances and one utilized vertical distances. In all of them, he consistently obtained—with an increasing distance (D)—a value for the mean error divided by the distance that first decreased and then, with further growth of D, increased again. Specifically:

| At D | 2.5 | 5 | 10 | 20 | 40 | 80 | 160 |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| No. 1 Horiz. | $\frac{1}{39}$ | $\frac{1}{52}$ | $\frac{1}{65}$ | $\frac{1}{76}$ | $\frac{1}{69}$ | $\frac{1}{48}$ | $\frac{1}{66}$ |
| No. 2 Horiz. | $\frac{1}{30}$ | $\frac{1}{48}$ | $\frac{1}{60}$ | $\frac{1}{112}$ | $\frac{1}{81}$ | $\frac{1}{58}$ | $\frac{1}{41}$ |
| No. 3 Vertic. | $\frac{1}{32}$ | $\frac{1}{41}$ | $\frac{1}{60}$ | $\frac{1}{55}$ | $\frac{1}{57}$ | $\frac{1}{46}$ | $\frac{1}{36}$ |

In contrast, <term>Weber's Law</term><note>The principle that the just-noticeable difference between two stimuli is a constant ratio of the original stimulus. In this context, it suggests that the "relative error" (error divided by distance) should remain constant regardless of how long the line is.</note> requires an equality of the aforementioned fractional values for all D in each of the three series.

Incontrovertibly, these results are very striking compared to those obtained by myself, Volkmann, and Solger. The reason for this discrepancy can only be sought in the differing procedure. Now, when one experimentally controls the trials of others, it is customary to do so either by the same procedure (with increased care where possible) or by an improved procedure, in order to eliminate deficiencies one believes to have noticed in the earlier observations. Instead, Chodin—without having noted any deficiencies in the earlier experiments or having conducted comparative trials with his own—adopted a procedure that was questionable from the outset, namely the following:

> "A fine line was drawn on paper with a pencil, upon which one of the distances was indicated with fine cross-strokes; then, on both sides of it (or above and below), the distance which appeared equal to the eye was marked with a cross-stroke in the continuation of the same line. This new distance (<term>error distance</term><note>original: "Fehldistanz"; the distance as subjectively estimated by the participant, which inevitably deviates from the objective "normal" distance.</note>) was measured by means of a precise scale and estimation down to 0.1 millimeters."

Now, it seems obvious to me that with this procedure, the uncertainty of the hand could not be corrected; because of this, the error distance could sometimes deviate from the <term>normal distance</term><note>The standard or target distance that the subject is trying to replicate.</note> by slightly more than the <term>difference threshold</term><note>original: "Unterschiedsschwelle"; the minimum amount by which stimulus intensity must be changed in order to produce a noticeable variation in sensory experience.</note>. However, as previously discussed (p. 113), it is a fundamental principle of the <term>method of mean errors</term><note>A psychophysical method where the subject adjusts a stimulus until it matches a standard; the average of these attempts reveals the subject's precision.</note> that the deviation between the normal distance and the error distance must always turn out smaller than the difference threshold—that is, it must remain imperceptible to the eye. This is ensured by the procedure usually adopted...

...possible corrections of the setting can be achieved in every case. Perhaps, however, Chodin also proceeded in such a way that, instead of marking the "error distance" <note>The distance produced by the test subject intended to match the standard distance.</note> in a single stroke, so to speak, he first attempted to make it as equal as possible to the **normal distance** <note>The standard or reference distance used for comparison.</note> by shifting a pencil point back and forth along the longitudinal line before fixing its position. But in that case, he had a normal distance situated between two small cross-marks, yet an error distance situated between one small cross-mark and a point formed by the tip of an obliquely held pencil. It is obvious that this cannot be accepted as reliably comparable without further justification.

Naturally, it must be assumed that if comparison errors occurred for one reason or another, these would have the greatest influence on the smallest distances, whereas larger distances should align better. And indeed, one can see that the relative "just noticeable differences"—represented by the fractional values in the previous table—fluctuate so irregularly in the first and third rows (from approximately 10 to 160 mm) that one can see in them a confirmation rather than a refutation of <term>Weber's Law</term> <note>The principle that the perceived change in a stimulus is proportional to the initial intensity of the stimulus.</note> within those limits; only the second row aligns less well.

Still, one might suspect that these experiments prove a deviation from <term>Weber's Law</term> regarding **visual estimation** <note>original: "Augenmaß"; the ability to judge distances or sizes by sight alone.</note> at smaller stimulus sizes—a deviation that does indeed occur in other areas of research. However, this is decidedly contradicted by the micrometric experiments of Volkmann and his fellow observers. While they consistently find a deviation, it is only a micrometric one, which at values of 5 mm almost disappears when weighed against the variable error through which the law must be validated, as will be shown in the following section b).

In any case, the results of Chodin's questionable experiments cannot invalidate the results of other researchers who, without being subject to similar suspicions, have produced mutually consistent findings. One notes with some regret that Chodin did not even attempt to resolve the contradiction between his results and those of earlier observers; he could not simply assume that his results rendered the work of previous observers obsolete.

### b) Micrometric experiments by Volkmann and his co-observers.

Following this, I come to those experiments by Volkmann and his co-observers which were conducted with very small distances within the limits of 0.2 to 1.4 mm. However, a link between these and the previous non-micrometric experiments is provided by a series (p. 124) conducted by Volkmann himself with the micrometric apparatus using distances of 1 to 5 mm, which will be included below under 1).

In total, there are eight series in question: three by Volkmann himself and five by his student co-observers—Appel (two series), Jahn, Geiß, and Krause. Of these, the series listed below under 2), 3), 4), and 8) were already considered in the *Elements* <note>Referring to Gustav Fechner's "Elements of Psychophysics" (1860), a founding text of experimental psychology.</note> (Vol. I, pp. 220 ff.) based on manuscript communications, and are reproduced in Volkmann’s *Physiological Investigations* <note>A. W. Volkmann’s "Physiologische Untersuchungen im Gebiete der Optik" (1863), a major work on the physiology of vision.</note> along with those added later. One will find that an even more precise method of calculation has been used for all of these than before, although this does not significantly change the results.

The procedure for the micrometric experiments, according to pages 3 and 97 of the *Physiological Investigations*, was as follows. It employed three parallel silver wires, 0.05 mm thick and 10 mm long, which appeared as dark lines when viewed against the bright sky. The two outermost wires could be moved with the help of a very precise **screw micrometer** <note>A measuring device that uses a calibrated screw to move parts with extreme precision, allowing for measurements of minute distances.</note> without disturbing their parallelism, allowing them to be brought as close as desired to the fixed central wire. Once the **normal distance** <note>The standard reference distance used for comparison.</note> was established by the spacing between one of the outer threads and the center one, the **error distance** <note>The distance adjusted by the test subject to match the standard reference.</note> was determined by shifting the third wire, "making it equal to the normal distance as far as visual judgment allows." The size of the distance can be measured to within 0.01 mm and estimated to within 0.001 mm.

Of the following eight experimental series, the first seven—just like the earlier ones with larger distances—were conducted with horizontal distances between vertical threads; the last, the eighth series, used vertical distances between horizontal threads.

All experiments with horizontal distances (1–7) were conducted by alternating the position of the normal distance between the right and left sides; the experimental series with vertical distance (8) alternated between an upper and lower position for the normal distance. Subsequently, the sums resulting from both positions were combined.

<meta>This page continues the analysis of micrometric experiments, specifically addressing the mathematical reconciliation between observations at very small scales and Weber’s Law. The previous page introduced the experimental setup using silver wires; here, the author explains why the "constant" errors that appear at tiny distances do not invalidate the proportional nature of Weber's Law seen at larger scales.</meta>

It becomes evident that observations at such small distances are only satisfied if one considers that the source of pure random errors—which, in the sense of <term>Weber’s Law</term> <note>Weber’s Law states that the perceived change in a stimulus is proportional to the initial intensity of the stimulus; here, it means error increases as distance increases.</note>, are subject to proportionality with the distance—is combined with a source of random errors that are independent of the distance. These independent errors, taken by themselves, would yield a <term>mean error</term> <note>The average amount by which an observation differs from the true value.</note> that is constant at all distances or, given a fixed number of observations, a constant <term>sum of errors</term>.

However, this does not contradict the results obtained previously with larger distances, where no such complexity appears and Weber's Law emerges in its pure form. This is because the errors independent of distance, when measured by their average value, are very small; consequently, at any significant distance, they noticeably disappear compared to the errors dependent on distance. Even in the series of experiments with distances of 1 to 5 mm, they exert only a little influence and can be completely neglected at 10 mm. Conversely, at very small distances, the errors proportional to the distance itself become so small that they noticeably disappear compared to the constant errors independent of them. It will be the task of the calculation to demonstrate that this is indeed the case.

Now, for a given number of observations, let the sum of errors found for a given distance *D*, which depends on both sources simultaneously, be *S*; let *DW* be the sum of errors proportional to *D* (where *W* is the sum of errors for the unit of distance if the source of these errors existed alone), and *V* be the sum of errors independent of distance if the source of those errors existed alone. By virtue of the interaction of these error sources, according to known laws of probability $^1)$, one has:

->S$^2$ = V$^2$ + D$^2$ W$^2$, therefore<-
->S = $\sqrt{V^2 + D^2 W^2}$<-

According to these formulas, it is now necessary to determine *V* and *W* from the experiments. By recalculating the values of *S* using the given *D* and the discovered *V* and *W*, we can see whether the observed and calculated values of *S* at different distances truly agree closely enough to grant confidence to the formula and, consequently, to the <term>decomposition principle</term> <note>The mathematical method of breaking down a total observed error into its constituent parts (constant vs. proportional).</note> upon which it is based. I shall come to this below.

***

and I believe that the results of the comparison between calculation and observation can be considered very satisfactory. For the sake of brevity, I will refer to $V$ as <term>Volkmann’s Constant</term><note>Alfred Wilhelm Volkmann (1801–1877), a physiologist who studied vision and worked closely with Fechner.</note> and $W$ as <term>Weber’s Variable</term>, as I did previously. This is even though the designation of $V$ as a constant is only to be understood in the sense that $V$ does not change with the distance ($D$); nevertheless, it represents a <term>sum of errors</term> in itself, while $DW$ is to be regarded as constant for the unit of distance.

In "Elements" Volume I, page 230, I stated the viewpoint that led Volkmann to suspect the existence of a constant like $V$ from the very beginning, although he was not led to a calculation by it. He finds the reason in <term>Weber’s view</term><note>Referring to Ernst Heinrich Weber’s idea that our sense of touch or sight is based on the number of sensory receptors (like those in the retina) stimulated.</note> that the magnitude of a distance is estimated according to the number of <term>retinal elements</term><note>The individual light-sensitive cells (rods and cones) in the eye.</note> which it encompasses between its points, as can be seen further in the place cited <note>original: "a. a. O." (*am angegebenen Ort*)</note>. In the meantime, after a new discussion of the experiments, I no longer believe myself that the previous attempt to explain the complication—to which Weber’s Law is subject at small distances—is tenable. If the $V$ values had the presupposed organic basis, they would have to be found to be noticeably constant across different experimental series by the same observer after being reduced to comparable values based on the number of observations. However, as will be seen later, they change no less than the $W$ values according to the times of the experiments. In what follows, any attempt to explain them is also set aside, and we shall merely investigate, after citing the experiments themselves, whether our formula is sufficient to represent them.

Volkmann himself has, of course, recently contradicted this representation, stating on page 125: "If the distances with which one performs the compensation experiments become very small, the influence of their dimension finally disappears completely 1), so that the sums of errors for noticeably different distances yield equal values. — Fechner was not yet aware of this fact and therefore, in the discussion of the smallest visible differences in size, put forward a hypothesis which is not tenable in view of my more recent experiences. Fechner suspected that the sums of errors, and accordingly the smallest recognizable differences, were two-part quantities: one part, $W$, corresponded to Weber’s Law and was proportional to the distances; the other part, $V$, on the other hand, was independent of the distances and thus constant. This hypothesis corresponded in a fairly satisfactory manner to the sums of errors of four series of experiments performed by me and one of my students. Only the sums of errors of the smallest distance fell out of the series, which Fechner believed he could attribute to <term>irradiation interference</term><note>A visual effect where light spreads from a bright area into a dark one, potentially blurring the edges of very small objects.</note>. <meta>This page continues Fechner’s technical defense of his psychophysical equations. He is specifically addressing the relationship between the distance (D) of a visual stimulus and the resulting sum of errors (S) in perception. He argues that the mathematical patterns seen in the data are not errors in his theory, but rather expected results of the formula itself, even at extremely small distances.</meta>

"...accidental disturbances, but rather depends on the fact that the <term>sums of errors</term><note>In psychophysics, this refers to the total amount of deviation between a subject's perception and the actual physical measurement.</note>, which accumulate during observations of the smallest distances, still depend on specific constant causes."

But these statements are based on misunderstandings.

Firstly, the new experiments by Volkmann and his co-observers—Jahn, Geiß, and Krause—align in their progression and results with the experiments I used in the *Elements* <note>Referring to Gustav Fechner’s foundational work, *Elemente der Psychophysik* (Elements of Psychophysics), published in 1860.</note>, and the noticeable constancy of the sums of errors at very small values of $D$ <note>$D$ stands for *Distanz* (distance).</note> is not in contradiction with my formula, but rather a consequence of it.

Secondly, in the *Elements*, I considered only the sums of errors occurring at the very smallest distance $D$ in Volkmann's earlier experiments (cited below under 2 and 3) to be distorted by <term>irradiation</term><note>A visual effect where light spreads from a bright area to a dark area on the retina, making objects appear larger or blurred.</note>, and I did so according to Volkmann's own statements (*Elem.* I. 220); for this reason, I must also exclude them from the following calculation, as they do not fit into the series of the others. See the table on page 348.

To initially determine $V$ and $W$ in the simplest possible way, and thus obtain approximate values to which the correction process according to the <term>method of least squares</term><note>A mathematical technique used to find the best-fitting curve for a set of data points by minimizing the gaps between the data and the curve.</note> can be applied, one can proceed as follows:

If the number of distances is $n$, one should sum the values of $S²$ obtained from $S$ for the $n/2$ smallest distances and likewise for the $n/2$ largest distances. Let the first sum be called $A$ and the latter $B$. In the same way, sum the values of $D²$ for the $n/2$ smallest and the $n/2$ largest distances. These sums are called $a$ and $b$. Then one has:

->A = n/2 V² + aW²<-
->B = n/2 V² + bW²<-

->and accordingly<-

->W² = (B — A) / (b — a)<-
->V² = (2 (A — aW²)) / n<-

If $n$ were odd, one would use $(n-1)/2$ instead of $n/2$, in which case the middle $S²$ is excluded from consideration in the determination. The result of this method, which I call the <term>summation method</term>, generally differs only slightly from the result of the most precise method—the method of least squares—as can be seen from the table on page 347.

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s technical discussion on the mathematical methods used to analyze experimental data. Having established that his formula for the "sum of errors" (S) remains valid even at small distances (D), he now explains a transition in his statistical approach—moving from a simpler calculation to a more rigorous application of the Method of Least Squares to ensure the highest possible accuracy.</meta>

In the *Elements* <note>Referring to Fechner's 1860 work, *Elemente der Psychophysik*.</note>, I based the latter method on the principle that the sum of the deviations between the calculated and observed $S^2$ should be a minimum; however, since $S$ itself is directly observed, rather than $S^2$, the calculation method must be considered even more precise if the sum of the squares of the deviations between the calculated and observed $S$ is the smallest possible. Although this method is considerably more laborious without leading to results significantly different from the previous one, I have subsequently applied it not only to the newer experiments but also recalculated the earlier ones accordingly. According to the form of the equation:

->S = √ (V² + D² W²)<-

however, the method can only be used for small corrections by starting from approximate values of $V$ and $W$; thus, I have used the values obtained with the <term>summation method</term><note>A simpler statistical technique for estimating parameters before refining them with more complex calculations.</note>, which are to be included in the table on page 347, as starting values for $V$ and $W$, and based the correction on the formula:

->∂S = (V ∂V + D² W ∂W) / √ (V² + D² W²)<-

Only in the series designated below as 1) and 7) was it necessary to go beyond the first correction.

In case 1), the distances *D* are so large that *V* almost disappears in comparison to *D*² *W*²; whereas in 7), the *V* is so large compared to *D*² *W*² that *W* almost disappears in comparison to *V*. If one were to harbor a suspicion that errors had crept into the calculation of *V* and *W* themselves, it would be easy to counter this suspicion by applying the same values to the calculation of *S*, but with some small changes in either the positive or negative direction; one will always find the sum of the squares of the deviations between the calculated and observed *S* values to be larger than when the *V* and *W* values given in the table are used.

The experiments were conducted with the help of a screw micrometer at a 200 mm <term>viewing distance<note>The distance between the eye and the object being measured.</note></term> according to the following procedure: "A <term>reference distance<note>Original: "Normaldistanz". The length adjusted by the observer to find the threshold of detection.</note></term> which, again alternating, appears a minimum amount larger or smaller." The obtained differences between the reference distance and the comparison distance are separated below into those for comparison distances that were too small and those that were too large, and their respective sums are listed as $+S$ and $-S$.

Volkmann (p. 131) performed 80 trials for each distance across 5 distances; Krause (p. 129) did so for only 3 distances. Specifically, 40 trials were performed with the reference distance on the right, and 40 with it on the left. Of these 40 trials, half served to produce distances that were too large, and the other half to produce distances that were too small. To obtain the <term>just noticeable difference</term> for each distance, each of the following $\pm S$ values would still need to be divided by 40.
