### c) By Chodin.

Chodin also conducted two series of experiments using the <term>method of just noticeable differences<note>original: "Methode d. e. m. U." (eben merkliche Unterschiede). This is a psychophysical technique where a researcher determines the smallest change in a stimulus that a subject can actually perceive.</note></term>; the results of which generally agree with the progression of his results cited above, obtained via the <term>method of mean errors<note>original: "Methode der m. F." (mittleren Fehler). A method where the subject adjusts a stimulus until it matches a standard; the "error" is the difference between the match and the standard.</note></term>. On the other hand, they deviate from the progression of the results of Volkmann and his fellow observer Krause in a similar manner as his previous results.

His procedure, following the one mentioned above (p. 340), was this: On both sides of the horizontal distance marked as above, "not an equal line, but a line larger or smaller by a detectable difference was drawn," and the total sum of the positive and negative differences obtained, for both the right-hand and left-hand positions, was added together.

After this sum was divided for each distance—first by the number of trials conducted, and second by the distance itself—the following values of the relative <term>just noticeable difference<note>original: "relativen eben m. U." The ratio of the smallest detectable change to the total size of the stimulus.</note></term> were obtained:

| D | 2.5 | 5 | 10 | 20 | 40 | 80 | 160 |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| No. 4 | 1/17 | 1/29 | 1/37 | 1/53 | 1/44 | 1/39 | 1/43 |
| No. 5 | 1/26 | 1/39 | 1/45 | 1/37 | 1/36 | 1/32 | 1/30 |

Naturally, the objections already raised against the previously cited experiments also apply to these. Even here, however, one can observe that in series No. 4, the values from D = 10 to 160 could serve more to confirm than to refute <term>Weber’s Law<note>Weber's Law suggests that the ability to perceive a change in a stimulus is proportional to the original magnitude of the stimulus. In this context, it would mean the relative difference (the fractions in the table) should remain constant.</note></term> within these limits, whereas series No. 5 decidedly contradicts it.

### d) By Wundt on changes in the convergence position of the eyes.

Wundt provides the following experiments in his *Physiological Psychology* <note>original: "Physiol. Psychol." refers to Wilhelm Wundt’s foundational work, *Grundzüge der physiologischen Psychologie* (Principles of Physiological Psychology), II. 94.</note>, along with many explanations and conclusions which I will omit here, as we are only interested in the confirmation that Weber's Law receives in the near constancy of the relative just noticeable differences in the <term>convergence position<note>Convergence refers to the simultaneous inward movement of both eyes toward each other to maintain focus on an object as it moves closer.</note></term> of the eyes, denoted hereafter as *v*. His statements read literally as follows:

> "Through a horizontal slit in an upright board, look with both eyes at a white wall in the distance. Between this wall and the eyes, a vertically suspended black thread, kept taut by a weight, is moved back and [forth]..."

Despite all these irregularities, the very close agreement between the observed and calculated remains visible in the vast majority of values and thus in the general progression of the values.

Should the calculation principle challenged by Müller be incorrect, one would have to expect a deviation between observation and calculation in a *constant direction*, especially at the smallest and largest values of $D$. Taking all of this together, in response to Müller's declaration—which was based on an incomplete investigation—that the incorrectness of my **decomposition principle** <note>The "Zerlegungsprincip" is Fechner’s mathematical method of separating different types of errors (like constant versus variable errors) to better understand sensory thresholds.</note> has been placed "beyond all doubt," I can only offer the counter-declaration: that the correctness of this principle is as well-secured by a complete discussion of the existing facts and the application of the most precise calculation methods as can possibly be demanded by the nature of these experiments. 3) On p. 213, Müller remarks "it should be taken into account that, according to Volkmann's later visual estimation experiments, the relative value of the average error increases with the size of the main distance, not only when comparing very small distances, but also when using larger distances from 1 to 60 mm..." By this, Müller can only mean the experiments conducted by Solger under Volkmann's direction, which are cited on p. 338; however, in those, if one disregards the first two distances in III and the first in IV, one can only speak of an agreement with **Weber's Law** <note>Weber's Law suggests that the smallest noticeable difference in a stimulus is proportional to the original intensity of the stimulus.</note> through a noticeable constancy of $S/D$ <note>The ratio of the sensitivity/error ($S$) to the total distance ($D$).</note>. Contrary to the somewhat large values of $S/D$ at the smallest distances, $S/D$ does not increase with increasing distance, as Müller says, but rather decreases, as one can see for oneself on p. 338.

4) Müller rejects the interpretation of the **Volkmann constant** <note>A fixed value Fechner introduced in his formulas to account for the physical limitations of the eye.</note> I gave in the "Elem." <note>Fechner’s foundational work, *Elemente der Psychophysik* (Elements of Psychophysics, 1860).</note>, simply because "it is [based on other facts] hardly subject to doubt that every precise comparison of two spatial magnitudes, lines, angles, or surfaces makes use of eye movements and is fundamentally only a comparison of the **muscle sensations** <note>The physical feeling of the eye muscles moving as they scan a shape or distance.</note> accompanying those eye movements." Now, I suspect this myself and have already expressed it elsewhere. But this would not in itself prevent this primary influence, which varies with distance, from being complicated by a small secondary influence depending on the dimensions of the **retinal elements** <note>The individual light-sensitive cells (photoreceptors) in the retina; Fechner theorized their physical spacing might set a "floor" for how small a distance the eye can perceive.</note>. In the meantime, I have already stated that I have dropped that previously established hypothesis regarding the reason for the constant $V$—which, however, does not alter the fact of the constant itself—for other reasons.

### 5) 
Regarding the experiments by Volkmann cited on page 350, which used the method of the **just noticeable difference** <note>original: "e. m. U.", or *eben merklicher Unterschied*. This is the smallest change in a stimulus, such as weight or light, that a person can actually detect.</note>, Müller (p. 207) states he "cannot see the benefit of switching the sign of the just noticeable difference. One generally measures the **difference sensitivity** <note>original: "U. E.", or *Unterschiedsempfindlichkeit*</note> associated with a stimulus magnitude *r* by setting it as the reciprocal of the just noticeable increase *S* to the given stimulus intensity, but not as the reciprocal of the previously mentioned decrease *d* of the same, which—as the just noticeable increase to the lower stimulus intensity *r — d*—is generally somewhat smaller. Strictly speaking, one introduces a new measure of difference sensitivity if one, following Volkmann, sets it as the reciprocal of the average value of *S* and *d*."

However, it seems to me that Müller overlooks the fact that even if one has unilaterally determined *S* as an increase to the distance *r*, one can just as easily view the found *S* conversely as a decrease relative to the resulting distance *S + r*, without thereby introducing a new measure of difference sensitivity. Taking the matter in the first way is merely a one-sided *psychological* and *experimental* direction of comparison, and Volkmann was therefore quite right to add experiments with −*S* to those with +*S* to compensate for **constant errors** <note>In scientific measurements, a "constant error" is a systematic bias that consistently pushes results in one direction, as opposed to random fluctuations.</note>. It has only been shown, according to my mathematical treatments of his experiments above, that the constant error for +*S* and −*S* is so different that it is more practical to calculate both separately rather than combined.

### 6) 
Müller finds (p. 206) the results of my series of experiments cited on page 350 to be "at least for the time being, completely useless for a testing of **Weber's Law** <note>Weber’s Law is a fundamental principle in psychophysics stating that the change in a stimulus that will be just noticeable is a constant ratio of the original stimulus.</note>, according to the explanations in § 26 ff. [of his writing]," and therefore does not go further into these experiments. I believe, however, after what was said in Section VII against Müller's interpretation of the **method of average errors** <note>original: "m. F.", or *mittlere Fehler*. A method where a subject tries to match a stimulus to a standard, and the researcher measures the average deviation.</note> in § 26 ff., that my experiments are still as good in this regard as they were before.

### 7) 
On p. 209, Müller remarks that Chodin <note>A. Chodin was a researcher known for studying the sensitivity of the eye to various distances.</note> "following Volkmann’s example, identifies the average value of pure variable errors with the largest unnoticeable difference, which naturally must behave exactly like the smallest detectable difference."

But I find nothing of this identification in either Chodin or Volkmann. Both only investigate the question of Weber's Law regarding one value as well as the other, without explaining or indirectly suggesting in any way that they consider both to be the same.

8) Müller returns (p. 210), when comparing Chodin's experiments with Volkmann’s, to his undeniably incorrect interpretation of the way Volkmann proceeded with the **Method of Average Error** <note>original: "m. F." or *mittlerer Fehler*. This is a statistical method where a subject tries to match a stimulus to a standard, and the "average error" in their accuracy is measured.</note>, a matter about which the necessary points have already been stated on page 117.

9) No less does he return to the idea (p. 209, 211, 213) that **visual estimation experiments** <note>original: *Augenmaßversuche*</note> conducted according to the Method of Average Error can only be asserted as valid for **Weber's Law** <note>Weber's Law suggests that the smallest change in a stimulus that can be detected is a constant proportion of the original stimulus.</note> insofar as the mean error obtained therein remains proportional to the **just noticeable difference** <note>original: "e. m. U." or *eben merklicher Unterschied*</note> (or the value representing it) at different distances; my remarks in Section II run contrary to this.

In doing so, Müller admits (p. 209) that the existing experiments, insofar as they offer a basis for comparison, prove a similar course for both, at least within certain limits. In fact, the micrometric experiments of Volkmann and Krause under section A. b. seem suited for a comparison with the micrometric experiments of the same observers under B. b. However, Krause's experiments cannot be counted here because, according to both methods, they consistently prove only that for Krause, at very small distances, the component of the mean error dependent on distance—just like that of the just noticeable difference—disappears noticeably compared to the independent component; whereas Volkmann’s experiments provide no certain decision for other reasons. Since Müller, in his comparison, ignores the decomposition of the obtained values into two components, the significance of his comparison disappears for me entirely.

## XXVIII. Notes on my series of weight experiments.

In the years 1855–1858, I conducted a number of larger series of weight experiments according to the **Method of Right and Wrong Cases** <note>original: "r. u. f. F." or *rechte und falsche Fälle*. This method involves presenting two slightly different stimuli and asking the subject to identify which is greater; the frequency of correct answers determines the threshold of perception.</note>. An account of these was given in general in *Elements of Psychophysics*, Volume I, pages 93 ff., 182 ff., and 305 ff., and results from them were specifically cited in relation to Weber's Law and the **Parallel Law** <note>The *Parallelgesetz* was Fechner's theory that if two stimuli are increased by the same ratio, the sensation of their difference remains constant.</note>. However, until now, the specific experimental data themselves and a discussion of them—from which many other results could be drawn—have not been published. Now, it is indeed my intention, after

Since I have frequently had occasion in this writing to refer back to these experiments regarding relationships that were not yet discussed in the *Elements* <note>referring to his seminal 1860 work, *Elements of Psychophysics*</note>, I wish to record here at least the most essential circumstances of the individual experimental series, so that these references do not appear to be "floating in the air." Regarding the general manner in which they were operated, I must refer to the *Elements*. In general, it was done such that every circumstance to be tested in comparison with others—such as the size of the primary weights, additional weights, the lifting hand, and temporal determinations—was included in the experiment equally often in methodical alternation, ascending and descending. The temporal and spatial positions were methodically rotated to allow for the elimination of constant errors. To record the relevant circumstances, I will also add an overview of the resulting distribution of $r, f, z$ <note>These represent the categories of responses: *richtig* (right), *falsch* (false), and *zweifelhaft* (doubtful/zero). I had the intention to further expand the experiments already conducted: namely, to bring the experiments on the duration of lifting and the interval between the two lifts of each double-lifting to a larger number (recorded below under Nos. 4 and 5), and partly to undertake experiments with variation of the interval between the individual double-lifts, and finally those with variation of the lifting height (which until now was everywhere 2 inches 9 lines <term>Parisian measure</term> <note>The "Paris inch" was a pre-metric unit of length, approximately 2.7 centimeters, slightly longer than the English inch. To this, I add the following remarks. The apparatus I used for the experiments is now no longer in my hands, but in Müller's <note>referring to Georg Elias Müller, a younger psychologist who often critiqued and refined Fechner's work</note>. It could one day pass into other hands, and thus an occasion might arise to reproach me for inaccuracies upon re-examining the lead weights (which are marked with the number of grams they weigh). Some may not have exactly the weight indicated and, as I expressly note, they truly require re-examination and, if necessary, correction before new experiments are performed with them. The reason for this is as follows. When I received the apparatus and weights from the **mechanic** <note>an instrument maker</note>, I found, upon careful re-examination, that some weights were a little too large and others a little too small compared to the correct weight. The former I corrected myself by filing them down; the latter I corrected during the experiments by adding small sheets of tin foil. All my experiments mentioned in the *Elements* were conducted in this way. Before the intended continuation of the experiments, and to save myself the effort of adding tin foil, I returned the weights that were too small to the mechanic to bring them to the correct weight by adding a bit of lead; but I cannot vouch for whether this was done correctly, as it...

I also do not want to omit mentioning, after the fact, that the ingenious device—by which the weight apparatuses can rotate freely around horizontal axes and orient themselves automatically according to gravity when lifted—is not my own invention; rather, I owe it to a suggestion by <term>Volkmann</term> <note>Alfred Wilhelm Volkmann (1801–1877), a physiologist who collaborated closely with Fechner on the study of sensations.</note>.

In the following, the number of cases is determined by the number of <term>double-lifts</term> <note>A "double-lift" consists of lifting two weights in succession to compare them, whereas a "simple lift" refers to lifting just one weight once.</note>, rather than the number of simple lifts as in the *Elements* <note>original: "Elem.", referring to Fechner’s 1860 book *Elements of Psychophysics*</note>; thus, the figures are only half as large as the reports in the *Elements*. Specifically, every "case" requires a double-lift—that is, the lifting of both the one and the other weight. **P** denotes the smaller, primary weight; **D** denotes the <term>additional weight</term> <note>original: "Zusatzgewicht"</note>, the size of which is consequently not given by its absolute value but in relation to **P**. Most frequently, **D = 0.04 P** and **= 0.08 P** are used. The gram serves as the unit of weight.

**One-handed trials** are those where both weights are lifted with the same hand; **two-handed trials** are those where one weight is lifted with one hand and the other with the opposite hand. However, the one-handed trials are always fully comparable and were performed in equal numbers with the **Left (L)** and the **Right (R)**, which should not be confused with "two-handed" in the sense described above.

There are 8 main experimental series: 5 one-handed and 3 two-handed. In each main series, on every day of experimentation, an equal number of trials were performed under the "normal conditions" specified in *Elements* I. 97 ff. (unless an exception is noted). In addition to these main series with given **D** values, there are 3 "side series" without **D**—that is, with two equal weights—conducted for comparison with main series No. 1, 2, and 6; these were inserted on special days between the trial days of the main series. The trials of these side series, as well as several <term>fatigue series</term> <note>Trials conducted to measure how physical exhaustion affects the accuracy of weight perception.</note> which are also to be regarded as side series, are therefore not counted among the 8 main series, though the side series without **D** are given special consideration at the end.

...[The number of] cases of a series or a larger division of the same is understood [as follows]. In the <term>one-handed procedure</term> <note>A method where the subject lifts weights using only one hand to compare them, rather than using both hands simultaneously.</note>, the total series is divided between the **Left (L)** and **Right (R)** hands, and when using additional weights (**D**) of different sizes, the series is divided into equal sections among them. This is done similarly according to the four different temporal and spatial positions to allow for the <term>elimination of constant errors</term> <note>"Constant errors" refer to predictable biases, such as a person consistently perceiving the second weight lifted as heavier simply because of the order.</note>, as well as according to **ascending ↑** and **descending ↓** orders. One can see from the last vertical column that the ratio of the doubtful cases ($\Sigma z$) to the total number ($\Sigma n$) varies greatly depending on the series, rising from a single amount to nearly double. # XXIX. Sound experiments by Nörr and Wundt with subsequent remarks on the method of just noticeable differences.

In the "Elements" <note>Fechner refers here to his seminal 1860 work, *Elemente der Psychophysik* (Elements of Psychophysics).</note> Vol. I, page 177 ff., I mentioned the experiments of Volkmann <note>Alfred Wilhelm Volkmann (1801–1877), a physiologist and close collaborator of Fechner.</note> conducted according to the method of just noticeable differences <term>e. m. U. (eben merkliche Unterschiede): a psychophysical method where a subject determines the smallest detectable difference between two stimuli.</term>, which provided a confirmation of Weber's Law <note>Weber's Law states that the smallest noticeable difference between two stimuli is a constant proportion of the original stimulus.</note>.

Such a highly desirable replication, using the <term>method of right and wrong cases<note>A procedure where a subject compares two stimuli, and the researcher records the frequency of correct, incorrect, and doubtful judgments to determine sensory thresholds.</note></term>, has since been carried out first by Nörr at the instigation of Vierordt <note>OCR reads "Bierordt," likely a transcription of Karl von Vierordt (1818–1884), a pioneer in medical physics.</note> in his physiological institute; secondly, very recent experiments—which may be summarized as Wundt’s experiments—were carried out by Wundt <note>Wilhelm Wundt, often called the "father of experimental psychology."</note> with the assistance of several of his students in his psycho-physiological institute, again according to the <term>method of just noticeable differences<note>A procedure where the difference between two stimuli is gradually increased or decreased until the subject can just barely perceive the change.</note></term>. In both instances, these were performed with far-reaching success in favor of Weber’s Law. As usually happens with successive treatments of the same field of observation by different researchers—and is to be expected everywhere in a difficult field—progress has asserted itself from the earlier to the later studies (that is, from Volkmann’s to Wundt’s experiments), and thus the confirmation of Weber’s Law has grown.

Now, I am certainly aware that Vierordt, having an interest in the Nörr experiments conducted in his institute, is by no means inclined to unreservedly agree with Wundt’s experiments regarding the circumstances by which they go beyond those of Nörr and Volkmann. His remarks in this regard are therefore to be awaited before one decides between the investigations of Nörr and Wundt where they deviate from one another; I also regret that I cannot personally wait for the results of the discussions expected on this matter. For the time being, however, I can only stick to the data as far as they are available, and I will therefore, after some preliminary discussions, communicate excerpts of both Nörr's and Wundt's investigations, each in its own context. Fortunately, the discrepancies between the two do not concern the question of the law's validity—which is affirmed by both investigations—but only the question of the greater or lesser adequacy of the investigation in demonstrating this validity <sup>1)</sup>.

### (VIII) To add some supplementary remarks (under C) regarding the method of just noticeable differences <note>original: "e. m. U.," abbreviation for *eben merkliche Unterschiede*</note>.

These are the designations that I applied in the presentation of *Nörr’s* experiments, and I will also maintain them in the following introductory observations, provided nothing else is noted; however, in *Tischer’s* treatise, the designations for the presentation of *Wundt’s* experiments are chosen differently, insofar as in the more general observations here, the greater height of fall is designated with *H*, the smaller with *h*, the greater weight with *P*, and the smaller with *p* ¹), while in the experimental tables the designations are specialized even further, which we shall come to later.

Now, if two sound stimuli *R₀*, *R₁* are calculated according to the values *H₀*, *H₁*, *M₀*, *M₁* <note>Height and Mass</note> entering into them, then the testing of *Weber’s* Law according to the method of just noticeable differences <note>original: "d. e. m. U.," abbreviation for *der eben merklichen Unterschiede*</note> can be done either by presenting two sound stimuli *R₀*, *R₁* for observation, modifying them until they present a just noticeable difference, and then changing both in the same proportion so that the absolute values *R₀*, *R₁* change but their ratio *R₁/R₀* remains the same, and seeing whether the just noticeable difference for sensation always remains just noticeable, as is required for the confirmation of *Weber’s* Law. *Volkmann* proceeded in this manner according to the description given in "Elements" <note>original: "Elem.," referring to Fechner's *Elemente der Psychophysik*</note> Vol. I, p. 178.

However, one can also proceed by not taking the same *R₁/R₀* from the outset while modifying *R₁* and *R₀*, but rather by modifying *R₁* against a given *R₀* until the difference between the two reaches a just noticeable difference; one then repeats this with different values for *R₀*, for which a different *R₁* will be found, and sees whether one arrives at the same ratio *R₁/R₀*, as is required by *Weber’s* Law. *Wundt* proceeded in this manner.

Finally, *Nörr*, using the method of right and wrong cases <note>original: "d. r. u. f. F.," abbreviation for *der richtigen und falschen Fälle*, a statistical method for determining thresholds</note>—corresponding to *Volkmann* using the method of just noticeable differences—proceeded by maintaining the same ratio *R₁/R₀* while changing the absolute values *R₀*, *R₁* and seeing whether the same percentage ratio

...of correct cases was achieved, as is required by **Weber’s Law**.

Regarding the derivation of a value *R* <note>sound intensity</note> from its components *M* <note>mass/weight</note> and *H* <note>height of fall</note>, it should first be noted that the square of the velocity *c*, with which the ball strikes the surface, is proportional to the height of fall *H*; thus, the <term>kinetic energy; original: *lebendige Kraft*, a 19th-century term for $mv^2$</term> of the impact is proportional to *MH* or *Mc²*. Now, sound intensity has been measured physically and objectively by the kinetic energy of the sound vibrations, and insofar as one considers these proportional to the kinetic energy of the ball's impact, we would be justified from the outset and without further ado in setting the sound intensity *R* proportional to *MH* or *Mc²*. 

But this is not self-evident, because the kinetic energy of the falling ball must first be communicated to the plate, setting it into vibrations, and these must be communicated to the air and the ear; it remains questionable whether, through the course of these transmissions, a kinetic energy proportional to the *Mc²* of the ball actually reaches the ear. Be that as it may, it is proved directly by the following circumstance that the sound intensity cannot be set proportional to the *Mc²* or *MH* of the falling ball. Were it proportional to them, then when changing *M* and *H* to any other values *M₁* and *H₁*, the sound should be heard as being of equal intensity if:

->*MH = M₁H₁*, therefore *Mc² = M₁c₁²*.<-

But **Vierordt** has made the interesting discovery—which forms, so to speak, the starting point of a new experimental measurement theory of sound intensity—that this is not the case; indeed, it fails completely. His experiments on this are contained in the *Journal of Biology* <note>original: *Zeitschr. f. Biol.*</note> 1878, p. 300 ff. At first, he concluded from these experiments that the sound is instead heard with equal intensity when:

->*Mc = M₁c₁* or *MH⁰·⁵ = M₁H₁⁰·⁵*,<-

according to which, for a given *M*, the sound intensity is to be set proportional to *H⁰·⁵* instead of *H*—that is: proportional to *c* instead of *c²*; and **Nörr** based his calculation of sound intensity upon this, setting generally:

->*R = MH⁰·⁵ = Mc*<-

In the meantime, both later experiments by **Oberbeck** (in *Poggendorff's Annals* <note>original: *Pogg. Ann. N. F.*</note> XIII, 222), using a principle other than Vierordt’s, and Vierordt’s own later experiments (in *Journal of Biology* XVII, 361 ff.) have led to an exponent of *H* other than 0.5. Let this be generally designated as ε <note>the Greek letter epsilon</note>.

<summary>This page discusses the mathematical relationship between the physical impact of a falling ball and the perceived intensity of the resulting sound, highlighting Vierordt's discovery that perceived intensity is proportional to velocity rather than the total kinetic energy.</summary>
<keywords>Weber's Law, sound intensity, kinetic energy, Vierordt, Nörr, height of fall, velocity, experimental psychophysics</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the mathematical and experimental investigation into the measurement of sound intensity. The previous page introduced the problem of whether sound intensity (R) is directly proportional to the kinetic energy of a falling ball (Mass times Height, or MH) or follows a more complex power law.</meta>

— 372 —

**Oberbeck** found that instead of an exponent of $e = 0.5$, values of 0.629 to 0.638 were applicable for lead balls falling onto wood, and 0.656 for stone balls; meanwhile, **Vierordt’s** later experiments with lead balls falling onto a tin plate yielded an exponent of 0.589, which he abbreviated to 0.59, as the most applicable. According to **Oberbeck**, however, the sound remains proportional to the mass, though large sound intensities grow somewhat more slowly than the weights.

Despite all this, it is important to note that for experiments testing **Weber’s Law**, it is generally indifferent whether we introduce the absolute acoustic stimulus as being proportional to $MH$ or $MH^{0.5}$, or to any other power of $H$—in short, whatever value we give to $e$—provided that it remains constant for all values of $M$ and $H$ used in the experimental series.

In fact, if we set $R_0 = M_0H_0^e$ and $R_1 = M_1H_1^e$, then the ratio $R_1 / R_0$—the constancy of which is required to achieve an equally noticeable sensation of difference—becomes:

->$\frac{M_1 H_1^e}{M_0 H_0^e} = \frac{M_1}{M_0} \left(\frac{H_1}{H_0}\right)^e$<-

Thus, $e$ can have any value; as long as it remains constant for all $M$ and $H$, the absolute value of the previous expression will change, but its constancy—which is what matters—will not. It is therefore simplest to take the value $e = 1$, and consequently to set $R$ simply as $MH$ and the ratio as $R_1 / R_0 = (M_1 H_1) / (M_0 H_0)$. Now, where $M_1 = M_0$ is used (as in **Nörr’s** experiments), $M_1$ and $M_0$ cancel each other out in the previous expression, and one can consider **Weber’s Law** confirmed if the same <note>original: e. m. U., abbreviation for *eben merkbarer Unterschied*</note> <term>just noticeable difference</term> or the same percentage of correct cases is found for the same ratio of $H_1 / H_0$ while the absolute magnitudes of $H_1$ and $H_0$ are varied.

It would be different, of course, if $e$ were to change depending on the magnitude of $M$ and $H$.

Now, the following circumstance causes some embarrassment. Experiments to test the law cannot, of course, be carried out without changing $M$ and $H$; furthermore, these values varied within wide limits in the experiments of both **Volkmann** and **Nörr**. In those studies, not only was no account taken of any variation in $e$—meaning its constancy was tacitly assumed—but such constancy must be assumed in order to find a strict verification of the law in these experiments. For

What would be the use if, with the same ratio of $\frac{\text{H}_1}{\text{H}_0}$ and varying absolute sizes of H₁ and H₀, one always found the same just noticeable difference <note>Ebenmerklichkeit: the smallest change in a stimulus that can be detected</note> or the same percentage of correct cases, if the value of ε changed in an unknown way across different values of H and M? In such a case, the constancy of the ratio $\frac{\text{R}_1}{\text{R}_0}$ <note>the ratio of perceived stimulus intensities</note> would be lost even while the ratio $\frac{\text{H}_1}{\text{H}_0}$ remained constant, despite the fact that the constancy of $\frac{\text{R}_1}{\text{R}_0}$ is the very foundation being relied upon.

On the other hand, the fact that a law emerged from the experiments of Volkmann and Nörr—which otherwise could not have been inferred from those trials—speaks in favor of the constancy of ε.

However, Wundt’s experiments on the measurement of sound intensity, which served as the introduction to his research on Weber’s Law <note>The principle that the perceived change in a stimulus is proportional to the initial intensity of the stimulus</note>, have decisively shown that ε is not independent of the absolute values of H and M. Instead, it increases as M and H increase; furthermore, it changes according to the impact surface <term>Fallunterlage: The specific material or base upon which the weight is dropped to produce a sound</term>. Moreover, the variation of ε according to M and H is not insignificant. Consequently, Wundt felt compelled to specifically determine the corresponding values of ε for the values of H₀, M₀, H₁, and M₁ that he employed, or to use only those values of H and M for whose combination ε had already been determined—a determination that could be carried out according to the principle applied by Vierordt. That is to say, if the sound produced using M₀ and H₀ was found to be equal to the sound from M₁ and H₁, one had to set:

->M₀H₀<sup>ε</sup> = M₁ H₁<sup>ε</sup><-

->from which ε = $\frac{\log \frac{\text{M}_0}{\text{M}_1}}{\log \frac{\text{H}_1}{\text{H}_0}}$<-

or, using Wundt’s notation (p. 370):

->pH<sup>ε</sup> = Ph<sup>ε</sup><-

->and from this ε = $\frac{\log \frac{\text{P}}{\text{p}}}{\log \frac{\text{H}}{\text{h}}}$<-

Since the confirmation of **Weber’s** law <note>A fundamental principle in psychophysics stating that the just-noticeable difference between two stimuli is proportional to the magnitude of the stimuli.</note> has now emerged from **Wundt’s** experiments based on the **special calculation** of **e** <note>Referring to the exponent ε (epsilon) used to calculate sound intensity from the mass and drop height of a ball.</note> for the applied drop heights and weights, the question arises: how could the law be confirmed by **Volkmann’s** and **Nörr’s** experiments **without such a calculation**, based on the assumption of a constant **e**, or to put it another way, how can one still regard it as confirmed by those experiments?

I confess that I cannot provide a definitive resolution to this difficulty; yet it seems to me that the following can be said about it.

Regarding **Volkmann’s** experiments, one may first remark in general that the method of estimating the just noticeable difference <note>The threshold at which a subject can first perceive a difference between two stimuli.</note> upon which these experiments are based was perhaps too uncertain to allow differences depending on the inconstancy of **e** to emerge clearly. However, one must also not overlook that **Volkmann** operated with **steel balls** falling on **steel**, whereas **Wundt’s** experiments—which speak against the constancy of **e**—were conducted with **lead balls** falling on **wood**, which are indisputably subject to a certain deformation, particularly at great drop heights. It thus remains to be investigated whether a much greater constancy of **e** would not be shown with **steel balls** on **steel** than with **lead balls** on **wood**. Although it is probable that the bouncing of the **steel balls**—about which **Volkmann** provides no data—will be stronger than that of the **lead balls**, if (as is not improbable) the loss of living force <note>original: "lebendige Kraft"; a historical term for kinetic energy.</note> resulting from this for the production of sound is proportional to the sound intensities, then this would seem to bring no essential disturbance. Meanwhile, if one examines the results of **Nörr’s** experiments more closely, the striking contradiction disappears, which they seem to stand in with **Wundt’s** experiments at first glance. **Nörr** conducted three series of experiments, in each of which the **M$_0$** <note>Initial mass or weight of the falling object.</note> ascended through seven values from 6.7 to 1,025,100 milligrams, while the corresponding **H$_0$** <note>Initial drop height.</note> partly ascended and partly descended. Each of these series gives, for the seven **M$_0$** with their corresponding **M$_1$** <note>The second mass used for comparison.</note>, seven percentages of correct cases; the equality of these percentages within each series is required for the confirmation of **Weber’s Law** <note>The principle that the perceived change in a stimulus is proportional to the initial stimulus.</note>. But a closer inspection shows, firstly, that these values—as well as the values for **t** <term>t-value</term> <note>A statistical value derived from the "fundamental table" of psychophysics used to measure the precision of a subject's sensory discrimination.</note> derivable from them according to the **Fundamental Table**—fluctuate significantly, so that the influence of a variation in *e* <note>The exponent used to calculate sound intensity from physical force.</note> can be partially hidden within this. Secondly, in all three series, the two heaviest balls yield percentages of correct cases, and thus values of **t**, which are considerably larger than the average of the other values in the same series; indeed, in the second and third series, they are even larger than every other individual value in the same series, as will be seen on p. 382. Previously, I was inclined to attribute this to a lack of comparability between the two heaviest balls and the others, insofar as those were exceptionally made of iron while the rest were of lead, and it is indeed possible that something depends on this; however, it is more likely that the increase of *e* with the increase of **M$_0$** (where **M$_1$** was equal throughout) is responsible for it.

Nevertheless, **Nörr’s** experiments could be considered a welcome support and supplement regarding the testing of **Weber’s Law**, partly because the deviation in the two largest **M$_0$** did not stand out too far from the fluctuations in the other values, because it allowed for a not improbable explanation, and in no case could it be seen as an upper deviation from the law in the same sense as occurs with light; for according to that, the percentages of correct cases for the highest **M** should have decreased rather than increased.

Aside from the different primary methods and ways of calculation in **Nörr’s** and **Wundt’s** experiments, the following points are also worth noting for a comparison between them, which are partly more favorable to one and partly to the other.

**Nörr’s** experiments were conducted solely by **Nörr** himself, while **Wundt’s** were performed by a majority of observers, which [provides] a useful

The number of individual trials in Nörr’s study is significantly larger than the total number of trials that I have grouped together as "Wundtian"; however, the method of **r. u. f. F.** <term>right and wrong cases</term> <note>German: "richtige und falsche Fälle." A method where a subject judges whether a comparison stimulus is greater, lesser, or equal to a standard.</note> also requires a comparatively larger number of trials than the method of **e. m. U.** <term>just noticeable difference</term> <note>German: "eben merklicher Unterschied." The smallest detectable difference between two stimuli.</note>. 

Nörr’s trials were distributed over two semesters without a specifically stated distribution pattern; as a rule, however, observations were never made for longer than half an hour at a time. Consequently, the entirety of the trials is divided into different "trial fractions." In contrast, the Wundtian trials were conducted by each observer in immediate succession, with the longest series of trials (Series XIV by **Merkel** <note>Julius Merkel, a researcher in Wundt’s laboratory.</note>) continuing for three hours. 

Regarding Nörr, this allows for the concern that a comparable state of differential sensitivity could not be guaranteed across the different trial fractions over the course of a year. Conversely, regarding the Wundtian experiments, one must consider that during a three-hour continuation of trials, the progress of fatigue and practice could hardly be absent; in any case, there is no evidence to prove that such influences were excluded. 

In this regard, it would have seemed important to me not to neglect the general rule for experiments on **Weber’s Law** <note>The psychological law stating that the change in a stimulus that will be just noticeable is a constant ratio of the original stimulus.</note>: namely, to conduct the trials in equal numbers in ascending and descending order of stimulus magnitudes—in this case, sound intensities. This is done partly to detect any possible influence from the sequence of trials and partly to compensate for it, especially since the sequence from smaller to larger stimuli (and vice versa) also gains influence through contrast effects. However, nothing at all is mentioned in **Tischer’s** <note>Ernst Tischer, whose acoustic experiments are being critiqued here.</note> treatise regarding the sequence maintained during the trials. 

As far as the influence of fatigue is concerned, one would expect no disadvantage for the validity of Weber's Law, provided that according to the **Parallel Law** <note>The principle that if fatigue affects the perception of both the standard and comparison stimuli equally, the ratio between them (and thus the law) remains valid.</note>, the fatigue extends to the different stimuli simultaneously. However, the determination of the average relative **e. m. U.** <note>just noticeable difference</note> could certainly be influenced by it, and in any case, the reliability of the trials toward their end could be diminished by a weakening of attention. 

Furthermore, progress in "practice"—of the kind where a smaller and smaller difference gradually becomes noticeable—would also have to be detrimental to the validity of Weber’s Law. That such an effect could indeed exert itself within a three-hour trial duration is quite possible to imagine, as I witnessed such an effect firsthand at the end of a long series of trials during my participation in **Volkmann’s** <note>Alfred Wilhelm Volkmann, a physiologist who collaborated with Fechner on psychophysical studies.</note> sound experiments.

### A) Nörr’s Experiments.

Without changing the factual basis of Nörr’s <note>Friedrich Nörr was a researcher who conducted early psychophysical experiments on the perception of sound intensity.</note> experiments, I will nevertheless allow myself some deviations from the author’s presentation in this report for formal reasons.

The following remarks are intended for orientation regarding the author’s own presentation.

Nörr still relies on the earlier view of Vierordt <note>Karl von Vierordt (1818–1884), a German physiologist who developed methods for measuring blood flow and sound perception.</note> that the sound intensity *R* can be measured by <term>Mc</term> <note>Momentum: Mass (M) multiplied by velocity (c). Early researchers used this physical calculation to estimate the "strength" of a sound produced by a falling object.</note>, where *c* denotes the terminal velocity of the fall, calculated from the height *H*. For the primary sound, where $H = H_0$, the value *c* is designated as $c_0$; for the comparison sound, where $H = H_1$, it is designated as $c_1$. The values for $c_0$ and, accordingly, $R_0 = Mc_0$ are provided by Nörr in Table II, page 302 of his treatise. In his seven experimental tables cited from page 306 onwards—corresponding to the seven applied drop weights $M_0$ ranging from 6.7 to 1025100 milligrams—the headings for all three main series specify the $M_0$ (which are equal to $M_1$), as well as $H_0$ and $H_1$. The first vertical column then contains, under **I**, the value $M_0c_0$ (the value of the primary sound according to the above calculation); under **II**, **III**, and **IV**, it contains the value of the corresponding comparison sound in the three main series (which I have distinguished as I, II, and III). The figures in the second vertical column, headed “Difference of both sound intensities in f''”, are obtained by expressing the relative differences of the first column—that is,

  Mc₁ — Mc₀     c₁ — c₀
———————— = ———————
     Mc₀           c₀

—as percentages through multiplication by 100. Thus, in the first of these tables on page 307, the figures 4.42, 8.85, and 17.4 are obtained for the three main series. Accordingly, the alleged *h* values in Table XII, page 316, are obtained by taking the values $t = hD = hM(c_1 - c_0)$ derived from the fundamental table <note>The "Fundamental Table" refers to Fechner's standardized mathematical tables used to calculate the probability of perceiving a difference between two stimuli.</note> according to the *r, f, z* values, and dividing them by the value

  c₁ — c₀
———————
     c₀

  c₁ — c₀
———————

is held constant.

The experiments were conducted at Vierordt’s Physiological Institute, which is located outside the city and is fairly well protected from disturbing daytime noise. They were performed with the assistance of the institute servant, Nagel, who was already practiced in such experiments. “From the outset, a strictly methodical distribution of the experiments into individual trial segments (hours, days, or even just weeks) had to be foregone,” and consequently, nothing is specified regarding this. As a rule, to prevent fatigue, experiments never lasted longer than about half an hour. The total number of experiments was distributed over two semesters.

Measures for the comparability and reliable execution of the experiments were taken, which should be consulted in the original. In total, seven spheres of different <term>mass (M)</term> were used; the two heaviest were made of polished iron, the others of lead. Each sphere was dropped from two different heights *H* with an interval of approximately three seconds between them, in order to generate a difference in the objective sound stimuli toward which the observer’s attention was to be directed. Naturally, the sphere falling from the greater height had to produce an objectively louder sound than the one falling from the lower height, but subjectively it could appear otherwise. Depending on whether the direction of the difference was judged correctly, incorrectly, or if no difference was found, these were categorized as "right," "wrong," and "null" cases, which the author designates as *R*, *F*, and *U* respectively, but for which I use the customary designations *r*, *f*, and *z* <note>In the psychophysics of this era, 'r' stands for *richtig* (right), 'f' for *falsch* (false), and 'z' for *Zweifelsfälle* (doubtful or null cases where no difference is perceived).</note> here. The total number of cases obtained with a given difference in *H*, $r + f + z$, is called *n*, as is usual. To compensate for <term>constant errors</term> <note>Constant errors: Systematic biases, such as the "time-order error," where the second of two identical sounds is often perceived as louder or softer simply because of its position in the sequence.</note> depending on the chronological order, the greater fall height was applied first in some trials and the smaller height first in others; these trials are distinguished as A and B. To obtain a definitive result, the average of the percentage values obtained in both cases was used for calculation.

The weights are expressed in milligrams, the fall heights in millimeters.

Regarding the designations, the details given on page 369 apply, to which the following should be added:

->Absolute difference $H_1 - H_0 = U$<-

->Relative difference $\frac{H_1 - H_0}{H_0} = \frac{U}{H_0} = u$<-

->Logarithm $\log \frac{H_1}{H_0} = d$<-

->Percentage of right cases increased by $\frac{z}{2}$<-

->$= \frac{r + \frac{z}{2}}{n} 100 = r' 100$<-

The fact that I add half of the *z* cases to the *r* cases when utilizing the *r*, *f*, *z* data is, I believe, justified by the discussions in Section V. This corresponds to the principle of dividing *z* that I designated as "I"; however <note>Fechner’s "Principle I" for handling uncertain cases assumes that if a subject cannot detect a difference, there is a 50% statistical probability they would have guessed correctly anyway, so half of these "null" cases are added to the "right" count.</note>...

...I will also proceed to a comparative consideration of the <term>Müllerian principle of division</term> for the *z* cases <note>original: "Müllerschen Theilungsprincipes der z". This refers to Georg Elias Müller’s mathematical method for distributing "doubtful" or "null" responses between the "right" and "wrong" categories to allow for better statistical analysis.</note>, which I have designated as II.

Since the same mass (*M*) was used for both heights $H_0$ and $H_1$ in all experiments—meaning $M_1 = M_0$ was taken throughout—the value of *M* cancels out in the ratio $\frac{M_1 H_1}{M_0 H_0}$. Furthermore, provided that the constant $\epsilon$ remains stable as Nörr assumed, the specific value of $\epsilon$ becomes irrelevant (see p. 372). For the sake of simplicity, we can set $\epsilon = 1$, and therefore treat the <term>stimulus (R)</term> <note>In these early psychophysical formulas, *R* stands for *Reiz* (the German word for stimulus).</note> as proportional to the height *H*. Accordingly, the ratio $\frac{R_1}{R_0}$ can be replaced by $\frac{H_1}{H_0}$, and the relative difference $\frac{R_1 - R_0}{R_0}$ can be replaced by $\frac{H_1 - H_0}{H_0} = u$. Consequently, confirmation of <term>Weber’s Law</term> <note>Weber's Law: The psychological principle stating that the perceived change in a stimulus is proportional to the initial intensity of the stimulus. In this context, the same ratio of drop heights should yield the same accuracy in judgment, regardless of how heavy the weights are.</note> can be found if the same percentage of correct cases ($r'_g$) is obtained at the same ratio $\frac{H_1}{H_0}$—or the same value $d = \log \frac{H_1}{H_0}$—even when the absolute values of $H_0$ and $H_1$ are changed. If I refer more frequently to *d* than to $\frac{H_1}{H_0}$ in the following, it is because *d* will eventually be useful from another perspective beyond just the application of Weber’s Law.

The author’s experiments can be separated into three main series, which shall be designated as I, II, and III ¹), and depending on whether an $H_1$, *d*, or *n* belongs to one or another series, the corresponding index will be attached below. On page 316 in Table XII of his treatise, Nörr bases the confirmation of Weber’s Law on the equality of $h$ in each vertical column, rather than on the equality of $t = hD$ <note>$D$ represents the difference between stimuli. In psychophysics, $t$ should remain constant if the ratio of the difference to the stimulus is constant.</note>. This is an oversight, because the equality of $r$ and $f$ <note>$r$ (right) and $f$ (false) are the proportions of correct and incorrect judgments.</note>, which is fundamentally at issue here, depends according to the fundamental formulas and the nature of the experiments not on the equality of $h$, but on the equality of $t = hD$. However, if one looks closer, the values taken for $h$ are, according to the way they were calculated, actually values of $hMc₀$, where $c₀$ is taken from the third vertical column of Table II on page 302 as the impact velocity corresponding to $H₀$; and it can be shown with some complexity that $Mc₀$ is proportional to $D$. I have indeed carried this out according to both my own and Müller’s determination of $t$; however, I refrain from citing these determinations because, while the $t$ values from the previous table appear slightly higher for both Fechner and Müller, the proportions have not changed in any significant way. According to my method of determination, one $t$ (in series III, No. 6) and according to Müller’s method, even three $t$ values (III, No. 3, 4, and 6) drop out of the calculation when full **elimination** <note>The statistical process of removing constant errors from the data to isolate the variable of interest.</note> is performed, as so-called **misfires** <note>original: "Fehlschläge"; cases where the experimental data is so inconsistent that the standard mathematical formulas cannot be applied.</note> (p. 54) occur; this is what led me to remain with the results of the incomplete elimination.

Following this, we turn to some secondary points.

In each of the seven horizontal rows, besides the experiments with an $H_1$ different from $H_0$, there were also experiments mixed in where $H_0$ was compared with itself—meaning the difference $D = 0$. In short, these were so-called **catch trials** <note>original: "Vexirversuche"; "trick" trials where no real difference exists, used to test the subject's bias or reliability.</note>, from which it could be inferred whether the first or second sound heard had a tendency to appear stronger. In most individual cases, both appeared equal; however, insofar as unequal judgments occurred, it was the second sound that more often appeared as the stronger one. If we designate with (1), (2), and (0) the cases where the first sound appeared stronger, the second sound appeared stronger, or both appeared equal, respectively, then the sums obtained directly for the seven weights were $\Sigma(1) = 139$, $\Sigma(2) = 170$, and $\Sigma(0) = 398$. However, the absolute numbers of catch trials varied greatly across the different weights; if one takes the percentage figures for each weight specifically and adds them together, the sum is $\Sigma(1) = 136.45$, $\Sigma(2) = 165.8$, $\Sigma(0) = 397.75$, or simply as a percentage: $\Sigma(1) = 19.49$; $\Sigma(2) = 23.69$; $\Sigma(0) = 56.82$.

Based on this, one could ask about the magnitude and direction of the **constant time error** <note>original: "constante Zeitfehler"; a systematic bias where the order of presentation (which stimulus comes first) affects the subject's judgment of intensity.</note> that appeared in the comparison of series A and B when $H_0$ and $H_1$ were different. From the results of the catch trials, it was already foreseeable that the B experiments (where the stronger sound followed) would yield larger $r$ and $r'$ values than the A experiments. Indeed, among all 21 partial series, only the first (I. 1) showed a predominance of A over B regarding the size of $r$; otherwise, B predominated everywhere. The following procedure serves to determine the constant error more precisely.

Let $C$ be the **constant error** <term>constant error: a systematic bias in measurement or perception that consistently shifts results in one direction, such as always perceiving the second of two sounds as louder.</term>, then for $\frac{r'}{n}$ one should look for the corresponding $t$ <note>In this statistical method, $t$ represents a value derived from the probability of a correct response, serving as a measure of the subject's sensitivity.</note> on sides A and B, respectively $t_A$ and $t_B$; set $t_A = h (D - C)$ and $t_B = h (D + C)$, so that $t_A + t_B = 2hD$ and $t_B - t_A = 2hC$. Consequently, $\frac{t_B - t_A}{t_A + t_B} = \frac{C}{D}$, which is the relative constant error; when multiplied by $D$ <note>$D$ represents the actual physical difference between the two stimuli.</note>, this gives the absolute error. $h$ <note>The precision measure $h$ represents the subject's sensitivity or the "sharpness" of their perception.</note>, obtained by dividing $t$ by $D$, remains constant during the variation of $t$. Strictly speaking, this only holds as long as $D$ remains small relative to $R_0$ <note>$R_0$ denotes the initial or base stimulus intensity.</note>. In a general and strict sense, however, $t$ should be taken as proportional to $\log R_1 - \log R_0 = d$ <term>d: the logarithmic difference between two stimuli, a key component of the Weber-Fechner Law</term> rather than to $R_1 - R_0$, since, according to the discussions in Section X, part 1, strictly speaking, it should be set as $hd$ rather than $hD$. Provided that in our experiments $R_0$ is represented by $MH_0$, $D$ by $M(H_1 - H_0)$, and $d$ by $\log \frac{H_1}{H_0}$, we should also expect the $t$ values of our three main series to be approximately proportional to the $D$ values understood in this way—or, since the $M$ values are common to all three main series, to the $U = H_1 - H_0$ values of the same, or more precisely to the $d$ values understood in this way—but this is by no means confirmed. In general, therefore, one can set $\frac{t^2}{d} = p^2$, or $\frac{t}{\sqrt{d}} = p$, where $p^2$ and $p$ are noticeably constant.

Admittedly, one might seek the reason for this anomalous regularity in the fact that the variability of $\varepsilon$ <note>$\varepsilon$ likely refers to a constant error or a specific threshold value in the precision formula.</note> could not be taken into account when calculating the results of Nörr's experiments <note>Friedrich Nörr was a researcher who conducted early psychophysical experiments, often cited by Fechner.</note> alongside changes in $M$ and $H$. <meta>This page transitions from the author's own statistical analysis to a review of sound intensity experiments conducted by others. It specifically introduces the methodology used in Wilhelm Wundt’s laboratory to test the relationship between physical stimulus and sensory perception.</meta>

### B) Wundt’s Experiments¹).

The general circumstances of these experiments have already been discussed in the introduction. Regarding the details, I will mostly let Tischer’s own treatise speak for itself; however, to make it easier to distinguish the literal communications of the original text from the transitional sentences inserted by me, the latter shall be kept in a smaller print.

> "The experiments were carried out according to a procedure essentially already used by Vierordt <note>Karl von Vierordt (1818–1884) was a German physiologist who pioneered methods for measuring the intensity of sensory stimuli.</note>. A larger ball of weight **P** fell from a smaller, constant height **h** onto the base being investigated at any given time. With the sound produced by this, a sound following shortly after (or preceding shortly before) was compared, which was produced by a smaller ball of weight **p** falling from a greater height **H**. The observer or comparer—who turned their back to the manipulator tasked with dropping the balls, so as not to be influenced in their judgment by the sight of the fall heights and weights used—had to state which of the two sound intensities was the greater. According to this statement, the height **H** was adjusted until a difference between the two sound intensities was no longer perceived. In doing so, **H** was first made so small that the sound of the smaller ball was noticeably weaker than the other, and gradually increased to the value **H'**, where both sounds appeared equally strong; then **H** was taken so large that the corresponding sound was noticeably stronger than that of the large ball, and gradually pushed down to the value **H''**, where again both sound intensities showed no more difference. The values **H'** and **H''** were not equal to each other, but rather **H' < H''**; the mean value **1/2 (H' + H'')** was taken as that fall height at which the sound intensity of the..."

> “The two sounds to be compared with each other, following one another at time intervals of about one second, were produced by lead balls whose weight ratio was either 1 or lay between the limits of 1 and 2, and which fell from corresponding heights onto the base (3). The person performing the comparison took up a comfortable position from which they could see nothing of my [Tischer’s] manipulations performed on the drop apparatus—neither the magnitude of the changed drop heights nor the sequence of the sounds, which occurred in irregular alternation, sometimes in one direction and sometimes in the other. The distance of the ear from the sound source was 1 to 2 m. One of the two balls (p) always fell from the same height *h* during each test series and produced a <term>sound stimulus<note>Original: "Schallreiz." The physical energy of the sound intended to evoke a sensory response.</note></term> *r*, for which the <term>difference threshold<note>Also known as the "just-noticeable difference," this is the minimum amount by which stimulus intensity must be changed in order to produce a noticeable variation in sensory experience.</note></term> was to be determined. The other ball p’ fell at the beginning of each test series from that height h’ at which, according to Table IX, the associated sound r’ was perceived as equal to sound r, and was gradually increased to the value h’$_0$, at which r’ appeared just barely stronger than r. Regarding the determination of h’$_0$, it must be mentioned that when h’$_0$ was nearly reached, the judgment of the person comparing fluctuated during repeated sound sequences, in that sometimes r’ > r and sometimes r’ = r was stated...”

->The ratio $\frac{\Delta r}{r}$ between the <term>difference threshold<note>The minimum amount by which a stimulus intensity must be changed in order to produce a noticeable variation in sensory experience.</note></term> $\Delta r$ and the<-
associated stimulus r was calculated in the following way. According to our experiments, two threshold values were obtained for each r, namely $\Delta r_o = r'_o - r$ and $\Delta r_u = r - r'_u$. The average $1/2 (\Delta r_o + \Delta r_u)$ of both was regarded as the actual threshold value $\Delta r$, and consequently

->$\frac{\Delta r}{r} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{\Delta r_o + \Delta r_u}{r}$<-

was established. In order to work not with absolute values but only with the ratios of the <term>drop heights<note>The height from which the ball was dropped to create the sound stimulus.</note></term>, I did not determine the magnitudes $\Delta r_o$ and $\Delta r_u$, but rather the magnitudes

->$1 + \frac{\Delta r_o}{r} = \frac{r'_o}{r}$ and $1 - \frac{\Delta r_u}{r} = \frac{r'_u}{r}$<-

calculated according to the formulas

->$\frac{r'_o}{r} = \frac{p'}{p} \left(\frac{h'_o}{h}\right)^\epsilon = a$, $\frac{r'_u}{r} = \frac{p'}{p} \left(\frac{h'_u}{h}\right)^\epsilon = b$.<-

Then it is simply

->$\frac{\Delta r}{r} = \frac{1}{2} (a-b)$.<-

In the first and largest series of experiments, which was intended to enable a judgment on the applicability and practical feasibility of the procedure just described, the sounds were compared by Mr. Merkel. <meta>This page continues the analysis of experimental data regarding auditory thresholds, calculating the mathematical "difference sensitivity" based on the values of a and b derived in the previous tables. It specifically addresses why values might vary between different drop heights.</meta>

A greater agreement among the individual values of $\frac{a-b}{2}$ could hardly be expected, given that all experiments reported in the table above were carried out within a period of three hours. The fact that the values associated with the constant <term>drop height</term> <note>German: Fallhöhe. The height from which a weight is dropped to create a sound of specific intensity.</note> h = 20 cm turn out somewhat larger than those corresponding to height h = 60 cm is explained by the arrangement of the experiments. For in truth, through these experiments, it was not the <term>just-noticeable</term> <note>The "just-noticeable difference" (JND) is the smallest change in stimulus that a person can detect.</note> but rather the just-above-noticeable differences that were determined; consequently, due to our procedure, the values for $h'_o$ <note>The "upper" height limit where a change in sound was first perceived.</note> had to turn out somewhat too large, and the values for $h'_u$ <note>The "lower" height limit where a change was first perceived.</note> somewhat too small. Since the absolute values of these "height errors" at h = 20 will be nearly equal to those at h = 60, it is clear that they must exert a larger, more visible influence on the small heights around 20 than on the large heights around 60; thus, the enlargement of $\frac{\Delta r}{r}$ <note>A mathematical ratio representing the change in stimulus intensity relative to the original stimulus.</note> is more prominent in the first case than in the latter.

The mean of all $^1/_2$(a—b) is $\frac{7,21}{18} = 0.4055 \dots$, thus, for Mr. **Merkel** the result is the

->reciprocal <term>difference sensitivity</term> <note>Unterschiedsempfindlichkeit; a measure of how finely a subject can distinguish between two stimulus intensities.</note> $\frac{\Delta r}{r} = \frac{2}{5}$.<-

If one wishes, however, to consider $\frac{\Delta r_o}{r}$ as the reciprocal difference sensitivity, then one has

->the mean of all *a* values equal to $1.48 = 1 + \frac{\Delta r_o}{r}$,<-

and thus the difference sensitivity corresponding to an **increase** of the <term>stimulus</term> <note>Reiz; in this case, the sound produced by the falling weight.</note> is $\frac{\Delta r_o}{r} = 0.48$. On the other hand, the

->mean of all *b* values is equal to $0.68 = 1 - \frac{\Delta r_u}{r}$,<-

and the difference sensitivity corresponding to a **decrease** of the stimulus is $\frac{\Delta r_u}{r} = 0.32$.

The mean **fluctuation** <note>Schwankung; refers to the statistical deviation of individual test results from the calculated average.</note> of the $^1/_2$(a—b) values in the table above around their overall mean is 0.022889, and its ratio to the $^1/_2$(a—b) mean is equal to

->$\frac{22889}{405556} = 0.0564.$<-

Thus far concludes the essential factual and computational content of the investigation in question, according to its editing as presented in Tischer's treatise <note>Ernst Tischer was a student of Wundt; his 1883 dissertation focused on sound intensity.</note>. The factual content remains, in any case, a highly valuable enrichment of <term>Psychophysics</term> <note>The scientific study of the relationship between physical stimuli and the sensations they produce.</note>; however, the method of calculation seems to me to require some changes and explanations in certain respects, though this does not change anything in the result favorable to <term>Weber's Law</term> <note>A psychological law stating that the change in a stimulus that will be just noticeable is a constant ratio of the original stimulus.</note>, regarding which the following remarks are made.

-> $\Delta_o = r_o - r;$ $\Delta_u = r - r_u$ <-
-> $\frac{r_o}{r} = 1 + \frac{\Delta_o}{r} = a;$ $\frac{r}{r_u} = 1 + \frac{\Delta_u}{r_u} = \frac{1}{b}$ <-
-> $\frac{\Delta_o}{r} = a - 1;$ $\frac{\Delta_u}{r_u} = \frac{1}{b} - 1.$ <-

It should be noted that $\Delta_o$ and $\Delta_u$ are the absolute difference thresholds, or <term>just noticeable differences</term> <note>original: "eben merkliche Unterschiede"; often abbreviated in psychophysics as JND</note>, in the upward and downward directions. In contrast, $\frac{r_o}{r}$ and $\frac{r}{r_u}$ represent the upper and lower <term>ratio thresholds</term> <note>The ratio threshold is the proportion by which a stimulus must be increased or decreased for a person to perceive a change.</note>.

Furthermore, it should be remembered that, according to <term>Weber’s Law</term> <note>A fundamental principle in psychophysics stating that the change in a stimulus that will be just noticeable is a constant ratio of the original stimulus.</note>, the upper and lower ratio thresholds are fundamentally equal, even if they vary in experiments due to chance. However, the absolute upper and lower difference thresholds are fundamentally *not* equal according to Weber’s Law. This is because, according to this law, the difference threshold is larger between large stimuli and smaller between small stimuli; in the case of the upper difference threshold, the <term>stimulus</term> <note>original: "Reiz" ($r$)</note> is related to a larger stimulus, while in the case of the lower, it is related to a smaller stimulus. Furthermore (under No. 16), a principle not yet known will be proven: that according to Weber's Law, the ratio of the upper to the lower difference threshold $\frac{\Delta_o}{\Delta_u}$ is equal to the ratio threshold $\frac{r_o}{r}$ or $\frac{r}{r_u}$, which is equal on both sides.

In addition, the following further remarks are made.

1) The confirmation of Weber's Law can be based equally on the constancy of the ratio threshold or the constancy of the <term>relative JND</term> <note>original: "e. m. U." (eben merklicher Unterschied)</note> in different parts of the stimulus scale. This applies if the ratio threshold is understood as the ratio of two stimuli that produce a just noticeable or just vanishing difference. The relative JND, or relative difference threshold, is the just noticeable difference itself divided either by the smaller stimulus, the larger stimulus, or the mean of both stimuli; this is indifferent, provided that the constancy of one of these ratios implies the constancy of the other. One must simply remain consistent with whichever convention is chosen in this regard.

2) The author adheres to the constancy of the relative JND. However, insofar as such a value is determined in the experiments on both the upper and lower side of $r$ (that is, between $r_o, r$, and $r, r_u$ respectively), he takes the arithmetic mean of the two. If one now asks whether, in principle, $A$ or $V$ is to be preferred as a mean between ratios, the following circumstance speaks in favor of $V$. A ratio, e.g., $\frac{2}{3} = 0.6667$, can just as well be written as $\frac{3}{2} = 1.5$, depending on whether one takes the denominator or the numerator as the unit with which the other value is compared; this choice is arbitrary.<sup>1)</sup> Let us call one form—perhaps the one first arrived at—the **direct** form, and the other the **reciprocal** form. Now, if a mean is to be drawn from two ratios, we call the **direct mean** that which is drawn from the direct ratios, and the **reciprocal mean** that which is drawn from the reciprocal ratios.

Now, we may demand of the method of calculating the mean that, regardless of the arbitrary choice to operate with direct or reciprocal ratios, the reciprocal mean should agree with the direct mean to produce one and the same result—that is, by inversion, it should reproduce the direct mean. The <term>calculation of the arithmetic mean</term> <note>original: "arithmetische Mittelziehung"</note> does not satisfy this condition, whereas the <term>determination of the ratio mean</term> <note>original: "Verhältnißmittelbestimmung"; this refers to the geometric mean.</note> does satisfy it; the first determination is therefore ambiguous, while the other is unambiguous. One can see this

---

1) Only when comparing a magnitude with the measurements of a scale is it not arbitrary; because these measurements are fixed and given, and thus form a common foundation for all magnitudes to be compared with one another. But where it is a matter of drawing a mean between ratios—in which the denominator and numerator may be altered, whether by chance or by <term>errors of estimation</term> <note>original: "Schätzungsirrthümer"</note>, in order to compensate for inaccuracies as much as possible—the arbitrariness indeed exists to consider one value or the other as that by which the other is to be measured. If we, for example, find $\frac{r_0}{r}$ as the <term>upper ratio threshold</term> <note>original: "obere Verhältnißschwelle"</note>, then both $r$ and $r_0$ can, through false estimation, give a false value for this threshold. One will not be able to say that $r_0$ can only be thought of according to its ratio of increase against $r$ as $\frac{r_0}{r}$, but just as well $r$ can be thought of according to its ratio of decrease against $r_0$ as $\frac{r}{r_0}$; it is therefore arbitrary whether one operates with $\frac{r_0}{r}$ or $\frac{r}{r_0}$.

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s mathematical argument regarding why the "ratio mean" (geometric mean) is the only logically sound way to average ratios or proportions. He is responding to potential critics who might use the arithmetic mean. The previous page ended mid-sentence, discussing how the arithmetic mean fails to maintain consistency when switching between direct and reciprocal ratios.</meta>

[...one can] express it generally in letters, but also illustrate it using any numerical examples. In fact, let:
-> $\frac{a}{b}$ , $\frac{c}{d}$ <-
be the two ratios considered **direct**, then
-> $\frac{b}{a}$ , $\frac{d}{c}$ <-
are their reciprocal values. If one calculates the <term>arithmetic mean</term> <note>The standard average: adding values and dividing by the total count.</note> from both arrangements, one has:
-> direct $\frac{1}{2} (\frac{a}{b} + \frac{c}{d})$ ; reciprocal $\frac{1}{2} (\frac{b}{a} + \frac{d}{c})$ <-

The second mean should now, through inversion—whereby it is known as the **harmonic** mean relative to the direct one—lead back to the direct mean. However, that is not the case, because $\frac{2}{\frac{b}{a} + \frac{d}{c}}$ is not equal to $\frac{1}{2} (\frac{a}{b} + \frac{c}{d})$ , and generally, the harmonic mean is not equal to the direct one unless the two ratios are identical. If, on the other hand, we take the <term>ratio mean</term> <note>Original: "Verhältnißmittel." This refers to the geometric mean.</note>, we have:
-> direct $\sqrt{\frac{a}{b} \cdot \frac{c}{d}}$ , reciprocal $\sqrt{\frac{b}{a} \cdot \frac{d}{c}}$ , <-
where the latter reproduces the former through inversion.

To be sure, where the values $\frac{a}{b}$ and $\frac{c}{d}$ lie very close to one another, $A$ <note>the arithmetic mean</note> also corresponds very closely with $V$ <note>the ratio mean</note>; where they do not, they can fall far apart, as one can convince oneself through self-made examples.
What holds true for the mean of **two** ratio values also holds true for the mean of any number of them; and since the values $a$ and $b$ in the tables, as well as the $\frac{1}{b}$ ratios to be derived from $b$, are proportions, then whenever mean values are to be calculated from them, one should use $V$ rather than $A$.

I am well aware that <term>calculating the arithmetic mean</term> <note>original: "arithmetische Mittelziehung"</note> from ratios is quite common; and since one is generally dealing with ratios that are close to each other, and means from empirical values always remain burdened with a certain uncertainty anyway, it usually matters little in practice. This would likely also be the case in the present investigation; nevertheless, $V$ remains preferable to $A$.

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s mathematical argument regarding why the "ratio mean" (geometric mean) is logically and practically superior to the arithmetic mean when calculating averages of ratios. He is specifically addressing the efficiency of logarithmic calculation in psychophysical data.</meta>

At first glance, the calculation of the <term>ratio mean</term> <note>The geometric mean, which Fechner argues is the correct way to average proportions.</note> might seem more cumbersome than the <term>arithmetic mean</term>, and one might therefore be tempted to prefer the latter for practical purposes when dealing with ratios that lie close to one another, where the two means do not differ to any significant degree. Indeed, when using <term>Tischer's tables</term> <note>Tables developed by Friedrich Tischer to assist in calculating Weber’s Law and other psychophysical constants.</note> to obtain the arithmetic mean $a$, one simply needs to add the values of $a$ and divide by their total number, doing the same for $b$; by contrast, to calculate the ratio mean, one must proceed through <term>logarithms</term>. However, one must consider that in order to add a series of ratios $a$ or $b$, each one must first be individually reduced to <term>decimal fractions</term>—a tedious task that easily invites calculation errors, and which must have preceded the determination of $a$ and $b$ in Tischer’s tables. In light of this, one might actually find the calculation of the ratio mean more practical, as it spares one this individual labor. If the ratios from which the mean is to be drawn are:

->$\frac{\alpha_1}{\beta_1}, \frac{\alpha_2}{\beta_2}, \frac{\alpha_3}{\beta_3} \dots$<-

and their number is $n$, then to calculate the ratio mean, one will indeed have to find the logarithms of all $\alpha$ as well as all $\beta$; after that, however, the mean is found simply as the number in the <term>logarithm tables</term> for:

->$\frac{\Sigma \log \alpha - \Sigma \log \beta}{n}$<-

In contrast, to calculate the arithmetic mean, one would first have to bring every $\frac{\alpha}{\beta}$ to its decimal value, and for that, one would most likely prefer using logarithmic mediation; however, for that purpose, every $\log \alpha - \log \beta$ must be calculated **separately** and then converted back to a number in the tables.

5) If we henceforth make use of the ratio mean instead of the arithmetic mean, the mean between the upper and lower <term>relat. e. m. U.</term> <note>Relative "eben merkliche Unterschiede" or just-noticeable differences. This is a core concept in Fechner's law, relating the size of a stimulus change to the baseline stimulus.</note> will no longer be determined as:

->$\frac{1}{2} (\frac{\Delta_o}{r} + \frac{\Delta_u}{r_u})$, but rather $\sqrt{\frac{\Delta_o \cdot \Delta_u}{r \cdot r_u}}$<-

and this value is to be substituted first for $\frac{a - b}{2}$. We can, however, also use a simpler formula instead, which—like $\frac{a - b}{2}$—is a function of $a$ and $b$, if we the [sentence continues on next page]

To obtain the resulting mean ratio threshold from the total set of *a* and <sup>1</sup>/<sub>*b*</sub> values, we sum the logarithms of all *a* and <sup>1</sup>/<sub>*b*</sub> (3.07223 + 3.02644 = 6.09867).
